An inner screw is sometimes added to pump down the centre. Using it for thin liquids. Undersized drive for the torque. Difficult cleaning between batches. Polymers, adhesives, pastes, greases and other very viscous batches.

s: A flat disc with bent teeth around its edge, running very fast. It breaks up powders and agglomerates in a liquid.
x: The disc runs at high tip speed. Liquid is flung outward and returns above and below the disc, forming a rolling doughnut pattern. Powder drawn into the vortex is sheared at the teeth and wetted out. Tip speed (pi x D x N) is the key setting, commonly about 18 to 25 m/s. The doughnut pattern needs the right disc diameter, height above the bottom and liquid depth. Little bulk pumping, so a slow anchor or second agitator is often added for large or viscous batches. Generates heat; long runs can raise batch temperature. Wrong disc-to-tank ratio or liquid depth, which loses the doughnut flow. Running it as a general blender. Ignoring heat build-up. Powder wetting, pigment and filler dispersion, paints, inks and suspensions.

s: A fast rotor spinning inside a slotted stator. Liquid is forced through a narrow gap, giving very high shear.
x: The rotor draws liquid and solids into the head from below. Material is forced out through the stator slots at high speed. The intense shear in the gap breaks droplets and agglomerates. Used for emulsions, fine dispersions and deagglomeration. Available as batch (top-entry), bottom-entry or inline units. Bulk circulation in the tank is weak, so a separate agitator is often needed. Heat input is significant on long runs. Relying on it for bulk mixing of a large tank. Running it dry or uncovered. Ignoring temperature rise. Creams, emulsions, suspensions, dissolving gums and powders, and particle size reduction in liquids.

s: An impeller on a hollow shaft. Low pressure at the blade tips sucks headspace gas down the shaft and disperses it into the liquid.
x: Holes near the top of the hollow shaft sit in the gas headspace. At speed, low pressure behind the impeller blades draws gas down the shaft. The gas leaves at the blade tips as fine bubbles and is recirculated continuously. Recirculates unreacted gas, which suits dead-end hydrogenation without an external compressor. Needs a minimum speed and correct submergence before it starts to draw gas. Gas induction rate depends on speed, submergence and liquid properties; use vendor data. Running below the onset speed so no gas is drawn. Wrong liquid level, which uncovers or floods the shaft openings. Hydrogenation, oxidation and other gas-liquid reactions in autoclaves.

s: The agitator inside an Agitated Nutsche Filter Dryer (ANFD). Its blades can be raised and lowered to reslurry, smooth, dry and finally discharge the cake.
x: During filtration the agitator is raised clear of the cake. For a reslurry wash it is lowered and turned to mix the cake into the wash liquid, then raised while the wash is filtered off. Turning in the smoothing direction levels the cake and closes cracks, so wash liquid and gas do not bypass. During drying it turns slowly to break lumps and expose fresh cake to the heated plate and walls. To discharge, it is lowered step by step and turned in the direction that sweeps the dry cake to the side discharge valve. Blade height is set hydraulically or mechanically. Cutting into a dense or hard cake is limited by torque, so it is lowered in small steps. Torque, not power number, is the main design limit. The drive is sized for peak torque when the blades cut into dense or sticky cake. Reslurry washing usually washes better than displacement washing for cracked or compressible cakes, at the cos

s: Lower pressure Same liquid = Lower boiling point

x: Leave 10 to 20 °C between steam temperature and the process setpoint so the jacket can still drive heat in.

s: Same gas Fixed volume: pressure follows absolute temperature
x: The gauge falls on a cold morning without any gas leaving. Compare readings at the same temperature, and never heat a cylinder with a flame.

s: 1 litre of liquid nitrogen about 694 litres of gas
x: You cannot smell or see the danger: the fog is condensed water, not the nitrogen. Use oxygen monitors and ventilation wherever cryogens are handled.

t: Animation: Pressure Drop in a Line
s: Double the flow about four times the pressure drop
x: One pipe size smaller costs roughly three times the pressure drop at the same flow. Fittings, strainers and partly shut valves add to it.

s: PD pump: flow stays nearly constant Centrifugal: flow falls as pressure rises
x: Never close the discharge of a PD pump: pressure rises until something gives. Fit a relief valve. A worn gear pump loses flow at high pressure because more liquid slips back.

s: Vertical tank: volume level Horizontal drum: it is not
x: At 25% level a horizontal drum holds only about 20% of its volume. Dished ends add a little more; use a strapping table for custody figures.

s: Bigger difference in volatility = Fewer stages
x: Real columns run above minimum reflux and need more stages than N min . A tray is less than one theoretical stage, so divide by tray efficiency.

s: At the azeotrope, vapour = liquid: distillation stops separating
x: Measured data put the 1 atm azeotrope at 89.4 mol% and 78.2 °C; this simple model gives 91.5%. The trend with pressure is the point: real ethanol water loses its azeotrope at around 0.1 bar.

s: Toluene + water boil together at 84 °C, below either liquid alone
x: The batch is dry when the head temperature climbs to the pure solvent boiling point and the trap stops filling. Poor separation in the trap, or a wet return line, sends water back into the batch.
Measure α in a Büchner trial on the real slurry before choosing a filter. Fines from crystallization raise α sharply.
Numbers are illustrative. The shape is real: the constant-rate period scales with bed depth, and the falling-rate tail gets longer as heat and vapour have further to travel.

s: Bed pressure drop rises with gas flow, then levels off at the bed weight
x: Fluid bed dryers usually run at a few times U mf . Wet, sticky product or a blocked distributor plate leaves dead zones that dry unevenly; keep U/U mf and bed depth the same on scale-up.

s: Double the speed four times the G-force
x: Higher G drains the cake drier and faster, but compressible cakes can pack tight and blind. Always check the basket load limit at the chosen speed.

s: Half the particle size a quarter of the settling speed

t: Animation: Gas Absorption in a Scrubber
s: More liquid per unit gas = More removed
x: Below A = 1 adding stages barely helps: the liquid is the limit. Absorption takes the gas into the liquid; adsorption holds it on a solid surface such as activated carbon.

t: Animation: Extraction: One Wash or Several
s: Same solvent split into several washes = More extracted
x: Good extraction also needs enough mixing to reach equilibrium and enough settling time for a clean split. Emulsions and a rag layer lose more product than the sum suggests.

s: Finer product = Much more energy per tonne
x: Mill ranges overlap and depend on the product; the bands are a rough guide. Mesh sizes are US standard sieves.

t: Animation: Area per Volume Falls on Scale-up
s: Volume grows with D³, jacket area only with D²
x: Lab: about 4 minutes to heat 40 K. A 10 m³ reactor with the same U takes about an hour and a half. The same loss of area limits how fast an exotherm can be removed.

t: Animation: Heat Generation vs Heat Removal
s: Reaction heat grows exponentially, cooling grows only in a straight line
x: Where the lines cross the batch holds steady. Raise the coolant past the critical point, or lose cooling area or agitation, and the lines never meet: temperature climbs on its own. Calorimetry measures the heat curve before scale-up.

s: Warmer cooling water smaller temperature difference less duty
x: Shaded area is the driving force. On a hot afternoon a condenser sized for 25 °C water can lose a third of its duty, and solvent slips through to the vacuum pump.

t: Animation: Chiller Capacity and Hot Weather
s: Hotter air at the condenser = Less cooling from the same chiller
x: Dirty condenser coils and hot air recirculating back into the fans make it worse. A TCU that cannot reach setpoint on summer afternoons is often a chiller at its limit, not a TCU fault.

t: Animation: Glycol vs Brine Freezing Point
s: More antifreeze = Lower freezing point, up to a limit
x: Brine is cheap and transfers heat well but its chlorides corrode carbon and stainless steel. Glycol needs inhibitor and turns viscous when cold, so pumps and heat transfer suffer at high strength. Values are approximate.

t: Animation: Residence Time: Tank vs Tube
x: A well-mixed tank runs at the outlet concentration, so it needs more volume for the same conversion. A batch reactor behaves like a plug-flow tube in time.

s: Conversion = A used Yield = B made Selectivity = B made / A used

t: Animation: Supersaturation and the Metastable Zone
s: Cool past solubility: supersaturated. Cool too far: a shower of new crystals
x: Unseeded, nothing happens until the limit line, then nucleation crashes the concentration and makes fines. Seeding in the shaded zone and cooling slowly keeps the batch close to the solubility curve and grows bigger crystals. The zone often narrows at plant scale.

s: Some solids and acids release heat as they dissolve
x: Add the solid, or the concentrated acid, slowly into water with stirring and cooling, never water into acid. Values are approximate and ignore heat lost to the vessel.

s: Same power per volume, bigger tank = Longer to mix
x: If a fast reaction finishes before the feed is mixed in, selectivity changes on scale-up. Feed near the impeller, slow the addition, or check that blend time stays well below reaction time. A sample taken before blending is complete is not representative.

s: Each rule keeps one thing the same, and changes the rest
x: Constant P/V suits blending and gas dispersion; constant tip speed suits shear-sensitive solids and crystals. Constant Reynolds is rarely usable. Constant blend time needs impossible power at plant scale.

s: Rate is set by the slower step: gas dissolving or the reaction itself
x: If the rate rises with agitator speed, gas transfer is the limit, and it will change on scale-up. Gas-inducing impellers, higher pressure and good catalyst suspension all help.

s: Each rinse dilutes what is left by the same factor
x: This assumes the residue dissolves in the rinse. Several small rinses beat one big one. Swab and rinse-sample results, not the sum, prove the vessel clean.

s: pKa belongs to the acid; pH belongs to the solution
x: A buffer works best within one pH unit of its pKa. Ionised forms dissolve in water; neutral forms extract into organic solvent.

s: An ageing probe gives a weaker signal per pH unit
x: A two-point calibration corrects the slope; most labs replace a probe below about 90%. Temperature also changes the slope, so use automatic temperature compensation. Coated or dried-out glass gives slow, drifting readings.

s: RTD: resistance rises with temperature Thermocouple: a small voltage from two metals
x: RTDs are more accurate and stable up to about 400 600 °C. Thermocouples go hotter, respond faster and are rugged, but a few microvolts of noise is a whole degree. Both read the thermowell, not the liquid, so lag and immersion matter.
Current does not drop along long cables the way voltage does, and the "live zero" at 4 mA lets the DCS tell a true zero from a cut wire. The same two wires also power the transmitter.

s: Too little gain: slow. Too much gain: overshoot and oscillation
x: An oscillating loop usually has too much gain or too little integral time. Cut the gain first, then check the valve for stiction and the measurement for noise before retuning.

t: Animation: Motor Load, Current and Heating
s: More load = More current; heating rises with current squared
x: Even at no load the motor draws magnetising current. Low supply voltage, unbalanced phases, a thick or cold product, a worn pump, or a blocked cooling fan all push current and winding temperature up. Single-phase motors suit small loads; three-phase gives smooth torque and smaller cables for the same power.

s: Too thin a cable runs hot and drops voltage
x: Current ratings shown are typical for PVC copper cable in conduit. Grouping, ambient temperature and installation method change them, so size cables from your local wiring code, not from this chart.

s: Cool air below its dew point and water condenses
x: Relative humidity changes with temperature; dew point does not. That is why compressed air is specified by pressure dew point: below it, water drops out in the lines.

s: Ultimate vacuum = pump limit + leak / pump speed
x: If the vacuum stalls, isolate the pump and do a rate-of-rise test on the vessel. Warm seal water raises the pump limit; at 35 °C it is about 56 mbar. Solvent vapour in the ring does the same.

s: Every extra bar of pressure costs about 6 8% more power
x: Single-stage estimate. Generate air at the lowest pressure the users need, and fix leaks: a 3 mm hole at 7 bar wastes several kW around the clock.

t: Animation: Flash Point and Flammable Range
s: Above its flash point, a solvent gives off enough vapour to ignite
x: Inerting the headspace with nitrogen removes the oxygen instead of the vapour. Classified-area equipment (intrinsically safe or flameproof) removes the spark. Fight solvent fires with foam, CO₂ or dry powder; water spreads them.

s: Hotter = Faster corrosion; a small rise can move a metal out of range
x: Compatibility charts give one temperature and concentration. Chlorides, oxidisers and crevices cause local pitting that a weight-loss average hides: stainless steel can pit while the coupon looks fine. Test coupons in the real process stream.

s: Two metals in contact: the less noble one corrodes faster
x: Simplified: real rates depend on the electrolyte and how far apart the metals sit in the galvanic series. Insulating gaskets, sleeves and washers break the circuit; if metals must touch, make the anode the large part.

s: Too little squeeze leaks; too much cracks and extrudes
x: Also check the stretch on the inside diameter (keep under about 5%) and that the elastomer suits the fluid and temperature: the wrong rubber swells, hardens or dissolves however well it fits.

s: A few mg of sample and an empty reference are heated side by side; the heat-flow difference shows melting and exotherms
x: The peak area is the energy: here about 848 J/g, so with c′p ≈ 1.8 J/g·K the adiabatic rise would be about 471 K. DSC is a quick screen. Its onset depends on scan rate and is far above the temperature at which a big insulated vessel can start to self-heat.

s: About 8 mL of sample in a closed test cell with a pressure transducer, heated in a ramp
x: Below the onset the pressure just follows the solvent’s vapour pressure. Where the measured line leaves the dashed curve, the sample is making gas. That gas is what the relief system has to vent, and DSC cannot see it.

s: Heat, wait, search: step the temperature until the sample heats itself, then keep the surroundings at the same temperature so no heat is lost
x: The staircase is heat-wait-search. Once the sample warms itself faster than 0.02 K/min, the guard heaters follow it, so no heat leaks away: just like the centre of a large, poorly cooled vessel. The steep climb gives the adiabatic rise, the self-heat rate and the TMRad. The thick bomb absorbs some heat, so results are scaled by the φ-factor.

t: Animation: RC1: Reaction Calorimetry and Accumulation
s: Run the real process in a jacketed lab reactor; the jacket heat balance gives the heat release rate as you dose B (shaded: dosing)
x: If B reacted the moment it went in, the heat would follow the dashed line. It lags, so unreacted B builds up: here up to about 23 % at 120 min. If cooling fails at that moment, all of it can still react. That is what sets the MTSR.

t: Animation: TMRad and TD24: How Much Time Is Left?
s: Time to maximum rate under adiabatic conditions falls exponentially as the start temperature rises
x: Every ten degrees or so cuts the time to runaway roughly in half. TD24, about 120 °C here, is a common reference: above it, a batch that loses cooling could reach maximum rate within a day. Values like these come from ARC or isothermal DSC kinetics, not from a single DSC onset.

s: Agitator design basics: radial and axial impellers, power number, baffles, tip speed and how to choose an impeller for blending, solids or gas.
x: Agitator Design Basics Process Design · Mixing · October 2026 Ask why a reactor has the agitator it has, and the answer is often “it came with the vessel”. Yet the agitator decides whether solids stay suspended, whether two liquid phases react, whether a crystallisation gives fines, and how fast heat reaches the jacket. This article explains what agitators do and how to read the numbers behind them. In this article What the agitator has to do Basics Radial and axial impellers Basics Power number and power draw Working level Baffles and vortexing Working level Choosing an impeller Going deeper Questions people ask What the agitator has to do Basics Mixing is not one thing. Liquid-liquid dispersion: needs shear to br

t: What the agitator has to do Basics
x: Mixing is not one thing. Each duty needs something different: Blending miscible liquids: needs bulk flow around the whole vessel. Solids suspension: needs upward flow along the base to lift particles. Liquid-liquid dispersion: needs shear to break drops, and flow to keep them dispersed. Gas dispersion (hydrogenation, oxidation): needs high shear at the impeller to break bubbles. Heat transfer: needs flow past the jacket wall. Before choosing an impeller, decide which duty matters most for this process.

A radial impeller (Rushton turbine, flat-blade turbine, the retreat-curve impeller of glass-lined reactors) throws liquid outward to the wall, where it splits into two loops, one above and one below. It produces high shear near the blades. An axial impeller (pitched-blade turbine, hydrofoil, marine propeller) pumps liquid down the shaft to the base and back up the walls in one big loop: efficient for blending and solids suspension. Try it: pick an impeller and change the speed. Watch the flow pattern and how the power changes with the power number.

t: Power number and power draw Working level
x: P = Np × ρ × N³ × D⁵ P in W, Np power number (a property of the impeller shape, constant in turbulent flow), ρ density in kg/m³, N speed in revolutions per second, D impeller diameter in m. Typical turbulent power numbers in baffled vessels: Rushton turbine about 5, pitched-blade turbine about 1.3, hydrofoil about 0.3. Glass-lined retreat-curve impellers are lower and depend strongly on the baffling. A 0.6 m Rushton at 100 rpm in a liquid of 900 kg/m³ draws about 1.6 kW; a hydrofoil of the same size at the same speed draws about 0.1 kW, but moves a similar amount of liquid. Two things follow from the equation. Power rises with the cube of spe

Without baffles, a centrally mounted impeller in a low-viscosity liquid mostly spins the liquid round as a whole. A vortex forms, air is drawn in, little top-to-bottom mixing happens, and the power number drops sharply. Standard practice is four wall baffles, each one-tenth to one-twelfth of the vessel diameter wide. Glass-lined reactors use one or two beaver-tail or finger baffles through the top nozzles, which give less complete baffling, so their mixing is gentler than a fully baffled steel vessel at the same speed.

Duty Usual choice Blending low-viscosity liquids Hydrofoil or pitched-blade turbine Solids suspension Pitched-blade or hydrofoil, pumping down, low clearance from the base Gas dispersion Rushton or concave-blade turbine, gas sparged under the impeller Liquid-liquid dispersion Pitched-blade or Rushton, depending on drop size needed Viscous liquids (above roughly 10,000 cP) Anchor or helical ribbon, close to the wall Glass-lined, corrosive service Retreat curve or glass-lined pitched-blade, with finger or beaver-tail baffle Tall vessels need two or more impellers on the shaft, spaced about one diameter apart. Check that the lowest impeller is c

Choosing an impeller without deciding the main mixing duty. No baffles with low-viscosity liquids. Raising speed or impeller size without checking motor power (N³, D⁵). Lowest impeller uncovered at minimum volume. Scaling up by rpm instead of P/V or tip speed.

t: What is the power number of an impeller?
x: A constant for the impeller shape: about 5 Rushton, 1.3 pitched blade, 0.3 hydrofoil.
To stop swirl and vortexing and create top-to-bottom flow.

t: Which impeller is best for solids suspension?
x: An axial impeller pumping down, close to the base.

s: How an agitated thin film dryer (ATFD) works and is sized: heat flux, evaporation capacity, its role in ZLD, and fixes for wet product and sticking.
x: Agitated Thin Film Dryer (ATFD) Process Design · Evaporation and Drying · October 2026 The agitated thin film dryer is the last step in most zero liquid discharge plants: it takes the thick concentrate from the MEE and turns it into a dry, free-flowing salt. It also dries and concentrates heat-sensitive and viscous products that no other evaporator can handle. Its secret is a rotor that keeps spreading a thin film on the heated wall. This article explains how it works, how to estimate its capacity, and what goes wrong. In this article How an ATFD works Basics Where it is used Basics Estimating capacity Working level Operating it well Working level Common problems Going deeper Questions people ask How an ATFD works Basics An ATFD is a vertical cylinder with a heating jacket (steam or thermic fluid) and a high-speed rotor inside, carrying blades or wipers set a few millimetres from the wal

An ATFD is a vertical cylinder with a heating jacket (steam or thermic fluid) and a high-speed rotor inside, carrying blades or wipers set a few millimetres from the wall. Feed enters at the top and the blades spread it into a thin, turbulent film on the hot wall. Water or solvent evaporates quickly from the thin film; the vapour flows up to a condenser, and the dried solid or concentrate is scraped down and leaves at the bottom. Because the rotor keeps renewing the film, it can handle liquids that become pastes and then powders on the way down, which would block any tube evaporator.

Zero liquid discharge : drying MEE concentrate to a salt that goes to a hazardous waste facility. Heat-sensitive products : short residence time (seconds to a few minutes) under vacuum. Solvent recovery from residues and viscous mother liquors. A related machine, the agitated thin film evaporator (ATFE or wiped film evaporator), concentrates a liquid without drying it, often as a stage before the dryer.

Q = U × A × (Tsteam - Tproduct) Evaporation ≈ Q / λ Feed capacity = evaporation / (fraction of the feed evaporated). For a feed with solids fraction s dried to 5 % moisture, the fraction evaporated is 1 - s/0.95. A 10 m² ATFD with U = 690 kcal/h·m²·°C and 60 °C between steam and product transfers about 4,14,000 kcal/h and evaporates about 766 kg/h of water. With a feed of 35 % solids, about 63 % of the feed must evaporate, so the ATFD can take about 1,200 kg/h of feed and gives about 450 kg/h of salt. U falls sharply as the product thickens, and varies widely between products, so real sizing uses pilot trials or the supplier's data on your co

Steady feed : rate and concentration swings cause wet product one hour and an overheated, sticky wall the next. A feed tank with level control and a metering pump helps. Watch motor current : it rises as the product thickens and is the best online signal of what is happening inside. Steam pressure : higher temperature raises capacity but can make some salts sticky or decompose organics. Find the window for your product. Vapour line and condenser : size them for the full evaporation, and keep the scrubber or vent condenser working for volatile organics.

Wet or lumpy product : feed too high, steam pressure low, or feed too dilute. Product sticking to the wall : some salt mixtures go through a sticky phase; adjust temperature, blade clearance or feed rate. High rotor current, trips : overload from too much solid, or blades rubbing. Blade and wall wear : abrasive salts; inspect clearances at each shutdown. Corrosion : concentrated chloride brines are aggressive; check the material of construction. See materials of construction .

Sending dilute feed to the ATFD instead of concentrating it in the MEE first. Sizing from a generic U without trials on the actual concentrate. Unsteady feed rate and concentration. Ignoring the rising motor current. Wrong material of construction for chloride brines.

t: What is an ATFD used for?
x: Drying MEE concentrate to salt in ZLD, and handling viscous or heat-sensitive liquids.

t: How do you estimate ATFD capacity?
x: Duty = U × A × ΔT; evaporation = duty / latent heat; feed = evaporation / fraction evaporated.

t: Why concentrate in an MEE before the ATFD?
x: The MEE uses far less steam per kg of water than the ATFD.

s: Batch time vs cycle time, how to find the bottleneck equipment in a multi-step batch, batches per week and practical ways to debottleneck.
x: Batch Cycle Time and Debottlenecking Plant Engineering · Capacity · October 2026 “We need 20 % more output by next quarter.” Every plant manager hears this. The usual reaction is to speed up whatever step looks slow, and often nothing changes. Output in a batch plant is set by one piece of equipment, and until you find it, every improvement elsewhere is wasted effort. This article shows how to find it and what to do about it. In this article Two different times Basics The bottleneck sets the pace Basics Drawing the Gantt chart Working level Ways to debottleneck Working level Where the hidden hours are Going deeper Campaigns, shared equipment and real schedules Going deeper Questions people ask Two different times Basics Batch time is how long one batch takes from the first charge to packed product: the time a single lot spends in the plant. Cycle time is the interval between one batch st

Batch time is how long one batch takes from the first charge to packed product: the time a single lot spends in the plant. Cycle time is the interval between one batch starting and the next one starting. In a plant with several pieces of equipment in series, these are very different, because while batch 1 is in the dryer, batch 2 can already be in the reactor. Output depends only on cycle time: Batches per week = available hours per week / cycle time Use realistic available hours: 168 minus planned maintenance, cleaning between products and typical downtime.

t: The bottleneck sets the pace Basics
x: Think of a line of people passing buckets. However fast the others are, buckets arrive at the end only as fast as the slowest person can pass them. In a batch plant, each piece of equipment can hold only one batch at a time, so a new batch can start only when the busiest piece of equipment is free. That equipment is the bottleneck , and its total occupancy per batch is the cycle time. Take a simple API step: Equipment Work in it per batch Occupancy Reactor R-101 Charge 1 h, react 6 h, distil 4 h, transfer 1 h 12 h Centrifuge C-101 Spin, wash, unload 4.5 h Dryer D-101 Load, dry, cool, unload 14 h Packing Sift, pack, label 2 h One batch takes 1

t: Drawing the Gantt chart Working level
x: A Gantt chart puts each piece of equipment on its own row and time along the bottom. Each batch is a coloured block in each row. Drawing three or four batches makes the bottleneck obvious: it is the row with no gaps, and every other row has idle time waiting for it. Try it: the dryer row has no gaps, so it is the bottleneck. Add a second dryer, then shorten distillation, and watch the batches per week change. Then try shortening a step that is not on the bottleneck. Draw the chart with what actually happens on the shop floor, not with the batch card times. Take the last ten batch records and use the median for each step, including waits.

Only time saved on the bottleneck increases output. So work on the bottleneck, in roughly this order of cost: Remove waiting time on the bottleneck. Material sitting in the dryer waiting for an LOD result, an operator, or a free packing room. Often free. Move work off the bottleneck. Cool the product in a separate hopper rather than in the dryer; do a filter-dryer's wash in the centrifuge instead. Shorten the bottleneck step itself. Better vacuum, higher jacket temperature within the product's limits, a lower final cake moisture from the centrifuge (see the centrifuge article ). Add parallel equipment. A second dryer working alternate batches

t: Where the hidden hours are Going deeper
x: When you compare batch records with the batch card, the extra hours usually come from things nobody calls a process step: In-process QC waits: sample taken, equipment held while the lab works through its queue. Agree sample priority for bottleneck equipment, or move the hold to a cheaper vessel. Shift handovers and breaks at a critical step: schedule so that long unattended steps span the handover. Utilities: chilled brine shared between reactors, so cooling takes twice as long when two batches need it together; vacuum that falls off when three vessels pull at once. Cleaning and line clearance between batches and products. Material not ready:

t: Campaigns, shared equipment and real schedules Going deeper
x: Real multi-product plants are messier. A reactor may serve two steps of the same product, or two products. Then its occupancy per batch of final product is the sum of all its uses. Product changeovers add cleaning time that is shared over the campaign length, so longer campaigns raise average output but tie up working capital and warehouse space. For a plant with many products and shared equipment, a spreadsheet with occupancy per equipment per product, multiplied by the demand plan, quickly shows which equipment is loaded above about 85 % (where queues build up and schedules slip) and which is lightly used. Above about 85 % utilisation, smal

Speeding up a step that is not on the bottleneck and expecting more output. Calculating capacity from batch card times instead of actual batch records. Ignoring cleaning, QC waits and changeovers. Buying a new reactor when the dryer is the bottleneck. Planning for 100 % utilisation of the bottleneck.

t: What is the difference between batch time and cycle time?
x: Batch time is how long one batch takes end to end (32.5 h in the example). Cycle time is the interval between batches, set by the bottleneck (14 h).

t: How do you find the bottleneck?
x: Total the occupancy of each piece of equipment per batch, including waits, cleaning and transfers. The longest is the bottleneck.

t: Does speeding up a non-bottleneck step help?
x: No. It shortens the batch time but not the cycle time, so output stays the same.

s: The Boilers Act, 2025 for chemical plants: what changed from 1923, registration and inspection, certified operators, accidents and good practice.
x: Boilers Act, 2025: Compliance for Plants Statutory Compliance · Utilities · October 2026 Almost every chemical plant has a boiler, and a boiler holds a great deal of stored energy. India replaced the century-old Indian Boilers Act, 1923 with the Boilers Act, 2025, in force from 1 May 2025. The basic duties are familiar: register, inspect, operate with certified people and report accidents. It is a general guide, not legal advice; the Act, the rules, your state’s notifications and your own licence conditions always prevail. In this article What changed Basics Registration and inspection Basics Certified persons Working level Accidents Working level Good boiler house practice Going deeper Questions people ask What changed Basics The Boilers Act, 2025 modernises the 1923 law. A Central Boilers Board regulates design, manufacture, erection and use, aiming for uniform registration and inspect

The Boilers Act, 2025 modernises the 1923 law. A Central Boilers Board regulates design, manufacture, erection and use, aiming for uniform registration and inspection across states. Several minor offences have been decriminalised, with fines converted into penalties decided by adjudication. Rules, regulations and orders made under the old Act continue until replaced, so existing procedures carry on while new ones are notified.

A boiler covered by the Act must be registered before use and may be used only with a valid certificate after inspection by the inspecting authority, with periodic inspections thereafter. Steam pipes and fittings covered by the Act are included. Any repair or alteration of the pressure parts needs the authority’s approval, using a certified boiler repairer.

Boilers must be operated under the charge of persons holding the required certificate of proficiency or competency, with qualifications prescribed by the government, and repairs done by certified repairers. Shift planning should make sure every shift has a certified attendant; see HR in plants .
Boiler accidents must be reported to the inspecting authority, and an inquiry is held in the manner the state prescribes. Leave the scene undisturbed except for rescue and making safe.

t: Good boiler house practice Going deeper
x: Test safety valves, low-water cut-offs and flame failure trips on a schedule and record them. Control feed water quality and blowdown to prevent scale and corrosion; see steam system efficiency . Keep the boiler log, the inspection certificate and repair records in the boiler house. Never bypass a trip to keep the plant running. On the plant Treat the boiler certificate expiry date like a licence: put it on the compliance register with a reminder well ahead, because the inspection needs a planned shutdown and steam for the plant during it.
Running on an expired certificate. Repairs to pressure parts by uncertified welders. No certified attendant on night shift. Bypassed low-water trips. Poor water treatment causing tube failures.

t: When did the Boilers Act, 2025 come into force?
x: On 1 May 2025, replacing the Indian Boilers Act, 1923.

t: Do rules under the old Boilers Act still apply?
x: Rules, regulations and orders under the 1923 Act continue until new ones are notified under the 2025 Act.

Planning a batch on one comes down to a few numbers: how hard it spins the cake (G-force), how much cake fits in one load, and how much liquid it can squeeze out. This article builds them up from the basics, then covers the limits that matter on the plant: the lip, the load rating and the residual moisture. t: How a basket centrifuge separates Basics
s: Centrifuge Cake Weight & G-Force: How a Basket Centrifuge Works in Numbers
x: The basket is a perforated drum lined with a filter cloth. Slurry is fed in while it spins. The spin flings everything outwards: solids pack against the cloth as a cake, and the liquid is pushed through the cake and the cloth and out through the holes. Once the feed stops, the basket keeps spinning to spin the cake dry, then the cake is washed (if needed), spun again and discharged, by a scraper (peeler) or by hand through the bottom. It is the same physics as a Nutsche filter, with one big difference: instead of 0.5–1 bar of vacuum or gas pressure pushing the liquid, the spinning liquid itself presses on the cake, and at normal speeds that p

s: Centrifuge Cake Weight & G-Force: How a Basket Centrifuge Works in Numbers
x: G-force tells you how many times stronger than gravity the push is. It comes from the centripetal acceleration ω²r divided by g: G = ω² r / g = (2πN/60)² r / 9.81 G = 1.118 × 10^-5 × r (cm) × N² = 1.12 × r (mm) × (N/1000)² Two things to remember. G grows with the square of speed, so a basket at 1,400 rpm works the cake about twice as hard as at 1,000 rpm. And G is proportional to radius, so it is not the same everywhere: it is highest at the basket wall and lower at the inner surface of the cake.

t: Cake volume and weight per load Working level
s: Centrifuge Cake Weight & G-Force: How a Basket Centrifuge Works in Numbers
x: The cake forms a hollow cylinder (an annulus) against the basket wall. Its volume is the basket's volume minus the empty core: Cake volume = H × (π/4) × [D² - (D - 2t)²] Cake weight = cake volume × bulk density of the wet cake D basket diameter, H basket height, t cake thickness. Use the bulk density of the actual discharged wet cake of your product, not a handbook value. The cake cannot be thicker than the lip allows. The lip is the ring at the top of the basket; its opening diameter sets the maximum cake thickness, (D - Dlip) / 2. Feed beyond that and slurry spills over the lip into the filtrate side.

s: Centrifuge Cake Weight & G-Force: How a Basket Centrifuge Works in Numbers
x: A 1,200 mm (48”) basket, 600 mm high, lip opening 900 mm, running at 1,000 rpm. Planned cake 120 mm thick, wet cake bulk density 700 kg/m³. G at the wall = 1.12 × 600 × (1,000/1,000)² ≈ 670 G G at the cake surface (r = 480 mm) ≈ 540 G Lip limit = (1,200 - 900) / 2 = 150 mm → 120 mm is fine Cake volume = 0.6 × π/4 × (1.2² - 0.96²) ≈ 0.244 m³ Cake weight = 0.244 × 700 ≈ 171 kg per load If the batch produces 900 kg of wet cake, that is about five and a half loads, so plan six. Each load has feed, spin-dry, wash, spin-dry and discharge steps, so the number of loads, not the spin itself, usually decides the batch time. Try it: the basket is seen f

t: The pressure that drives liquid out Going deeper
s: Centrifuge Cake Weight & G-Force: How a Basket Centrifuge Works in Numbers
x: During the feed, a layer of liquid sits on top of the cake. Spinning, that liquid presses outwards like a column of water pressing on the bottom of a tank, except the “gravity” is hundreds of G. The pressure across the cake and cloth is: ΔP = ρliquid × ω² × (rwall² - rliquid surface²) / 2 In the example, with a 30 mm liquid layer on the cake (liquid surface at 450 mm radius) and liquid of 900 kg/m³, ΔP = 900 × 104.7² × (0.6² - 0.45²) / 2 ≈ 7.8 bar. A vacuum Nutsche can never exceed about 0.9 bar. That is the real reason a centrifuge filters and dewaters faster: the same cake resistance equation applies, with a much bigger pressure. Once the l

t: Load, speed and safety limits Going deeper
s: Centrifuge Cake Weight & G-Force: How a Basket Centrifuge Works in Numbers
x: Maximum load and speed are linked. The basket's stress depends on load × speed². The nameplate gives a maximum load at maximum speed; a denser product or a heavier load means a lower allowed speed. Never exceed both. Imbalance. Uneven feeding, or a cake that slumps on one side, makes the basket wobble. Feed at low speed and evenly, and respect the vibration trip. Flammable solvents. A spinning basket full of solvent-wet cake, with fast-moving liquid and plastic cloth, is a static and flammable-vapour hazard. x: Chemical Warehouse Management Plant Departments · Warehouse · October 2026 A chemical warehouse is not just a store. It holds flammable, corrosive, toxic and reactive materials side by side, keeps GMP status for every container, and feeds the plant with exactly weighed charges. Most of its rules exist because something went wrong somewhere. In this article Every container has a status Basics Segregation of incompatible materials Basics Flammable solvents Working level FIFO, FEFO and stock accuracy Working level Dispensing and reconciliation Going deeper Questions people ask Every container has a status Basics Each container shows its material, lot number and status: Quarantine , Approved , Rejected or Under test . Rejected material is kept in a locked, separate area until it is returned or destroyed. In a warehouse management system the status is controlled in software, but a physical la

t: Every container has a status Basics
x: Each container shows its material, lot number and status: Quarantine , Approved , Rejected or Under test . Rejected material is kept in a locked, separate area until it is returned or destroyed. In a warehouse management system the status is controlled in software, but a physical label still matters for anyone walking the floor.

Store materials by hazard, not by alphabet. The classic separations: Oxidisers (nitrates, peroxides, hypochlorite, permanganate) away from flammables and organics. Acids away from bases , and acids away from cyanides and sulphides, which release toxic gas. Water-reactive materials (sodium metal, hydrides, acid chlorides, thionyl chloride) in dry areas, away from sprinklers where possible and from aqueous materials. Pyrophoric catalysts kept wet and in closed containers. Toxic and highly potent materials in a restricted area. The safety data sheet (section 7, handling and storage, and section 10, stability and reactivity) is the starting point

Solvents in drums and tanks bring the most risk. In India, petroleum products and many flammable liquids are covered by the Petroleum Rules and licensing by PESO, with limits on quantity and separation distances; the site’s licence states what may be stored where (see PESO licensing ). Good practice: Drum stores with ventilation, flameproof electrics, bunding and spill kits. Earthing and bonding for drum transfer; see static electricity and solvent fires . Tank farms with dykes, nitrogen blanketing where needed, and breather valves sized for breathing losses . No storage of solvents in production areas beyond the shift requirement.

t: FIFO, FEFO and stock accuracy Working level
x: FIFO (first in, first out) issues the oldest lot first. FEFO (first expiry, first out) issues the lot that expires or reaches retest first, which matters when lots arrive with different shelf lives. Bin cards or system locations, regular cycle counts and immediate recording of every movement keep the stock accurate; an inaccurate stock is how a plant runs short of a material the system says it has.

Dispensing turns approved stock into weighed charges for a specific batch. It is done in a dispensing booth with extraction (often a downflow booth for powders), on calibrated balances checked daily, with each charge labelled for the batch, double-checked and recorded. Potent materials need containment. Afterwards, issued, used and returned quantities are reconciled; an unexplained difference is a deviation. Finished API is stored according to its label conditions (for example below 25 °C, protected from light), with temperature and humidity monitored and mapped across the store so the worst spot is known. On the plant Walk the store once a w

Storing by supplier or alphabet instead of hazard. Rejected material left in the approved area. Drum transfers without earthing. Issuing the newest lot because it is easiest to reach. Balances not checked before dispensing.

t: What is the difference between FIFO and FEFO?
x: FIFO issues the oldest received stock first; FEFO issues the stock with the earliest expiry or retest date first. FEFO is preferred where shelf lives differ.

t: Which materials should never be stored together?
x: Oxidisers with flammables, acids with bases, acids with cyanides or sulphides, and water-reactive materials with aqueous materials. Check section 10 of the SDS for each material.

t: Why is warehouse temperature mapping done?
x: To find the warmest and coldest spots so that materials with storage conditions are kept where those conditions are actually met.

s: Chiller vs VAM: Calculations and Running Cost
x: Electric (vapour compression) chiller: refrigerant boils in the evaporator and takes heat from the chilled water; the compressor raises its pressure; it condenses in the condenser and gives the heat to cooling water; an expansion valve drops the pressure again. The compressor is where the electricity goes. Vapour absorption machine: water is the refrigerant. It boils at very low pressure (about 8 mbar abs, around 4 °C) in the evaporator and chills the water. Concentrated lithium bromide solution absorbs the vapour. A generator heated by steam or hot water boils the water back out of the solution, and a condenser turns it to liquid again. Inst

s: Chiller vs VAM: Calculations and Running Cost
x: 120 m³/h of chilled water from 12 °C to 7 °C: 120 × 5 / 3.024 ≈ 198 TR (6,00,000 kcal/h). The compressor draws 140 kW: 0.71 kW/TR, COP 5.0. That is a normal water-cooled screw chiller.

s: Chiller vs VAM: Calculations and Running Cost

Making cold at -5 °C simply takes far more work than at 7 °C, so only compare brine chillers with other brine chillers at the same temperatures. And use the right cp: treating glycol as water here would overstate the load by about 9 %. Measurement tips: temperature sensors in thermowells close to the machine, calibrated together (0.25 °C error on a 5 °C ΔT is 5 % error in TR); a clamp-on ultrasonic flow meter on a straight run;

s: Chiller vs VAM: Calculations and Running Cost
x: Heat input (kcal/h) = TR × 3,024 / COP Steam (kg/h) = heat input / hfg (kcal/kg) at the supply pressure Hot water (m³/h) = heat input / (1 × ΔT × 1,000) A 200 TR double-effect VAM (COP 1.3) on 8 barg steam needs 200 × 3,024 / 1.3 ≈ 4,65,000 kcal/h, about 960 kg/h of steam or 4.8 kg/h per TR. A 100 TR single-effect machine (COP 0.7) on 90 °C hot water cooled by 10 °C needs about 4,32,000 kcal/h, or 43 m³/h of hot water: a good use for DG jacket water, hot condensate or process cooling water that would otherwise go to a cooling tower.

t: The cooling tower each one needs Working level
s: Chiller vs VAM: Calculations and Running Cost
x: Both machines reject their heat to the cooling tower: the cooling load plus whatever drove the machine. Electric chiller: cooling + compressor power ≈ 1.2–1.25 × cooling VAM: cooling × (1 + 1/COP) ≈ 1.77 × cooling (double effect), ≈ 2.4 × (single effect) Replacing a 200 TR electric chiller with a VAM therefore needs a cooling tower about 40 % bigger, more condenser water flow, and more make-up water. Count this before deciding.

t: Which is cheaper to run? Going deeper
s: Chiller vs VAM: Calculations and Running Cost
x: Electric chiller cost per year = TR × kW/TR × hours × ₹/kWh VAM cost per year = TR × steam (kg/h per TR) / 1,000 × hours × ₹/tonne + auxiliary power cost Break-even steam cost = (chiller kW/TR - VAM auxiliary kW/TR) × ₹/kWh / (steam per TR-hour in tonnes) With 0.85 kW/TR for the chiller (including its share of pumps and cooling tower fans), 0.15 kW/TR of VAM auxiliaries, power at ₹8/kWh and 4.6 kg/h of steam per TR, the break-even is about ₹1,200 per tonne of steam. Steam from furnace oil at ₹3,700 per tonne never gets there; steam from a well-run biomass boiler can come close; waste heat, exhaust gas or back-pressure steam from a turbine bea

x: Raise the chilled water set point as far as the process allows: roughly 2–3 % power saved per 1 °C. Keep the condenser water cold and the condenser tubes clean: roughly 2–3 % per 1 °C colder. Run one chiller well loaded rather than two lightly loaded, unless the machines are designed for good part-load efficiency. Find the cause of a low chilled water ΔT: too much flow, three-way valves bypassing, or an oversized pump. Insulate and seal chilled water and brine lines; wet insulation is both a heat gain and a corrosion problem.

s: Chiller vs VAM: Calculations and Running Cost
x: COP = 3.517 / (kW/TR). At 0.7 kW/TR the COP is about 5.0; at 1.2 kW/TR it is about 2.9.

t: How much steam does a VAM use per TR?
s: Chiller vs VAM: Calculations and Running Cost

x: A compressor squeezes atmospheric air to 6–8 barg. Squeezing air heats it, so an aftercooler cools it and most of its moisture condenses and is drained. A dryer removes more, a receiver stores a buffer, and a pipe network carries it to the users: valves and actuators, instruments, pneumatic pumps, filter blowing, conveying. The catch is efficiency. Most of the electricity a compressor draws becomes heat in the compressor, not useful work at the user. t: How do you measure compressed air leakage?

s: How to build consumption norms and cost per kg for an API or chemical process: yield, raw material and solvent use, recovery and conversion cost.
x: Consumption Norms and Cost per kg Process Design · Costing · October 2026 Sooner or later every process engineer is asked: what will this cost per kilogram? The answer decides whether a product is launched, which route is chosen and where improvement effort goes. Building it is not difficult, but it needs care with yields, solvent recovery and the costs that come per batch rather than per kilogram. This article walks through it with a worked example. In this article Yield: molar and weight Basics Consumption norms Basics Building the cost per kg Working level Where the money really is Working level Lab numbers vs plant numbers Going deeper Questions people ask Yield: molar and weight Basics Chemists usually report molar yield : moles of product made per mole of limiting starting material, as a percentage. Costing usually needs weight yield : kilograms of product per kilogram of starting

s: Consumption Norms and Cost per kg
x: Chemists usually report molar yield : moles of product made per mole of limiting starting material, as a percentage. Costing usually needs weight yield : kilograms of product per kilogram of starting material. They differ by the ratio of molecular weights: Weight yield = molar yield × (MW product / MW starting material) × stoichiometric ratio A molar yield of 85 % on a reaction where the product weighs 1.2 times the starting material gives a weight yield of 1.02 kg/kg. Mixing the two up is one of the most common errors in early costing. Always say which you mean.

s: Consumption Norms and Cost per kg
x: A consumption norm is how much of each input is used per kilogram of finished product. For raw materials: Norm (kg/kg) = quantity charged per batch / product per batch For solvents, only the part that isn't recovered and reused counts: Solvent norm = charged × (1 - recovery fraction) / product per batch Norms are also the best way to track a plant. A rising solvent norm points straight to a recovery or loss problem, before anyone looks at the cost report. The material balance article shows how to find where the losses are.

s: Consumption Norms and Cost per kg
x: Take one stage. Per batch, charge 500 kg of starting material at ₹800/kg, 300 kg of reagent at ₹250/kg, and 2,000 kg of toluene at ₹90/kg with 90 % recovered. Theoretical output is 600 kg; at 85 % yield, 510 kg. Conversion cost (utilities, labour, maintenance, QC, effluent treatment and overheads) is about ₹1.2 lakh per batch. Raw materials: (500 × 800 + 300 × 250) / 510 = ₹931 per kg. Solvent make-up: 2,000 × 0.10 × 90 / 510 = ₹35 per kg. Conversion: 1,20,000 / 510 = ₹235 per kg. Total: about ₹1,202 per kg. Try it: move the yield and the solvent recovery and watch the cost per kg. All the numbers are illustrative, not from a real product. Fo

The picture flips for cheap chemistry. In a bulk intermediate made from inexpensive raw materials in a lot of solvent, solvent loss and conversion cost can dominate. s: Flow chemistry for process engineers: residence time, tube and plate reactors, heat transfer and safety, what flow does badly, and scale-up by numbering up.
x: Continuous and Flow Chemistry Scale-up · Continuous Processing · October 2026 Instead of filling a 6,000 L reactor and waiting, a flow reactor pumps reagents through a tube a few millimetres wide, and product comes out continuously at the other end. It sounds like a lab curiosity, but flow chemistry is now used at production scale for reactions that are too fast, too hot or too hazardous to run safely in batch. This article explains how it works and where it fits. In this article The idea: time becomes distance Basics Why flow can do things batch cannot Basics Sizing a simple flow reactor Working level What flow does badly Working level Scaling up and running a flow process Going deeper Questions people ask The idea: time becomes distance Basics In a batch reactor, the reaction proceeds in time: so many hours at temperature. In a flow reactor, it proceeds along the tube: each bit of flui

t: The idea: time becomes distance Basics
x: In a batch reactor, the reaction proceeds in time: so many hours at temperature. In a flow reactor, it proceeds along the tube: each bit of fluid enters, reacts as it travels, and leaves after the residence time: Residence time τ = reactor volume V / volumetric flow Q A 6 mm tube 40 m long holds about 1.1 L. At 100 mL/min, the residence time is about 11 minutes. Run it continuously and it processes 144 L a day, from a reactor you can carry. Try it: change the tube diameter, length and flow and see the residence time, throughput and heat transfer area per volume compared with batch reactors.

t: Why flow can do things batch cannot Basics
x: Heat transfer: area per volume is 4/d for a tube. A 6 mm tube has about 670 m²/m³; a 6 kL batch reactor has about 2. Strongly exothermic reactions that would need hours of slow dosing in batch can run in seconds to minutes. Small inventory: only a litre or so is reacting at any moment. If something goes wrong, the energy available is tiny compared with a full batch. Hazardous intermediates (diazonium salts, azides, organolithiums) can be made and used immediately without accumulating. Precise residence time: stopping a reaction at exactly the right point helps with consecutive side reactions. See reactor selection . Extreme conditions: temper

t: Sizing a simple flow reactor Working level
x: Find the residence time needed from batch kinetics or small flow trials at the chosen temperature. Choose the throughput: product per day = flow × concentration × molar mass × time. At 100 mL/min, 0.5 mol/L and a molar mass of 250 g/mol, that is about 18 kg per day. Reactor volume = flow × residence time. Check mixing at the inlet: fast reactions need a good mixer (T-piece, static mixer or micromixer), because laminar flow in small tubes mixes slowly by itself. Check pressure drop through the tube and mixers, and that the pumps can deliver steady, pulse-free flow.

t: What flow does badly Working level
x: Solids: precipitates and slurries block narrow channels. This is the most common reason flow projects fail. Keep everything in solution, or use reactors designed for slurries (CSTR cascades, oscillatory baffled reactors). Slow reactions: a 10-hour reaction needs a very long tube or very low flow. Batch is usually simpler. Many steps with different conditions can be linked, but every step adds pumps, mixers and control, and the slowest step sets the pace. Start-up and shut-down produce off-specification material, which must be planned for.

t: Scaling up and running a flow process Going deeper
x: Flow processes scale by running longer, by using a larger reactor of the same design (keeping heat transfer and mixing similar), or by numbering up : several identical reactors in parallel. Each keeps the same conditions that worked in development, which avoids many of the scale-up surprises of batch. See lab to plant scale-up . Continuous processes also need continuous quality control. Process analytical technology (inline IR, UV or Raman) watches the product stream in real time, and a diverter valve sends out-of-specification material to waste or recycling. In GMP manufacture, the batch is defined by time or quantity, with traceability of a

Choosing flow for a reaction that forms solids. Ignoring mixing at the inlet of a fast reaction. Pulsing pumps that make residence time uneven. No plan for start-up and shut-down material. Converting a whole process when one hazardous step would do.

t: Why is flow chemistry safer for exothermic reactions?
x: High area per volume removes heat fast, and the reacting inventory is tiny.

t: What are the main limitations of flow chemistry?
x: Solids, slow reactions, multi-step complexity, and start-up/shut-down material.

s: Cooling tower calculations: range, approach, heat load in kcal/h and TR, evaporation loss, drift, blowdown, make-up and cycles of concentration.
x: Cooling Tower Calculations Explained Utilities · Cooling Water · Updated October 2026 The cooling tower decides the condenser water temperature for every chiller, solvent condenser and reactor jacket in the plant, and it is usually the biggest single user of fresh water on site. Four numbers describe it: range, approach, evaporation and cycles of concentration. Here is how to calculate each one and what it tells you. t: How a cooling tower cools water Basics
x: Hot water is spread over the fill so that a large surface of water meets moving air. About 1 % of the water evaporates for every 6–7 °C of cooling, and the latent heat it takes cools the rest. Because the cooling comes from evaporation, the limit is the air's wet bulb temperature, not its dry bulb. On a humid monsoon day with a 29 °C wet bulb, no tower can deliver 28 °C water. Hot water falls over the fill while the fan draws air through it. A small part of the water evaporates into the air, and that evaporation is what cools the rest.

Range = hot water in - cold water out Approach = cold water out - wet bulb Effectiveness = Range / (Range + Approach) = Range / (hot water in - wet bulb) The range is fixed by the plant: heat load divided by water flow. The approach is what the tower controls. A tower designed for 4 °C approach that now gives 7 °C at the same wet bulb has a problem: scaled or broken fill, blocked distribution nozzles, a fan with the wrong blade angle or a slipping belt, or air short-circuiting from the outlet back to the inlet.

Heat rejected (kcal/h) = flow (m³/h) × 1,000 × 1 × Range In TR: kcal/h / 3,024 For 500 m³/h cooled from 37 to 32 °C: 500 × 1,000 × 5 = 25,00,000 kcal/h, about 827 TR. A cooling tower serving a chiller rejects the chiller's cooling load plus its compressor power, about 1.2–1.25 times the chiller TR. For a VAM it is about 1.8 times, because it also rejects the steam's heat.

Evaporation E (m³/h) = 0.00085 × 1.8 × circulation (m³/h) × Range (°C) Drift D = drift % × circulation Cycles of concentration COC = conductivity (or chloride) of circulating water / that of make-up Blowdown B = E / (COC - 1) - D Make-up M = E + B + D = E × COC / (COC - 1) The evaporation formula is a field approximation: about 0.15 % of the flow per degree of range. It assumes all the heat leaves as latent heat; in dry weather a little leaves as sensible heat and actual evaporation is slightly lower.

t: A water-saving case: raising the cycles Working level
x: A 1,000 m³/h tower with a 6 °C range evaporates about 9.2 m³/h. At 3 cycles the make-up is 9.2 × 3/2 ≈ 13.8 m³/h. At 5 cycles it is 9.2 × 5/4 ≈ 11.5 m³/h: about 55 m³ a day less make-up, and about 55 m³ a day less blowdown going to the ETP. Above about 6 cycles the saving per extra cycle gets small, while the scaling and corrosion risk keeps rising. What limits the cycles is the make-up water: hardness and alkalinity (calcium carbonate scale), silica, chloride (corrosion of stainless and carbon steel) and the treatment programme. Ask your water treatment supplier for the maximum safe cycles for your make-up analysis, and control the blowdown

t: Why the approach matters to the whole plant Going deeper
x: Every degree the cooling water runs warmer costs energy and capacity elsewhere. An electric chiller uses roughly 2–3 % more power for each 1 °C rise in condenser water temperature. Solvent condensers lose capacity, vacuum systems lose vacuum, and batch cooling times stretch. A 2 °C approach improvement on the tower is often worth more in the chiller house than in the cooling tower itself.

Log hot water, cold water and wet bulb every shift; trend the approach against the wet bulb. Measure the circulating flow at least once a year (ultrasonic meter) to confirm the heat load. Inspect the hot water basin and nozzles, the fill, the drift eliminators and the fan blade angle. Compare make-up meter readings with the calculated make-up; a big gap means leaks or uncontrolled overflow. Check the conductivity controller and the blowdown valve actually work. Run fans on cold-water temperature, with VFDs where possible, so they slow down in winter.

t: What is the formula for cooling tower evaporation loss?
x: E (m³/h) = 0.00085 × 1.8 × circulation (m³/h) × range (°C), about 0.15 % of the flow per degree of range.

t: How are cycles of concentration measured?
x: Divide the conductivity (or chloride) of the circulating water by that of the make-up water. Chloride is more reliable when treatment chemicals add conductivity.

t: What is a good cooling tower approach?
x: About 3–5 °C at design wet bulb for most process towers. Watch the trend: an approach that creeps up at the same load and wet bulb means the tower needs attention.

s: Crystallisation scale-up: solubility and supersaturation, metastable zone width, seeding, cooling profiles, oiling out and what changes at plant scale.
x: Crystallisation Scale-up Scale-up · Solids · October 2026 In API manufacturing, crystallisation is where the product gets its purity, its form and its particle size. It is also the step that most often behaves differently in the plant: the lab gave nice prisms that filtered in minutes, and the plant gives a paste that blocks the centrifuge. The cause is nearly always supersaturation: how much of it was created, how fast, and where in the vessel. This article explains crystallisation from that one idea. In this article Solubility and supersaturation Basics Nucleation vs growth Basics The metastable zone Working level Seeding and cooling profiles Working level Antisolvent and reactive crystallisation Working level What changes at plant scale Going deeper Oiling out, polymorphs and other surprises Going deeper Questions people ask Solubility and supersaturation Basics Every compound has a s

Every compound has a solubility in a solvent: the most that can stay dissolved at a given temperature. For most organic compounds it rises with temperature. Dissolve the product hot, cool it, and the solution ends up holding more than it can at the lower temperature. That excess is supersaturation , and it is the driving force for crystallisation: Supersaturation ΔC = C - C*(T) or as a ratio S = C / C*(T) C: concentration in solution; C*: solubility at the current temperature. We create supersaturation by cooling, by evaporating solvent, by adding an antisolvent in which the product is poorly soluble, or by a reaction that forms the less solu

Supersaturation can be used up in two ways: Nucleation: new crystals form from nothing. It needs high supersaturation and happens suddenly, in a burst, producing a large number of tiny crystals. Growth: dissolved molecules attach to crystals that already exist. It works at low supersaturation and makes existing crystals bigger. A good crystallisation is mostly growth: few crystals, growing large and evenly. A bad one is mostly nucleation: a shower of fines that are hard to filter and wash, hold more mother liquor (and its impurities) and dry slowly. Controlling crystallisation means keeping supersaturation in the range where growth wins.

A clear solution can be cooled some way below its saturation temperature without crystallising. The region between the solubility curve and the point where it finally nucleates on its own is the metastable zone . Its width (MSZW) is typically a few degrees to about 20 °C of undercooling. It is not a fixed property: faster cooling, weaker agitation and higher purity all make it wider. Inside the zone, crystals that are already present grow, but new ones form only slowly. Cross the upper limit and the solution nucleates suddenly, usually at a temperature that varies from batch to batch. Try it: a solution saturated at 70 °C is cooled to 10 °C.

t: Seeding and cooling profiles Working level
x: Seeding takes nucleation out of the hands of chance. You add crystals of the right form at a chosen point inside the metastable zone, so growth starts on them at low supersaturation. Good practice: Seed about a quarter to a third of the way into the metastable zone: past saturation so the seed doesn't dissolve, but far from the limit. Use 0.5–2 % by weight of seed, milled or sieved to a known size, and of the correct polymorph. Add it as a slurry in the same solvent, not as a dry powder that floats on the surface. Hold for 30–60 minutes after seeding before cooling further, so the seed surface “heals” and starts to grow. Then cool. At the sta

t: Antisolvent and reactive crystallisation Working level
x: With an antisolvent (water into a methanol solution, heptane into ethyl acetate), supersaturation is created where the antisolvent meets the solution: at the feed point. Local supersaturation there can be far higher than the average in the vessel. The same applies to reactive crystallisation, such as adding acid to form a salt. So: Add slowly, especially at first; seed after the first portion. Feed into a well-mixed zone near the impeller, not onto the surface or down the wall. Consider reverse addition (solution into antisolvent) only if the lab has shown it gives the right form.

t: What changes at plant scale Going deeper
x: Cooling is slower and less even. The plant can't cool as fast as the lab, which is often good for crystal size, but the jacket wall is much colder than the bulk. Supersaturation near the wall causes encrustation and fines. Limit the jacket-to-batch temperature difference (often 10–15 °C) during crystallisation. Mixing is slower. Antisolvent and reagent feed points matter much more. See the mixing scale-up article . Agitator tip speed is higher. At the same power per volume, the plant impeller tip moves faster and can break needle-like crystals, creating fines. Check the crystal habit under the microscope. Time is longer. Holds at the end of c

t: Oiling out, polymorphs and other surprises Going deeper
x: Oiling out (liquid-liquid phase separation) happens when the product separates as an oil instead of crystals, usually because supersaturation is too high or the temperature is above the product's melting point in that solvent mixture. The oil later solidifies into a lump that traps impurities. Seed above the oiling-out temperature, and add antisolvent more slowly. Polymorphs are different crystal forms of the same molecule, with different solubility, stability and bioavailability. The form that crystallises can depend on solvent, temperature, supersaturation and seed. Always seed with the right form, confirm the form by XRD on plant batches,

Cooling at a fixed rate with no seed and accepting whatever nucleates. Adding dry seed powder onto the surface. Cooling fast right after seeding. Pouring antisolvent onto the surface or down the wall. Scaling up without checking the plant's jacket temperature difference and agitator tip speed.

t: What is the metastable zone width?
x: The undercooling a clear solution can take before nucleating on its own, typically a few degrees to 20 °C.

t: When and how much should you seed?
x: About a quarter to a third into the metastable zone, with 0.5–2 % seed of the right form, then hold 30–60 minutes.
It cools slowly while crystal surface is small and faster as it grows, keeping supersaturation low and even.

x: Distillation Basics Process Design · Separation · October 2026 Distillation is the workhorse of every chemical plant: solvent recovery, purification, removing water before a reaction. Most engineers can run a still, but fewer can say why one separation needs five trays and another needs fifty, or why turning up the reflux sometimes fixes the purity and sometimes doesn't. This article builds the picture from one idea: vapour is richer in the more volatile component than the liquid it boils from. In this article The one idea behind distillation Basics Relative volatility: how easy is the separation? Basics What a theoretical stage is Basics McCabe-Thiele: counting the stages Working level Choosing the reflux ratio Working level From theoretical stages to a real column Working level Batch distillation in pharma plants Going deeper Questions people ask The one idea behind distillation Basics

t: The one idea behind distillation Basics
x: Boil a mixture of methanol and water and the first vapour that comes off is richer in methanol than the liquid was, because methanol has the higher vapour pressure. Condense that vapour, boil it again, and it gets richer still. A distillation column simply does this boiling and condensing many times over, in one piece of equipment. Vapour rises, liquid falls, and on each tray or each bit of packing they meet, swap some molecules, and part again. That is all. Everything else in distillation design is about how many of those contacts you need and how much liquid you must send back down the column to make them work.

t: Relative volatility: how easy is the separation? Basics
x: Relative volatility, α, measures how strongly the light component prefers the vapour compared with the heavy one: α = (yA/xA) / (yB/xB) ≈ P^satA / P^satB (for ideal mixtures) x is the mole fraction in the liquid, y in the vapour. The equilibrium curve is y = αx / (1 + (α - 1)x). Some feel for the numbers: α above 3: easy. A few stages do the job. Acetone from water is in this range at low acetone concentrations. α around 1.5 to 2.5: normal. Ten to thirty stages. α below 1.2: hard. Many stages and high reflux; ask whether another method would be cheaper. α = 1: an azeotrope. Ordinary distillation cannot pass it, whatever the column. Ethanol an

t: What a theoretical stage is Basics
x: A theoretical stage (or ideal stage) is a contact where vapour and liquid mix long enough to reach equilibrium and then separate cleanly. Real trays don't quite get there, so a real column needs more trays than theoretical stages. But theoretical stages are the right way to think first, because they depend only on the chemistry and the reflux, not on the hardware. The reboiler counts as one theoretical stage. A partial condenser also counts as one; a total condenser does not.

t: McCabe-Thiele: counting the stages Working level
x: The McCabe-Thiele diagram is the classic way to see a binary separation. It has three lines: the equilibrium curve : what composition of vapour sits above each liquid; the operating lines : a mass balance that links the liquid leaving one stage with the vapour coming up from the one below. Above the feed (rectifying section) the slope is R/(R + 1), where R is the reflux ratio; below the feed (stripping section) it is steeper; the 45° diagonal, where x = y. Starting at the top product composition, step horizontally to the equilibrium curve (one stage of equilibrium), then vertically to the operating line (mass balance to the next stage down),

t: Choosing the reflux ratio Working level
x: Two limits frame every design: Nmin = ln[ (xD/(1 - xD)) × ((1 - xB)/xB) ] / ln α (Fenske, at total reflux) Rmin: the reflux at which the operating line touches the equilibrium curve (a pinch) For our example: Nmin = ln(19 × 19) / ln 2.5 ≈ 6.4 stages, and Rmin ≈ 1.1. At total reflux you need the fewest stages but produce nothing; at minimum reflux you need infinite stages. Between them is a trade-off: Every unit of reflux has to be boiled in the reboiler and condensed again. Reboiler duty ≈ (R + 1) × D × latent heat, so steam and cooling water costs rise in step with R + 1. Fewer stages means a shorter, cheaper column. The economic optimum is

t: From theoretical stages to a real column Working level
x: Trays: real trays = theoretical stages ÷ overall efficiency. Typical efficiencies are 0.5 to 0.8 for solvent systems, lower for viscous liquids. Tray spacing is usually 450–600 mm. Packing: packed height = theoretical stages × HETP. Structured packing gives HETP of roughly 0.3–0.5 m; random packing (rings) 0.4–0.8 m. Packing has a low pressure drop, so it is the usual choice for vacuum distillation and for the small columns on top of batch stills. Diameter is set by the vapour load: too small and the column floods; too large and liquid doesn't distribute evenly on packing or trays weep at low load. Design around 70–80 % of flooding. Add a mar

t: Batch distillation in pharma plants Going deeper
x: Most solvent distillation in API and intermediate plants is batch: a reactor acts as the reboiler, with a short packed column, a condenser, a reflux divider and receivers. The pot composition keeps changing, so the top composition falls during the run unless the reflux ratio is raised. Operators usually run it in cuts: total reflux to establish the column; a low-boiler fore-cut, collected separately; the main solvent cut at a moderate reflux ratio, raising it as the top temperature starts to climb; an intermediate cut (slop) to be recycled into the next batch; the residue left in the pot. Watch the top temperature, not just the time. For a so

Designing from a single relative volatility for a mixture with water. Expecting distillation to break an azeotrope. Turning up reflux on a column that is already flooding. Ignoring liquid distribution in packed columns. Running batch cuts by the clock instead of the top temperature.
How much more the light component prefers the vapour than the heavy one. Above 2 the separation is easy; below 1.2 it is hard.

t: What is the minimum reflux ratio?
x: The reflux at which the separation needs an infinite number of stages. Practical designs use 1.2 to 1.5 times the minimum.

t: How do you convert theoretical stages to real trays?
x: Divide by the tray efficiency (0.5–0.8), or for packing multiply by the HETP (0.3–0.8 m).

s: Drug Manufacturing Licence and Schedule M
x: Manufacturing licences are granted by the State Licensing Authority (the state drugs controller), with joint inspection by central and state drugs inspectors before grant. Since a 2017 amendment, licences remain valid unless suspended or cancelled, provided a retention fee is paid before the end of every five years from issue; late payment attracts a monthly late fee, and non-payment beyond six months leads to deemed cancellation.

s: Drug Manufacturing Licence and Schedule M
x: Each product must be approved and endorsed on the licence before commercial manufacture. New drugs need approval from the central regulator, CDSCO, before the state can add them. A new product introduced through technology transfer therefore needs its licence endorsement planned alongside its trial batches.

s: Drug Manufacturing Licence and Schedule M
x: Schedule M was revised at the end of 2023 to bring Indian GMP close to international standards, with a pharmaceutical quality system, quality risk management, product quality review, validation, qualification of equipment and computerised systems, and stronger data integrity. Large manufacturers had to comply first; for smaller manufacturers with turnover below ₹250 crore, the deadline was extended to 31 December 2025. See QA and GMP .

s: Drug Manufacturing Licence and Schedule M
x: Licensed premises are inspected at least once every three years, or more often based on risk, and also after complaints or quality failures. Export sites are additionally inspected by foreign regulators and customers. Inspection readiness is a habit, not an event: current SOPs, complete batch records, closed deviations and CAPA, and trained people.

s: Drug Manufacturing Licence and Schedule M
x: Other approvals that often sit with the drug licence: a WHO-GMP certificate or certificate of pharmaceutical product for export markets, NOCs for export, and registration of controlled substances where the process uses them; see NDPS compliance and regulatory affairs . On the plant Keep a table of every product made on site against its licence endorsement and consent listing. The two documents are issued by different departments and drift apart unless someone checks.

s: Drug Manufacturing Licence and Schedule M
x: Commercial batches before the product is endorsed on the licence. Missing the five-yearly retention fee. Treating Schedule M as paperwork rather than a quality system. Inspection preparation only when an inspection is announced. Licence and pollution consent listing different products.
