s: Drying of wet cakes: drying curves, why plant drying is slower than lab, dryer types (VTD, ANFD, RCVD, FBD), residual solvent and endpoints.
x: Drying and Dryer Scale-up Scale-up · Solids · October 2026 Drying looks like the simplest step in the process: put the wet cake in, heat it, wait. Yet it is often the bottleneck of the whole plant, and where batches fail on LOD, residual solvent or degradation. The reason is that drying happens in two very different stages, and the second one, which barely shows in the lab, can take most of the time in the plant. This article explains drying from the basics and what to expect when you scale it up. In this article What happens when a cake dries Basics The drying curve Basics Why the plant is so much slower Working level Choosing a dryer Working level Temperature, form and residual solvent Working level Knowing when it's dry Going deeper Questions people ask What happens when a cake dries Basics A wet cake from a centrifuge or filter holds solvent in two places: free solvent in the spaces

t: What happens when a cake dries Basics
x: A wet cake from a centrifuge or filter holds solvent in two places: free solvent in the spaces between particles and on their surfaces, and bound solvent inside pores, in crystal defects or held as a solvate. Free solvent evaporates easily once heat reaches it. Bound solvent first has to travel out of the particle, which is slow and doesn't speed up much however hot the jacket is. To evaporate solvent you need heat (its latent heat) and a way to carry the vapour away (vacuum or a gas stream). Vacuum lowers the boiling point, so the solvent evaporates at a temperature the product can tolerate.

Plot LOD (loss on drying) against time and you see two periods: Constant-rate period: particle surfaces are wet, and solvent evaporates as fast as heat arrives. The product sits near the solvent's boiling point at the dryer pressure, well below the jacket temperature. LOD falls in a straight line. Falling-rate period: below the critical moisture content , the surfaces dry out. Now the rate is set by how fast solvent moves out from inside the particles. The rate falls, LOD approaches its final value slowly, and the product temperature rises toward the jacket temperature. The falling-rate period is the trap. It has little solvent left to remove

t: Why the plant is so much slower Working level
x: In a contact dryer (a vacuum tray dryer, filter-dryer or conical dryer), heat comes through the heated wall or plates. The drying rate per kilogram of cake depends on how much heated area each kilogram has, and that falls as the bed gets deeper: Drying rate per kg ∝ U × A × (Tjacket - Tproduct) / mcake ∝ ΔT / bed depth A lab tray of 2 cm cake dried at 60 °C reaches 0.5 % LOD in about 1.4 hours. The same cake in a filter-dryer with a 30 cm bed has 15 times less area per kilogram and takes about 22 hours, 14 of them in the falling-rate period. Raising the jacket to 80 °C, if the product allows, brings it to about 14 hours. Reducing the bed dept

Dryer Good for Watch out for Vacuum tray dryer (VTD) Small batches, sticky or heat-sensitive products, many products Manual loading and unloading, operator exposure, slow Agitated nutsche filter-dryer (ANFD) Filtration, washing and drying in one closed vessel; potent and toxic products Deep beds, slow falling-rate period, agitator causing agglomerates or attrition Rotary cone vacuum dryer (RCVD) Free-flowing powders, gentle tumbling, good mixing Lumps and balling with sticky cakes Fluid bed dryer (FBD) Fast drying of granular, free-flowing solids with hot gas Dust explosion risk with solvents and fines; needs inert gas for flammable solvents

t: Temperature, form and residual solvent Working level
x: Product temperature limit: below the temperature where it melts, sinters, degrades or changes form. During the constant-rate period the product stays cool even with a hot jacket, but in the falling-rate period it heats up toward the jacket temperature. Many plants run a hot jacket first and lower it later. Solvates and hydrates: some products hold solvent or water in the crystal. Drying too hard can remove it and change the form; drying too gently can leave too much. The form must be checked by XRD at the end of drying. Residual solvent limits: ICH Q3C sets limits for solvents in drug substances. For example, toluene is limited to 890 ppm and

t: Knowing when it's dry Going deeper
x: The definitive answer is a sample tested for LOD or residual solvent. But samples take time, so watch the online signs too: Product temperature rising toward the jacket temperature: the constant-rate period is over. Dryer pressure falling toward the pump's no-load vacuum: little vapour is being produced. Condensate collection in the receiver slowing to a stop. Sample at the point the trend says it should be dry, not on a fixed clock. If the falling-rate period is the bottleneck, look at reducing particle porosity in crystallisation, at better deliquoring, or at a short slurry wash with a lower-boiling solvent to displace a high-boiling one be

Estimating plant drying time from a lab oven tray. Running the jacket at full temperature into the falling-rate period without checking product temperature limits. Passing LOD but never testing residual solvent. Drying a 30 % LOD cake when better deliquoring could bring it to 20 %. Fluid-bed drying flammable solvent-wet product with air.

t: Why is plant drying so much slower?
x: The plant bed is much deeper, so heated area per kilogram is much smaller. 1.4 hours in a lab tray can become about 22 hours in a filter-dryer.

t: What are the constant-rate and falling-rate periods?
x: First, wet surfaces evaporate as fast as heat arrives; then solvent must move out of the particles and the rate falls.

t: How do you know drying is complete?
x: By LOD or residual solvent test, guided by product temperature, vacuum level and condensate rate.

x: Dust Explosions Process Safety · Fire and Explosion · October 2026 Most people in a solvent plant respect solvent vapour, but treat powder as harmless: it is just the product, sitting in a bag. Yet many organic powders, APIs, intermediates, sugar and starch among them, explode as violently as a gas when they are dispersed as a cloud. This article explains when and why a dust explodes, how to read the test data, and the controls that actually protect a plant. In this article How a powder can explode Basics The explosion pentagon Basics Reading the test data: Kst, Pmax, MIE Working level Hybrid mixtures: powder plus solvent Working level Prevention and protection Working level Secondary explosions and Imperial Sugar Going deeper Questions people ask How a powder can explode Basics A lump of sugar burns slowly. Grind it to a fine powder and blow it into the air, and every particle is surrou

t: How a powder can explode Basics
x: A lump of sugar burns slowly. Grind it to a fine powder and blow it into the air, and every particle is surrounded by oxygen with a huge surface area to react. A flame can then pass from particle to particle fast enough to build pressure inside equipment or a building: a dust explosion. Roughly, any solid that can burn can explode as a dust if it is fine enough, typically below about 500 µm, and especially below 100 µm. That includes most organic chemicals, APIs, excipients, food powders, plastics and metal powders such as aluminium. Inert inorganic salts don't.

A fire needs the three sides of the fire triangle: fuel, oxygen and ignition. A dust explosion needs two more: the dust must be dispersed as a cloud, and the cloud must be confined so pressure can build. Take away any one of the five and there is no explosion. Try it: tap a side of the pentagon to remove it, and see how plants remove each one in practice. Dispersion is what makes dust different from a vapour. A layer of powder on a floor is not an explosion hazard by itself; the same powder blown into the air is. That's why the places to worry about are where powder is airborne: inside mills, sieves, blenders, fluid bed dryers, cyclones, bag

t: Reading the test data: Kst, Pmax, MIE Working level
x: A powder's explosion behaviour is measured in standard tests. The main numbers: Property What it means Typical range KSt (bar·m/s) How violent the explosion is: maximum rate of pressure rise, normalised to volume St 1: up to 200; St 2: 200–300; St 3: above 300 Pmax (bar g) Highest pressure in a closed vessel Usually 7–10 bar g MIE (mJ) Smallest spark that ignites the dust cloud From below 3 mJ (very sensitive) to above 1,000 mJ MIT (°C) Minimum ignition temperature of a cloud and of a 5 mm layer Cloud often 400–600 °C; layers much lower LOC (% O2) Oxygen below which the dust cannot explode Often 9–14 % with nitrogen MEC (g/m³) Minimum explosi

t: Hybrid mixtures: powder plus solvent Working level
x: Pharma and fine chemical plants have a special problem: powders that are wet with solvent, or charged into vessels containing solvent vapour. A dust cloud mixed with flammable vapour is a hybrid mixture . Even solvent vapour well below its LFL makes the dust far easier to ignite, often reducing the MIE to that of the solvent, and makes the explosion more violent. Practical rules: Charging powder into a reactor containing solvent: treat it as a solvent vapour hazard first, and inert the vessel. See inerting and LOC . Drying solvent-wet product in a fluid bed: use nitrogen in a closed loop, not air, unless testing shows the hybrid mixture can't

Prevention stops an explosion starting: Avoid clouds and layers: closed transfer systems, dust extraction at charging points, and housekeeping with industrial vacuum cleaners rated for combustible dust, never compressed air or brooms. Control ignition sources: earthing and bonding, Type C or D FIBCs, magnets and metal detectors ahead of mills, temperature limits for equipment surfaces, and hazardous area zoning (Zone 20, 21, 22 for dust) with suitably rated electrical equipment. Inert equipment where clouds are unavoidable and the dust is sensitive: mills, blenders, dryers. Protection limits the damage when one does start: Explosion venting:

t: Secondary explosions and Imperial Sugar Going deeper
x: A primary explosion inside equipment is often fairly small. But its pressure wave shakes loose dust settled on beams, ducts, cable trays and floors, raising a large cloud through the building, and the flame from the primary ignites it. This secondary explosion causes most of the deaths and damage in major dust incidents. On 7 February 2008, at the Imperial Sugar refinery in Port Wentworth, Georgia, a primary explosion in a steel belt conveyor under the sugar silos set off secondary explosions that spread through the packing buildings. Fourteen workers died and dozens were injured. The US Chemical Safety Board found heavy accumulations of suga

Assuming a powder is safe because it is “just the product”. No dust explosion test data for products that are milled, sieved or fluid-bed dried. Cleaning with compressed air, which creates the cloud. Ignoring hybrid mixtures when charging powders into solvent. Explosion vents that discharge into a work area or are blocked.
The dust deflagration index: St 1 up to 200, St 2 200–300, St 3 above 300 bar·m/s. It sizes vents and suppression.
A dust cloud with flammable vapour. It ignites more easily and burns more violently than the dust alone.
A primary blast raises settled dust into a cloud that then explodes, usually causing most of the damage.

Electrical installations are governed by the Central Electricity Authority’s safety regulations and inspected by the state Electrical Inspector, while hazardous areas need equipment certified for flammable atmospheres. It is a general guide, not legal advice; the Act, the rules, your state’s notifications and your own licence conditions always prevail. x: Effluent Treatment Basics Plant Engineering · Environment · October 2026 Pharmaceutical effluent is difficult: high COD, high salt, residual solvents and compounds that bacteria don’t like to eat. Treating it all together usually fails. Treating it well starts long before the ETP, with knowing which stream is which. This article explains the key parameters, the treatment steps, and why segregation is the most important design decision. In this article The numbers that describe effluent Basics Segregation: the first decision Basics High-COD and high-TDS streams Working level Biological treatment Working level Tertiary treatment and ZLD Going deeper Questions people ask The numbers that describe effluent Basics COD (chemical oxygen demand): the oxygen needed to oxidise everything organic chemically, in mg/L. The overall organic load. BOD (biochemical oxygen demand, usually 3 days at 27 °C

t: The numbers that describe effluent Basics
x: COD (chemical oxygen demand): the oxygen needed to oxidise everything organic chemically, in mg/L. The overall organic load. BOD (biochemical oxygen demand, usually 3 days at 27 °C in India): the oxygen bacteria use to eat the organics. The biodegradable part. BOD/COD ratio: above about 0.4, the effluent is reasonably biodegradable; below about 0.2, biology alone won't do much. TDS (total dissolved solids): salts from neutralisations and work-ups. High TDS, above roughly 1–2 %, inhibits normal biological treatment. pH, TSS, oil and grease, ammoniacal nitrogen and specific toxic compounds. Typical general discharge standards for inland surface

A small volume of mother liquor or aqueous layer can carry most of a site's COD and salt. Mixing it with large volumes of washings dilutes the concentration, but not the load, and turns it into a big stream that is hard to treat. Separate streams at the source: High-COD / high-TDS: aqueous layers, mother liquors, scrubber blowdowns. Send to stripping and evaporation. Low-COD / low-TDS: equipment washings, utility blowdowns, floor washings. Send to biological treatment. Collect high-strength streams in separate, labelled tanks with an analysis for each batch. The material balance of each process tells you in advance what each stream carries.

t: High-COD and high-TDS streams Working level
x: Solvent stripping: a steam stripper removes volatile solvents, recovering them and cutting COD. A few percent of methanol in an aqueous stream can be a large share of its COD. Neutralisation and pre-treatment: pH adjustment, removal of oil and suspended solids. Multiple effect evaporator (MEE): evaporates the water using steam several times over; a four-effect MEE typically evaporates around 3–3.5 kg of water per kg of steam. The condensate goes to biological treatment or reuse. Agitated thin film dryer (ATFD): dries the MEE concentrate to a solid salt, which goes to a hazardous waste facility.

Low-strength streams and MEE condensate go through a conventional sequence: equalisation (to even out swings in flow and composition), neutralisation, primary clarification, aeration (activated sludge or MBBR) and secondary clarification. Bacteria need steady conditions: sudden slugs of solvent, high salt or toxic compounds kill the biomass, and recovery takes weeks. Equalisation and stream control protect them. Try it: change the inlet COD and biodegradability (BOD/COD) and see whether the treated effluent meets a 250 mg/L COD limit. A rough model, but it shows why low-BOD/COD streams need segregation.

t: Tertiary treatment and ZLD Going deeper
x: After biology, tertiary steps polish the water: pressure sand filters, activated carbon, sometimes ozonation, and ultrafiltration plus reverse osmosis for reuse. In a zero liquid discharge scheme, RO permeate is reused as cooling tower or boiler feed make-up, and the RO reject goes back to the MEE, so no liquid leaves the site. ETP operating cost is dominated by steam for the MEE and ATFD, power for aeration, chemicals and hazardous solid disposal. The cheapest reduction is at source: recover solvents better, reduce salt by choosing reagents and work-ups carefully, and keep high-strength streams small. On the plant Track COD load (kg/day), no

Mixing high-strength mother liquors with large washing streams. Sending high-TDS effluent straight to biological treatment. Ignoring solvent content as a source of COD. Shock loading the aeration tank. Watching concentration instead of load.

t: What is the difference between COD and BOD?
x: COD is all oxidisable organics; BOD is the biodegradable part.
A multi-stage evaporator that reuses vapour, evaporating several kg of water per kg of steam.

t: What does zero liquid discharge mean?
x: No liquid leaves the site; water is reused and salts leave as solids.

s: Cut effluent COD, salt and volume before it reaches the ETP: load accounting, solvent in effluent, salt reduction, washing and segregation.
x: Reducing ETP Load at Source Plant Departments · Effluent Treatment · October 2026 An ETP can only treat what it receives. The cheapest kilogram of COD or salt is the one never sent to it. This article is about the decisions made in the production block and in R&D that set the ETP’s load and its operating cost. The ETP basics article covers the treatment steps themselves. In this article Account for load, stream by stream Basics Solvent in effluent is COD Basics Salt (TDS) is decided in the chemistry Working level Washing and cleaning practice Working level Segregate at the block Going deeper Questions people ask Account for load, stream by stream Basics Make a table of every effluent stream from every product: volume per batch, COD, TDS and the main solvent, and multiply by batches per month. COD load in kg = volume in m³ × COD in mg/L ÷ 1000. Sorting the table by load almost always show

t: Account for load, stream by stream Basics
x: Make a table of every effluent stream from every product: volume per batch, COD, TDS and the main solvent, and multiply by batches per month. COD load in kg = volume in m³ × COD in mg/L ÷ 1000. Sorting the table by load almost always shows that a handful of streams carry most of the COD and salt. Those are where effort pays.

t: Solvent in effluent is COD Basics
x: Dissolved solvent is often the biggest single COD contributor. Each kg of methanol needs about 1.5 kg of oxygen to oxidise completely, so 1 % methanol in water is roughly 15,000 mg/L of COD from the solvent alone; ethanol is about 2.1 kg O₂ per kg and acetone about 2.2. Recovering solvent from aqueous layers by distillation or a steam stripper both cuts COD and returns solvent to use. The solvent recovery calculator helps size the batch distillation.

t: Salt (TDS) is decided in the chemistry Working level
x: Every neutralisation makes salt, and salt ends up in the MEE and ATFD, the most expensive part of the ETP. Ways to reduce it: Use the minimum excess of acid and base; follow the stoichiometry in the reaction builder . Choose reagents that leave less salt or a recoverable by-product (for example recovering ammonium sulphate or sodium sulphate as a saleable product where quality allows). Reuse dilute brine washes for the next batch’s first wash where QC agrees. Recycle mother liquors when the impurity build-up allows.

t: Washing and cleaning practice Working level
x: Washings are usually low in concentration but high in volume. Counter-current washing (the last, cleanest wash of one batch becomes the first wash of the next), measured wash volumes instead of “wash till clear”, and cleaning procedures validated for the minimum effective volume cut volume a lot. Spills and leaks of mother liquor into floor drains are a hidden high-COD stream; keep floor drains separate from process drains.

t: Segregate at the block Going deeper
x: Collect high-COD and high-TDS streams in labelled, dedicated tanks at the production block, analyse each batch, and send them to stripping or evaporation; send low-strength washings to biological treatment. Mixing a small strong stream into a large weak one dilutes it but does not reduce the load, and it turns an easy evaporation job into a large, difficult one. Report effluent performance as load per kg of product (kg COD/kg, kg TDS/kg, m³ effluent/kg). This makes products comparable and shows whether an improvement is real or only a dilution. On the plant Ask R&D for the expected composition of every aqueous layer in a new process before it

Measuring concentration, not load. Sending solvent-rich aqueous layers straight to the ETP. Using large acid or base excesses “to be safe”. Washing by eye instead of by volume. Process drains and floor drains connected together.

t: How do I estimate COD from a solvent concentration?
x: Multiply the solvent concentration in mg/L by its theoretical oxygen demand: about 1.5 for methanol, 2.1 for ethanol, 2.2 for acetone, 3.1 for toluene (kg O2 per kg solvent).

t: Why is salt so expensive to treat?
x: Dissolved salt does not break down; it must be evaporated out in an MEE and dried in an ATFD, which uses steam and creates solid waste for disposal.
Reusing the last, cleanest wash of one batch as the first wash of the next, so less fresh water is used for the same cleanliness.

A plant that buys, stores, uses or recovers ethanol or spirit needs to follow its state’s excise rules, which differ widely between states. In October 2024 a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court held, by majority, that states can regulate industrial alcohol as well as potable liquor. It is a general guide, not legal advice; the Act, the rules, your state’s notifications and your own licence conditions always prevail. s: Excise Licences for Ethanol and Spirit
x: Rectified spirit (about 95 % ethanol) and extra neutral alcohol : potable grade, most tightly controlled. Absolute alcohol (99.5 % or more): often used where water must be avoided. Denatured spirit: ethanol made unfit to drink by adding denaturants, with lighter controls; the denaturant must be acceptable to the process and to QC. t: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
s: Falling film evaporator basics: film formation, distributor, minimum wetting rate, heat transfer and area, multiple effects, MVR and common problems.
x: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized Process Design · Evaporation · October 2026 A falling film evaporator looks like a shell-and-tube exchanger standing on end, and that is nearly what it is. Liquid runs down the inside of the tubes as a thin film while steam condenses outside, and the vapour separates at the bottom. Because each drop spends only seconds in the heated tube, it is a favourite for heat-sensitive liquids and for effluent concentration in MEE plants. Its weak point is the film itself: if it breaks, the tube runs dry and fouls. This article explains how it works and how to keep the film whole. In this article How it works Basics Why choose a falling film Basics The distributor and the wetting rate Working level Sizing the heat transfer Working level Multiple effects and MVR Going deeper Common problems Going deeper Questions people ask How it works Basic

s: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
x: Feed enters the top head, above the tube sheet, and a distributor spreads it evenly over every tube. It runs down the inside wall as a thin film, typically a millimetre or less, heated by steam condensing on the shell side. The liquid boils at the film surface; vapour flows down the tube centre with the liquid, and both leave the bottom into a separator, where the vapour goes to a condenser or the next effect and the concentrate is pumped out, partly recirculated to the top if needed.

t: Why choose a falling film Basics
s: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
x: Short residence time , seconds per pass, so heat-sensitive products degrade less. Small temperature difference works well, because there is no hydrostatic head raising the boiling point at the bottom of the tube (unlike a rising film or natural circulation evaporator). That suits multiple effects and vapour recompression. High heat transfer coefficients for clean, low-viscosity liquids. It is a poor choice for liquids that crystallise or foul heavily in the tube, or are very viscous; forced circulation evaporators and agitated thin film dryers handle those. See the ATFD article .

t: The distributor and the wetting rate Working level
s: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
x: Everything depends on every tube getting enough liquid, all the way down. The measure is the wetting rate Γ: liquid flow per metre of tube perimeter. Γ = m / (N × π × d) m liquid flow (kg/s), N number of tubes, d tube inside diameter (m). Evaporation reduces Γ down the tube, so the bottom is the critical point. Below a minimum wetting rate the film breaks into rivulets, leaving dry patches that overheat and foul. The minimum depends on the liquid, surface and heat flux; designers often work with figures in the region of a few tenths of a kg/m·s for water-like liquids and check with the supplier. The figure uses 0.25 kg/m·s as an illustration.

t: Sizing the heat transfer Working level
s: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
x: Q = mevap × λ + mfeed × cp × (Tboil - Tfeed) A = Q / (U × ΔT) ΔT is the steam saturation temperature minus the boiling temperature of the liquid at the evaporator pressure, adjusted for boiling point elevation of concentrated solutions. Overall U for clean aqueous duty is often 1,300–2,600 kcal/h·m²·°C, falling with viscosity and fouling. Preheat the feed to its boiling point before it enters the tubes; otherwise the top of the tubes acts as a heater, not an evaporator. See heat exchanger design basics .

t: Multiple effects and MVR Going deeper
s: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
x: In a multiple effect evaporator (MEE) the vapour from one effect heats the next, which runs at a lower pressure and temperature. A four-effect plant evaporates roughly 3 to 3.5 kg of water per kg of steam. In mechanical vapour recompression (MVR) , a compressor or fan raises the vapour pressure slightly so it can heat the same evaporator, using electricity instead of steam. Falling film designs suit both because they work with small temperature differences. In pharma effluent plants, an FFE often forms the first effects of the MEE, followed by forced circulation effects as the liquid concentrates and an ATFD to dry it. See ETP basics .

s: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
x: Falling capacity : scaling in the tubes (check the ΔT needed for the same evaporation) or non-condensables blanketing the shell side (vent it). Dry tubes and fouling at the bottom : wetting rate too low; add recirculation. Carry-over of droplets into the condensate: separator overloaded, demister damaged or foaming. Uneven tube performance : distributor out of level or partly blocked.

s: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
x: Feeding below the boiling point so the top of the tubes only heats. No recirculation when most of the feed is evaporated. Distributor not levelled or inspected. Using an FFE for crystallising or very viscous liquids. Ignoring boiling point elevation of concentrated solutions.

s: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
x: Liquid flow per metre of tube perimeter: m / (N π d).

t: Why is a falling film evaporator good for heat-sensitive products?
s: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
x: Seconds of residence time and no hydrostatic head, so low temperatures work.

t: How much steam does a multiple effect evaporator save?
s: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
x: A four-effect unit evaporates about 3–3.5 kg of water per kg of steam.

s: Fault tree analysis for process plants: top and basic events, AND and OR gates, top event frequency, minimal cut sets and links to HAZOP and LOPA.
x: Fault Tree Analysis (FTA) Process Safety · Risk Assessment · October 2026 A HAZOP finds that a runaway is possible. LOPA estimates how likely it is with simple multiplication. But when the protection is a complicated system, two pumps, redundant trips, shared power supplies, you need a way to see exactly which combinations of failures lead to the accident. That is fault tree analysis: working backwards from the accident to every route that gets there. In this article The idea: start from the accident Basics AND and OR gates Basics Calculating the top event Working level Minimal cut sets Working level Common cause failures and where FTA fits Going deeper Questions people ask The idea: start from the accident Basics A fault tree starts with one undesired top event , such as “runaway reaction with reactor damage”, and asks: what must happen for this to occur? Each answer is broken down agai

t: The idea: start from the accident Basics
x: A fault tree starts with one undesired top event , such as “runaway reaction with reactor damage”, and asks: what must happen for this to occur? Each answer is broken down again, until you reach basic events whose failure rates you can estimate: a pump fails, a valve sticks open, an operator makes an error, a trip fails on demand. The result is a tree that shows, on one page, every route to the accident.

OR gate : the event above happens if any one of the events below happens. Too much reagent is dosed if the pump speed is wrong, or the control valve fails open, or the operator doses the wrong quantity. AND gate : the event above happens only if all the events below happen together. Damage occurs only if excess dosing happens and both protections fail. OR: P = 1 - (1 - P1)(1 - P2)… ≈ P1 + P2 + … (for small P) AND: P = P1 × P2 × … OR gates add up; AND gates multiply down. That is why protection works: putting independent protections under an AND gate makes the top event much rarer. Try it: change the frequency or probability of each basic even

t: Calculating the top event Working level
x: In the example, the three causes of excess dosing (0.05, 0.1 and 0.1 per year) combine through the OR gate to about 0.23 per year. The high-temperature trip fails on 1 demand in 100, and the relief is undersized for this case with a probability of 0.1, so both protections fail together with a probability of 0.001 per demand. The top event frequency is 0.23 × 0.001 ≈ 2.3 × 10^-4 per year. Halving the operator error rate barely changes this; improving the trip to SIL 2 (0.001) cuts it tenfold. Mixing units is the common trap: initiating causes are frequencies (per year), while protections are probabilities of failure on demand (no units). Only

A cut set is a combination of basic events that together cause the top event. A minimal cut set is one where removing any event stops it being a cut set. In the example the minimal cut sets are {A, D, E}, {B, D, E} and {C, D, E}. Two things to look for: Single-event cut sets : one failure alone causes the accident. These need attention first. Events that appear in every cut set , like D and E here: improving them reduces every route at once.

t: Common cause failures and where FTA fits Going deeper
x: The AND gate only multiplies if the events are independent. Two trips on the same instrument air supply, two pumps fed from one electrical panel, or two sensors calibrated with the same faulty reference can fail together. These common cause failures often dominate the real risk and must be added as their own basic events. See LOPA and SIL on independence. FTA sits alongside other methods: HAZOP finds the scenarios, LOPA screens them with quick arithmetic, and FTA is used where the protection logic is complex, for SIL verification of redundant systems, or for investigating an incident to see which combinations of failures occurred. See HAZOP m

Putting two frequencies under an AND gate. Assuming protections are independent when they share a utility or a sensor. Using precise-looking numbers without stating where they came from. Improving events on OR branches when the AND gate matters more. Drawing a tree so detailed that nobody reviews it.

t: What is the difference between AND and OR gates in a fault tree?
x: OR: any input causes it (add). AND: all inputs together (multiply).

t: What is a minimal cut set?
x: The smallest combination of basic events that causes the top event.

t: How is FTA different from LOPA?
x: LOPA is quick layer arithmetic for one scenario; FTA models the full failure logic.
US NRC, Fault Tree Handbook , NUREG-0492, 1981 CCPS, Guidelines for Chemical Process Quantitative Risk Analysis , 2nd ed., 2000

s: Filtration calculation: cake and cloth resistance, the Ruth equation, specific cake resistance from a bench test, and scale-up to a Nutsche filter.
x: How to Calculate Filtration Performance Chemical Engineering · Solid–Liquid Separation · Updated October 2026 A 15-minute Büchner test in the lab can tell you whether the plant filtration will take one hour or eight, if you record the right numbers. This article explains what slows a filtration down, how to turn a simple bench trial into one number that scales (the specific cake resistance), and how to use it to predict a Nutsche filter or centrifuge batch. In this article What actually slows a filtration Basics The cake filtration equation Basics Running and reading a bench trial Working level Predicting the plant filter Working level Compressible cakes and why pressure disappoints Going deeper Fixing a slow cake Going deeper Questions people ask Have trial data? The Filtration Calculator fits the line and gives the cake resistance and flux. What actually slows a filtration Basics Liqui

t: What actually slows a filtration Basics
x: Liquid has to squeeze through two things: the filter cloth and the cake of solids building up on it. At the start there is no cake, so filtrate pours through. As solids deposit, the cake thickens and every layer adds resistance, so the flow keeps slowing. In almost every plant filtration the cake , not the cloth, ends up controlling the time. As the cake grows, each new layer of solids adds resistance, so the same pressure pushes less filtrate through.

The flow through a cake behaves like flow through any porous bed (Darcy's law): rate is proportional to pressure and area, and inversely proportional to viscosity and resistance. The resistance has two parts, the cake (which grows with the filtrate collected) and the cloth (fixed): dV/dt = ΔP · A / [ μ ( α c V / A + Rm ) ] V filtrate volume (m³), t time (s), ΔP pressure difference (Pa), A filter area (m²), μ filtrate viscosity (Pa·s), c dry cake mass per m³ of filtrate (kg/m³), α specific cake resistance (m/kg), Rm cloth resistance (1/m). Integrated at constant pressure, it becomes a straight line, which is the trick that makes it useful: t /

t: Running and reading a bench trial Working level
x: Use a Büchner or a small pressure filter with a known area, the same cloth or paper type as the plant if possible, and a vacuum or pressure close to the plant's. Record the filtrate volume at regular times, every 15–30 s, not just the total at the end. Note the slurry concentration so you know c.

A 20 cm² (0.002 m²) filter at 0.5 bar (50,000 Pa), filtrate viscosity 1 cP (0.001 Pa·s), c = 40 kg/m³: Filtrate V (mL) Time t (s) t/V (s/mL) 50 17.5 0.35 100 60 0.60 150 127.5 0.85 200 220 1.10 t/V rises by 0.25 s/mL for every 50 mL, a straight line. In SI units the slope is 5 × 10^9 s/m⁶ and the intercept 1 × 10^5 s/m³. Then: α = 2 × slope × A² × ΔP / (μ c) = 2 × 5×10^9 × (0.002)² × 50,000 / (0.001 × 40) = 5 × 10^10 m/kg Rm = intercept × A × ΔP / μ = 1×10^5 × 0.002 × 50,000 / 0.001 = 1 × 10^10 1/m Specific cake resistance α What it means Below 10^10 m/kg Fast-filtering, coarse crystals 10^10 – 10^11 Moderate: our example sits here 10^11 – 10

t: Predicting the plant filter Working level
x: The plant Nutsche has 2 m² of cloth and must collect 2 m³ of filtrate at the same 0.5 bar. Put the lab α and Rm back into the integrated equation with the plant area: Slope = μ α c / (2 A² ΔP) = 0.001 × 5×10^10 × 40 / (2 × 4 × 50,000) = 5,000 s/m⁶ Intercept = μ Rm / (A ΔP) = 100 s/m³ t = 5,000 × 2² + 100 × 2 ≈ 20,200 s ≈ 5.6 h The shortcut: what matters is filtrate per square metre. The lab filter collected 0.1 m³/m² in 220 s; the plant needs 1 m³/m², ten times more, and because the cake term goes with V², it takes roughly a hundred times longer. The cake will be 40 kg/m² of dry solids, several centimetres thick. Try it: the same 2 m² Nutsche

t: Compressible cakes and why pressure disappoints Going deeper
x: The equation assumes α stays constant. For hard, regular crystals it nearly does. Many organic products, amorphous solids, and anything with fines form compressible cakes: pressing harder squeezes the pores shut, so α rises with ΔP. A common fit is α = α0 ΔP^n, with n between 0 (incompressible) and 1 (so compressible that more pressure gains nothing). To find out, run the bench trial at two pressures, say 0.5 and 1.5 bar. If α triples, n ≈ 1 and the plant should not expect a pressure filter to beat a vacuum one. Run the lab trial near the plant pressure, never extrapolate far.

t: Fixing a slow cake Going deeper
x: Because α depends on the particles, the cheapest fix is usually upstream, in the crystallisation: Grow bigger crystals: slower cooling or antisolvent addition, seeding, and a hold before filtering. Resistance rises steeply as particle size falls. Avoid fines: reduce agitator speed or impeller tip speed during crystallisation and transfer; pumps with high shear crush crystals. Raise the temperature of the filtration if the product allows: filtrate viscosity falls and the time falls with it. Filter aid (diatomaceous earth, perlite) for gelatinous or very fine solids, if the product can tolerate it. Thinner cakes: split the batch into two loads,

Recording only the final volume and time: one point can't separate cake from cloth resistance. Testing at a very different pressure from the plant on a compressible cake. Forgetting that slurry from the lab beaker is not the same as slurry after a plant transfer pump. Ignoring temperature: filtrate viscosity can change by half between 20 and 50 °C.

t: How do you calculate specific cake resistance?
x: Plot t/V against V from a timed trial, fit a line, and use α = 2 × slope × A² × ΔP / (μ c).

t: What is a good specific cake resistance?
x: Below 10^10 m/kg is fast, 10^10–10^11 moderate, 10^11–10^12 slow, and above 10^12 very slow.

t: Does doubling the pressure halve the filtration time?
x: Only for an incompressible cake. For compressible cakes the resistance rises with pressure and the gain is much smaller.

The fire NOC from the state fire service confirms a building has the fire protection its occupancy needs; keeping that protection working every day is the site’s job. It is a general guide, not legal advice; the Act, the rules, your state’s notifications and your own licence conditions always prevail. s: Fire NOC and Fire Protection for Chemical Plants
x: Fire safety is regulated by each state under its fire services law, generally referring to the National Building Code of India (Part 4, Fire and Life Safety). Industrial buildings with hazardous occupancy need a fire NOC from the state fire service, first at the building plan stage and then before occupation, with renewal at the interval the state sets. Any change of building use, layout or hazard level needs an amended NOC.

t: Protection systems for a chemical plant Basics
s: Fire NOC and Fire Protection for Chemical Plants
x: Hydrant system: fire water tank, jockey, main electric and diesel pumps, ring main and hydrants with hoses. Sprinklers and water spray for buildings and for cooling tanks and structures. Foam systems for solvent tank farms and drum stores; water alone is poor on many solvent fires. Fire detection and alarm: smoke and heat detectors, flame detectors in solvent areas, gas detectors for flammable vapours. Extinguishers of the right type (foam, CO₂, dry powder) at each location.

s: Fire NOC and Fire Protection for Chemical Plants
x: Most plant fires start from solvent vapour meeting an ignition source. Prevention: earthing and bonding , inerting , flameproof electrics, hot work under permit , good housekeeping, and keeping solvent stocks in production areas to the shift requirement.

s: Fire NOC and Fire Protection for Chemical Plants
x: Run fire pumps weekly, including the diesel pump, and check auto-start on pressure drop. Test hydrants, sprinklers, detectors and alarms on a schedule and record the results. Keep the fire water tank full and its level indicated. Inspect and refill extinguishers as required.

t: Fire teams and drills Going deeper
s: Fire NOC and Fire Protection for Chemical Plants
x: Train a fire team on every shift, with clear roles in the on-site emergency plan , and practise with real equipment. Agree in advance how the state fire service will reach the site, where it will connect, and what information it will need on arrival, including a list of chemicals and their locations. On the plant Check the diesel fire pump at night. A pump that starts only when the day-shift fitter is there to prime it is not a fire pump.

s: Fire NOC and Fire Protection for Chemical Plants
x: Fire NOC not amended after a layout change. Water used where foam is needed. Diesel fire pump never test-run on auto-start. Hydrants blocked by stored material. Fire team only on the day shift.

s: Fire NOC and Fire Protection for Chemical Plants

t: Why is foam used for solvent fires?

x: Foam forms a blanket on the liquid surface that cuts off oxygen and vapour; water can spread a burning solvent that floats on it.

t: How often should fire pumps be tested?
s: Fire NOC and Fire Protection for Chemical Plants

s: kLa and gas-liquid mass transfer: Henry's law, when a hydrogenation is mass-transfer limited, why plant kLa is lower, and how pressure and agitation help.
x: Gas-Liquid Reactions and kLa Scale-up · Reaction Engineering · October 2026 A hydrogenation that finishes in an hour in the lab autoclave takes six hours in the plant, and the impurity profile changes too. The catalyst is the same, the temperature and pressure are the same. What changed is how fast hydrogen gets from the gas into the liquid. This article explains gas-liquid mass transfer and the one number, kLa, that describes it. In this article The path of a hydrogen molecule Basics kLa and the transfer rate Basics Which step limits the rate? Working level Why plant kLa is lower Working level Improving mass transfer Going deeper Questions people ask The path of a hydrogen molecule Basics For hydrogen to react, it has to travel: from the gas bubble across a thin liquid film into the bulk liquid, then through the liquid to a catalyst particle, into its pores and onto the metal surface. E

t: The path of a hydrogen molecule Basics
x: For hydrogen to react, it has to travel: from the gas bubble across a thin liquid film into the bulk liquid, then through the liquid to a catalyst particle, into its pores and onto the metal surface. Each step has a resistance. The slowest one sets the overall rate. In most hydrogenations with an active catalyst, the slow step is the first: gas into liquid.

t: kLa and the transfer rate Basics
x: Rate of transfer = kLa × (C* - C) kLa: volumetric mass transfer coefficient (1/s), the product of the liquid-film coefficient kL and the bubble surface area per volume a. C*: gas solubility at the interface; C: dissolved concentration in the bulk. C* follows Henry's law: proportional to the gas partial pressure. Hydrogen is poorly soluble; in methanol roughly 0.004 mol/L per bar (the hydrogen solubility calculator gives it for 16 solvents). At 5 bar, C* ≈ 0.02 mol/L. With kLa = 0.1 s^-1, the maximum transfer rate (when C is near zero) is 0.1 × 0.02 × 3,600 ≈ 7 mol/L per hour.

t: Which step limits the rate? Working level
x: Compare the maximum transfer rate with the rate the catalyst could achieve if hydrogen were plentiful (the kinetic rate): Mass-transfer limited: the catalyst could go faster, but hydrogen can't arrive fast enough. Dissolved hydrogen is near zero. The rate rises with pressure and agitation, but not with more catalyst. Kinetically limited: hydrogen is plentiful; the catalyst is the bottleneck. The rate rises with catalyst loading and temperature, but not with agitation. Try it: change the pressure, kLa and catalyst-limited rate. See which one limits, and how long it takes to take up 3 mol/L of hydrogen (a nitro reduction at 1 mol/L). A simple l

t: Why plant kLa is lower Working level
x: Typical values: lab autoclaves with gas-inducing stirrers reach 0.1–1 s^-1; plant hydrogenators often 0.02–0.2 s^-1. The reasons: Plant agitators run at lower power per volume than small lab stirrers. Gas enters from the headspace by surface entrainment, which becomes much less effective in tall vessels. Gas-inducing impellers lose efficiency with depth. So a reaction that was kinetically limited in the lab can become mass-transfer limited in the plant, with a longer cycle time and a different impurity profile. With the default values in the figure, lowering kLa from 0.1 to 0.03 s^-1 stretches the reaction from about 40 minutes to over an hou

Raise the pressure within the vessel rating: C* rises in proportion. Improve gas dispersion: gas-inducing hollow-shaft impellers, a sparger below a Rushton-type turbine, or an external loop reactor with an ejector. Increase agitator power where the motor and seal allow. Use the right fill level: too full and the surface entrainment drops; too empty and the impeller is uncovered. Mass transfer also gives a safety handle: in a mass-transfer limited hydrogenation, cutting the hydrogen supply or stopping the agitator stops the reaction and its heat quickly. But it works in reverse too: restarting a stopped agitator with hydrogen pressure on can r

Adding more catalyst to a mass-transfer limited reaction. Assuming lab reaction times will hold in the plant. Ignoring hydrogen starvation as a source of impurities. Restarting the agitator under hydrogen pressure without thought. Overfilling a hydrogenator with a gas-inducing impeller.
The mass transfer coefficient times interfacial area per volume, in 1/s.

t: How do you know if a hydrogenation is mass-transfer limited?
x: If the rate changes with agitation speed, mass transfer limits it.

t: Why are hydrogenations slower in the plant?
x: Plant kLa is usually lower, so hydrogen dissolves more slowly.

x: Hydrogen comes from hydrogenations, hydride and metal quenches (NaH, LiAlH4, NaBH4, sodium), and metals in acid. x: Glass-Lined Reactor Care Plant Engineering · Equipment Care · October 2026 A glass-lined reactor costs a lot, takes months to replace, and can be ruined in seconds by a dropped spanner or a blast of steam into a cold jacket. Yet it will last decades if a handful of rules are followed. This article explains how the lining works, what damages it, and how to inspect and repair it. In this article How a glass lining works Basics Thermal shock Basics Mechanical and chemical damage Working level Electrostatic damage Working level Inspection and repair Going deeper Questions people ask How a glass lining works Basics A glass-lined reactor is a carbon steel vessel with a layer of special glass, typically about 1–2 mm thick, fused onto the inside at high temperature. The glass is applied so that it is held in compression by the steel as they cool; glass is very strong in compression and weak in t

t: How a glass lining works Basics
x: A glass-lined reactor is a carbon steel vessel with a layer of special glass, typically about 1–2 mm thick, fused onto the inside at high temperature. The glass is applied so that it is held in compression by the steel as they cool; glass is very strong in compression and weak in tension. Anything that puts the glass in tension, such as a sudden temperature change, an impact or flexing of the steel, can crack or chip it. Once the glass is breached, the process liquid reaches the steel and corrodes it quickly.

Glass and steel expand at different rates. A sudden temperature difference between the glass surface and the steel behind it creates stress in the glass. Manufacturers publish charts of the allowable temperature difference, which depend on the vessel temperature and on whether you are heating or cooling. Typical dangerous situations: Charging cold liquid into a hot empty vessel, or hot liquid into a cold one. Switching the jacket from steam straight to brine, or brine to steam. Spraying cold wash water onto a hot wall. Ramp the jacket temperature in steps, clamp the jacket set point within the allowed difference in the DCS, and drain the jack

t: Mechanical and chemical damage Working level
x: Impact: dropped tools, sample thieves, scrapers, solids charged from height. Use protective covers on the manhole and non-metallic tools. Agitator problems: a bent shaft or worn bearing lets the impeller strike the wall or baffle. Check runout after maintenance. External damage: welding on the outside of the jacket or nozzles destroys the glass behind it. Never weld on a glass-lined vessel. Chemicals: glass resists almost all acids, but is attacked by hydrofluoric acid and fluorides, hot concentrated phosphoric acid, and alkali, increasingly so with temperature and pH. Prolonged boiling water also slowly attacks glass.

Glass is an insulator. When non-conductive liquids such as toluene or heptane are stirred, filtered or sprayed into a glass-lined vessel, charge can build up on the glass surface until it discharges through the lining to the steel, leaving a pinhole. It is also an ignition risk. Remedies include conductive glass, earthed tantalum or PTFE-coated probes in contact with the liquid, slower filling through dip pipes, and adding conductive solvents where the process allows. See static electricity .

Visual inspection at every opportunity: chips, dull or rough patches (chemical attack), rust stains (breach). Spark (holiday) testing: a high-voltage brush passed over the glass shows sparks where there is a pinhole or crack to the steel. Use the voltage recommended by the manufacturer for the glass thickness. Thickness measurement of the glass with a magnetic gauge shows gradual chemical wear. Repairs: small defects are sealed with tantalum plugs and screws or tantalum patches, with PTFE gaskets; larger areas with repair cements or sleeves. Repairs are compatible with fewer chemicals than the original glass, so note them in the vessel histor

Steam straight into the jacket of a cold vessel, or brine into a hot one. Metal tools and sample thieves inside the vessel. Hot caustic cleaning. Welding on the jacket or nozzles. Ignoring static with non-conductive solvents.

t: What causes thermal shock in glass-lined reactors?
x: A sudden temperature difference between glass and steel, which puts the glass into tension.
HF and fluorides, hot concentrated phosphoric acid, and hot alkali.
A high-voltage test that sparks through pinholes to show defects.

x: Groundwater NOC for Industries Statutory Compliance · Water · October 2026 Many plants draw process and utility water from borewells. Groundwater abstraction by industry needs a no-objection certificate, from the Central Ground Water Authority or, in several states, a state authority. The NOC sets how much may be drawn and comes with metering and recharge conditions. It is a general guide, not legal advice; the Act, the rules, your state’s notifications and your own licence conditions always prevail. In this article Who issues the NOC Basics Typical conditions Basics Know your water balance Working level Reducing abstraction Working level Keeping the NOC Going deeper Questions people ask Who issues the NOC Basics The Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) issues NOCs under its 2020 guidelines through an online portal, in states that do not have their own groundwater regulator. Several sta

The Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) issues NOCs under its 2020 guidelines through an online portal, in states that do not have their own groundwater regulator. Several states, including Punjab, Haryana, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and others, have their own authorities and rules, which apply instead. New industrial NOCs are generally not given in over-exploited areas, which makes groundwater status a site-selection question.

A maximum permitted abstraction in m³/day. A tamper-proof digital flow meter on each borewell, with telemetry where required. Piezometers to monitor water level, with regular reporting. Rainwater harvesting and recharge structures. Payment of groundwater abstraction charges, which vary with the area’s groundwater status. Periodic renewal.

t: Know your water balance Working level
x: Make a site water balance: borewell abstraction, uses (process, cooling tower make-up, boiler feed, washing, domestic) and outflows (evaporation, effluent, product). Cooling tower make-up is often the largest use; see cooling tower calculations . The balance shows whether the permitted quantity is enough for the next expansion.

Recycle treated effluent and RO permeate to cooling towers, as in zero liquid discharge schemes. Return steam condensate to the boiler; see steam system efficiency . Raise cooling tower cycles of concentration with good water treatment. Harvest rainwater from roofs for recharge or use.

Read meters daily and keep records; report as the NOC requires; maintain recharge structures; renew in time. An expansion that needs more water needs an amended NOC before it starts, alongside the amended pollution consent . On the plant Put the borewell meter reading on the daily utility report next to production. Water per kg of product is one of the easiest numbers to improve once people see it every day.

Drawing more than the permitted quantity. Meters not working or not read. Recharge structures neglected. Expansion planned without checking water availability. Assuming CGWA rules apply in a state with its own authority.

They are not exotic: sodium hydride, lithium aluminium hydride, thionyl chloride, sodium azide. What they share is that their hazard is greatest at the end of the reaction, when the excess has to be destroyed. This article covers the main ones and the principles of a safe quench. t: Why the quench is the dangerous step Basics
x: During the reaction, the reagent is consumed under conditions somebody designed carefully. The quench is different: it destroys whatever is left, often an uncertain amount, with water or an alcohol, releasing heat and gas. It is often written in the batch record as a single line (“quench with water”) and done near the end of a long shift. Many incidents follow that pattern.

Reagent Main hazards Key precautions Sodium hydride (usually 60 % in mineral oil) Hydrogen with water, alcohols and acids; known thermal runaways in DMF, DMSO and DMAc Avoid NaH with DMF/DMSO at elevated temperature unless tested; quench slowly with IPA before water; inerted vessel and safe H2 vent Lithium aluminium hydride Violent reaction with water, hydrogen; ether solvents Controlled quench (for example the Fieser method: water, 15 % NaOH, water in a 1:1:3 ratio by weight of LAH); keep cold; vent H2 Thionyl chloride Releases SO2 and HCl; violent with water Distil off the excess before quench; route vents to a caustic scrubber sized for th

t: Designing a safe quench Working level
x: Know how much is left. Use the stoichiometry and an in-process check, not “excess”. The amount of reagent left decides the heat and gas. Control by addition rate. The quench should be dose-controlled: heat and gas come out as you add, and stop when you stop. That needs the quench reagent to react quickly at the quench temperature. Too cold and it accumulates, then reacts all at once. Choose the direction. Adding quench to the reaction (normal quench) or the reaction to the quench (reverse quench) gives very different local concentrations. Reverse quench into a large volume of cold quench solution often gives better control of heat and gas. Us

t: Gas evolution and venting Working level
x: Every mole of NaH gives a mole of hydrogen. Six kilograms of NaH (250 mol) releases about 5.6 Nm³ of hydrogen. Over 2 hours that averages 2.8 Nm³/h, but the peak rate is often higher. The vent line, flame arrester and scrubber must handle the peak without pressurising the vessel, and the headspace must stay inerted so the hydrogen has no oxygen to burn with inside the vessel. Try it: change the amount of excess NaH and the addition time. The curve shows the average hydrogen rate; compare it with what the vent can take. The same logic applies to CO2 from bicarbonate quenches (foaming), SO2 and HCl from thionyl chloride, and nitrogen from azide

Run the quench in the reaction calorimeter at the plant addition rate, measuring heat and gas. See how to read RC1 data . DSC the reaction mixture before quench, especially reagent/solvent combinations with known incidents. Calculate peak gas rate and check the vent and scrubber capacity. See scrubber design . Write the quench into the batch record as a controlled step with rate, temperature limits and stop conditions, not a single line. On the plant If a quench “isn't doing anything”, stop adding. A quench that seems not to react is the most dangerous kind: the reagent is accumulating, and when it starts, it will all go at once.

Quenching an unknown excess. Quenching too cold, so the quench reagent accumulates. Adding the quench faster because nothing seems to happen. Vent lines sized for normal breathing, not for quench gas. Using DMF or DMSO with NaH at elevated temperature without testing.

t: Why is NaH in DMF dangerous?
x: The combination can decompose exothermically at moderate temperature; several runaways have been reported.

t: How much hydrogen does sodium hydride give on quench?
x: One mole of H2 per mole of NaH, about 0.93 Nm³ per kg of pure NaH.

x: HAZOP Made Practical Process Safety · Hazard Studies · October 2026 Most engineers first meet a HAZOP as a long meeting with a projector, a stack of P&IDs and a spreadsheet that grows by a hundred rows a day. Done well, it is the single best way to find out how a design can go wrong before it does. Done badly, it is a box-ticking exercise that misses the one scenario that matters. This article explains how a HAZOP works, step by step, and what separates a useful one from a ritual. In this article The idea behind a HAZOP Basics The method: node, intent, guideword, deviation Basics Filling one row properly Working level Ranking risk and deciding actions Working level HAZOP for batch processes Going deeper What makes a HAZOP good Going deeper Questions people ask The idea behind a HAZOP Basics A process design describes how the plant is supposed to behave. Accidents happen when it behaves d

t: The idea behind a HAZOP Basics
x: A process design describes how the plant is supposed to behave. Accidents happen when it behaves differently: too much flow, no cooling, the wrong material, a step done out of order. A HAZOP (hazard and operability study) is a disciplined way of imagining those departures from design, one at a time, with a team that between them knows the chemistry, the equipment and how the plant is really operated. The method was developed at ICI in the 1960s and is now described in IEC 61882. Its strength is that it doesn't rely on anyone's memory of past incidents: it forces the team to consider deviations systematically, including ones nobody has seen ye

t: The method: node, intent, guideword, deviation Basics
x: Pick a node. A section of the P&ID with one clear purpose: the reagent dosing line and reactor, the condenser and receiver, the transfer to the centrifuge. State the design intent. What the node is meant to do, with numbers: “Dose 800 kg of reagent into R-101 over 4 hours at 60 °C, with the agitator running and the jacket on cooling water.” Combine a guideword with a parameter to get a deviation. Guidewords: No, More, Less, As well as, Part of, Reverse, Other than . Parameters: flow, temperature, pressure, level, composition, agitation, time. For each meaningful deviation, ask: What could cause it? What would happen? What protects us now? Is

t: Filling one row properly Working level
x: Take More flow of reagent during dosing. A weak row reads: “Cause: pump problem. Consequence: high temperature. Safeguard: operator.” It is useless, because nobody can act on it. A good row is specific enough that someone who wasn't in the room understands it: Causes: dosing pump speed set too high after maintenance; control valve FCV fails open; operator increases rate to finish before shift change. Consequence (without safeguards): reagent accumulates faster than it reacts; heat release exceeds jacket cooling; batch temperature rises; if cooling then fails, the MTSR exceeds the solvent boiling point and the reactor pressurises. Existing saf

t: Ranking risk and deciding actions Working level
x: Most companies rank each scenario on a risk matrix: severity of the consequence (from minor injury to multiple fatalities or a major release) against likelihood (from “has happened on this site” to “not expected in the plant's life”). The ranking decides whether the existing safeguards are enough or an action is needed. For high-severity scenarios, a matrix alone is too coarse. Layer of Protection Analysis (LOPA) is the usual next step: it counts the independent protection layers, gives each a credit (typically a tenfold risk reduction for a good alarm with operator response or a basic trip), and checks whether the total meets the company's t

t: HAZOP for batch processes Going deeper
x: A continuous plant runs in one steady state, so nodes based on equipment work well. A batch plant runs through a sequence of steps, and the same reactor is a charging vessel, a reactor, a distillation pot and a crystalliser on the same day. For batch processes, it works better to take the batch record steps as nodes and add timing guidewords: Early / Late: sampling done before the reaction is complete; quench added late. Before / After: solvent charged before the vessel is inerted; heating started before the agitator. Longer / Shorter: hold time extended over a weekend; dosing completed in half the time. Other than: wrong drum, wrong reactor,

t: What makes a HAZOP good Going deeper
x: Up-to-date P&IDs. A HAZOP on drawings that don't match the plant reviews a plant that doesn't exist. Walk the line first. The right people. An independent facilitator, a good scribe, the process engineer, and an operator or supervisor who knows how things are really done at 3 a.m. Process safety data in hand. Reaction heat, MTSR, TD24, gas evolution, flash points, toxicity. Without them, the team guesses at consequences. Short sessions. Four to five hours a day. After that, quality drops sharply and rows become copy-paste. Actions closed, not just raised. Track them with owners and dates, and review the closure. An open HAZOP action is a know

Writing consequences with the safeguards working, so every scenario looks minor. Counting the alarm and the trip on the same sensor as two layers. Skipping “obvious” deviations because the team is experienced. No reaction hazard data, so runaway scenarios are judged by feel. Actions that say “be careful”.
A structured team review that applies guidewords to process parameters, node by node, to find deviations from design intent and check that each has adequate safeguards.
No, More, Less, As well as, Part of, Reverse and Other than; for batch processes also Early, Late, Before and After.

t: Who should be in a HAZOP team?
x: An independent facilitator, a scribe, the process engineer, operations, and instrument, maintenance and safety specialists as needed: usually five to eight people.

s: Heat exchanger sizing basics: heat duty, LMTD, counter vs co-current flow, overall U, typical U values, fouling, the F factor and a worked example.
x: Heat Exchanger Design Basics Process Design · Heat Transfer · October 2026 Every heat exchanger, from a reactor jacket to a shell-and-tube condenser, is sized with one short equation: Q = U × A × ΔT. The skill is in the three pieces: how much heat you must move, what temperature difference you really have, and how well heat crosses the wall once the exchanger has been in service a year. This article walks through each one and finishes with a full sizing example. In this article Step 1: the heat duty Basics Step 2: the temperature difference (LMTD) Basics Counter-current vs co-current Working level Step 3: the U value Working level Fouling: designing for the dirty exchanger Working level A full worked example Working level F factor, pinch and choosing the type Going deeper Questions people ask Step 1: the heat duty Basics The duty is the heat that must move from the hot stream to the cold

The duty is the heat that must move from the hot stream to the cold stream per hour. With no phase change: Q = m × cp × (Tin - Tout) Q in kcal/h when m is in kg/h and cp in kcal/kg·°C. With condensation or boiling, add m × latent heat. The duty must balance: what the hot side loses, the cold side gains (minus a few percent lost to the surroundings). Use this to find the flow you need on the other side. If 4,000 kg/h of a solvent stream with cp 0.48 cools from 120 to 60 °C, the duty is 4,000 × 0.48 × 60 ≈ 1,15,200 kcal/h. Cooling water warming from 30 to 40 °C then needs 1,15,200 / (1 × 10) ≈ 11,520 kg/h, about 11.5 m³/h.

The temperature difference between the two streams is not constant: it is large at one end of the exchanger and smaller at the other. The right average is not the simple arithmetic mean but the log mean : LMTD = (ΔT1 - ΔT2) / ln(ΔT1 / ΔT2) ΔT1 and ΔT2 are the hot-minus-cold temperature differences at the two ends. The log mean is always smaller than the arithmetic mean, and the difference grows as the two end differences move apart. When one end difference gets very small, the LMTD falls sharply and the area shoots up: that is the “temperature pinch” designers watch for.

In counter-current flow the streams enter at opposite ends; in co-current (parallel) flow they enter at the same end. For our example, hot 120 → 60 °C and cold 30 → 40 °C: Counter-current: ΔT1 = 120 - 40 = 80, ΔT2 = 60 - 30 = 30. LMTD = 50 / ln(2.67) ≈ 51.0 °C . Co-current: ΔT1 = 120 - 30 = 90, ΔT2 = 60 - 40 = 20. LMTD = 70 / ln(4.5) ≈ 46.5 °C . Counter-current needs about 9 % less area here. The bigger advantage is that it allows the cold outlet to get hotter than the hot outlet (a “temperature cross”), which co-current can never do. Co-current is still used where you want to limit the wall temperature for a heat-sensitive product, because t

t: Step 3: the U value Working level
x: U, the overall heat transfer coefficient (kcal/h·m²·°C), is how easily heat crosses from one fluid to the other. It combines the film on the hot side, the wall, the film on the cold side and any fouling, all as resistances in series: 1/U = 1/hhot + twall/kwall + 1/hcold + Rf The worst resistance dominates. A gas or a viscous liquid on one side caps U, whatever you do on the other side. Typical overall values for preliminary sizing: Service Typical U (kcal/h·m²·°C) Water to water, shell-and-tube 690 – 1,300 Organic solvent to cooling water 260 – 520 Condensing steam to water 1,300 – 3,450 Condensing solvent vapour to cooling water 430 – 860 Ga

t: Fouling: designing for the dirty exchanger Working level
x: A clean exchanger only stays clean for a few weeks. Scale from cooling water, polymer or tar from process streams and corrosion products all add resistance. Designers allow for this with a fouling factor: 1/Udirty = 1/Uclean + Rf With Uclean = 430 kcal/h·m²·°C and Rf = 0.00058 m²·h·°C/kcal: 1/U = 0.00233 + 0.00058 = 0.00291, so Udirty ≈ 345. The exchanger needs 25 % more area. Typical Rf values (m²·h·°C/kcal): treated cooling tower water 0.00023–0.00047, river or untreated water 0.00058–0.0012, clean organic solvents 0.00023, heavy or polymerising streams 0.00058 and up. Be careful not to stack margins: a generous fouling factor, plus a 20 %

t: A full worked example Working level
x: Cool 4,000 kg/h of process stream (cp 0.48 kcal/kg·°C) from 120 to 60 °C with cooling water from 30 to 40 °C, in a shell-and-tube exchanger E-101. Duty: Q = 4,000 × 0.48 × 60 = 1,15,200 kcal/h. Cooling water: 1,15,200 / (1 × 10) = 11,520 kg/h, about 11.5 m³/h. LMTD, counter-current: 51.0 °C. U: organic to water, clean 430, with Rf 0.00058 gives 345 kcal/h·m²·°C. Area: A = Q / (U × LMTD) = 1,15,200 / (345 × 51.0) ≈ 6.5 m² . Co-current would need 1,15,200 / (345 × 46.5) ≈ 7.2 m². Specify the exchanger at 6.5 m² plus a modest margin (10–15 %), and check the tube-side velocity: cooling water below about 1 m/s fouls fast.

t: F factor, pinch and choosing the type Going deeper
x: The F correction factor. Real shell-and-tube exchangers with more than one tube pass are neither pure counter-current nor co-current. The LMTD is multiplied by a correction factor F (from charts or equations, based on the four temperatures): Q = U × A × F × LMTD. If F falls below about 0.8, the design is inefficient and sensitive; use more shells in series or a true counter-current design. Approach temperature. The smallest temperature difference anywhere in the exchanger. Below about 5–10 °C for liquids, area grows very fast for little extra heat recovered. That is why a cooling water exchanger rarely cools a process stream below about 38–40

Using the arithmetic mean temperature difference instead of the LMTD. Forgetting the latent heat when a solvent vapour condenses. Stacking fouling factor, area margin and conservative U on top of each other. Ignoring non-condensables in vacuum condensers. Taking U from a table for a viscous or gas service where it can be ten times lower.
The effective average temperature difference along an exchanger: (ΔT1 - ΔT2) / ln(ΔT1/ΔT2).
It gives a higher LMTD (51 against 46.5 °C in the example), so less area, and it allows a temperature cross.
An extra resistance for deposits: 1/Udirty = 1/Uclean + Rf. An Rf of 0.0005 takes U from 500 to 400.

s: Heat load for a jacketed batch reactor: sensible and latent heat, Q = UAΔT, wetted area, heat-up and cool-down time and solvent recovery time.
x: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time Chemical Engineering · Heat Transfer · Updated October 2026 “How long will it take to heat the batch?” and “How long to strip the solvent?” are two questions every shift asks. Both come from the same two ideas: how much heat the batch needs, and how fast the jacket can push it through the reactor wall. Get those right and you can predict batch time cycles, spot a fouled jacket, and explain why the last 10 °C of cooling always takes forever. In this article How much heat does the batch need? Basics How fast can the jacket deliver it? Basics Heat-up and cool-down time Working level Solvent recovery time Working level Wetted area and reactor occupancy Going deeper What sets U, and how it decays Going deeper Questions people ask Just need the number? The Heat Load & Recovery Calculator works it out, including wetted area from reactor occupancy. How

t: How much heat does the batch need? Basics
s: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time
x: Heat goes into a batch in two ways. Sensible heat raises its temperature; you can feel it, hence the name. Latent heat changes liquid into vapour without changing the temperature; it is hidden, which is what “latent” means. A boiling batch can take heat all day and stay at the same temperature, because every kilocalorie is going into vapour. Sensible heat Q = M × cp × ΔT (kcal) Latent heat Q = mvapour × λ (kcal) For a sense of scale: heating 1 kg of water by 1 °C takes 1 kcal, but boiling it off takes 539 kcal. For toluene the numbers are about 0.41 kcal to warm it 1 °C and 86 kcal to boil it. Boiling is where the energy goes.

t: How fast can the jacket deliver it? Basics
s: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time
x: Heat flows from the jacket into the batch through the reactor wall, and the rate depends on three things: Q (kcal/h) = U × A × ΔT U: overall heat transfer coefficient (kcal/h·m²·°C), how easily heat crosses the wall. A: wetted area (m²), only the part of the wall with liquid behind it. ΔT: jacket temperature minus batch temperature. That last term is the one people underestimate. Heat flow is proportional to the temperature difference, so as the batch gets close to the jacket temperature, heat flow tails off. That single fact explains most of what follows. Only the jacket area with liquid behind it transfers heat well. Above the liquid level

t: Heat-up and cool-down time Working level
s: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time
x: Because the heat flow falls as the batch warms, the temperature does not rise in a straight line. It rises quickly at first and then creeps towards the jacket temperature. With the jacket at a constant temperature Tj (condensing steam is close to this), the time to go from T0 to T is: t = (M × cp) / (U × A) × ln[(Tj - T0) / (Tj - T)] M × cp / (U × A) is the batch's time constant: the bigger the batch or the worse the heat transfer, the slower it responds.

s: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time
x: A 5 KL glass-lined reactor with 4,000 kg of batch (cp ≈ 0.48 kcal/kg·°C), 9 m² of wetted area and U ≈ 300 kcal/h·m²·°C. Heat from 30 to 80 °C on 3 barg steam (143.6 °C): M cp / UA = 4,000 × 0.48 / (300 × 9) ≈ 0.71 h ≈ 42 min t = 42 × ln[(143.6 - 30) / (143.6 - 80)] = 42 × ln(1.79) ≈ 25 min Now cool it back from 80 to 40 °C with cooling water at 32 °C: t = 42 × ln[(80 - 32) / (40 - 32)] = 42 × ln(6) ≈ 76 min Three times longer for a smaller temperature change. When the batch is at 40 °C, the cooling water has only 8 °C of driving force left. This is why plants switch to chilled water or brine for the last part of a cool-down. Try it: the same

s: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time
x: Once the batch is boiling, the temperature stops rising and every kcal from the jacket goes into vapour: Vapour rate (kg/h) = Heat duty (kcal/h) / λ (kcal/kg) Recovery time (h) = solvent to recover (kg) / vapour rate (kg/h) 500 kg of solvent with λ = 86 kcal/kg, and a jacket that can deliver 34,400 kcal/h at the boiling temperature: Vapour rate = 34,400 / 86 = 400 kg/h → time = 500 / 400 ≈ 1.25 h Add the heat-up time before boiling starts, and expect the last part to be slower than the first: the wetted area shrinks and, with mixed solvents, the boiling point rises as the light solvent leaves. The solvent recovery article covers boiling point

t: Wetted area and reactor occupancy Going deeper
s: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time
x: A reactor's jacket area on the datasheet is the full jacket. The area that matters is the part covered by liquid inside. For a vertical reactor with a 2:1 dished bottom head: The bottom head holds a volume of πD³/24 and has an inside area of about 1.08 D². Above the head, each metre of liquid height in the shell adds πD m² of wetted wall. So the wetted area depends on how full the reactor is. A 5 KL reactor (about 1.75 m diameter) at 80 % occupancy has roughly 9–11 m² wetted, depending on how high the jacket goes; at 30 % (near the end of a solvent strip) only about 5 m². Since Q = U A ΔT, the jacket delivers half the heat just when the opera

t: What sets U, and how it decays Going deeper
s: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time
x: U is not one property; it is several resistances in series, like resistors in a circuit: 1/U = 1/hinside + wall thickness / kwall + 1/hjacket + fouling resistances The biggest one wins. In a glass-lined reactor the glass layer (k ≈ 0.86 kcal/h·m·°C) is a large resistance, so U is typically 215–345 kcal/h·m²·°C. In stainless steel with good agitation and steam, 430–690 is common. Viscous batches, poor agitation and scale in the jacket all pull it down. The practical check: record the heat-up time of a standard batch when the reactor is clean. If the same batch takes 30 % longer a year later, U has dropped by about 30 %, and the jacket probably

s: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time
x: Using the full jacket area from the datasheet instead of the wetted area. Using an average ΔT as if the batch temperature were fixed, which underestimates heat-up time near the end. Forgetting the reactor steel and the jacket contents in M cp for short batches; they can add 10–20 %. Taking latent heat at atmospheric pressure for a vacuum recovery (it is a little higher at lower temperatures). Designing a cool-down on cooling water alone when the target is within 10 °C of the cooling water temperature.

t: How do you calculate the heat-up time of a jacketed reactor?
s: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time
x: t = (M cp / UA) × ln[(Tj - T0) / (Tj - T)]. For the 4,000 kg example on 3 barg steam, about 25 minutes from 30 to 80 °C.

t: Why does cooling take longer than heating?
s: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time
x: The driving force is smaller. Cooling water at 32 °C has only 8 °C of driving force when the batch is at 40 °C, while steam at 144 °C still has over 60 °C when the batch reaches 80 °C.

t: How do you calculate solvent recovery time?
s: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time
x: Vapour rate = heat duty / latent heat; time = solvent mass / vapour rate. 500 kg at 86 kcal/kg and 34,400 kcal/h takes about 1.25 hours of boiling.
