s: Practical risk assessment in chemical plants: HIRA for activities, JSA for jobs, the risk matrix, the hierarchy of controls and links to HAZOP.
x: Risk Assessment: HIRA, JSA and the Risk Matrix Plant Departments · Risk Assessment · October 2026 HAZOP looks at the process design. Most injuries, though, happen during ordinary activities: charging powders, sampling, changing a filter cloth, working at height. HIRA and JSA are the tools for those. Done honestly, they are short, practical and make work safer; done as paperwork, they are neither. In this article HIRA: hazard identification and risk assessment Basics The risk matrix Basics JSA: breaking a job into steps Working level Hierarchy of controls Working level Where HIRA and JSA fit Going deeper Questions people ask HIRA: hazard identification and risk assessment Basics A HIRA covers each area or activity: list the routine and non-routine tasks, identify the hazards in each (chemical exposure, fire, pressure, moving machinery, manual handling, height, electricity, heat), estimate

t: HIRA: hazard identification and risk assessment Basics
s: Risk Assessment: HIRA, JSA and the Risk Matrix
x: A HIRA covers each area or activity: list the routine and non-routine tasks, identify the hazards in each (chemical exposure, fire, pressure, moving machinery, manual handling, height, electricity, heat), estimate the risk with existing controls, and decide whether more control is needed. It is reviewed periodically and after any change or incident.

s: Risk Assessment: HIRA, JSA and the Risk Matrix
x: Risk combines severity (from first aid to fatality or major release) and likelihood (from very unlikely to frequent), usually each on a 1–5 scale. Risk score = severity × likelihood, and bands such as low, medium, high and unacceptable decide the action. Example: a solvent drum transfer without earthing, severity 4 (fire with possible serious injury), likelihood 3: score 12, high. With bonding, earthing and a dip pipe, likelihood drops to 1: score 4, low. The method is simple; the value is in the honest discussion behind the numbers.

t: JSA: breaking a job into steps Working level
s: Risk Assessment: HIRA, JSA and the Risk Matrix
x: A job safety analysis takes one specific job, for example opening a filter dryer to discharge wet cake, and breaks it into steps. For each step: the hazard, the control, and who is responsible. It is best done with the people who do the job, at the place where it is done. The JSA then becomes the basis of the SOP, the training and the permit .

s: Risk Assessment: HIRA, JSA and the Risk Matrix
x: Elimination: remove the hazard (a closed charging system instead of manual tipping). Substitution: a less hazardous material or form (a solution or paste instead of a dusty powder). Engineering controls: local exhaust, containment, interlocks, guards, earthing. Administrative controls: procedures, permits, training, signs, job rotation. Personal protective equipment: the last line, not the first. A risk assessment whose only actions are “use PPE” and “be careful” has not been finished.

t: Where HIRA and JSA fit Going deeper
s: Risk Assessment: HIRA, JSA and the Risk Matrix
x: HIRA and JSA cover activities and occupational hazards. Process hazards, deviations of flow, temperature and pressure, are covered by HAZOP , with LOPA where the consequence is severe, and by thermal safety studies for reactions. Chemical exposure assessment compares expected exposure with occupational exposure limits and decides containment, especially for potent APIs. Together they form the site’s risk register, reviewed when anything changes through management of change . On the plant Do the JSA for a non-routine job at the job location, with the people who will do it, on the day. A desk JSA written last year rarely knows that the platform

s: Risk Assessment: HIRA, JSA and the Risk Matrix
x: HIRA copied from another area and never reviewed. Scores adjusted to avoid actions. JSA written without the people who do the job. Relying on PPE instead of engineering controls. Not reviewing the assessment after an incident or change.

t: What is the difference between HIRA and JSA?
s: Risk Assessment: HIRA, JSA and the Risk Matrix
x: HIRA assesses the hazards of all activities in an area. A JSA breaks one specific job into steps and lists the hazard and control for each.

t: How is a risk score calculated in a risk matrix?
s: Risk Assessment: HIRA, JSA and the Risk Matrix
x: Severity times likelihood, each usually on a 1 to 5 scale, with bands deciding what action is needed.

t: What is the hierarchy of controls?
s: Risk Assessment: HIRA, JSA and the Risk Matrix
x: Elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls and PPE, in order of effectiveness.

s: How to read a P&ID: equipment tags, line numbers, valve and line symbols, ISA 5.1 instrument letters, control loops and interlocks. Interactive explorer.
x: How to Read a P&ID Plant Engineering · Drawings · October 2026 The first time someone hands you a P&ID, it looks like a circuit diagram that fell into a bowl of alphabet soup. A week later you can't imagine working without it. The P&ID is the one drawing that shows how the plant is really put together: every line, valve, instrument and interlock. This article teaches you to read one, using a simple reactor example with generic tags. In this article What a P&ID is (and is not) Basics Equipment and their tags Basics Lines and line numbers Basics Valves and fittings Working level Instrument bubbles and ISA letters Working level Control loops and interlocks Going deeper How to trace a line on site Going deeper Questions people ask What a P&ID is (and is not) Basics A PFD (process flow diagram) tells the story of the process: main equipment, main streams, temperatures, pressures and flows fro

t: What a P&ID is (and is not) Basics
x: A PFD (process flow diagram) tells the story of the process: main equipment, main streams, temperatures, pressures and flows from the heat and material balance. It fits a whole plant on a few sheets. A P&ID (piping and instrumentation diagram) tells you how to build and run it: every pipe with its size and class, every valve, every instrument and what it is connected to, every vent, drain, sample point, utility connection, interlock and relief device. It is drawn schematically, not to scale: a pump drawn next to a reactor might be 30 metres away on site. For where things physically are, you need the layout and isometric drawings. The P&ID is

Each piece of equipment gets a tag: a letter code for its type and a number, often starting with the area or block. Codes differ between companies, but a common pattern is: Code Equipment Example R Reactor R-101 V / T Vessel / storage tank V-102, T-103 E Heat exchanger, condenser E-101 P Pump P-101A/B (A and B: duty and standby) C / K Centrifuge / compressor C-101 F / D Filter / dryer F-101, D-101 The legend sheet, usually the first sheet in the set, defines the codes and symbols for that project. Read it before anything else.

A thick solid line is a main process line; a thinner solid line is a secondary or utility line. Instrument signals are drawn differently: dashed lines for electrical signals, lines with short cross-hatches for pneumatic (air) signals, and a line of small circles or a dash-dot pattern for software or data links. Arrows show the direction of flow, and an off-page connector (an arrow-shaped box) shows where the line continues on another sheet. Every pipe has a line number. A typical format: 50 – PS – 101 – A1 50: nominal size in mm (or 2″). PS: service code, here process solvent. 101: sequence number. A1: piping class, which fixes material, pres

Most valve symbols start from two triangles touching at their tips (a “bow-tie”), which is a gate valve. Variations on it: Globe valve: bow-tie with a solid dot in the middle. Used for throttling. Ball valve: bow-tie with a circle in the middle. Quick on/off. Butterfly valve: a line with a short bar across it, or a bow-tie with a vertical line. Check (non-return) valve: a bow-tie with one triangle filled, or an arrow with a bar, pointing in the allowed flow direction. Control valve: a bow-tie with an actuator drawn on top: a dome for a diaphragm actuator. Labels FC (fail closed) or FO (fail open) tell you what it does when air or power fails.

t: Instrument bubbles and ISA letters Working level
x: Instruments are drawn as circles (bubbles). The line through the middle tells you where the instrument is seen: No line: mounted in the field, locally. Solid line: in the main control room panel. Dashed line: behind the panel or in a local panel. A circle inside a square: a function in the DCS or PLC, shown on the operator screen. Inside the bubble are letters and a loop number, following ISA-5.1. The first letter is what is measured; the following letters are what the instrument does. First letter (measured) Following letters (function) F flow, L level, P pressure, T temperature I indicate, R record, C control A analysis (O2, pH), S speed, W

t: Control loops and interlocks Going deeper
x: All instruments with the same number form one loop. Follow it: TE-101 senses the batch temperature, TT-101 sends it to the DCS, TIC-101 compares it with the set point, and TV-101 on the jacket cooling water opens or closes. Once you see a loop as sensor, controller and final element, every loop on the drawing reads the same way. Safety functions are drawn separately. An interlock or trip often appears as a diamond or a hexagon with a number (I-101) and a note, or as a separate safety instrumented function with its own sensor, such as TSHH-105 tripping the dosing valve XV-105. Check two things: Independence. Does the trip have its own sensor,

t: How to trace a line on site Going deeper
x: Start from a piece of equipment you can find on site, such as the reactor nozzle. Follow the line on the P&ID valve by valve, writing down the line number and each valve. On site, follow the same line. Every valve, instrument, reducer and branch should match the drawing, in the same order. Mark differences in red on a copy: a valve that doesn't exist, a bypass nobody drew, a temporary hose that became permanent. Send the marked-up copy for as-built correction through change control. On the plant New engineers learn a plant fastest by tracing lines with an experienced operator. It is also the cheapest HAZOP preparation there is: most surprises

Reading gets easier once you have drawn a few. The free P&ID drawing tool has ISA instrument symbols, line numbering and a title block, and downloads PDF or DXF for AutoCAD. This 2-minute video shows the whole workflow.

Reading the P&ID as a layout and expecting things to be where they are drawn. Ignoring the piping class at the end of the line number. Missing the FC/FO label on a control valve. Treating a control alarm and a trip on the same sensor as two protections. Trusting a drawing that hasn't been walked since commissioning.

t: What is the difference between a PFD and a P&ID?
x: The PFD shows the main equipment, streams and the heat and material balance. The P&ID shows every line, valve, instrument and interlock needed to build and operate the plant.
Temperature indicating controller. The first letter is the measured variable; the rest are functions.

t: How do you read a line number?
x: Size, service code, sequence number and piping class, for example 50-PS-101-A1. The legend sheet defines the exact format.

x: How to Read DSC, ARC, RC1 and TSU Data Process Safety · Thermal Hazards · October 2026 A thermal safety report lands on your desk: a DSC trace, an ARC plot on a log scale, an RC1 curve and a TSU pressure chart. Each says something different about the same chemistry, and each can mislead you if read carelessly. This article explains, from the basics, what each instrument does, how to read its key features, and which questions each one can and cannot answer. In this article Why four different tests Basics DSC: the first screen Basics Reading a DSC trace Working level TSU: screening for gas Working level RC1: the reaction as it runs Working level ARC: the runaway in slow motion Going deeper Putting it together Going deeper Questions people ask Why four different tests Basics Two questions decide whether a process is thermally safe. First, the desired reaction : how much heat does it release

s: How to Read DSC, ARC, RC1 and TSU Data
x: Two questions decide whether a process is thermally safe. First, the desired reaction : how much heat does it release, how fast, and how much could still be released if cooling failed? Second, the undesired reaction : at what temperature does the mixture start to decompose, how much energy and gas does that release, and how quickly does it run away? No single instrument answers both well, so we use a set: Test Sample What it measures Main question it answers DSC 2–10 mg, sealed crucible Heat flow while heating at a fixed rate Is there an exotherm, where, and how big? TSU A few grams, closed cell Temperature and pressure while heating Does dec

s: How to Read DSC, ARC, RC1 and TSU Data
x: Differential scanning calorimetry heats a few milligrams of sample and an empty reference side by side at a steady rate, typically 2–10 °C/min, and records the extra heat the sample absorbs or gives out. It is fast, cheap and needs very little material, so it is the first test for every intermediate, reaction mixture, distillation residue and isolated solid. Use a sealed high-pressure crucible (gold-plated steel is common) for anything containing solvent. In an open pan, the solvent evaporates with a large endotherm that can hide a decomposition exotherm completely.

t: Reading a DSC trace Working level
s: How to Read DSC, ARC, RC1 and TSU Data
x: Try it: pick an instrument and tap the numbered points on its curve. The curves are illustrative, not from a real compound. On a DSC trace (check the axis label: most safety labs plot exo up ), read four things: Endotherms (downward peaks): melting, boiling, desolvation. Not hazards themselves, but a melt just before a decomposition often means the decomposition is fast. Onset : where the exotherm leaves the baseline. It depends on heating rate and sensitivity. A DSC at 5 °C/min detects onset much later than the temperature at which a large, insulated plant batch would start to self-heat. It is a marker, never a safe operating limit. Energy :

t: TSU: screening for gas Working level
s: How to Read DSC, ARC, RC1 and TSU Data
x: A thermal screening unit (TSU) heats a few grams of sample in a closed metal cell, usually at a slow ramp (often around 1–2 °C/min), recording both temperature and pressure. It fills the gap between DSC and ARC. The pressure trace is the valuable part: Below the onset, pressure rises gently and reversibly with the solvent's vapour pressure. At the exotherm, temperature and pressure jump together. The rates dT/dt and dP/dt show how violent it is. After cooling back to room temperature, any pressure left is non-condensable gas . Gas generation often decides relief sizing and can be more dangerous than the heat itself.

A calibration heater of known power, fired before and after the reaction, gives UA. From one run you get: Reaction heat ΔHr in kcal/mol, from integrating the heat flow, and the adiabatic temperature rise. Heat release rate : the plateau during dosing tells you the cooling the plant must provide per kg. x: HR in Chemical and Pharma Plants Plant Departments · Human Resources · October 2026 A plant runs on people working shifts around the clock with hazardous chemicals under GMP. HR in such a plant is far more than payroll: it decides whether every shift has enough trained people, whether training records stand up to an audit, and whether contract and permanent staff work safely side by side. A post manned 24 hours, 7 days a week needs 168 hours of cover every week. With a 48-hour working week, that is 168 ÷ 48 = 3

s: HR in Chemical and Pharma Plants
x: Start from posts, not people: how many operators, chemists and technicians each area needs on each shift. A post manned 24 hours, 7 days a week needs 168 hours of cover every week. With a 48-hour working week, that is 168 ÷ 48 = 3.5 people per post. Allowing about 10 % for leave and absence gives 3.5 ÷ 0.9 ≈ 3.9, so plan 4 people per round-the-clock post . A block with 6 posts per shift therefore needs about 24 people, plus supervisors and relievers for training. The occupancy chart of the products tells you which areas are busy at once, which sets the posts per shift.

s: HR in Chemical and Pharma Plants
x: Plants recruit graduate engineer trainees and chemists from campuses, experienced operators and technicians, and specialists for QC, QA, EHS and maintenance. Tests and interviews should check what the job really needs: reading a P&ID, basic calculations, chemical safety awareness, attitude to procedures. Induction covers site safety rules, emergency response, GMP basics, data integrity, and a walk through the plant with a mentor before any independent work.

s: HR in Chemical and Pharma Plants
x: In a GMP plant, an untrained person may not perform a GMP task, and the training record must prove it. A competency matrix lists every person against every SOP and task with their status: trained, qualified to work independently, or qualified to train others. Training on a new or revised SOP is completed before the SOP becomes effective. Good training mixes: Classroom sessions on GMP, safety and the chemistry of the process. On-the-job training with a qualified operator, signed off by observation. Periodic refreshers and drills: fire, spill, gas leak, evacuation. Training on lessons from incidents and deviations, so the same mistake is not re

The principal employer remains responsible for their safety on site and must check that the contractor meets statutory obligations: registration and licence where required, wages, provident fund and ESI, appointment letters and working hours. Contract workers need the same safety induction, PPE and permit discipline as permanent staff; many serious incidents involve contractors doing non-routine work.

Engagement and retention matter more in plants than many assume: an experienced shift operator who leaves takes years of process knowledge with them. s: How much hydrogen dissolves in methanol, toluene, THF, IPA and water, how pressure and temperature change it, and why hydrogenations are mass-transfer limited.
x: Hydrogen Solubility in Solvents Reaction Engineering · Hydrogenation Hydrogen barely dissolves in anything. At 25 °C and 1 bar of hydrogen, a litre of methanol holds about 8 mg, toluene or IPA about 6 mg and water only 1.6 mg. The amount rises in proportion to pressure and, in organic solvents, slightly with temperature. Because the liquid holds so little, plant hydrogenations are almost always limited by how fast the gas dissolves, not by the catalyst. In this article Henry's law for hydrogen Pressure: the strongest lever Temperature: the opposite of most gases Which solvent holds the most How much hydrogen is in your batch What it means on the plant Questions people ask Henry's law for hydrogen At the pressures used in pharma and fine-chemical hydrogenations (up to about 100 bar), dissolved hydrogen follows Henry's law: xH2 = pH2 / H(T) pH2 = Ptotal, abs - pvap, solvent x mole fraction

At the pressures used in pharma and fine-chemical hydrogenations (up to about 100 bar), dissolved hydrogen follows Henry's law: xH2 = pH2 / H(T) pH2 = Ptotal, abs - pvap, solvent x mole fraction of hydrogen in the liquid; H Henry's constant (MPa), which depends on the solvent and temperature. Use the hydrogen partial pressure, not the gauge reading: add 1.013 bar to the gauge pressure and subtract the solvent's vapour pressure. For hydrogen the Henry's constants are large: about 140 MPa in n-hexane, 320 MPa in toluene, 630 MPa in methanol and 7,200 MPa in water at 25 °C. A large constant means low solubility. The hydrogen solubility calculato

Solubility is directly proportional to the hydrogen partial pressure. In methanol at 25 °C: Hydrogen pressure Dissolved H2, mg/L 1 bar g 14.7 4 bar g 38.6 10 bar g 86.4 The gas–liquid transfer rate is kLa × (C* - C), and C* is this solubility. So doubling the hydrogen pressure roughly doubles the maximum rate at which hydrogen can reach the catalyst. That is why a reaction that crawls at 2 bar g can run well at 8 bar g in the same reactor.

t: Temperature: the opposite of most gases
x: Most gases dissolve less as the liquid warms. Hydrogen in organic solvents does the opposite: dissolving is slightly endothermic, so solubility rises with temperature. Brunner's measurements at BASF show the mole fraction rising by about 15–25 % from 25 to 50 °C in ten common solvents. In water hydrogen solubility falls slightly up to about 50 °C and then rises slowly. At a fixed total pressure there is a catch: the solvent's vapour pressure also rises and takes a growing share of the headspace. In toluene at 4 bar g the dissolved hydrogen goes from 29 mg/L at 25 °C to 36 mg/L at 60 °C and 39 mg/L at 80 °C. In methanol, whose vapour pressure

Per mole, non-polar solvents dissolve the most hydrogen: n-hexane about 7 × 10^-4 mole fraction at 1 atm and 25 °C, toluene 3.2 × 10^-4, DMF and NMP about 1.4 × 10^-4. Per litre the picture changes, because small molecules pack more moles into a litre: Solvent mg/L per bar H2, 25 °C n-Hexane 10.8 Methanol 8.0 Acetone 7.7 Ethanol 7.0 THF 6.6 Toluene 5.9 DMF 3.8 NMP 2.9 Water 1.6 Between the common organic solvents the difference is at most two to three times, so a solvent change rarely rescues a slow hydrogenation on its own. Water is the outlier: a water-rich solvent mixture holds much less hydrogen than the dry solvent.

t: How much hydrogen is in your batch
x: Take 2,000 L of methanol at 25 °C under 4 bar g hydrogen: pH2 = 5.013 - 0.169 (methanol vapour pressure) = 4.84 bar x = 0.484 MPa / 626 MPa = 7.7 × 10^-4 → 38.6 mg/L Dissolved hydrogen in 2,000 L ≈ 77 g Now compare with what the reaction needs. Reducing 1 kmol of a nitro group to an amine consumes 3 kmol of hydrogen, about 6 kg. The liquid holds about 1 % of that at any moment. Every gram the catalyst uses must be replaced by fresh gas dissolving from the bubbles. With a kLa of 0.1 s^-1, the most methanol can take up at 4 bar g is roughly 7 mol of hydrogen per litre per hour. A large reactor with poor gas dispersion may reach only a tenth of

t: What it means on the plant
x: Raise the pressure first. It raises solubility, and with it the transfer rate, in direct proportion. Check the reactor's design pressure and the relief settings first. Then improve gas dispersion. A gas-inducing or hollow-blade impeller, a sparger under the impeller, and enough power per volume raise kLa far more than extra catalyst does. Lab rates do not scale directly. A small autoclave with a fast stirrer can have several times the plant kLa. If the lab reaction was already mass-transfer limited, the plant will be slower unless pressure or agitation make up the difference. Dissolved hydrogen leaves when the pressure drops. When the reactor

t: How much hydrogen dissolves in a solvent?
x: Very little: at 25 °C and 1 bar of hydrogen, about 8 mg/L in methanol, 6 mg/L in toluene or IPA, and 1.6 mg/L in water. It rises in proportion to the hydrogen pressure.

t: Does hydrogen dissolve better at higher temperature?
x: In organic solvents, yes, by roughly 15–25 % from 25 to 50 °C. In water it falls slightly up to about 50 °C. At a fixed total pressure, the solvent's rising vapour pressure takes back part of the gain.

t: Why is my hydrogenation slow at plant scale?
x: Usually because hydrogen cannot dissolve fast enough. Higher pressure and better gas dispersion help more than extra catalyst.

t: Is dissolved hydrogen a hazard when the reactor is opened?
x: Yes: it comes out of the liquid as the pressure drops. Vent safely and purge with nitrogen before opening or filtering.

s: Safe hydrogenation: the N2-H2-N2 purge sequence, pyrophoric Pd/C and Raney nickel catalysts, charging and filtering, heat release and leak detection.
x: Hydrogenation Safety Process Safety · Hazardous Operations · October 2026 Hydrogenation is one of the most useful reactions in API manufacturing and one of the most unforgiving. It combines a gas that ignites from almost any spark with catalysts that can catch fire on their own in air, usually in a flammable solvent, under pressure. Most hydrogenation fires happen not during the reaction but before and after it: at charging, purging and filtration. This article explains why, and the procedures that prevent them. In this article Why hydrogen is different Basics The purge sequence Basics Pyrophoric catalysts Working level Charging and filtering catalyst safely Working level Heat, pressure and leaks Going deeper Questions people ask Why hydrogen is different Basics Very wide flammable range: about 4 to 75 % in air, compared with roughly 1 to 7 % for toluene. Tiny ignition energy: about 0.02

Very wide flammable range: about 4 to 75 % in air, compared with roughly 1 to 7 % for toluene. Tiny ignition energy: about 0.02 mJ, around ten times less than most solvent vapours. A static spark you would never feel is enough. Low LOC: about 5 % oxygen with nitrogen, lower than most solvents, so inerting must be tighter. Leaks easily: the smallest molecule, so it escapes through joints that hold other gases. It is lighter than air and collects under roofs. Nearly invisible flame in daylight.

The rule is simple: hydrogen and air must never meet in the vessel . Every hydrogenation follows the same pattern: Charge the vessel and inert it: pressure-purge with nitrogen, typically three cycles, until oxygen is below about 1 %. Pressure-purge with hydrogen to displace the nitrogen. React under hydrogen pressure. Vent the hydrogen to a safe location and purge with nitrogen until hydrogen is below a safe level (often under 1 %). Only then open the vessel or transfer the slurry for filtration. Try it: run the correct sequence, then skip the first nitrogen purge. The headspace passes through the flammable range as hydrogen enters air. Each

Palladium, platinum and nickel catalysts are pyrophoric: dry, and especially when they have absorbed hydrogen, they can heat up and ignite on contact with air. Add a flammable solvent and you have the fuel, the ignition source and the oxygen together. Pd/C and Pt/C are supplied about 50 % water-wet to reduce this risk. Keep them wet. Raney nickel is stored under water and is strongly pyrophoric when dry. Spent catalyst is more dangerous than fresh: it carries absorbed hydrogen and organic residue.

t: Charging and filtering catalyst safely Working level
x: Charge wet catalyst into an inerted vessel, ideally as a slurry in water or the reaction solvent through a closed charging system. Never sprinkle dry catalyst into a solvent in air. Filter under nitrogen in a closed filter: candle, sparkler or enclosed Nutsche. Open-top filtration of a catalyst slurry is a classic fire scenario. Never let the catalyst cake suck dry while air can reach it. Wash with solvent and then water, and keep the cake covered. Store spent catalyst under water in closed, labelled containers, and send it for recovery promptly. Earth the filter and the receiving vessel: catalyst slurry in a low-conductivity solvent charges

t: Heat, pressure and leaks Going deeper
x: Many hydrogenations are strongly exothermic; nitro reductions release over 120 kcal per mol of nitro group. Because the reaction usually can't go faster than hydrogen dissolves, the hydrogen feed rate and agitation control the heat release. That is useful, but it means an agitator restart after a stop, or a sudden pressure increase, can release accumulated heat quickly. See gas-liquid mass transfer . Pressure relief sized for the worst case, including runaway of the substrate if it is thermally unstable. Leak test the system with nitrogen at operating pressure before every campaign. Hydrogen detectors at high points, with ventilation and alar

Introducing hydrogen into a vessel that was never purged with nitrogen. Letting the catalyst cake dry on the filter. Opening the reactor before purging out the hydrogen. Leak testing only once, at commissioning. Venting hydrogen inside a building or under a canopy.

t: What is the flammable range of hydrogen?
x: About 4–75 % in air, with a minimum ignition energy around 0.02 mJ.
Dry Pd/C can ignite in air; water-wetting makes it much safer to handle.

t: Why purge with nitrogen before hydrogen?
x: So hydrogen never mixes with air; adding it to air passes through the flammable range.

s: Nitrogen inerting basics: the flammability diagram, LOC and safe oxygen targets, pressure, vacuum and sweep purging, blanketing and O2 measurement.
x: Inerting and Limiting Oxygen Concentration Process Safety · Fire and Explosion · October 2026 “The reactor is under nitrogen.” Everyone in a solvent plant has said it, and it is one of the most reassuring and least checked sentences in process safety. Inerting is powerful: take enough oxygen away and solvent vapour simply cannot burn, whatever sparks fly. But it only works if the oxygen really is low, and the only way to know is to understand the numbers and measure them. This article explains both. In this article Why removing oxygen works Basics The flammability diagram Basics How low is low enough? Working level Getting there: three ways to purge Working level Staying there: blanketing and leaks Working level Measuring oxygen, and the hazard to people Going deeper Questions people ask Why removing oxygen works Basics A fire needs fuel, oxygen and an ignition source. In a solvent plant

A fire needs fuel, oxygen and an ignition source. In a solvent plant, fuel is always present and ignition sources are hard to eliminate completely: static, hot surfaces, sparks from metal, a pyrophoric catalyst. Oxygen is the one side of the triangle we can control reliably, by replacing air with nitrogen. You don't need to remove all the oxygen. Below a certain level, the flame can't sustain itself because there isn't enough oxygen to release heat faster than the surrounding gas absorbs it. That level is the limiting oxygen concentration (LOC) .

Picture a chart with solvent vapour along the bottom and oxygen up the side. Mixtures of solvent with plain air lie on a line that starts at 21 % oxygen and falls slightly as vapour displaces air. Along that line, the mixture burns only between the lower flammable limit (LFL) and the upper flammable limit (UFL) : around 1–7 % for toluene, 6–36 % for methanol. Add nitrogen and you move downward. The flammable range narrows as oxygen falls, until the LFL and UFL boundaries meet at a nose. The oxygen level at that nose is the LOC. Below it, no solvent concentration can burn. Try it: the shaded region is flammable for a typical solvent. Move the

t: How low is low enough? Working level
x: Operating right at the LOC leaves no room for error: a small leak, a slow analyser or a gust of air through a manhole would put you into the flammable region. NFPA 69 sets the margin: With continuous O2 monitoring: operate at least 2 percentage points below LOC Without continuous monitoring: no more than 60 % of LOC For LOC = 10 %: 8 % with an analyser and interlock, 6 % without. Many plants simply use 5 % as a standard target for all solvent work. That is easier to remember and gives margin for hydrogen-free systems, but check it against the LOC if hydrogen or another low-LOC gas can be present.

Pressurise the vessel with nitrogen, let it mix, vent back to atmosphere, repeat. Each cycle reduces the oxygen by the ratio of the absolute pressures: O2 after n cycles = O2 initial × (Plow / Phigh)^n Purging to 2 barg (3.01 bar abs) and venting to 1.01 bar abs multiplies the oxygen by 0.34 each cycle: 21 → 7.1 → 2.4 %. Two cycles reach a 5 % target. Check the vessel's rating first: a glass-lined reactor or a vessel with a sight glass may not take 2 barg. Try it: change the nitrogen pressure and run the purge. Higher pressure means fewer cycles, but more nitrogen per cycle.

Pull a vacuum, break it with nitrogen, repeat. The same ratio applies: vacuum to 100 mbar and break to atmosphere multiplies oxygen by about 0.1 per cycle, so one cycle takes 21 % to about 2 %. It is very nitrogen-efficient and is the usual choice for vessels rated for full vacuum. It must be done before solvent is charged, or the vacuum will pull solvent vapour to the pump.

Blow nitrogen in at one end and let it out at the other. With perfect mixing, oxygen falls as C = C0 × e^-volumes, so about one volume change takes 21 % to 8 % and 1.4 volumes to 5 %. In practice mixing is far from perfect, so plan on three to five volume changes and measure the outlet. Sweeping is the right method for long pipes and for vessels that can't take pressure or vacuum.

t: Staying there: blanketing and leaks Working level
x: Purging gets the oxygen down; blanketing keeps it down. A small nitrogen pressure (typically 20–100 mbarg) held by a regulator stops air coming in as the vessel breathes. Every time something happens, ask whether oxygen came in: Opening a manhole to charge solids lets air in. Keep a nitrogen flow at the manhole while it is open, or use a closed charging system, and re-purge before heating. Cooling a vessel under a fixed amount of gas pulls a vacuum, which pulls air through any leak. Keep the blanket supply open while cooling. Drawing liquid out lowers the pressure the same way. Vacuum distillation pulls in air through every leaking gland and

t: Measuring oxygen, and the hazard to people Going deeper
x: Without a measurement, “inerted” is a hope. Options range from a portable analyser used to check after each purge, to a fixed analyser on the vent line, interlocked to stop heating or charging if oxygen rises. Calibrate it regularly, check that the sample point represents the vessel (not just the nitrogen inlet), and remember that solvent vapour in the sample can affect some sensors. The same nitrogen that protects the vessel kills people. Air with less than about 18 % oxygen impairs judgement, and a few breaths of near-pure nitrogen cause collapse without warning, because the body senses carbon dioxide, not low oxygen. Treat an inerted vesse

Assuming the vessel is inert because nitrogen was connected, without measuring. Forgetting to re-purge after opening a manhole for charging. Breaking vacuum with air after distillation. Assuming a mixture above the UFL is safe. Treating nitrogen as harmless around people.

t: What is the limiting oxygen concentration?
x: The oxygen level below which no mixture can burn, roughly 9–12 % for common solvents with nitrogen and about 5 % for hydrogen.

t: What oxygen level should we keep?
x: At least 2 points below the LOC with continuous monitoring, or 60 % of the LOC without (NFPA 69).

t: How many purge cycles are needed?
x: Each cycle multiplies oxygen by Plow/Phigh. At 2 barg, two cycles take air to about 2.4 %.

s: How plant instruments measure pressure, temperature, level and flow: RTDs, thermocouples, DP, radar, magnetic, Coriolis and vortex meters, calibration.
x: Process Instrumentation Basics Plant Engineering · Instrumentation · October 2026 Every decision on a plant starts with a number from an instrument. When that number is wrong, everything built on it is wrong too: the batch goes off temperature, the tank overflows, the yield seems to fall. Instrument engineers don’t need to be the only ones who understand how these readings are made. This article covers the four main measurements, how each instrument works, and where each one fools people. In this article Pressure Basics Temperature Basics Level Working level Flow Working level Accuracy, turndown and calibration Going deeper Questions people ask Pressure Basics Know which pressure you are reading. Gauge pressure (barg) is relative to the atmosphere; absolute pressure (bar abs, mbar abs) is relative to vacuum. For vacuum work always use absolute transmitters: a gauge reading of -0.95 bar m

Know which pressure you are reading. Gauge pressure (barg) is relative to the atmosphere; absolute pressure (bar abs, mbar abs) is relative to vacuum. For vacuum work always use absolute transmitters: a gauge reading of -0.95 bar means a different absolute pressure on different days and at different altitudes. Bourdon gauges for local reading; transmitters (strain gauge or capacitance sensors) send 4–20 mA signals to the DCS. Diaphragm seals protect the sensor from corrosive, crystallising or viscous fluids. The fill fluid adds temperature error and slows the response. A pressure gauge on the suction of every important pump is worth its cost

RTD (Pt100): platinum resistance; accurate and stable, the usual choice up to about 400 °C. Thermocouple: two dissimilar metals produce a voltage; robust, wide range, less accurate. Type K is common for high temperatures. Thermowell: protects the sensor but adds delay. A heavy thermowell in a slow-moving liquid can lag the real temperature by minutes, which matters a great deal in an exothermic reaction. In glass-lined reactors the temperature probe is usually inside a baffle. If the baffle isn't covered by liquid at low volume, it reads vapour temperature, not batch temperature.

Differential pressure: level = ΔP / (ρ g). Accurate only if the density is right; a change from water to toluene (1,000 to 867 kg/m³) shifts the reading by 15 %. Radar (non-contact) and guided-wave radar: unaffected by density; foam, vapour and agitators can confuse non-contact radar. Load cells: weigh the whole vessel; excellent for batch charging and mass balances, but piping stresses, nitrogen pressure and agitator vibration affect them. Sight glass and level gauges: local check; keep them clean and protected. Level switches for high-high trips should be independent of the level transmitter used for control.

Meter How it works Good for Limitations Orifice plate (DP) Flow ∝ √ΔP across a restriction Clean liquids, gases, steam; cheap Narrow turndown (about 3–4:1); permanent pressure loss Magnetic Voltage induced in a conductive liquid moving through a magnetic field Water, aqueous solutions, slurries Does not work with solvents and other non-conductive liquids Coriolis Mass flow from the twisting of vibrating tubes Mass flow and density of any liquid; batch dosing Cost; pressure drop in small sizes Vortex Frequency of vortices shed from a bluff body Steam, gases, clean liquids Needs a minimum velocity Rotameter Float rises in a tapered tube Local i

t: Accuracy, turndown and calibration Going deeper
x: Read the accuracy statement carefully. “±0.1 % of span” means the same absolute error at every reading, so the relative error grows at low readings. “±0.2 % of reading” stays proportional. For an orifice meter at 10 % flow, the DP is only 1 % of span, and a ±0.1 % of span transmitter gives about ±5 % error in flow. Turndown is the ratio of maximum to minimum flow the meter can measure accurately. Size meters for the normal flow, not the design maximum times a safety factor, or the plant will spend its life at the bottom of the range. Calibration checks the instrument against a reference; a loop check confirms that the value in the DCS matches

Magnetic flowmeters on solvent lines. DP level transmitters left calibrated for the wrong density. Gauge-pressure transmitters for vacuum control. Orifice meters sized for the maximum and run at 10 % flow. Control and trip sharing one level transmitter.

t: Why can magnetic flowmeters not measure solvents?
x: They need a conductive liquid; most solvents have almost no conductivity.

t: What is the difference between RTD and thermocouple?
x: RTDs are more accurate and stable; thermocouples cover wider ranges more robustly.

t: What does accuracy as a percentage of span mean?
x: A fixed error over the full range, which becomes large relative to small readings.

s: Reactor jackets, limpet (half-pipe) coils, dimple jackets and internal coils: jacket velocity, film coefficients, overall U and multi-fluid service.
x: Reactor Jackets and Limpet Coils Process Design · Heat Transfer · October 2026 Heat-up and cool-down times on a plant reactor are often blamed on the vessel size or the glass lining. Sometimes the real culprit is the jacket: cooling water creeping through a wide annulus at a few centimetres per second. This article explains the main jacket types, why velocity on the jacket side matters, and when it stops mattering. In this article Jacket types Basics Why jacket-side velocity matters Basics Film coefficients and overall U Working level Steam, water, brine and thermic fluid Working level Multi-fluid jackets and practical problems Going deeper Questions people ask Jacket types Basics Conventional jacket: an outer shell around the vessel, with a gap of typically 50–100 mm. Simple and cheap, good for steam. For liquids, the flow area is huge and the velocity very low unless agitation nozzles

Conventional jacket: an outer shell around the vessel, with a gap of typically 50–100 mm. Simple and cheap, good for steam. For liquids, the flow area is huge and the velocity very low unless agitation nozzles or a spiral baffle are fitted. Half-pipe or limpet coil: a pipe cut in half lengthwise and welded in a spiral around the vessel. Small flow area, so high velocity and good heat transfer with liquids. Strong, so it suits high-pressure utilities and thin vessel walls. Dimple jacket: a thin sheet with pressed dimples welded to the vessel. Light and cheap, used for moderate pressures. Internal coils: extra area inside the vessel, at the cos

Take a 3 m³ vessel, 1.6 m in diameter. A 50 mm conventional jacket has a flow area of about 0.27 m². Twenty m³/h of cooling water flows through it at about 0.02 m/s: barely moving. The jacket-side film coefficient is then only a few hundred kcal/h·m²·°C, set mostly by natural convection. The same 20 m³/h through an 80 NB half-pipe coil (flow area about 0.0024 m²) runs at over 2 m/s, and the film coefficient rises to around 6,500 kcal/h·m²·°C. Agitation nozzles in a conventional jacket, which inject water tangentially to create swirl, give something in between. Try it: change the cooling water flow and compare the overall U for three jacket de

t: Film coefficients and overall U Working level
x: 1/U = 1/hprocess + twall/kwall + Rfouling + 1/hjacket The overall coefficient is limited by the worst resistance. With a slow conventional jacket, the jacket side dominates and U is about 190 kcal/h·m²·°C. With agitation nozzles, U roughly doubles. With a half-pipe coil, the jacket side almost disappears from the sum, and U is limited by the process side and the wall: about 470 kcal/h·m²·°C in this example. Going faster on the jacket side beyond this gains little. For glass-lined vessels, the glass layer (about 1–2 mm, with thermal conductivity around 0.86 kcal/h·m·°C) adds a resistance of the same order as the process film, so U is usually 1

t: Steam, water, brine and thermic fluid Working level
x: Steam: condensing film coefficients are very high, so a conventional jacket is fine. Inlet at the top, condensate out at the bottom through a steam trap. Air and non-condensables must be vented or they blanket the surface. Cooling water and chilled water: velocity matters, as above. Inlet at the bottom so the jacket stays full and air is pushed out at the top. Brine and glycol: more viscous at low temperature, so film coefficients are lower; velocity matters even more. Thermic fluid (hot oil): for temperatures above about 180 °C without high-pressure steam. Lower film coefficients than steam; usually in half-pipe coils.

t: Multi-fluid jackets and practical problems Going deeper
x: Most multi-purpose reactors switch the same jacket between steam, water and brine. That is convenient but causes trouble if not done carefully: Drain and blow out the previous fluid before switching. Water left in a jacket that receives brine dilutes the brine and can freeze; steam into a jacket full of brine causes water hammer. Thermal shock: switching from steam to cold brine on a glass-lined vessel can crack the glass. Respect the manufacturer's temperature-difference limits. See glass-lined reactor care . Fouling: cooling tower water scales jackets over the years. A periodic acid clean of the jacket, done under a permit, can restore a su

Expecting good cooling from water in a conventional jacket with no nozzles. Feeding cooling water from the top and trapping air. Switching utilities without draining the previous fluid. Blaming the glass for slow cooling without checking the jacket side. Never cleaning scaled jackets.
A half-pipe spiral welded to the shell: high velocity and strong.

t: Why is cooling slow in a conventional jacket?
x: Water moves very slowly in the wide annulus, so the film coefficient is low.

t: What overall U can a reactor jacket achieve?
x: About 170–520 kcal/h·m²·°C for stainless, 170–345 for glass-lined.

t: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
s: Why reactions behave differently at plant scale: area to volume, heat-up, mixing, dosing and solids, with a practical tech transfer checklist.
x: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes Scale-up · Technology Transfer · October 2026 The chemist hands over a procedure that works perfectly in a 1-litre flask. The first plant batch takes three times longer, gives a sticky solid that won't filter and misses the impurity limit. Nobody did anything wrong. The chemistry is the same, but almost everything around it has changed. This article explains what changes with scale, why, and how to check it before the first plant batch instead of after. In this article The chemistry stays, the physics changes Basics Heat: the biggest change Basics Mixing and dosing Working level Solids: crystallisation, filtration and drying Working level Time itself Working level The checklist Going deeper Questions people ask The chemistry stays, the physics changes Basics Reaction kinetics, equilibrium and solubility don't depend on the size of the vessel. What does

t: The chemistry stays, the physics changes Basics
s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: Reaction kinetics, equilibrium and solubility don't depend on the size of the vessel. What does depend on size is everything that moves heat and material around: how fast you can heat or cool, how quickly a drop of reagent mixes in, how long a transfer takes, how deep the filter cake is. In the lab these are so fast that they disappear. In the plant they can become slower than the chemistry, and then they control the result. So the question for every step is: in the lab, which was faster, the chemistry or the physics? And will that still be true in the plant?

s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: Make a vessel twice as wide (keeping the same shape) and its volume grows eight times, but its wall area only four times. Volume grows with the cube of size, area with the square. So the cooling area per litre falls as the vessel gets bigger: Area per volume ∝ V^-1/3 From 1 L to 6,000 L: 6,000^1/3 ≈ 18, so about 18 times less jacket area per litre. That has three consequences. Heating and cooling take roughly 18 times longer for the same temperature difference (and plant jackets often have a lower U than a thin glass flask in a bath, so it can be worse). An exotherm that a flask absorbed easily may exceed the plant's cooling. And a quench or

s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: A magnetic stirrer in a flask blends in a few seconds. A plant reactor at a typical power input takes tens of seconds to a few minutes; at the same power per volume, blend time grows roughly with V^2/9, about 7 times from 1 L to 6,000 L, and much more if the agitator is less powerful per litre than the lab. This matters when: a fast reaction competes with a side reaction , and local excess reagent near the feed point favours the impurity. Feed below the surface near the impeller, not onto the surface; two liquid phases need to stay dispersed for the reaction to proceed; solids need to stay suspended , especially dense catalysts or heavy cryst

t: Solids: crystallisation, filtration and drying Working level
s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: Solids cause more scale-up failures than reactions do. Slower cooling in the plant changes the supersaturation profile, so crystals nucleate differently: often finer, sometimes a different polymorph. Fines filter slowly; filtration time grows with the square of the cake depth, and a plant centrifuge or filter-dryer cake is far deeper than a Buchner funnel's. Wash efficiency falls in deep cakes, and drying a deep bed takes much longer than a thin layer in a lab oven. Run the lab crystallisation at the plant's real cooling rate and agitation, and measure filtration resistance (see the filtration article ). Seed at a defined temperature to contr

s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: Everything takes longer in the plant: charging 200 kg of solid by hand, transferring 4,000 L through a 50 mm line, sampling and waiting for the lab, heating, cooling. A reaction mixture that sat for 20 minutes in the lab may sit for 8 hours in the plant, sometimes overnight. If the product, an intermediate or a reagent degrades in that time, the impurity profile changes. Ask the chemists for hold-time studies : keep each key mixture at its process temperature for several times the expected plant duration and measure what happens. It is cheap in the lab and saves batches. On the plant The best technology transfer meetings I've seen include an

s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: Reaction calorimetry for every exothermic step: heat, accumulation, MTSR, gas evolution. DSC/ARC on reaction mixtures, isolated intermediates and residues. Criticality class for each step, and the relief scenario it implies. Flash points, static risk, inerting needs and dust explosion data for powders.

s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: Minimum stir volume and maximum working volume of each vessel at every step, including after distillation. Jacket service (steam, hot water, brine) and the temperatures it can reach. Materials of construction: glass-lined, SS316, Hastelloy; gaskets and seals compatible with every chemical and solvent. Filter or centrifuge area, cake depth and dryer capacity per batch.

s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: Plant heat-up, cool-down and dosing times calculated, and tested in the lab at those times. Order and method of addition: liquid dosing, solid charging, subsurface feed. Hold-time data for every intermediate stage. Sampling points, in-process tests, specifications and lab turnaround time. Solvent recovery: can the recovered solvent be reused, and is there an azeotrope?

s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: Batch record written in plant language, with ranges, not single values. HAZOP or what-if review of the process in the actual equipment. Operator training before the first batch, with the chemist present for the first runs. Effluent and waste: quantities, treatability at the ETP, and any special disposal.

s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: Copying lab addition times into the plant batch record. Assuming the lab crystallisation will filter the same at plant scale. No hold-time data, so a weekend stop becomes a failed batch. Checking that the batch fits the reactor at the start, but not after a distillation or a dilution. Reaction safety data done after the first plant batch instead of before.

t: Why does heat transfer get worse on scale-up?
s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: Area per litre falls as V^-1/3: about 18 times less from 1 L to 6,000 L, so heating and cooling take much longer.

t: What should a scale-up checklist cover?
s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: Safety data, heat, mixing and dosing, solids, equipment fit, materials, sampling, hold times, utilities, recovery, waste and documentation.

t: Should the plant batch match the lab procedure exactly?
s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: The chemistry should; times and addition methods often must change, after testing them in the lab under plant-like conditions.

s: Legal metrology for plants: which weighing instruments need stamping, weighbridge re-verification, and how it differs from GMP calibration.
x: Legal Metrology: Weighbridges and Balances Statutory Compliance · Weights and Measures · October 2026 A plant weighs everything: raw materials at the gate, charges in dispensing, product into drums. Two separate systems check those weighings. Legal metrology, under the Legal Metrology Act, 2009, protects trade; GMP calibration protects product quality. Plants need to satisfy both. It is a general guide, not legal advice; the Act, the rules, your state’s notifications and your own licence conditions always prevail. In this article What legal metrology covers Basics How it differs from GMP calibration Basics Packaged commodities Working level Weighbridge practice Working level Why it matters beyond compliance Going deeper Questions people ask What legal metrology covers Basics Weighing and measuring instruments used in trade , where a quantity decides what is paid or delivered, must be of

Weighing and measuring instruments used in trade , where a quantity decides what is paid or delivered, must be of an approved model, verified and stamped by the state legal metrology department, and re-verified periodically. In a plant this mainly means the weighbridge at the gate and the scales used for invoicing or dispatch. Weighbridges are ordinarily re-verified every twelve months; check your state’s rules for each instrument type.

t: How it differs from GMP calibration Basics
x: GMP requires every balance used for dispensing, in-process checks or QC to be calibrated against traceable standards at a set frequency, with a daily check before use, whether or not it is used in trade. Legal metrology stamping does not replace this, and GMP calibration does not replace stamping. A dispatch scale may need both. See warehouse dispensing and QC lab basics .

Products sold in packaged form to consumers are covered by the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, which set labelling and net quantity requirements. Bulk API sold in drums to other manufacturers is generally treated differently from consumer packs; confirm with the state department how your products are covered.

Keep the verification certificate displayed and the stamp intact. Check zero and use a known test weight or vehicle regularly between verifications. Compare gate weight with the supplier’s invoice; persistent differences point to the weighbridge, the supplier, or losses in transit. Keep the platform clean and the load cells protected from water.

t: Why it matters beyond compliance Going deeper
x: Raw material reconciliation, consumption norms and solvent accounting all start with the gate weight. An unverified weighbridge reading can be challenged by a supplier or customer, and an inaccurate one hides losses. On the plant When the weighbridge and the supplier disagree, weigh a known reference load. It settles the argument in minutes.

Weighbridge re-verification overdue. Assuming GMP calibration covers legal metrology, or the reverse. No checks between annual verifications. Ignoring persistent gate-versus-invoice differences. Repairs to a stamped instrument without re-verification.

t: How often must a weighbridge be re-verified?
x: Ordinarily every twelve months by the state legal metrology department.

t: Does GMP calibration replace legal metrology verification?
x: No. Legal metrology protects trade and is done by the state department; GMP calibration protects quality. A scale used for both purposes needs both.

t: Which law governs weights and measures in India?
x: The Legal Metrology Act, 2009 and its rules, enforced by state legal metrology departments.

s: Statutory testing of hoists, cranes, lifting tackle, pressure vessels and air receivers: competent persons, intervals, registers and safe use.
x: Statutory Testing: Lifting Equipment and Pressure Vessels Statutory Compliance · Equipment · October 2026 Hoists that lift drums to a reactor manhole, chain blocks in maintenance, air receivers and nitrogen buffer vessels all need periodic examination by a competent person. These tests are easy to forget because the equipment seems to work fine until the day it does not. It is a general guide, not legal advice; the Act, the rules, your state’s notifications and your own licence conditions always prevail. In this article Which law applies Basics Lifting equipment Basics Pressure vessels and air receivers Working level Registers Working level Safe use Going deeper Questions people ask Which law applies Basics Under the Factories Act, 1948, lifting machines, chains, ropes and tackle had to be thoroughly examined by a competent person at least once in every 12 months, and hoists and lifts ev

s: Statutory Testing: Lifting Equipment and Pressure Vessels
x: Under the Factories Act, 1948, lifting machines, chains, ropes and tackle had to be thoroughly examined by a competent person at least once in every 12 months, and hoists and lifts every 6 months, with pressure plant examined and tested periodically. The OSH Code, 2020 has replaced the Factories Act, and these requirements now come through the Code and the rules notified by each state; see the new labour codes . Pressure vessels for compressed and liquefied gases above 1,000 litres also fall under PESO’s SMPV(U) Rules, and boilers under the Boilers Act .

s: Statutory Testing: Lifting Equipment and Pressure Vessels
x: Each item has a unique number, its safe working load marked, and a test certificate. Examined by a competent person at the required interval; load tested after repair or modification. Inspected by the user before each use: hooks, safety latches, wire rope and chain wear, brakes, limit switches. Defective slings and tackle removed and destroyed, not set aside.

t: Pressure vessels and air receivers Working level
s: Statutory Testing: Lifting Equipment and Pressure Vessels
x: Pressure vessels are examined internally and externally, and hydrostatically tested at the intervals and pressures set by the applicable rules and design code, by a competent person. Safety valves are tested and set at the vessel’s design pressure or below, see relief valve sizing . Ultrasonic thickness checks track corrosion between tests; see maintenance planning .

s: Statutory Testing: Lifting Equipment and Pressure Vessels
x: Keep one register of all statutory equipment: number, location, safe working load or design pressure, last examination, next due date, certificate reference and the competent person. Put the due dates on the compliance calendar and plan tests into shutdowns.

s: Statutory Testing: Lifting Equipment and Pressure Vessels
x: Most lifting incidents come from use, not equipment: wrong sling angle, overloading, standing under a load, untrained operators. Plan non-routine lifts with a lifting plan and a JSA . On the plant Colour-code lifting tackle by the quarter in which it was last inspected. Anyone can see at a glance whether a sling is in date.

s: Statutory Testing: Lifting Equipment and Pressure Vessels
x: Examinations overdue because nobody owns the register. Uncertified chain blocks brought in by contractors. Safety valves set above design pressure. No load test after repairs. Damaged slings kept “for emergencies”.

t: How often must lifting equipment be examined?
s: Statutory Testing: Lifting Equipment and Pressure Vessels
x: The Factories Act required lifting machines and tackle every 12 months and hoists and lifts every 6 months; the OSH Code rules notified by each state now apply.

t: Who can certify lifting equipment and pressure vessels?
s: Statutory Testing: Lifting Equipment and Pressure Vessels
x: A competent person recognised under the applicable rules.

t: Which pressure vessels fall under PESO?
s: Statutory Testing: Lifting Equipment and Pressure Vessels
x: Vessels storing compressed or liquefied gases above 1,000 litres water capacity, under the SMPV(U) Rules, 2016, with some exclusions.

s: Line sizing basics: recommended velocities, Reynolds number, friction factor, the Darcy equation, fittings and static-safe velocities for solvents.
x: Line Sizing and Pressure Drop Process Design · Fluid Flow · October 2026 Choosing a pipe size looks like a small decision, but it fixes the pump head, the energy bill, whether the pump cavitates, whether a solvent line charges up with static, and whether the line erodes or blocks. Most of it comes down to one number, velocity, and one equation for friction. This article goes through both, with the rules of thumb engineers actually use. In this article Start with velocity Basics Reynolds number: laminar or turbulent Basics Friction loss: the Darcy equation Working level Fittings, valves and equivalent length Working level Special cases: solvents, slurries, viscous liquids, gases Going deeper Questions people ask Start with velocity Basics v = Q / A = 4Q / (π D²) v in m/s, Q in m³/s, D the pipe's inside diameter in m (not the nominal size). Typical design velocities for liquids: Service Ty

v = Q / A = 4Q / (π D²) v in m/s, Q in m³/s, D the pipe's inside diameter in m (not the nominal size). Typical design velocities for liquids: Service Typical velocity Why Pump suction 0.6–1.5 m/s Low friction keeps NPSH available high Pump discharge 1.5–3 m/s Balance of pipe cost and pumping energy Gravity drain 0.3–1 m/s Little head available; avoid running full of vapour Cooling water headers 1.5–2.5 m/s High enough to limit fouling Low-conductivity solvent into a tank ≤ 1 m/s until the inlet is submerged Static charge generation For 20 m³/h of water: 40 NB gives 4.2 m/s (too fast), 50 NB 2.6 m/s (good for a discharge), 80 NB 1.2 m/s (good

t: Reynolds number: laminar or turbulent Basics
x: Re = ρ v D / μ Below about 2,300 the flow is laminar: smooth layers, friction proportional to velocity. Above about 4,000 it is turbulent: eddies, friction roughly proportional to velocity squared. Water at 2.6 m/s in a 50 NB line has Re ≈ 135,000, well into turbulence. A 100 cP oil at the same velocity has Re ≈ 1,200, which is laminar, and behaves very differently.

t: Friction loss: the Darcy equation Working level
x: ΔP = f × (L / D) × ρ v² / 2 f is the Darcy friction factor: 64/Re for laminar flow; for turbulent flow from the Moody chart or the Colebrook or Swamee-Jain equations, depending on Re and the pipe roughness (about 0.045 mm for commercial steel). For 20 m³/h of water in 50 NB steel, f ≈ 0.02 and the loss is about 1.3 bar per 100 m. In 80 NB it falls to about 0.18 bar per 100 m. That is the trade-off: friction falls steeply with diameter (roughly as D^-5 at constant flow), while pipe cost rises with diameter. Velocities of 1.5–3 m/s for pumped liquids sit near the economic optimum for typical plant lengths.

t: Fittings, valves and equivalent length Working level
x: Elbows, tees, valves, strainers and entrances add loss. Two ways to include it: K values: ΔP = K × ρ v²/2 for each fitting. Typical K: standard 90° elbow 0.3–0.75, open gate valve 0.15, open globe valve 6–10, swing check 2, tank entrance 0.5, exit 1. Equivalent length: each fitting adds the friction of a straight length, for example about 30 pipe diameters for an elbow. In compact plant piping, fittings often account for more loss than the straight pipe. A Y-strainer that is half blocked can account for more than everything else together; that's why strainers get differential pressure gauges.

t: Special cases: solvents, slurries, viscous liquids, gases Going deeper
x: Solvents and static: keep low-conductivity solvents at 1 m/s or less into tanks until the fill pipe is submerged, and at most about 7 m/s anywhere. See static electricity . Slurries: keep velocity above the settling velocity of the solids, often 1.5–2.5 m/s, and avoid dead legs and low points where solids collect. Viscous liquids: flow is often laminar and loss rises with viscosity; heat tracing or a larger line can save a lot of pump power. Use a positive displacement pump. Gases and vapours: much higher velocities (10–30 m/s for process gas, lower for vacuum lines where every millibar matters). Vacuum lines from a condenser to the pump shou

Using the nominal size instead of the inside diameter. Sizing pump suction lines like discharge lines. Ignoring fittings and strainers in compact piping. Filling solvent tanks at high velocity through a top nozzle. Forgetting that viscous liquids may be laminar.

t: How do you calculate pressure drop in a pipe?
x: Darcy: ΔP = f × (L/D) × ρv²/2, plus fittings.

s: LOPA basics: scenarios, initiating event frequencies, independent protection layers, tolerable risk targets, and what SIL 1 and SIL 2 really mean.
x: LOPA and SIL Basics Process Safety · Risk Assessment · October 2026 A HAZOP finds a scenario: cooling water fails during dosing and the reactor could run away. Everyone agrees it is serious. But is the alarm enough? Do we need a trip? How reliable must it be? LOPA, layer of protection analysis, answers those questions with simple arithmetic instead of opinion. This article shows how it works and what a SIL rating actually means. In this article The idea: layers like slices of cheese Basics What counts as a protection layer Basics The LOPA arithmetic Working level Closing the gap: SIF and SIL Working level Keeping the SIL real Going deeper Questions people ask The idea: layers like slices of cheese Basics No single safeguard is perfect. The alarm might be ignored, the trip valve might stick, the rupture disc might be the wrong size. A plant is safe when there are enough independent layers

t: The idea: layers like slices of cheese Basics
x: No single safeguard is perfect. The alarm might be ignored, the trip valve might stick, the rupture disc might be the wrong size. A plant is safe when there are enough independent layers that the chance of all of them failing together is very small. Picture slices of Swiss cheese: an accident happens only when the holes line up. LOPA puts numbers on this. Start with how often the cause happens, multiply by the chance each layer fails when needed, and compare the result with what the company accepts as tolerable.

t: What counts as a protection layer Basics
x: Only independent protection layers (IPLs) get credit. A safeguard is an IPL only if it is: Independent of the initiating event and of the other layers. A high-temperature alarm on the same sensor as the control loop that failed is not independent. Effective : able to stop the scenario on its own, in time, if it works. An operator needs a clear alarm and enough time, often at least 10 minutes, to act. Auditable : tested and maintained, with records. Typical credits, as probability of failure on demand (PFD): Layer Typical PFD Risk reduction Alarm with operator response (enough time, clear procedure) 0.1 10× Basic process control system functio

Frequency of outcome = initiating event frequency × PFD1 × PFD2 × … × conditional modifiers Conditional modifiers include the probability that someone is present (occupancy) or that a release ignites. Use them with care and only where justified. Take the scenario: cooling water fails during exothermic dosing (0.1 per year, a typical value for a utility failure), leading to a runaway that could rupture the reactor and kill an operator. The company's tolerable frequency for a single fatality is 10^-5 per year. High-temperature alarm, operator stops dosing: × 0.1 Area manned half the time: × 0.5 Result: 0.1 × 0.1 × 0.5 = 5 × 10^-3 per year, 500

t: Closing the gap: SIF and SIL Working level
x: When the existing layers don't reach the target, the usual answer is a safety instrumented function (SIF) : its own sensor, logic solver and final element, separate from the control system. Its safety integrity level (SIL) is set by the risk reduction still needed: Gap up to 10×: no SIF needed if another IPL can do it; otherwise SIL 1 is ample. Gap of 10–100×: SIL 1. Gap of 100–1,000×: SIL 2. Gap above 1,000×: SIL 3 is possible but rare and expensive in chemical plants; usually it is better to change the process (smaller batch, slower dosing, a different solvent). SIL is a property of the whole function, not of a transmitter. A SIL 2 sensor c

t: Keeping the SIL real Going deeper
x: Proof testing at the interval the calculation assumed, testing the whole loop from sensor to valve, with results recorded. Bypass management : a bypassed SIF provides no protection. Bypasses need permits, compensating measures and a time limit. Demand tracking : if the SIF trips more often than the LOPA assumed, the initiating frequency was wrong and the analysis must be redone. Management of change for set points, logic and hardware. See management of change . On the plant The most useful LOPA output is often not the SIL number but the list of layers you were already relying on. Each one becomes a safety-critical element with an owner and a

Giving credit to two layers that share a sensor or valve. Counting procedures and training as protection layers. Using a fire-sized relief valve as a layer for a runaway. Specifying a SIL and never proof testing the loop. Stacking optimistic conditional modifiers to make the numbers work.
A method that multiplies an initiating frequency by the failure probability of each independent layer and compares it with a target.

t: What is the difference between SIL 1 and SIL 2?
x: SIL 1 reduces risk 10–100×; SIL 2, 100–1,000×.

t: Can an operator alarm be a protection layer?
x: Yes, usually a 10× credit, if independent and with enough time to act.

t: Maintenance Planning: Preventive, Predictive, MTBF and MTTR
s: Maintenance planning for chemical plants: breakdown, preventive and predictive maintenance, criticality, MTBF, MTTR, availability and spares.
x: Maintenance Planning: Preventive, Predictive, MTBF and MTTR Plant Departments · Maintenance · October 2026 Maintenance decides whether the plant runs when production needs it. Good maintenance is mostly invisible: the planned job done on time, the spare on the shelf, the bearing changed before it seized. This article covers the strategies and the few numbers that tell you if they are working. In this article Breakdown, preventive and predictive Basics Criticality decides the strategy Basics MTBF, MTTR and availability Working level Repeated failures Working level Spares, safety and GMP Going deeper Questions people ask Breakdown, preventive and predictive Basics Breakdown (run to failure): fix it when it fails. Acceptable for cheap, non-critical items with a spare available. Preventive (time-based): service at fixed intervals or running hours: lubrication, seal and gasket changes, filter

s: Maintenance Planning: Preventive, Predictive, MTBF and MTTR
x: Breakdown (run to failure): fix it when it fails. Acceptable for cheap, non-critical items with a spare available. Preventive (time-based): service at fixed intervals or running hours: lubrication, seal and gasket changes, filter changes, calibration. Predictive or condition-based: measure condition and act when it deteriorates: vibration on pumps and agitators, thermography of electrical panels, oil analysis on gearboxes, ultrasonic thickness on vessels and lines.

s: Maintenance Planning: Preventive, Predictive, MTBF and MTTR
x: Rank each asset by the consequence of its failure: safety and environment, product quality, production loss, and repair cost. Critical items (the only reactor for a bottleneck step, the brine chiller, the main vacuum pump, the scrubber fan) get condition monitoring, strategic spares and priority. Low-criticality items can run to failure. This puts effort where it matters.

t: MTBF, MTTR and availability Working level
s: Maintenance Planning: Preventive, Predictive, MTBF and MTTR
x: MTBF (mean time between failures) = total operating time ÷ number of failures. MTTR (mean time to repair) = total repair time ÷ number of repairs. Availability = MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR). Example: a pump runs 4,000 hours in a period with 4 failures and 32 hours of total repair time. MTBF = 1,000 h, MTTR = 8 h, availability = 1,000 ÷ 1,008 = 99.2 %. Rising MTBF shows reliability is improving; falling MTTR shows the repair process (spares, skills, access) is improving.

s: Maintenance Planning: Preventive, Predictive, MTBF and MTTR
x: The same equipment failing again and again is the best place to invest effort. Record each failure with its cause, not just “seal replaced”. Common root causes in chemical plants: pumps running far from their best efficiency point, wrong seal flush plan, misalignment, corrosion from the wrong MOC, and dry running. See pump and seal troubleshooting and glass-lined reactor care .

t: Spares, safety and GMP Going deeper
s: Maintenance Planning: Preventive, Predictive, MTBF and MTTR
x: Keep critical spares based on lead time and consequence of failure, not just usage. All work follows permit to work and isolation . In GMP areas, maintenance on product-contact equipment is recorded in the equipment log, may need change control if anything is changed, and the equipment is cleaned and released by QA before use. Calibration of critical instruments follows a schedule with out-of-tolerance results investigated for impact on batches made since the last good calibration. On the plant Put the five worst bad actors, the equipment with the most breakdown hours last quarter, on the wall of the maintenance office with their MTBF. Fixing

s: Maintenance Planning: Preventive, Predictive, MTBF and MTTR
x: Same preventive schedule for every asset regardless of criticality. Failures recorded without a cause. Critical spares with long lead times not stocked. Calibration failures not checked for batch impact. Equipment returned to production without cleaning and release.

s: Maintenance Planning: Preventive, Predictive, MTBF and MTTR

s: Management of change in process plants: what counts as a change, temporary and organisational changes, MOC steps to PSSR, and Flixborough lessons.
x: Management of Change (MOC) Process Safety · Safety Management · October 2026 A plant that is safe on the day it is commissioned does not stay safe by itself. Every week someone swaps a valve, changes a set point, tries a new supplier or adds a hose “for now”. Each change on its own looks harmless. Management of change is the habit of stopping for a moment before each one and asking: what else does this affect? This article explains what counts as a change, how a good MOC works, and why it fails. In this article Why changes cause accidents Basics What counts as a change Basics The MOC steps Working level What a good review asks Working level Temporary, emergency and organisational changes Going deeper Flixborough: a temporary pipe Going deeper Questions people ask Why changes cause accidents Basics When a plant is designed, engineers think through how each part interacts with the others:

When a plant is designed, engineers think through how each part interacts with the others: the relief valve is sized for the nitrogen regulator, the pump for the line, the trip for the reaction. Those links are rarely written on the equipment. When one part is changed without looking at the links, the plant quietly loses protection it used to have, and nobody notices until the day it is needed. Investigations of major accidents keep finding the same thing: a change made with good intentions, by competent people, without anyone asking what else it affected.

t: What counts as a change Basics
x: Anything that alters the plant, the process or the way it is run, compared with what was reviewed and approved. That includes: Equipment and piping: new or modified equipment, a different material, a bigger pump, removed or added valves. Process conditions: temperatures, pressures, dosing times, batch sizes, beyond the approved range. Chemistry and materials: new solvents, reagents, suppliers or grades; a new product in an existing reactor. Controls and safeguards: set points, alarm limits, interlock logic, bypasses, relief devices. Procedures: changed sequences, skipped steps, new cleaning methods. Organisation: fewer operators per shift, a

Request: describe the change, why it is needed and what it replaces. Attach marked-up drawings. Classify: is it in kind? Minor or major? Permanent or temporary? The class decides how deep the review goes. Hazard review: a checklist for small changes, a what-if or HAZOP for larger ones, and reaction safety data for chemistry changes. Approve: by people with the authority and the knowledge, from production, engineering and safety, and quality where product is affected. Implement: build or change it as approved, not as convenient on the day. Pre-startup safety review (PSSR): walk it down before use. Built as approved? Drawings, SOPs and batch re

t: What a good review asks Working level
x: Does it change the relief scenarios or the relief load? (A bigger nitrogen regulator, a higher steam pressure.) See relief valve sizing . Does it change the reaction hazard : heat, gas, accumulation, MTSR? Does it remove or weaken a safeguard , even temporarily? Does it bring a new ignition source , flammable atmosphere or static risk? Are the materials compatible: pressure rating, temperature, corrosion, gaskets? Who needs to know? Procedures, drawings and training to update. On the plant The best MOC systems are quick for small changes and thorough for big ones. If filling in the form for a gasket takes a week, people stop filling it in, an

t: Temporary, emergency and organisational changes Going deeper
x: Temporary changes need the same hazard review as permanent ones, plus an expiry date and a named person responsible for removing them. Temporary hoses, bypasses and jumpers have a way of becoming permanent. Emergency changes , made at night to keep a batch safe, can be approved by a shift manager under a short procedure, but must go through the full review within a defined time, typically a day or two. Organisational changes are the most often missed: cutting a shift crew, outsourcing maintenance, or losing the one engineer who understood an old process. Ask the same question: which safeguards depended on these people or this knowledge?

t: Flixborough: a temporary pipe Going deeper
x: On 1 June 1974, at the Nypro plant in Flixborough, England, a cracked cyclohexane reactor was removed from a train of six. To keep production going, the engineers bridged the gap with a 20-inch temporary pipe with bellows at each end, supported on scaffolding. No design calculation was done for the bellows or the pipe under pressure, and no qualified engineer reviewed it. Two months later the bypass failed, releasing tonnes of cyclohexane, and the vapour cloud exploded. Twenty-eight people died and the site was destroyed. The investigation's lesson shaped modern MOC: a modification must be designed and reviewed to the same standard as the ori

Calling a different specification “like for like”. Temporary changes with no end date. Changing set points and alarm limits without MOC. MOC closed before drawings and SOPs are updated. Never applying MOC to staffing or organisational changes.

t: What is a replacement in kind?
x: A replacement that meets the original specification exactly. Anything different, even if better, is a change.
Yes, with the same review, an end date and a check that the plant is restored.

t: What is a pre-startup safety review?
x: A check before use that the change was built as approved and that drawings, procedures, training and actions are complete.
