x: Material and Energy Balance for Batch Plants Plant Engineering · Fundamentals · October 2026 Every chemical engineer learns material balances in the first year, then meets a real plant where the numbers never add up. 3,800 kg go into the reactor and only 3,670 kg come out the other end, and nobody can say where the rest went. Those missing kilograms are money, solvent emissions and sometimes a safety problem. This article shows how to do a balance that is useful on a real batch plant, and how to find what is missing. In this article The idea: what goes in comes out Basics Draw the boundary first Basics A batch mass balance Working level Component balances: following the solvent Working level The energy balance of a distillation Working level Finding the missing kilograms Going deeper Questions people ask The idea: what goes in comes out Basics Mass is conserved. For any part of a plant o

t: The idea: what goes in comes out Basics
s: Material and Energy Balance for Batch Plants
x: Mass is conserved. For any part of a plant over any period: In - Out + Generated - Consumed = Accumulated For total mass, nothing is generated or consumed by a chemical reaction, so for a complete batch (empty to empty) the balance is simply In = Out . For a single chemical, reactions do create and destroy it, so its balance needs the generation and consumption terms from the stoichiometry. Energy follows the same rule: heat in from steam, plus heat released by reaction, equals heat out to cooling water and surroundings, plus the change in the batch's own heat content.

s: Material and Energy Balance for Batch Plants
x: Most balance arguments are really arguments about the boundary. Before writing any numbers, draw a box on the process flow diagram and decide: What is inside: one reactor, a whole stage, or the whole plant? Over what period: one batch, a campaign, a month? Monthly balances smooth out batch-to-batch hold-up. Every stream crossing the line: raw materials, solvents, washes, nitrogen, water, steam condensate, vents, samples, effluent, product, residues. The streams people forget are almost always the small ones crossing the boundary sideways: the line wash, the sample, the vent to the scrubber, the water used to rinse the filter.

t: A batch mass balance Working level
s: Material and Energy Balance for Batch Plants
x: Take a reaction stage. Into the reactor go 500 kg of starting material, 300 kg of reagent, 400 kg of caustic lye, 2,000 kg of toluene and 600 kg of water: 3,800 kg in total. Out come 520 kg of dry product, 1,850 kg of recovered toluene, 1,160 kg of aqueous layer to the ETP and 140 kg of distillation residue: 3,670 kg. Closure = total out / total in × 100 = 3,670 / 3,800 = 96.6 % 130 kg unaccounted per batch. A batch balance closing within about 97–103 % is good, given weighing and level-gauge accuracy. Below that, something is being missed or lost. Try it: change how much toluene is recovered and how much dry product is made. Watch the unacco

To reduce consumption you need a balance on each important component, and toluene is the obvious one here: In: 2,000 kg charged (fresh plus recovered). Out: 1,850 kg recovered, plus toluene dissolved in the aqueous layer (toluene's solubility in water is about 0.05 %, so under 1 kg), plus toluene in the wet cake before drying, plus toluene in the residue, plus vapour lost through vents and vacuum. Heat needed = mbatch × cp × (Tboil - Tstart) + mdistilled × λsolvent Steam = heat needed / λsteam × (1 + losses) Distilling 1,850 kg of toluene (λ ≈ 86 kcal/kg at atmospheric pressure) takes 1,850 × 86 ≈ 1,59,100 kcal of latent heat. With steam at about 3.5 barg (λ ≈ 509 kcal/kg) that is 313 kg of steam, plus roughly 10–15 % for losses and heating the vessel: about 360 kg. Calibrate before chasing losses. Check hold-up. A batch balance is only exact from empty to empty. Material left in the reactor, filter, lines and dryer from one batch shows up in the next. Use campaign balances to average it out. List the unrecorded streams. Line washes, filter washes, samples, spillage, nitrogen sweeping vapour to the vent. Look at the vents. Every vessel that breathes during charging, heating or nitrogen purging carries solvent vapour out. Wit

s: Choosing materials of construction: SS304 and SS316L, duplex, Hastelloy, titanium, glass-lined steel, PTFE and FRP, corrosion types, PREN and gaskets.
x: Materials of Construction Plant Engineering · Materials · October 2026 “Use SS316, it’s stainless.” Many corrosion failures start with that sentence. Stainless steel resists a lot, but chlorides, hot caustic and reducing acids can destroy it quickly, while cheap carbon steel happily holds strong sulphuric acid. This article explains how the common plant materials behave, the forms of corrosion that catch people out, and how to choose. In this article The common materials Basics Forms of corrosion Basics Choosing by service Working level Gaskets, seals and linings Working level Checking and monitoring Going deeper Questions people ask The common materials Basics Carbon steel: cheap and strong. Fine for neutral solvents, steam, strong sulphuric acid at ambient, caustic at moderate temperature. Rusts in water and dilute acids. SS304 / SS316L: chromium forms a thin passive oxide film that pr

Carbon steel: cheap and strong. Fine for neutral solvents, steam, strong sulphuric acid at ambient, caustic at moderate temperature. Rusts in water and dilute acids. SS304 / SS316L: chromium forms a thin passive oxide film that protects the steel. Molybdenum in 316 improves resistance to chlorides. “L” means low carbon, which avoids corrosion at welds. Duplex stainless (2205): stronger and much more resistant to chloride stress-corrosion cracking than 316L. Nickel alloys (Hastelloy C-276, C-22): resist chlorides, many reducing acids and mixed acid streams. Expensive, used where stainless fails. Titanium: excellent in chlorides, wet chlorine a

General corrosion: even thinning, predictable from corrosion rate tables and coupons. See the corrosion coupon calculator . Pitting: local holes where the passive film breaks down, typically caused by chlorides. Can perforate a vessel while the rest looks perfect. The pitting resistance equivalent number, PREN = %Cr + 3.3 × %Mo + 16 × %N, ranks alloys: about 24 for 316L, 35 for duplex 2205, over 40 for super-duplex and Hastelloy. Stress-corrosion cracking (SCC): cracks from the combination of tensile stress and a specific environment, such as chlorides with 304/316 above about 50–60 °C, or hot caustic with carbon steel. Sudden and dangerous.

Try it: pick a service and see how the common materials generally behave. This is a first guide only; concentration, temperature and impurities change the answer. Selection should follow the worst condition the equipment will see, not the normal one: the cleaning cycle, the start-up with concentrated acid, the hot spot near the steam inlet, the chloride left from a previous product. In a multi-purpose plant, list every chemical the equipment may meet, including cleaning agents, and check them all. The materials compatibility tool helps with that list.

t: Gaskets, seals and linings Working level
x: A vessel in Hastelloy with the wrong gasket still leaks. Elastomers are usually the weakest link: EPDM: good for water, steam, dilute acids and alkali; swells in hydrocarbons and oils. Viton (FKM): good for hydrocarbons and many acids; poor in ketones, esters and amines. FFKM (perfluoroelastomer): resists almost everything; expensive. PTFE gaskets resist chemicals but creep under load; use filled or expanded PTFE and the right bolt torque.

Corrosion coupons in critical services, removed and weighed on a schedule. Ultrasonic thickness surveys on vessels and piping, compared with the minimum thickness from design. Material certificates and positive material identification (PMI) for alloy parts, so a carbon steel fitting doesn't end up in a Hastelloy line. Review materials through MOC whenever a new chemical or cleaning agent is introduced. On the plant Keep the failed part. A pitted gasket face, a cracked weld or a thinned elbow tells a corrosion specialist almost exactly what happened. Thrown into the scrap bin, it tells nobody anything.

Assuming stainless steel resists chlorides. Choosing material for the process but not for cleaning chemicals. Glass-lined vessels exposed to hot caustic. Elastomers chosen without checking every solvent. No PMI on alloy spares.

t: Why does stainless steel corrode in chloride solutions?
x: Chlorides break the passive film, causing pitting and stress-corrosion cracking.
%Cr + 3.3×%Mo + 16×%N; about 24 for 316L, 35 for duplex 2205.
Only cold and dilute; hot alkali dissolves glass.

s: MES and electronic batch records for pharma and fine-chemical plants: what MES does, paper vs eBMR, review by exception, Part 11 and Annex 11, and rollout.
x: MES and Electronic Batch Records Digitalization and AI · Plant Engineering · October 2026 AI basics AI plant examples Predictive maintenance Soft sensors Digital twins GenAI for SOPs and deviations Process historian MES and eBMR OEE in batch plants OT cybersecurity Plant KPI dashboard Digital business case Paper batch records catch mistakes days after they happen, during review. An electronic batch record stops many of them at the moment of entry, and lets QA review only what went wrong. This article explains what an MES does, how an eBMR compares with paper, how review by exception works (with a demo), the Part 11 and Annex 11 expectations, and how an implementation usually goes. In this article What an MES does Basics Paper BMR vs electronic batch record Basics Review by exception (demo) Working level Part 11, Annex 11 and data integrity Working level How an eBMR project goes Going dee

A manufacturing execution system (MES) runs production at ISA-95 level 3: between the DCS that controls equipment and the ERP that plans orders and stock. In a pharma or fine-chemical plant its core is the electronic batch record (eBMR or EBR) : the master recipe becomes a guided, step-by-step electronic workflow, and the executed record is captured as the batch runs. MES function What it replaces or adds Electronic batch record Paper BMR: instructions, entries, signatures, calculations Weighing and dispensing Hand-written weights; adds scale integration, material and container checks Material genealogy Tracing which raw material lots went in

t: Paper BMR vs electronic batch record Basics
x: Paper Electronic Wrong entry or calculation Found at review, days later Blocked or flagged at the moment of entry Missed step or signature Found at review The workflow will not move on without it Weights Written by hand Read from the balance, with container and lot checks Review Every page, every entry Review by exception: only flagged entries Data for analysis Locked on paper Searchable, comparable across batches Pharmaceutical Technology reports typical paper-based batch release of 10 to 40 days, an average of 48 hours to review a single batch report, and electronic batch records cutting manual data-entry time by at least 60%.

ISPE defines review by exception as an approach in which manufacturing and quality data are screened to present or report only critical process exceptions. Reviewers spend their time on what went wrong, not on confirming hundreds of entries that were checked automatically when they were made.

t: Review by exception: what the reviewer sees
x: An illustrative batch record with made-up values. Switch between full review and exceptions only. Full record Exceptions only

t: Part 11, Annex 11 and data integrity Working level
x: 21 CFR Part 11 (US) expects validated systems, secure computer-generated time-stamped audit trails, controlled access, and electronic signatures linked to their records. FDA’s 2003 scope guidance takes a risk-based view of which records need which controls. EU GMP Annex 11 covers computerised systems in the EU, and was being revised alongside the new draft Annex 22 on AI in 2025. Data integrity : FDA’s 2018 guidance expects records to be attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original or a true copy, and accurate.

t: How an eBMR project goes Going deeper
x: Fix the process on paper first. Harmonise BMRs across products; an electronic copy of a messy BMR is a messy eBMR. User requirements. Scope, interfaces, which checks are automatic, what counts as an exception (see URS to handover ). Master recipe design with production, QA and IT together: this is most of the work. Interfaces to ERP, balances, LIMS, DCS and historian. Validation under your computerised-system procedure, risk-based. Pilot one product, then roll out. Train operators on the floor, not in a classroom.

Copying the paper BMR screen by screen, including steps that only existed because paper could not check itself. Defining “exceptions” so widely that every batch has hundreds, and review by exception becomes full review again. No interface to balances or LIMS, so operators still type numbers in. Underestimating master recipe work and operator training.

t: What is the difference between MES and ERP?
x: ERP plans the business: orders, stock, purchasing, costs. MES runs production on the floor: batch records, dispensing, equipment status and genealogy. They exchange orders and results through interfaces.
An approach, defined by ISPE, in which manufacturing and quality data are screened so that reviewers see only critical process exceptions, instead of reading every entry of the batch record.

t: Is an electronic batch record required by Schedule M or FDA?
x: No regulation requires electronic records, but if you use them they must meet electronic-record expectations such as 21 CFR Part 11 in the US and EU GMP Annex 11, with validation, audit trails and access control.

x: Mixing Scale-up: From the Lab Flask to the Plant Reactor Chemical Engineering · Mixing · Updated October 2026 A reaction that worked perfectly in a 2-litre flask at 300 rpm is moving to a 20 KL reactor. What speed should the plant agitator run at? There is no single right answer, because you cannot keep everything the same when you make a vessel a thousand times bigger. You have to choose what matters most for your process, and accept that other things will change. This article explains the choice. t: What an agitator actually does Basics
s: Mixing Scale-up: From the Lab Flask to the Plant Reactor
x: An impeller does two jobs at once. It pumps : it moves the whole batch around the vessel so every part passes through the impeller zone regularly. And it shears : right at the blade tips the liquid is torn apart into small eddies, which breaks up droplets, disperses gas and, unfortunately, can break crystals. Different impellers split their effort differently. A Rushton (flat-blade) turbine throws liquid outwards and makes a lot of shear: good for gas dispersion. A pitched-blade turbine or hydrofoil pushes liquid down and around: good for blending and keeping solids suspended with less shear. An anchor scrapes the wall at low speed: good for

s: Mixing Scale-up: From the Lab Flask to the Plant Reactor
x: Reynolds number Re = ρ N D² / μ turbulent above about 10,000; laminar below about 10 Tip speed = π D N a measure of the shear at the blade tips Power P = Np ρ N³ D⁵ Np is the impeller's power number Power per volume P/V how hard the whole batch is being worked N is speed in revolutions per second and D the impeller diameter. Two things in the power equation are worth noticing: power rises with the cube of speed and the fifth power of diameter. Double the impeller diameter at the same speed and you need 32 times the power. That is why plant agitators run so much slower than lab stirrers. t: Worked example: 0.1 m to 1.0 m impeller Working level
s: Mixing Scale-up: From the Lab Flask to the Plant Reactor
x: A lab vessel (0.3 m diameter) with a 0.1 m Rushton turbine at 300 rpm, water-like liquid. The plant vessel is ten times bigger in every dimension: a 3 m tank with a 1.0 m impeller, about a thousand times the volume. Constant P/V: N2 = 300 × (0.1/1.0)^2/3 ≈ 65 rpm Constant tip speed: N2 = 300 × (0.1/1.0) = 30 rpm Constant Re: N2 = 300 × (0.1/1.0)² = 3 rpm The same lab result gives 65, 30 or 3 rpm. At 65 rpm the plant agitator draws about 6 kW (a thousand times the lab's 6 W). At 30 rpm it draws only 0.6 kW, but the batch is worked ten times less hard per cubic metre. At 3 rpm, nothing is really mixing. Try it: the impellers turn at their real

t: Which rule for which process Working level
s: Mixing Scale-up: From the Lab Flask to the Plant Reactor
x: Crystallisation and fragile solids: constant tip speed. Crystal breakage happens at the blade tips. Keep the tip speed the same as the lab (or below about 3–5 m/s) and accept slower blending. Blending, heat transfer, reactions with dosing, liquid–liquid or gas–liquid dispersion: constant P/V. These depend on how much energy goes into the whole batch. Keeping solids suspended: the just-suspended speed (Zwietering) scales as roughly D^-0.85, between the two rules. Constant P/V usually keeps solids off the bottom; constant tip speed may not. Check it. Viscous batches (laminar flow): scale-up is about keeping the whole batch moving, usually with

t: What changes no matter which rule you pick Going deeper
s: Mixing Scale-up: From the Lab Flask to the Plant Reactor
x: Blend time gets longer. In turbulent flow, the time to blend to 95 % uniformity is inversely proportional to speed for the same geometry. In the example, the lab blends in about 5 s; the plant takes about 25 s at constant P/V and about 55 s at constant tip speed. If your chemistry is fast compared with that (a quick neutralisation, a fast addition of a reactive reagent), the plant will see local hot spots or over-concentrated zones the lab never did. Slow the addition, or add near the impeller where mixing is most intense. Heat transfer area per volume falls. The vessel's surface area grows with diameter squared, its volume with diameter cube

s: Mixing Scale-up: From the Lab Flask to the Plant Reactor
x: Using one rule by habit without asking what the process actually needs. Comparing speeds between different impeller types as if their power numbers were the same. Scaling mixing correctly and forgetting that heat removal per volume fell tenfold. Ignoring the fill level: a reactor run at 30 % fill has the impeller near the surface and very different flow.

t: What are the main mixing scale-up rules?
s: Mixing Scale-up: From the Lab Flask to the Plant Reactor
x: For geometrically similar vessels, N2 = N1 × (D1/D2)^n, with n = 1 for constant tip speed, n = 2/3 for constant P/V (turbulent) and n = 2 for constant Reynolds number.

t: Which scale-up rule should I use?
s: Mixing Scale-up: From the Lab Flask to the Plant Reactor
x: Constant tip speed when shear damages the product, constant P/V when blending, heat transfer or mass transfer control the result. If you are unsure, calculate both and check what each does to the property you care about.

t: Why does blend time increase on scale-up?
s: Mixing Scale-up: From the Lab Flask to the Plant Reactor
x: Blend time in turbulent flow is inversely proportional to speed. Plant agitators turn much slower, so blending takes longer: about five times longer at constant P/V for a tenfold increase in impeller diameter.

x: MSIHC Rules: Emergency Planning for Chemical Plants Statutory Compliance · Process Safety · October 2026 The MSIHC Rules, 1989, made under the Environment (Protection) Act after Bhopal, apply to sites that handle listed hazardous chemicals above set quantities. Most solvent-heavy pharma sites cross at least one threshold. The rules require a site to know its major accident hazards, plan for them and practise. It is a general guide, not legal advice; the Act, the rules, your state’s notifications and your own licence conditions always prevail. In this article Does it apply to your site? Basics Safety report and safety audit Working level On-site emergency plan Basics Mock drills and the off-site plan Working level Major accident reporting Going deeper Questions people ask Does it apply to your site? Basics The rules list hazardous chemicals in their schedules, with threshold quantities fo

t: Does it apply to your site? Basics
s: MSIHC Rules: Emergency Planning for Chemical Plants
x: The rules list hazardous chemicals in their schedules, with threshold quantities for isolated storage and for industrial activity. Flammable liquids, toxic gases such as chlorine and ammonia, and many reactive chemicals are covered. Add up the maximum quantity of each listed chemical that can be on site, including tanks, drums and process inventory, and compare with the thresholds. Sites above the lower thresholds have duties such as identifying hazards and preparing an on-site emergency plan; sites above the higher thresholds have additional duties such as a safety report.

t: Safety report and safety audit Working level
s: MSIHC Rules: Emergency Planning for Chemical Plants
x: Sites in the higher tier prepare a safety report in the format the rules set, before starting the activity, describing the chemicals, processes, major accident hazards and controls. A safety audit is carried out and its report updated once a year. The tools are the ones used every day in process safety: HAZOP , LOPA , consequence analysis and HIRA .

s: MSIHC Rules: Emergency Planning for Chemical Plants
x: The occupier prepares an on-site emergency plan covering the credible major accidents (fire, explosion, toxic release), the emergency organisation (site main controller, incident controller, teams), alarms, assembly points, emergency control centre, fire and medical resources, communication with outside agencies and the public, and shutdown procedures. The site head is usually the site main controller; see the role of a site head .

t: Mock drills and the off-site plan Working level
s: MSIHC Rules: Emergency Planning for Chemical Plants
x: The on-site plan is rehearsed through mock drills every six months , with the findings recorded and acted on. The district authority prepares the off-site emergency plan for incidents that can affect people outside the fence and rehearses it at least once a year; the occupier supplies the information it needs. Persons likely to be affected by a major accident must be given information about the hazards and what to do.

s: MSIHC Rules: Emergency Planning for Chemical Plants
x: A major accident must be reported to the concerned authority (for factories, the Chief Inspector of Factories) within 48 hours, followed by a detailed report in the prescribed schedule. The investigation and the lessons should feed back into the safety report, the emergency plan and the management of change system. On the plant Run at least one mock drill a year at night or on a holiday, with the site head and fire team leaders absent. A plan that only works when everyone is on site is not an emergency plan.

It is a general guide, not legal advice: state rules are still being finalised, so confirm details with HR or a legal adviser. Industrial Relations Code, 2020: trade unions, standing orders, disputes, strikes, layoffs, retrenchment and closure. Code on Social Security, 2020: provident fund, ESI, gratuity, maternity benefit and coverage for gig and platform workers. s: The New Labour Codes: What Changes for Plants
x: The codes use one definition of wages for all statutory purposes. Allowances above 50 % of total remuneration are added back into wages. In practice, a salary structure with a small basic pay and large allowances now has a larger wage base for provident fund, gratuity, leave encashment, bonus and overtime. HR and finance usually need to restructure pay; employees may see a change in take-home pay against higher retirement benefits.

s: The New Labour Codes: What Changes for Plants
x: The 48-hour weekly limit remains; state rules can allow longer daily shifts within it. Overtime is paid at twice the ordinary rate of wages. Women may work in all establishments and on night shifts, with their consent and with the safety measures the rules require. Eligibility for annual leave with wages comes after 180 days of work in a year, instead of 240. For shift planning, check the state rules for daily hours, spread-over and rest intervals before changing a shift pattern. The HR article shows how to work out manpower for a round-the-clock post.

s: The New Labour Codes: What Changes for Plants
x: Appointment letters with the prescribed details are compulsory for every employee. Fixed-term employees get the same statutory benefits as permanent employees doing similar work, and become eligible for gratuity after one year of service instead of five. Social security coverage extends to gig and platform workers, with detailed schemes to be notified.

Process safety tools such as HIRA and JSA , permit to work and HAZOP remain the way a site actually meets these duties.

s: Where operating cost goes in an API plant and how to cut it: yield, solvent recovery, cycle time, utilities, effluent and measured cost projects.
x: Reducing OPEX in API Plants Plant Departments · Operational Excellence · October 2026 Operating expenditure decides whether a product makes money. In API manufacturing most of it is fixed by raw materials and yield, but the conversion cost, everything the plant spends to turn materials into product, is where engineers have the most control. This article shows where to look. In this article The cost buckets Basics Yield and recovery first Basics Cycle time Working level Utilities and effluent Working level Running cost projects Going deeper Questions people ask The cost buckets Basics Raw materials: reagents, starting materials, catalysts and solvents, net of recovery. Usually the largest share. Utilities: steam, power, chilled water and brine, cooling water, nitrogen, compressed air. Effluent and waste: ETP operation, MEE and ATFD steam, incineration and hazardous waste disposal. Manpowe

Raw materials: reagents, starting materials, catalysts and solvents, net of recovery. Usually the largest share. Utilities: steam, power, chilled water and brine, cooling water, nitrogen, compressed air. Effluent and waste: ETP operation, MEE and ATFD steam, incineration and hazardous waste disposal. Manpower, maintenance and overheads spread over batches; so a shorter cycle time lowers cost per kg. The consumption norms and cost per kg article shows how to build the cost sheet.

One percent of yield on an expensive step is usually worth more than any utility project. Look for losses in mother liquors (can a second crop or recycle recover product?), in transfers and filters, in drying (dust), and in rework. Solvent is the next lever: a recovery rate going from 85 % to 92 % cuts fresh solvent purchase by about half of what it was. See solvent recovery troubleshooting .

If a plant is sold out, every hour removed from the bottleneck step is extra output at almost no cost. Typical gains: faster heat-up and cool-down with better utility temperatures, parallel operations, shorter filtration by changing the crystallisation, removing waiting for QC by faster in-process methods. The debottlenecking article covers the method.

Steam: condensate recovery, trap maintenance, insulation, right pressure for the duty ( steam system efficiency ). Chilling: use cooling tower water or chilled water before brine; each lower level costs more power per kcal ( chillers and VAM ). Power: variable speed drives on pumps and fans, leaks in compressed air ( compressed air and nitrogen ). Effluent: reduce load at source ( ETP load reduction ).

A simple structure keeps cost work honest: a baseline from at least several months of actual data; an idea list with estimated saving, investment and effort; a quality and regulatory check (a change in solvent, vendor or process step needs change control and may need a filing); a trial; and a measured result against the baseline. Payback = investment ÷ annual saving. Track realised savings, not promised ones, and revisit the norms so the gain does not drift away. On the plant Before starting a cost project, write down the cost per kg from the books and from your own calculation. If they disagree by more than a few percent, find out why first;

Chasing small utility savings while yield losses go unnoticed. Counting savings that were never measured. Changing solvent or vendor without change control. Improving a step that is not the bottleneck. Letting norms drift back after a project ends.
Everything spent to turn raw materials into product: utilities, manpower, maintenance, effluent and overheads, usually expressed per kg of product.

t: Which OPEX lever is usually largest in API plants?
x: Yield and raw material consumption, including solvent recovery, usually outweigh utility savings.
Payback in years = investment divided by annual saving.

t: Why plant networks are different Basics
x: Office IT protects information. Operational technology (OT) , the DCS, PLCs, safety systems, historians and HMIs, controls physical equipment, so a cyber incident can mean a runaway reaction, a release or a fire, not just lost files. OT also runs for 15 to 20 years, often on old operating systems that cannot simply be patched on Tuesday night. The case every plant should know In 2017, attackers moved from the IT network into the OT network of a Middle East petrochemical facility and installed malware, later called TRITON, on its Triconex safety instrumented system controllers. The plant went to a safe state only because a bug in the malware t

The ISA/IEC 62443 series, developed by ISA and adopted by the IEC, is the main international standard set for securing industrial automation and control systems, built on shared responsibility between asset owners, suppliers, integrators and service providers. Its core design idea: Zones group assets that share a security level requirement: for example the safety system, the DCS of one block, the historian and MES servers. Conduits are the controlled paths between zones, each with a stated purpose, allowed protocols and its own controls. A path between zones that nobody designed is a finding, not a conduit. Security levels SL 1 to SL 4 descri
Twelve yes-or-no questions. The result is our own rough guide, not an IEC 62443 assessment.

CERT-In’s directions of 28 April 2022 under section 70B(6) of the IT Act require cyber incidents to be reported to CERT-In within six hours of noticing them or being told of them. CERT-In can give directions to service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporates and government organisations. Make sure your incident response plan names who reports, and that OT incidents are included, not only IT.

t: AI and remote access: design rules Going deeper
x: Data flows out, not in. Analytics and AI should read data from a historian copy in the DMZ, not connect to the DCS directly. No direct internet from control networks. Cloud tools reach plant data through the DMZ. Remote vendor access through one controlled gateway, with named accounts, approval for each session, recording, and nothing left permanently open. Models that write back (set points, recipes) need the same review as a control change: limits, interlocks untouched, operator override and management of change. Backups of DCS, PLC and SIS configurations kept offline and tested by restoring them.

A “temporary” remote-access modem or remote-desktop tool for a vendor, never removed. One flat network from the office to the PLCs. Shared operator passwords that never change. USB sticks moving between office and engineering stations. Backups that were never test-restored.

Protecting operational technology, the DCS, PLCs, safety systems, historians and HMIs that control physical processes, from cyber attacks and accidents. Failures can cause safety incidents and releases, not only data loss.

An international series of standards, developed by ISA and adopted by the IEC, for securing industrial automation and control systems. It uses zones, conduits and security levels and shares responsibility between asset owners, suppliers, integrators and service providers.

x: Permit to Work and Isolation Process Safety · Safe Work · October 2026 Most serious accidents during maintenance happen at the boundary between operations and maintenance: a line opened that was still connected to pressure, a pump started that someone was working on, a permit that didn’t survive a shift change. A permit to work is the system that manages that boundary. This article explains how it works, and how to isolate equipment properly. In this article What a permit to work is for Basics Types of permit Basics The isolation hierarchy Working level Lockout, tagout and verification Working level Handover: the Piper Alpha lesson Going deeper Questions people ask What a permit to work is for Basics A permit to work is a written agreement between the person in control of the plant and the person doing the work. It records what will be done, where, what hazards exist, how the equipment h

t: What a permit to work is for Basics
x: A permit to work is a written agreement between the person in control of the plant and the person doing the work. It records what will be done, where, what hazards exist, how the equipment has been made safe, what precautions are needed, and who has checked each one. Its value is not the paper but the conversation and checks it forces: the plant is handed over in a defined state, and handed back only when the work is complete and the equipment ready.

Hot work: welding, grinding, cutting, anything that makes sparks or flames. Needs gas testing and fire watch. Cold work / line break: opening process lines and equipment. Confined space entry: vessels, tanks, pits. Needs isolation, ventilation, atmosphere testing for oxygen, flammables and toxics, a standby person and a rescue plan. Electrical work and work at height , often as certificates attached to a main permit. Where several jobs touch the same equipment, they must be cross-referenced so one permit isn't closed while another depends on the same isolation.

Valves leak and get opened by mistake. The more severe the hazard, the more secure the isolation must be: Single closed valve: only for low-hazard fluids and short, simple jobs. Double block: two closed valves in series. Double block and bleed: two closed valves with a vent or drain open between them, so any leak through the first valve goes to the bleed, not to the work. Positive isolation: a spade (blind) or spectacle blind inserted, or a spool removed and the open ends blanked. Toxic, flammable, high-pressure or hot fluids, and any confined space entry, generally need positive isolation. The isolation points must be marked on a P&ID copy a

t: Lockout, tagout and verification Working level
x: Every energy source that could hurt someone must be isolated and locked: electrical supply, pneumatic and hydraulic power, stored pressure, springs, gravity (raised parts), and process chemicals. Each person working puts their own lock on the isolation (a multi-lock hasp or lock box) and only they remove it. Then verify : try to start the motor locally; check the pressure gauge reads zero and open the bleed; test the atmosphere before entry. An isolation that hasn't been tested is an assumption.

t: Handover: the Piper Alpha lesson Going deeper
x: On 6 July 1988, on the Piper Alpha platform in the North Sea, a pressure safety valve had been removed from a condensate pump for maintenance and replaced with a blind flange that was not leak-tight. The permit for that work was not effectively communicated at the evening shift handover. When the other pump tripped, the night shift started the pump with the missing valve. Condensate leaked, ignited and exploded, and the fires that followed destroyed the platform. 167 men died. The inquiry found weaknesses in the permit to work system, especially in shift handover and in cross-referencing permits. The lesson for every plant: a permit is only a

Signing permits in the office without visiting the job. Treating a stop button or a closed valve as an isolation. Not verifying the isolation before starting work. Permits not discussed at shift handover. Closing a permit while another job depends on the same isolation.

t: What is double block and bleed?
x: Two closed valves with an open bleed between them, so leakage goes to the bleed, not the work.
For toxic, flammable, high-energy fluids, long jobs and any confined space entry.
Isolating, locking and tagging every energy source, then verifying it before work.

s: PID control basics: P, I and D action, process gain, time constant and dead time, IMC tuning, cascade and split-range control and integral windup.
x: PID Control and Tuning Plant Engineering · Process Control · October 2026 A badly tuned temperature loop on a reactor shows up as a batch that swings 5 °C around its set point, a jacket valve that never stops moving, or a heat-up that overshoots into an exotherm. Most loops are tuned once at commissioning and never touched again. This article explains what a PID controller actually does and how to tune one sensibly. In this article Feedback control in one paragraph Basics P, I and D Basics Know the process: gain, lag and dead time Working level Tuning: a simple, safe method Working level Reactor temperature control in practice Going deeper Questions people ask Feedback control in one paragraph Basics A controller compares the measured value (the process variable, PV) with the set point (SP), and moves an output (usually a valve) to reduce the difference, the error. It repeats this many t

t: Feedback control in one paragraph Basics
x: A controller compares the measured value (the process variable, PV) with the set point (SP), and moves an output (usually a valve) to reduce the difference, the error. It repeats this many times a second. Everything else is about how much to move the valve for a given error, and how to avoid overreacting.

Output = Kc × [ e + (1/Ti) ∫ e dt + Td × de/dt ] Proportional (Kc): output proportional to the error now. More gain gives a faster response but, beyond a point, oscillation. Proportional action alone leaves a steady offset. Integral (Ti): keeps adding output while any error remains, so it removes the offset. A short integral time (strong integral action) causes overshoot and slow oscillation. Derivative (Td): reacts to how fast the error is changing, damping overshoot on slow processes. It amplifies noise, so it is often left at zero, except on slow temperature loops.

t: Know the process: gain, lag and dead time Working level
x: Most plant loops behave roughly like a first-order lag with dead time: Process gain K: how much the PV finally changes for a 1 % change in output. Time constant τ: how long it takes to get about 63 % of the way to its new value. Dead time θ: how long before anything happens at all. Thermowells, long pipes and jacket volumes add dead time. Dead time is what limits control. The bigger θ is compared with τ, the gentler the tuning must be. Find these three numbers with a simple step test: put the controller in manual, change the output by 5–10 %, and record the PV.

t: Tuning: a simple, safe method Working level
x: The IMC (internal model control) rules give robust PI settings from the step test, with one choice: the desired closed-loop speed λ. Choosing λ equal to the dead time is a reasonable start; a larger λ is gentler. Kc = τ / [K × (λ + θ)] Ti = τ For a process with K = 1, τ = 10 min and θ = 2 min, with λ = 2 min: Kc = 2.5 and Ti = 10 min. Compare that with a loop left at Kc = 1 and Ti = 5 min: slower to start, but overshooting because the integral is too strong. Try it: change gain, integral and derivative and watch the response to a set point step. Push the gain up until it oscillates, then press “Use IMC tuning”.

t: Reactor temperature control in practice Going deeper
x: Cascade control: the batch temperature controller (master) sets the jacket temperature set point; the jacket temperature controller (slave) moves the valves. The fast slave loop corrects utility disturbances before they reach the batch. Tune the slave first. Split range: one output drives cooling for 0–50 % and heating for 50–100 %. Check the overlap so both valves aren't open together, and that there's no dead band where nothing happens. Integral windup: during a long heat-up, the error stays large and the integral term keeps growing; when the batch reaches set point, the stored integral causes a big overshoot. Use anti-windup in the DCS, or

Tuning a loop without knowing the process dead time. Too much integral action, causing slow oscillation. No anti-windup on batch heat-up. Tuning the master loop before the slave loop. Blaming tuning for a sticky valve.

t: What does the integral term in PID do?
x: It removes steady offset; too much causes overshoot and oscillation.

t: What is cascade control on a reactor?
x: A batch controller setting a jacket controller, which moves the valves.

t: How do you tune a PI controller simply?
x: Step test, then IMC: Kc = τ/[K(λ+θ)], Ti = τ.

Administration, often with HR, EHS and legal, keeps the site legal to operate: licences, renewals, returns and the records inspectors ask for. This article is an engineer’s map of what exists and why. It is a general guide; the exact requirements depend on the state and on the site’s activities, so always check the current rules. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 repla

India’s four labour codes came into force on 21 November 2025. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 replaced the Factories Act, 1948 and related laws, so factory registration, safety officers, safety committees, hazardous process requirements, health checks and working hours now follow the Code and the rules notified by each state. Transition arrangements and state rules differ, so the site should confirm current forms and registers with its legal adviser. See the new labour codes for what changed.

Consent to Establish and Consent to Operate from the State Pollution Control Board under the Water Act, 1974 and Air Act, 1981, with limits on effluent, emissions, production capacity and products. Expansions need fresh consent, and many projects need environmental clearance first. Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules, 2016: authorisation, storage limits and manifests for waste sent to treatment and disposal facilities, with annual returns. Periodic environmental statements and monitoring reports as the consent requires.

Boilers: registration and periodic inspection; the Boilers Act, 2025 replaced the Indian Boilers Act, 1923 from 1 May 2025. Export markets add their own registrations and inspections; see regulatory affairs basics .

The practical tool is a single register: each licence or consent, the issuing authority, number, validity, conditions, renewal lead time, the owner, and the next return or inspection date. Conditions in consents, such as a production limit or a stack height, must also be checked against what the plant actually does, especially after expansions and new products. x: Pollution Control Consents: CTE, CTO and EC Statutory Compliance · Environment · October 2026 No chemical or pharma plant in India may be built or run without consent from the State Pollution Control Board. The consent fixes what the site may make, how much, and what it may discharge, so it quietly limits every new product and expansion. This article explains the consents and how to stay within them. It is a general guide, not legal advice; the Act, the rules, your state’s notifications and your own licence conditions always prevail. In this article Consent to establish and consent to operate Basics Categories and validity Basics What the consent conditions fix Working level Expansions and environmental clearance Working level Staying within consent Going deeper Questions people ask Consent to establish and consent to operate Basics Under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) A

t: Consent to establish and consent to operate Basics
s: Pollution Control Consents: CTE, CTO and EC
x: Under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 and the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, a plant needs two consents from the State Pollution Control Board (SPCB) or Pollution Control Committee: Consent to Establish (CTE): before construction starts, based on the proposed products, capacity, effluent and emissions, and the treatment planned. Consent to Operate (CTO): before production starts, after the board confirms the plant and its pollution controls are built as approved. It is renewed periodically. Applications are made online through the state’s consent management system.

s: Pollution Control Consents: CTE, CTO and EC
x: Industries are classed by pollution potential as red, orange, green or white. Synthetic organic chemicals and bulk drug manufacture are in the red category. Under the CPCB guidelines, a red category CTO is typically granted for 5 years, orange for 10 and green for 15, with white category industries exempt; states apply these with their own procedures, and some allow auto-renewal where nothing has changed.

t: What the consent conditions fix Working level
s: Pollution Control Consents: CTE, CTO and EC
x: The products and production capacity , often product by product. Effluent quantity and quality limits, or zero liquid discharge; see ETP basics . Stack emissions, stack heights and air pollution control equipment such as scrubbers . Water consumption, hazardous waste handling, monitoring and reporting. Special conditions such as online monitoring, green belt, and an annual environmental statement.

t: Expansions and environmental clearance Working level
s: Pollution Control Consents: CTE, CTO and EC
x: A new product, higher capacity or a new process usually needs an amended CTE before work starts and an amended CTO before production. Larger changes may first need environmental clearance (EC) under the EIA Notification, 2006, in which synthetic organic chemicals including bulk drugs are a listed activity; this involves an environmental impact assessment and, for category A projects, appraisal by the central expert committee. The EC timeline is long, so it belongs at the very start of project planning; see project execution .

s: Pollution Control Consents: CTE, CTO and EC
x: Keep a one-page sheet of every consent condition with the actual figure next to it: production by product, effluent flow and quality, emissions, water use, waste quantities. Review it monthly and before any new product or campaign. Apply for renewal well before expiry through the online system, with monitoring data ready. Technology transfers into the site should include a consent check alongside the PESO and waste checks. On the plant The most common consent problem is not pollution but paperwork: a product made on the site that is not listed in the CTO, or a capacity that crept above the consented figure after debottlenecking. t: The P-F curve: how much warning you get Basics
x: Most failures of rotating equipment give warning. P is the point where a coming failure first becomes detectable (a rise in vibration, a hot bearing); F is the functional failure (the pump stops delivering). The time between them is the P-F interval . Reliability-centred maintenance practice says to check at intervals of about half the P-F interval , or less for high-risk failure modes, so that at least one check falls inside the warning window with time left to plan the repair.

Enter your own estimates. The P-F interval comes from experience with that failure mode on that machine. x: Anomaly detection across many signals. A model learns how vibration, temperature, current and flow move together in normal running, and flags a pump that drifts away from its own normal, even when no single value has crossed an alarm limit. This is what Shell scaled to more than 10,000 pieces of equipment, with about 11,000 models in production. Context. In batch plants, an agitator’s current depends on the batch phase and fill level. Models that know the phase avoid the false alarms that make people ignore fixed limits. Remaining useful life. Predicting how many days are left needs a history of real failures with their signals. Most sites do

t: A practical pilot in 12 weeks Going deeper
x: Pick 10 to 20 critical machines with repeat failures and real production or safety impact. Use your criticality ranking and the last two years of breakdowns. Baseline them. Record failures, downtime hours and repair cost for the last two years, so savings can be measured later. Instrument the gaps. Add wireless vibration and temperature sensors where the DCS has nothing; bring everything into the historian. Start with limits, then models. ISO-based alarm zones give quick wins; anomaly models come once there are a few months of normal data. Close the loop. Every alert must create a work order in the CMMS with an owner, and every finding at ins

Monitoring everything instead of the 10% of machines that cause most of the loss. Fixed alarm limits on agitators and pumps whose normal values change with each batch phase. Sensors installed, data not stored, or stored without the equipment tag that links it to the CMMS. Calling a model “predictive” when there is no failure history to predict from. Skipping the baseline, so no one can prove the savings a year later.

t: What is the difference between preventive and predictive maintenance?
x: Preventive maintenance is done on a fixed schedule, whether or not the machine needs it. Predictive maintenance is done when measured condition, often analysed by software or machine learning, shows a failure is developing.

t: How often should vibration be checked?
x: Reliability-centred maintenance practice suggests a check interval of about half the P-F interval for that failure mode, shorter for high-risk failures. Machines with short P-F intervals are better monitored online.

t: Do we need machine learning for predictive maintenance?
x: No. Many sites get most of the benefit from good sensors, ISO-based vibration limits and a disciplined work-order process. Machine learning helps when many signals interact or normal values change with batch phase.

The BFD is the first picture: one block per step (reaction, work-up, isolation, drying, recovery), arrows for main streams with quantities per batch, and the solvents and wastes leaving each step. It is quick to draw, and it is where the first mass balance is closed. Everyone, including management, can read it.

For each step: what goes in, what comes out, and where every kg goes, including solvent losses and effluent. The energy balance gives heating and cooling duties, peak and average, which size utilities and set cycle times. See material and energy balance and the heat load calculator .

t: PFD, equipment list and occupancy Working level
x: The PFD shows the main equipment with key operating conditions and the major control loops. With it comes the equipment list (capacity, MOC, design pressure and temperature, agitator and jacket details) and an occupancy chart , a time chart of which equipment each step uses and for how long. The occupancy chart reveals the bottleneck and the achievable batches per month; see batch cycle time and debottlenecking .

Reactors: working volume at the largest step, with enough freeboard, and jacket area for the duty ( jacket and limpet coil design ). Agitators: type and power for the duty ( agitator design ). Heat exchangers and condensers ( heat exchanger basics ). Pumps, lines and pressure drop ( line sizing ), vacuum systems, scrubbers, filters and dryers. Relief devices for each overpressure scenario ( relief valve sizing ).

x: Process engineering supplies the control philosophy, interlocks, instrument ranges and line list for the P&ID , takes part in the HAZOP, and writes commissioning and start-up procedures. Once the plant runs, the job shifts to support: yield and cycle-time improvement, consumption norms, troubleshooting, capacity studies for new products and feasibility for the next expansion. On the plant Keep one live spreadsheet per product with the batch mass balance, utility duties and occupancy. Every question from management, costing, the ETP or projects can be answered from it in minutes.

Sizing from the lab procedure without a closed mass balance. Using average duties where the peak sets the equipment. No occupancy chart, so the real bottleneck is found after commissioning. Freeboard ignored for foaming or gassing steps. Documents not updated after plant changes.

t: What a process historian does Basics
x: The DCS shows what is happening now. A process historian remembers it: every temperature, pressure, flow, level, valve position and alarm, time-stamped, for years. In the ISA-95 picture of a plant it sits between control (level 2) and manufacturing operations (level 3), and it is the data source under almost every analytics and AI project. Troubleshooting: overlay last night’s trend on a good batch. Investigations: evidence for deviations and incidents (see deviations and CAPA ). Performance: cycle time, energy and utility consumption, OEE. Models: training data for soft sensors , predictive maintenance and digital twins .

t: Tags: names, units and context Basics
x: Each measured value is a tag . A historian with 20,000 tags called AI_1047 is almost useless; one with consistent names is a goldmine. A practical tag record holds: Field Example Why it matters Tag name (from the P&ID) B2-R201-TI-101 Links the data to the drawing and the equipment (see how to read a P&ID ) Description Reactor R-201 mass temperature People can find it Engineering unit and range °C, -20 to 150 No guessing between kg/h and m³/h Equipment and area R-201, Block 2 Lets analytics group tags by unit Compression settings Deadband 0.2 °C Decides how much detail is kept (below) GMP relevance Critical process parameter: yes Decides audit

t: Compression: how much detail is kept Working level
x: Storing every value every second for every tag is expensive, so historians discard points that add no information. Deadband (exception) compression discards small changes within a set band; it suits stepwise signals such as valve positions and levels. Swinging door compression keeps the points needed to represent the shape of a smooth signal, and is better for continuous data such as pressure and temperature. Set the band too wide and short spikes (the ones investigations need) disappear.
Simulated reactor temperature over one hour, sampled every 10 s, with a short spike at 38 minutes. Widen the deadband and watch what is lost. Deadband (°C): 0.2

t: Time, quality flags and context Working level
x: One clock. DCS, PLCs, historian, MES and LIMS must be synchronised to a common time source. A five-minute offset between the lab and the historian ruins soft sensors and confuses investigations. Quality flags. A good historian stores whether a value was good, bad (instrument fault) or substituted. Analytics must exclude bad values, not treat them as real. Batch context. Store batch ID, product and phase (charging, reaction, distillation) as events, so trends can be aligned batch by batch. This is usually supplied by the MES or the DCS batch engine (see MES and electronic batch records ).

t: Historians in GMP plants Going deeper
x: When historian data is used for GMP decisions, such as proving a critical process parameter stayed in range, it is a GMP record. FDA’s data integrity guidance (December 2018) expects such records to be attributable, legible, contemporaneously recorded, original or a true copy, and accurate, and 21 CFR Part 11 expects validated systems, secure time-stamped audit trails and controlled access. In practice: validate the interfaces for GMP tags, protect compression settings and tag changes under change control, and keep data for the retention period your quality system requires.

Tag names that do not match the P&ID, so nobody can find the right signal. Default compression on every tag, so short pressure spikes vanish from investigations. Clocks drifting apart between historian, MES and LIMS. Collecting data with no batch context, so batches cannot be compared. Changing compression or scaling on GMP tags without change control.
A database designed to store time-stamped process data (temperatures, pressures, flows, valve positions, alarms) from the DCS and PLCs for years, so trends can be reviewed, compared and analysed.

t: What compression setting should I use in a historian?
x: It depends on the signal: tight enough to keep the detail investigations and models need (short spikes, fast changes), loose enough to save storage. Deadband suits stepwise signals; swinging door suits smooth continuous signals. Critical GMP tags deserve deliberate, controlled settings, not defaults.

t: Is historian data a GMP record?
x: When it is used to make or support a GMP decision, such as showing a critical process parameter stayed in range, yes. It then needs data-integrity controls: validated interfaces, audit trails, access control and change control.

The decisions taken in the R&D lab fix most of the plant’s cost, waste and risk. This article covers how a good process is chosen and developed. s: Process R&D: Route Selection and Development
x: Several routes usually lead to the same molecule. They are compared on: Number of steps and overall yield: five steps at 80 % give 33 %; seven at 90 % give 48 %. Cost and availability of starting materials , and how many sources exist. Safety: energetic reagents (azides, nitro compounds, peroxides), highly exothermic steps, toxic gases, cryogenic temperatures. Waste and solvents: process mass intensity (kg of all inputs per kg of product), salt formed, solvent classes under ICH Q3C. Quality: where impurities form and whether later steps can remove them; genotoxic (mutagenic) impurity risk under ICH M7. Plant fit: equipment, MOC and operations

t: From a working reaction to a robust process Basics
s: Process R&D: Route Selection and Development
x: Development makes each step reliable: concentration high enough for good productivity, a workable order and rate of addition, a work-up that separates cleanly, an isolation that filters and dries well, and solvents that can be recovered. Each step is run several times to show it is reproducible, then at larger lab scale (1–5 L jacketed reactors) under conditions that resemble the plant.

t: Critical parameters and DoE Working level
s: Process R&D: Route Selection and Development
x: Not every parameter matters equally. Critical process parameters (CPPs) are those whose variation affects a critical quality attribute (purity, a specific impurity, polymorph, particle size). Design of experiments (DoE) varies several parameters together in a planned set of runs, finding the important effects and interactions with far fewer experiments than one-factor-at-a-time. The output is a proven acceptable range for each CPP, which becomes the range in the batch record.

s: Process R&D: Route Selection and Development
x: Before scale-up, each step is screened for thermal hazards: DSC on reaction mixtures and isolated intermediates, reaction calorimetry (RC1) for heat of reaction and accumulation, and adiabatic tests (ARC) for runaway behaviour. The results decide whether a step is dosing-controlled, how fast it can be dosed and what the cooling must handle. See how to read DSC, ARC, RC1 and TSU and semi-batch dosing and accumulation .

t: Impurity fate and purge Going deeper
s: Process R&D: Route Selection and Development
x: For each impurity, R&D works out where it forms, whether it reacts on, and how much each later step removes (the purge factor). Spiking studies, adding a known amount of an impurity and measuring how much survives, prove the control strategy. Mutagenic impurities need special attention: they must be controlled to very low levels, either by testing or by showing the process purges them reliably. On the plant The plant questions R&D should answer before a process leaves the lab: how long can each intermediate be held, what happens if dosing stops halfway, how does the filter cake behave at 30 cm instead of 2 cm, and what is in every aqueous lay

s: Process R&D: Route Selection and Development
x: Choosing the route with the fewest steps without checking safety and waste. Optimising yield at a concentration the plant cannot stir or filter. Skipping thermal screening because the lab batch “behaved”. Not studying hold times. No data on impurity purge, so every new impurity becomes a crisis.

s: Process R&D: Route Selection and Development
x: The total mass of all materials used (reagents, solvents, water) per kg of product. Lower is better; it is a simple measure of how wasteful a process is.

t: What is a critical process parameter?
s: Process R&D: Route Selection and Development
x: A parameter whose variation affects a critical quality attribute of the product, so it must be controlled within a proven range.

t: Why do DoE instead of changing one factor at a time?
s: Process R&D: Route Selection and Development
x: DoE finds the effects of several factors and their interactions with fewer experiments, which one-factor-at-a-time cannot do.

s: Stages of a plant project: URS, basic and detailed engineering, procurement, construction, commissioning, qualification and handover.
x: Project Execution: URS to Handover Plant Departments · Projects · October 2026 A new block or a capacity expansion is a long chain of decisions, each costing more to change than the one before. The cheapest moment to fix a layout, a material or a missing utility is on paper at the start. This article walks through the stages and what each must deliver. In this article URS and basic engineering Basics Detailed engineering Basics Procurement and construction Working level Mechanical completion, commissioning and qualification Working level Cost, schedule and handover Going deeper Questions people ask URS and basic engineering Basics The user requirement specification states what the facility must do: products and capacity, process steps, GMP grade of areas, containment, utilities, safety and environmental requirements. Basic engineering turns it into a process package : BFD, PFD, mass bala

The user requirement specification states what the facility must do: products and capacity, process steps, GMP grade of areas, containment, utilities, safety and environmental requirements. Basic engineering turns it into a process package : BFD, PFD, mass balance, equipment list, utility loads, layout and a cost estimate (often ±20–30 %) for approval.

Detailed engineering produces everything needed to buy and build: P&IDs after HAZOP, equipment datasheets, piping layouts and isometrics, civil and structural drawings, electrical and instrumentation design, HVAC for classified areas, and the fire and safety system design. The design qualification ( DQ ) checks the design meets the URS and GMP.

Long-lead items, such as glass-lined reactors, special alloy equipment, transformers and large chillers, are ordered first because they set the schedule. Vendors submit drawings for approval; factory acceptance tests (FAT) check equipment before dispatch. On site, construction follows the civil works, equipment erection, piping, electrical and instrumentation, with safety controlled by permits ( permit to work ) and regular inspections.

t: Mechanical completion, commissioning and qualification Working level
x: Mechanical completion: everything installed as per drawings; punch lists closed; pressure tests and line flushing done. Pre-commissioning: loop checks, motor rotation, interlock tests, utilities run in. Commissioning: water trials and solvent trials to test heating, cooling, vacuum, transfers and controls. Qualification: IQ, OQ and PQ for GMP equipment and systems, then process validation batches. A pre-startup safety review confirms the HAZOP actions are closed and the plant matches the design before the first chemical enters.

t: Cost, schedule and handover Going deeper
x: A project is controlled with a baseline schedule (critical path), a budget broken down by area and discipline, a change register and regular progress reviews. Late changes to P&IDs or layout are the main source of overruns. Handover gives production and maintenance the as-built drawings, equipment manuals, spares list, qualification reports, SOPs and trained people. A project closure report records cost, schedule and lessons learned for the next one. On the plant Bring the operators and maintenance team into the 3D model or layout review. They find the valve that cannot be reached, the filter that cannot be removed and the drain at the wrong

Starting detailed engineering with an incomplete URS. HAZOP done after piping is ordered. Ordering long-lead items late. Skipping water trials to save time. Handing over without as-built drawings and spares.
A user requirement specification: the document stating what a facility or equipment must do, used to design, buy and later qualify it.

t: What is the difference between FAT and SAT?
x: A factory acceptance test checks equipment at the vendor before dispatch; a site acceptance test checks it after installation at site.
The point when everything is installed and tested mechanically as per drawings, ready for pre-commissioning.

s: Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 for chemical sites: who must insure, no-fault relief, cover linked to paid-up capital, Environment Relief Fund.
x: Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 Statutory Compliance · Insurance · October 2026 If a chemical accident hurts people outside the plant or damages their property, the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 makes sure they receive immediate relief without having to prove anyone was at fault. Every owner handling hazardous substances above notified quantities must carry the insurance that pays for it. It is a general guide, not legal advice; the Act, the rules, your state’s notifications and your own licence conditions always prevail. In this article Who must insure Basics No-fault relief Basics Cover and the Environment Relief Fund Working level Penalties Working level Fitting it into the safety system Going deeper Questions people ask Who must insure Basics Every owner who handles a hazardous substance must take out an insurance policy before starting to handle it, and renew it so the c

Every owner who handles a hazardous substance must take out an insurance policy before starting to handle it, and renew it so the cover is continuous. A hazardous substance here means one classed as hazardous under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, in quantities above those notified by the central government. “Owner” includes the directors or managers in charge of a company. Government undertakings with a maintained fund are exempt.

After an accident, the owner must provide relief to affected members of the public for death, injury, sickness, lost wages and damage to private property, at rates set by the rules, without the claimant having to prove negligence. Employees are covered separately under workers’ compensation and social security law, not under this Act. The relief is in addition to any other compensation a court may award.

t: Cover and the Environment Relief Fund Working level
x: The policy must cover at least the undertaking’s paid-up capital (or, for non-companies, the market value of assets and stock), up to a prescribed maximum of no more than ₹500 crore. With the premium, the owner pays an extra amount, not more than the premium, which the insurer credits to the Environment Relief Fund .

Following the Jan Vishwas amendments in force from 1 April 2024, failing to insure attracts a penalty of the annual premium, up to twice that amount, with further penalties for continuing failure, imposed by an adjudicating officer, with appeals to the National Green Tribunal. Ignoring directions or obstructing officers carries larger penalties.

t: Fitting it into the safety system Going deeper
x: The insurance pays for relief; it does not reduce risk. The same hazardous substances that trigger this Act usually trigger the MSIHC Rules , so the hazard identification, emergency planning and off-site information duties go together. Keep the policy on the compliance register with its renewal date. On the plant When the company’s paid-up capital changes, for example after a fresh issue of shares, check the policy cover. The required minimum is linked to it.

Starting to handle a hazardous substance before the policy is in place. Letting the policy lapse at renewal. Cover below paid-up capital after a capital increase. Environment Relief Fund contribution not paid. Confusing this insurance with workers’ compensation.

t: Who must take insurance under the Public Liability Insurance Act?
x: Every owner handling a hazardous substance above the notified quantity, before starting to handle it.
No. Workmen are excluded; they are covered under workers’ compensation and social security law.

t: What is the minimum insurance cover?
x: At least the paid-up capital of the undertaking, up to a prescribed maximum of no more than Rs 500 crore.

x: Pump and Mechanical Seal Troubleshooting Plant Engineering · Rotating Equipment · October 2026 Centrifugal pumps are the most common machine in a chemical plant and the most common maintenance call. The same pump that ran for three years without trouble suddenly eats a seal every month. Usually the pump hasn't changed; the way it is being run has. This article explains how a centrifugal pump wants to be operated, what each symptom tells you, and why mechanical seals really fail. In this article Where a pump likes to run Basics How a mechanical seal works Basics Reading the symptoms Working level Seal flush and barrier plans Working level Why seals really fail Going deeper Making pumps reliable Going deeper Questions people ask Where a pump likes to run Basics A centrifugal pump has a curve: the head it makes falls as the flow rises. Where that curve crosses the system curve is where it a

t: Where a pump likes to run Basics
x: A centrifugal pump has a curve: the head it makes falls as the flow rises. Where that curve crosses the system curve is where it actually runs. Each pump also has a best efficiency point (BEP) , the flow at which the liquid enters and leaves the impeller smoothly. Near the BEP, forces on the shaft are balanced, vibration is low and the seal and bearings last. Far left of BEP (throttled hard, below about 60–70 %): liquid recirculates inside the impeller, the shaft deflects, the liquid heats up, vibration rises. At zero flow (dead-heading) the pump can boil its own contents. Far right of BEP (discharge wide open, above about 120 %): the pump ne

t: How a mechanical seal works Basics
x: Where the shaft passes through the casing, something has to stop the liquid escaping. Old pumps used packing (gland rope) that was designed to drip. Mechanical seals instead use two very flat rings, one rotating with the shaft and one stationary, pressed together by springs. Between them runs a liquid film about one micrometre thick. That film lubricates and cools the faces. With it, a seal lasts years; without it, the faces rub, overheat and crack, sometimes within a minute. Everything about seal reliability comes back to that film: keep it present, clean, cool and stable.

Try it: pick a symptom. The pump shows where to look, with the likely causes in order and the first check to make. Three measurements solve most pump problems: suction pressure , discharge pressure and motor current . With the head (discharge minus suction) and the current, you can place the pump on its curve and see whether it is running where you think it is. Fit pressure gauges on both sides of every important pump, not only on the discharge. Two quick checks catch a surprising number of faults: the direction of rotation (a reverse-running centrifugal pump still delivers some flow at reduced head, so it isn't obvious), and the shut-off hea

t: Seal flush and barrier plans Working level
x: API 682 numbers the arrangements that keep the seal environment healthy. The ones you'll meet most in chemical plants: Plan What it does Used for 11 Recirculates a little liquid from the discharge to the seal faces Clean, cool liquids; the most common single-seal plan 32 Injects clean liquid from an external source Dirty or crystallising liquids 52 Unpressurised buffer fluid between two seals, from a pot Volatile liquids where some leakage to the buffer is acceptable 53A/B/C Pressurised barrier fluid between two seals, from a pot or accumulator Toxic, flammable or crystallising products; nothing leaks to atmosphere 62 External quench on the a

t: Why seals really fail Going deeper
x: Seal manufacturers say that most failures are not the seal's fault, and in my experience they are right. Look at the failed parts before ordering a replacement: Heat-checked or cracked faces: dry running. The pump ran on an empty tank, against a closed suction valve, or with vapour at the faces. Fit a low-level or dry-run trip (power monitor) and fill and vent the pump before starting. Swollen, hard or cracked O-rings: wrong elastomer for the solvent. Viton swells in ketones such as acetone; EPDM swells in hydrocarbons; FFKM (perfluoroelastomer) resists almost everything but costs much more. Check compatibility for every solvent the pump sees

Size for the real duty , not the worst case times a safety factor. Use a VFD where flows vary, rather than throttling. Protect against dry running and dead-heading: a minimum-flow recirculation line, a power monitor that trips on low load, and interlocks on tank low level. Alignment after every maintenance job, ideally with a laser, and with pipework supported so it doesn't pull on the pump. Consider sealless pumps (magnetic drive or canned motor) for toxic or very volatile liquids. They have no seal to leak, but they hate dry running and solids even more than sealed pumps. Trend vibration and bearing temperature monthly on critical pumps. Pr

Replacing the seal without asking why it failed. Running an oversized pump throttled at a third of its BEP flow. Starting a pump before it is filled and vented. Choosing seal elastomers for the product but not for the cleaning solvent. No suction pressure gauge, so cavitation is guessed at, not measured.
Mostly because of conditions around them: dry running, lost flush, vibration, solids and incompatible elastomers.

t: What is the safe operating range?
x: Ideally 80–110 % of best efficiency flow, and generally within 70–120 %.

t: How do you know a pump is cavitating?
x: Crackling noise, fluctuating pressure and flow, lower head, and pitting on the impeller eye over time.

What size motor does the pump need? The answer takes about five minutes, if you know which numbers matter. This article starts from what “pump power” actually means and works up to the things that catch people out on a real plant: receiver pressure, motor margins, pump curves and NPSH. t: The idea in plain words Basics
s: Pump Power Calculation: From the Basics to the Plant Floor
x: A pump does one job: it gives energy to a liquid so the liquid can get somewhere it would not go by itself. Higher up, into a vessel at higher pressure, or simply through a long pipe that resists the flow. Think of carrying buckets of water up a staircase. The work you do depends on two things: how much water you carry each minute, and how high the stairs are. Pumps are the same. Flow is how much you carry; head is how high the stairs are. Multiply them (with the liquid's weight) and you get the power the liquid receives. The pump is not perfect, so it needs more power at its shaft than it gives to the liquid. The motor is not perfect either,

s: Pump Power Calculation: From the Basics to the Plant Floor
x: Head is energy per unit weight of liquid, expressed as a height in metres. It sounds abstract, but it is a useful trick: a pump that develops 30 m of head can lift any liquid 30 m, whether it is water, toluene or a heavy brine. The pressure it makes changes with the liquid's density; the head does not. That is why pump curves are drawn in metres. The total head a pump must deliver has three parts: Total head = static lift + pressure difference converted to head + friction losses. H = (z2 - z1) + (P2 - P1) / (ρ g) + hf Static head , z2 - z1: the height from the liquid level in the suction tank to the delivery point. Pressure head , (P2 - P1) /

t: The formula, and where 367 comes from Basics
s: Pump Power Calculation: From the Basics to the Plant Floor
x: Hydraulic power (kW) = ρ × g × Q × H / 1,000 Shaft power (kW) = Hydraulic power / ηpump Motor input power (kW) = Shaft power / ηmotor ρ is density in kg/m³, g is 9.81 m/s², Q is flow in m³/s, H is total head in m, and the efficiencies are fractions (0.65, not 65). On the plant, flow is read in m³/h, not m³/s. Put Q in m³/h and density as specific gravity, and all the constants fold into one number: Hydraulic power (kW) = Q (m³/h) × H (m) × SG / 367 367 = 3,600 × 1,000 / (1,000 × 9.81). It is worth remembering. If you think in horsepower, 1 hp = 0.746 kW.

t: Example 1: water to an overhead tank Working level
s: Pump Power Calculation: From the Basics to the Plant Floor
x: Water at 50 m³/h, total head 30 m (static lift plus friction, tank open to atmosphere). Pump efficiency 65 %, motor efficiency 92 %. Hydraulic power = 50 × 30 × 1.0 / 367 ≈ 4.09 kW Shaft power = 4.09 / 0.65 ≈ 6.29 kW Motor input = 6.29 / 0.92 ≈ 6.84 kW You would not buy a 6.84 kW motor; you pick a standard size. The next size up is 7.5 kW, and many plants would fit exactly that. Apply the stricter margin rule in the motor section below (125 % of 6.29 kW ≈ 7.9 kW) and it becomes the next size again, 9.3 kW (12.5 HP).

t: Example 2: solvent into a pressurised reactor Working level

x: This is closer to daily life in a pharma or chemical plant. Toluene (870 kg/m³, SG 0.87) is transferred at 20 m³/h into a reactor held at 2 barg under nitrogen. The storage tank is atmospheric. Where 4 kW IEC motors are stocked, that is the pick. Many Indian plants standardise on 3.7 kW (5 HP) instead, which is just short, so the next size, 5.5 kW (7.5 HP), is the safe choice. Run it at 80–110 % of the BEP flow and you get the catalogue efficiency, quiet running and long seal life. Run it far to the left (throttled hard) and efficiency falls, the liquid recirculates inside the casing, it heats up, and seals and bearings suffer. Far to the right, efficiency falls again and NPSH required shoots up. x: A pump can have the right motor and the right head and still not work, because the liquid boils in its own suction. If the pressure at the impeller eye drops below the liquid's vapour pressure, vapour bubbles form and then collapse violently as the pressure rises. That is cavitation: a gravel-like noise, falling flow, and pitted impellers.
