t: What is the formula for pump power?
s: Pump Power Calculation: From the Basics to the Plant Floor
x: Hydraulic power (kW) = ρ × g × Q × H / 1,000, with ρ in kg/m³, Q in m³/s and H in m. Divide by pump efficiency for shaft power, then by motor efficiency for motor input power.

t: What is the quick formula from m³/h?
s: Pump Power Calculation: From the Basics to the Plant Floor
x: Hydraulic power (kW) = Q (m³/h) × H (m) × SG / 367. For 50 m³/h of water at 30 m head, about 4.1 kW.

t: What is the difference between hydraulic power and shaft power?
s: Pump Power Calculation: From the Basics to the Plant Floor
x: Hydraulic power is what the liquid receives. Shaft power is what the pump takes at its shaft; it is higher because of losses inside the pump. Shaft power = hydraulic power / pump efficiency.

t: What is the pump capacity formula?
s: Pump Power Calculation: From the Basics to the Plant Floor
x: Turn the power formula round: Q (m³/h) = 367 × shaft power (kW) × pump efficiency / (H × SG). A 7.5 kW motor driving a 65 % efficient pump against 30 m of water gives roughly 55 m³/h. The pump curve gives the exact figure.

t: How do I convert pressure to head?
s: Pump Power Calculation: From the Basics to the Plant Floor
x: Head (m) = ΔP (Pa) / (ρ × 9.81). For water, 1 bar is about 10.2 m; for a lighter liquid the same pressure is more metres.

t: How much margin should a pump motor have?
s: Pump Power Calculation: From the Basics to the Plant Floor
x: A common rule is 125 % of shaft power up to 22 kW, 115 % from 22 to 55 kW and 110 % above that, then the next standard size. Also check the shaft power at the end of the pump curve.

x: QA and GMP for Plant Engineers Plant Departments · Quality Assurance · October 2026 Quality control tests the product; quality assurance makes sure the whole system that made it can be trusted. For engineers, QA shows up as signatures, deviation forms and change controls. Understanding why each exists makes them faster to complete and far more useful. s: QA and GMP for Plant Engineers
x: Good Manufacturing Practice asks one thing: can you prove every batch was made the approved way, by trained people, on qualified equipment, from approved materials, and that nothing unrecorded happened? For APIs the international reference is ICH Q7; in India the revised Schedule M of the Drugs Rules applies, and export customers bring their own regulators (US FDA, EU, WHO and others). The practical consequence is “if it isn’t written, it didn’t happen”. Records must be attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original and accurate, the ALCOA principle, which also applies to electronic data from DCS, balances and instruments.

s: QA and GMP for Plant Engineers
x: The BMR (or BPR) is the step-by-step instruction for a batch that becomes its record as it is filled in: materials dispensed with lot numbers, equipment used, each charge with quantity and time, temperatures, in-process results, yields, and the signatures of the person doing and the person checking each critical step. A well-written BMR reads like the process: one action per step, the target and the range, and space to record the actual. Engineers write BMR steps after technology transfer . A range that the plant cannot actually hold (for example “add over 30–35 minutes” with a manual valve) will produce deviations every batch.

t: Deviations: recording what went differently Working level
s: QA and GMP for Plant Engineers
x: A deviation is any departure from an approved instruction or specification: a temperature excursion, a wrong sequence, an equipment breakdown mid-batch, a missed sample. It is raised at once, contained (hold the batch, segregate material), classified by impact (critical, major, minor) and investigated. Planned deviations, approved in advance for a one-off change, are different from unplanned ones discovered after the fact.

t: Root cause and CAPA Working level
s: QA and GMP for Plant Engineers
x: A deviation is closed with a root cause and corrective and preventive actions . Corrective action fixes this occurrence; preventive action stops it happening again here or elsewhere. Useful tools: 5 Whys: keep asking why until you reach something you can change in the system, not a person. Fishbone (Ishikawa): man, machine, method, material, measurement and environment as headings for possible causes. Data: trend the same parameter over previous batches; a cause that also appeared in good batches is not the cause. “Operator error” followed by “operator retrained” is the weakest CAPA. Ask why the system allowed the error: confusing instruction

t: Change control and quality risk management Going deeper
s: QA and GMP for Plant Engineers
x: Any change that could affect the product, from a new vendor or a larger reactor to a modified cleaning procedure, goes through change control : describe the change, assess the impact (quality, regulatory filing, validation, safety, customers), approve it, implement it with any required studies, and verify it worked. It is the GMP twin of the process-safety management of change ; many sites link the two forms. The depth of assessment follows quality risk management (ICH Q9(R1)): severity, probability and detectability scored with a tool such as FMEA, so effort goes where risk is highest. ICH Q10 places all of this in a pharmaceutical quality s

s: QA and GMP for Plant Engineers
x: Filling the BMR at the end of the shift instead of as each step is done. Closing every deviation with retraining. Making a “small” change without change control because it seemed obviously safe. Ranges in the BMR that the equipment cannot hold. Not trending deviations, so the same one returns every month.

t: What is the difference between QA and QC?
s: QA and GMP for Plant Engineers
x: QC tests materials and products against specifications. QA owns the system: procedures, batch record review, deviations, change control, audits and final release.

s: QA and GMP for Plant Engineers
x: Corrective and preventive action: corrective action fixes the problem that occurred, preventive action stops it recurring.

s: QA and GMP for Plant Engineers
x: A data-integrity principle: records must be attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original and accurate. ALCOA+ adds complete, consistent, enduring and available.

x: QC Lab Basics for Plant Engineers Plant Departments · Quality Control · October 2026 Every batch leaves the plant on the strength of a QC report. Engineers who understand what the lab measures, how sure it is, and what happens when a result fails can design processes that pass first time and help the lab when they don’t. This article walks through the QC lab from the plant side. s: QC Lab Basics for Plant Engineers
x: A specification is the list of tests, methods and acceptance limits a material must meet. There are specifications for raw materials, intermediates, the final API, packing materials and even process water. A typical API specification covers: Description and identification: appearance, IR spectrum or HPLC retention time matching a reference standard. Assay: how much of the material is the compound itself, usually by HPLC or titration. Related substances (impurities): each known impurity, any unknown impurity and the total, by HPLC. Residual solvents: by headspace GC, against the limits of ICH Q3C. Water content (Karl Fischer) or loss on drying

t: Sampling: where most errors start Basics
s: QC Lab Basics for Plant Engineers
x: A result can only be as good as the sample. A sample must represent the whole batch: taken with a clean, dry, compatible tool, from the right places (top, middle and bottom of a drum or several bags of a lot), in a labelled container, and protected from moisture and light where needed. In-process samples from a reactor need the line flushed first so the sample is not the stale liquid sitting in the dip leg. Many “failures” turn out to be sampling problems: a wet sample from the top of a dryer, a mother liquor sample that crystallised in the bottle, or a sample taken before the batch was homogeneous.

t: HPLC, GC and the other workhorses Working level
s: QC Lab Basics for Plant Engineers
x: HPLC separates the components in a liquid sample on a column and measures each peak, usually by UV. It gives assay and impurity profile. The peak area is compared with a reference standard of known purity. GC does the same for volatile compounds. Headspace GC heats the sample in a sealed vial and injects only the vapour above it, which is how residual solvents are measured. Karl Fischer titration measures water specifically; loss on drying measures everything that leaves on heating (water and solvent), so the two can differ. Titration, IR, UV, melting point, specific optical rotation, particle size (laser diffraction) and XRD complete the too

t: Method validation in one paragraph Working level
s: QC Lab Basics for Plant Engineers
x: An analytical method must be shown to be fit for purpose before it is used for release. ICH Q2(R2), adopted in 2023 together with ICH Q14 on analytical procedure development, lists the characteristics to demonstrate: specificity, accuracy, precision (repeatability and intermediate precision), linearity and range, detection and quantitation limits for impurities, and robustness. When a method moves from R&D to the plant QC lab, a method transfer shows the receiving lab gets equivalent results on the same samples.

t: OOS and OOT: what happens when a result fails Going deeper
s: QC Lab Basics for Plant Engineers
x: An out-of-specification (OOS) result is outside the approved limit. An out-of-trend (OOT) result is within limits but unusual compared with previous batches or stability time points. Both are investigated, following the approach in the US FDA guidance on OOS investigations: Phase I, laboratory investigation: the analyst and supervisor check for an obvious lab error: wrong dilution, standard preparation, integration, instrument fault, system suitability. Only a documented, assignable lab error allows the result to be invalidated. Phase II, full-scale investigation: if no lab error is found, the investigation moves to production: the batch reco

s: QC Lab Basics for Plant Engineers
x: Sampling before the batch is homogeneous or from the wrong point. Treating loss on drying and water content as the same thing. Retesting until the result passes. Changing the process without telling QC, so the method meets an impurity it was never validated for. Not keeping reference and retained samples properly.

t: What is the difference between OOS and OOT?
s: QC Lab Basics for Plant Engineers
x: OOS is a result outside the specification limit. OOT is within the limit but out of line with the trend of previous results. Both need investigation; OOS can lead to batch rejection.

t: Why do residual solvent tests use headspace GC?
s: QC Lab Basics for Plant Engineers
x: Heating the sample in a sealed vial and injecting only the vapour measures the volatile solvents without putting the non-volatile API on the GC column.

s: QC Lab Basics for Plant Engineers
x: A check run before each analysis, such as resolution, injection repeatability and peak tailing, to show the instrument and method are working properly on that day.

s: Raw material control in API plants: specifications, vendor qualification, quarantine, sampling and release, consumption norms and inventory planning.
x: Raw Material Management Plant Departments · Raw Materials · October 2026 Raw materials are usually the largest part of the cost of an API, and a wrong or poor-quality material can spoil a batch long before anyone notices. Good raw material management connects purchase, stores, QC and production so the right material is in the right place, approved, at the right time. In this article Start with the specification Basics Vendor qualification Basics Receipt, quarantine, sampling and release Working level Consumption norms and yield Working level Inventory planning Going deeper Questions people ask Start with the specification Basics Each raw material has a specification agreed between R&D, QC and purchase: purity or assay, specific impurities that matter to the process (for example water in a reagent that will be used with an acid chloride, or a metal that poisons a catalyst), physical form

Each raw material has a specification agreed between R&D, QC and purchase: purity or assay, specific impurities that matter to the process (for example water in a reagent that will be used with an acid chloride, or a metal that poisons a catalyst), physical form and pack size. A key starting material, the first material that becomes part of the API structure, gets the tightest controls because its impurities can carry through to the product. A specification copied from a supplier’s catalogue usually misses the parameter your chemistry is sensitive to. Ask R&D: which impurity in this material has caused trouble in the lab?

Approved materials come only from approved vendors . Qualification typically includes a questionnaire, samples tested against the specification, a trial batch at plant scale, and for critical materials an audit of the vendor’s site. A second source is qualified the same way. Changing vendor for a key starting material is a change control and may need regulatory notification.

t: Receipt, quarantine, sampling and release Working level
x: Receipt: check the vehicle, seals, labels, quantity, the supplier’s certificate of analysis, and that the vendor is approved for that material. Quarantine: the material gets a GRN and an internal lot number and is labelled “Quarantine” in a segregated area or a locked system status. Sampling: QC samples a defined number of containers (a common plan is √n + 1 containers for a lot of n) in a sampling booth for materials that need protection. Testing and release: the material is tested (full or reduced testing for qualified vendors with periodic full checks) and labelled “Approved” or “Rejected”. Only approved material is dispensed. Approved mat

t: Consumption norms and yield Working level
x: The consumption norm is the planned kg of each raw material per kg of product. Comparing actual consumption with the norm batch by batch shows losses early: a solvent norm creeping up points to recovery problems ; a reagent above norm may mean a weighing error, a poor assay or a side reaction. The consumption norms article covers how to set and track them.

Inventory is a balance between running out (a stopped plant) and holding too much (cash locked up, retest dates expiring, storage limits). The usual tools: Requirement from the production plan: batches planned × norm per batch, plus losses. Lead time and safety stock: reorder when stock falls to (daily use × lead time) + safety stock. Imported or single-source materials need more safety stock. ABC analysis: the few high-value materials (A) get tight, frequent control; the many low-value ones (C) simpler rules. Storage limits: flammable solvents are limited by licence and tank capacity, not just by cash. Plan deliveries around them. On the pla

Specifications that do not include the impurity the process is sensitive to. Buying from a cheaper, unqualified source in a hurry. Using material past its retest date. Not reconciling actual consumption against norms every batch. Ignoring storage licence limits when ordering solvents.

t: What is a key starting material?
x: The material that becomes a significant structural part of the API and from which GMP controls apply. It needs the tightest specification and vendor control.

t: Why is raw material sampled even with a supplier CoA?
x: GMP requires the user to verify identity and quality. A qualified vendor may allow reduced testing, but identity is always confirmed and full testing is repeated periodically.

s: How to choose a reactor: batch, semi-batch, CSTR and plug flow compared on residence time, conversion, selectivity, heat removal and safety.
x: Reactor Selection: Batch, Semi-batch, CSTR or Flow Process Design · Reaction Engineering · October 2026 Most API and fine chemical plants are built around batch reactors, and for good reasons. But the choice of reactor type changes conversion, selectivity, safety and cost, and sometimes a different type solves a problem that no amount of batch optimisation can. This article compares the four basic reactor types and when each one makes sense. In this article The four basic types Basics Residence time and conversion Working level Selectivity: where the reactor type really matters Working level Heat removal and safety Working level Choosing in practice Going deeper Questions people ask The four basic types Basics Batch: everything charged, reacted, discharged. Flexible, simple, the standard multi-purpose plant reactor. Semi-batch: one reactant dosed into the other. The workhorse for exother

s: Reactor Selection: Batch, Semi-batch, CSTR or Flow
x: Batch: everything charged, reacted, discharged. Flexible, simple, the standard multi-purpose plant reactor. Semi-batch: one reactant dosed into the other. The workhorse for exothermic reactions because dosing controls the heat. See semi-batch dosing . Continuous stirred tank (CSTR): feed in and product out continuously, well mixed, so the whole contents sit at the outlet composition. Plug flow (PFR): a tube where each slice of fluid travels through without mixing with the slices before and after. Every slice behaves like a small batch reactor. Modern flow chemistry reactors approach this. See flow chemistry .

t: Residence time and conversion Working level
s: Reactor Selection: Batch, Semi-batch, CSTR or Flow
x: For a simple first-order reaction with rate constant k and residence time τ, the product kτ (the Damköhler number) sets conversion: Batch or plug flow: X = 1 - e^-kτ One CSTR: X = kτ / (1 + kτ) To reach 90 % conversion, a batch or plug flow reactor needs kτ = 2.3; a single CSTR needs kτ = 9, almost four times the volume. The reason is that the CSTR runs entirely at the outlet concentration, where the reactant is depleted and the rate is slow. Two CSTRs in series need about 1.9 times the plug flow volume; more tanks in series approach plug flow. Try it: set the conversion you need and compare the residence time each reactor type requires. The

t: Selectivity: where the reactor type really matters Working level
s: Reactor Selection: Batch, Semi-batch, CSTR or Flow
x: Conversion only costs volume. Selectivity costs yield and purity, and the reactor type affects it strongly: Consecutive reactions (A → desired B → unwanted C): plug flow or batch, stopped at the right time, gives the most B. A CSTR keeps B in the reactor with fresh conversion going on, so more C forms. Parallel reactions where the side reaction has a higher order in a reagent: keep that reagent dilute. Semi-batch dosing or a CSTR does this naturally. Fast reactions limited by mixing: local excess at the feed point gives impurities. Small, well-mixed flow reactors or good feed-point design help.

t: Heat removal and safety Working level
s: Reactor Selection: Batch, Semi-batch, CSTR or Flow
x: A large batch reactor has little cooling area per litre and holds the whole inventory of reactive material. A CSTR at steady state holds mostly converted material, so the energy available for a runaway is smaller. A flow reactor has a tiny volume and enormous area per volume, so it can run reactions that would be unsafe or impossible in batch: very fast, very exothermic, or with unstable intermediates that are made and consumed within seconds. The trade-off is complexity: continuous plants need steady feeds, accurate pumps, good analytics and a plan for start-up, shut-down and blockages.

s: Reactor Selection: Batch, Semi-batch, CSTR or Flow
x: It runs entirely at the low outlet concentration; for 90 % conversion about 3.9× the volume.

Engineers who know the basics avoid nasty surprises. s: Regulatory Affairs Basics for API Plants
x: US Drug Master File (DMF), Type II: a confidential file with the US FDA describing the manufacture and control of the API. The customer’s product application refers to it. EU Active Substance Master File (ASMF): similar, with an applicant’s part shared with the customer and a restricted part that only regulators see. Certificate of Suitability (CEP): issued by the EDQM when an API meets its European Pharmacopoeia monograph; customers in Europe and many other markets can use it instead of a full file. National registrations in other markets, often based on the same core data.

t: What is in the file Basics
s: Regulatory Affairs Basics for API Plants
x: Files follow the Common Technical Document format; the API section (3.2.S) covers general information, manufacturer and site, the description of the process with flow diagrams and process controls, control of materials including starting materials, critical steps and intermediates, process validation, characterisation and impurities, specifications and analytical methods with validation, reference standards, container closure and stability data.

t: Impurities: the questions regulators ask Working level
s: Regulatory Affairs Basics for API Plants
x: ICH Q3A: reporting, identification and qualification thresholds for organic impurities in new drug substances. ICH Q3C: residual solvent classes and limits. ICH Q3D: elemental impurities, including metal catalysts. ICH M7: mutagenic impurities, controlled to very low levels on a risk basis, and the nitrosamine requirements that followed. These connect directly to the plant: a new solvent, a different catalyst or a change in quench can introduce something the file does not cover.

t: Why plant changes need regulatory assessment Working level
s: Regulatory Affairs Basics for API Plants
x: Once a file is approved, changes are classified by their potential impact. Changing a starting material supplier, the route, a solvent, a critical parameter range, a specification, the manufacturing site or a major piece of equipment can require a notification or prior approval in one or more markets, with supporting data such as comparative batches and stability. Some changes take many months to approve. That is why every change control in a regulated plant includes a regulatory impact question, answered by regulatory affairs; see QA and change control .

s: Regulatory Affairs Basics for API Plants
x: Files are kept current with annual reports or updates, and ICH Q12 provides tools for managing post-approval changes more predictably. Regulators also inspect the site against what is filed: an inspector will compare the batch record, equipment and procedures with the file, so the plant and the file must tell the same story. On the plant Before a trial with a new solvent, vendor or larger reactor in a registered process, a two-line email to regulatory affairs asking “is this filed?” costs nothing and can save months.

s: Regulatory Affairs Basics for API Plants
x: Treating regulatory affairs as a typing department at the end. Plant changes made before the regulatory impact is known. Batch records that no longer match the filed process. New solvents or catalysts introduced without impurity assessment. Stability not started for changes that need it.

x: Relief Valve Sizing Basics Process Design · Pressure Protection · October 2026 A relief valve sits on top of a vessel for years doing nothing, and then has a few seconds to do its one job. Whether it succeeds depends on decisions made long before: which scenario it was sized for, whether the pipe to it is too long, whether someone fitted a valve underneath it. This article explains how relief sizing works, from the basic idea to an API 520 calculation, and where the common traps are. In this article Why vessels need relief Basics Set pressure, overpressure and MAWP Basics Finding the governing scenario Working level The fire case, worked through Working level Sizing the orifice with API 520 Working level Rupture discs and runaway reactions Going deeper Installation: where good sizing goes wrong Going deeper Questions people ask Why vessels need relief Basics Every vessel has a pressure i

Every vessel has a pressure it was designed for. Control systems, alarms and trips keep it well below that pressure most of the time. But all of them can fail: a control valve sticks open, cooling water stops, a fire starts under the vessel. The relief device is the last line of protection: a purely mechanical device that opens when the pressure reaches its set point and lets enough fluid out to stop the pressure rising further. “Enough” is the important word. A relief valve that opens but is too small simply slows the pressure rise, and the vessel still fails. Sizing is about matching the valve's capacity to the worst credible flow it must p

t: Set pressure, overpressure and MAWP Basics
x: MAWP (maximum allowable working pressure) is the highest pressure the vessel is certified for at its design temperature. It is on the nameplate. Set pressure is where the valve starts to open, normally at or below the MAWP. Overpressure is how far above MAWP the pressure may rise while the valve is discharging at full capacity: 10 % for a single valve on a process upset, 16 % with several valves, and 21 % for an external fire (ASME Section VIII and API 520/521). Relieving pressure = set pressure + overpressure. Sizing uses this pressure. Operating pressure should sit at least 10 % below set pressure, or the valve will simmer and leak.

t: Finding the governing scenario Working level
x: API 521 lists the causes of overpressure to consider. For a typical batch reactor in a pharma plant, the list usually narrows to: External fire around the vessel. Blocked outlet on a vent or condenser line while nitrogen or steam keeps flowing in. Control valve failure on the nitrogen supply, steam to the jacket, or a pump discharging into the vessel. Loss of cooling during reflux or reaction. Runaway reaction or decomposition. Tube rupture in a heat exchanger with a high-pressure side. Each credible scenario gives a relieving load. The largest one, the governing scenario , sets the size. Write all of them down with the reasoning: a future re

t: The fire case, worked through Working level
x: In a fire, the liquid inside boils and the vapour must escape. API 521 gives the heat absorbed by a vessel with adequate drainage and firefighting: Q = 43,200 × F × Awetted^0.82 (W) Awetted: wetted area in m², counted up to 7.6 m above grade. F: environment factor, 1.0 for a bare vessel, lower with approved insulation. Without adequate drainage, the constant is 70,900. Take a 6 m³ reactor holding toluene with a wetted area of about 12 m², set at 3 barg: Q = 43,200 × 12^0.82 W (API 521 constant, in watts) ≈ 331 kW ≈ 2,84,600 kcal/h. Relieving pressure = 3 × 1.21 + 1.01 ≈ 4.64 bar abs. Toluene boils at about 175 °C at this pressure, where its l

t: Sizing the orifice with API 520 Working level
x: For a gas or vapour in critical (choked) flow, which is almost always the case when the valve discharges to a header near atmospheric pressure: A = W / (C × Kd × P1 × Kb × Kc) × √(T × Z / M) A in mm², W in kg/h, P1 relieving pressure in kPa abs, T in K, M molar mass. C = 0.03948 × √[k (2/(k+1))^(k+1)/(k-1)] from the ratio of specific heats k. Kd = 0.975 for a preliminary valve size; Kb = 1 for conventional valves with low back pressure; Kc = 0.9 with a rupture disc upstream, otherwise 1. For toluene, k ≈ 1.09 gives C ≈ 0.0247. With W = 3,850 kg/h, P1 = 464 kPa, T = 448 K (175 °C + 273, the formula needs absolute temperature) and Z taken as 1:

t: Rupture discs and runaway reactions Going deeper
x: A rupture disc is a thin membrane that bursts at a set pressure. It opens fully in milliseconds, has no moving parts and is tight against leaks and corrosive vapours. But once burst, it stays open until replaced. Discs are used alone on reactors where a fast, large opening matters, and upstream of a relief valve to protect it from corrosion (with a pressure gauge between them to detect a leaking disc). A runaway reaction is a different problem from fire. As temperature climbs, the batch foams and swells, so the relief discharges a two-phase mixture of liquid and vapour. Two-phase flow needs a much larger area than vapour alone, often several

t: Installation: where good sizing goes wrong Going deeper
x: Inlet pressure loss above 3 % of set pressure makes the valve open and close rapidly (chatter), which can destroy it. Keep inlet lines short and at least the valve's inlet size. Back pressure from a long discharge line or a shared header reduces capacity. Above about 10 % of set pressure, use a balanced-bellows valve and the Kb correction. No isolation valve under a relief device unless it is locked or car-sealed open under a written procedure. A safe discharge: to a scrubber, flare, catch tank or a safe high point, never into a work area or back into a building. Testing: bench-test valves at the interval the inspection plan sets, and record

Sizing only for fire and never considering the runaway case. Using the set pressure instead of the relieving pressure in the formula. Isolation valves under relief valves left closed after maintenance. Long, small-bore inlet lines that make the valve chatter. Not revisiting relief sizing when a new product moves into an old reactor.
10 % above MAWP for a single valve on a process upset, 16 % with several valves, and 21 % for fire.

t: How is the fire case load calculated?
x: Q = 43,200 × F × A^0.82 W with adequate drainage; divide by the latent heat at relieving conditions.

t: Can a relief valve protect against a runaway?
x: Usually not if sized for vapour only. Runaways need two-phase sizing with DIERS methods and calorimetry data.

This article sets out what the role is accountable for and how good site heads organise their day. t: What the site head is accountable for Basics
s: The Role of a Site Head
x: A simple way to remember it is SQDCP , in that order of priority: Safety: people, process safety and the environment. The head of QA has independent authority to release or reject; the site head’s job is to protect that independence and make sure production is never rewarded for pushing a batch through. Customer audits and regulatory inspections are led with the site head present and responsible for the commitments made. See QA and GMP .

Weekly reviews : production plan versus actual, maintenance backlog, open deviations and CAPA, safety observations and near misses. Monthly reviews : KPIs, budget, people, capex, compliance register and management review of quality.

x: Scrubber Design for Process Vents Process Safety · Emissions · October 2026 The vent scrubber stands at the edge of the plant, usually forgotten until someone smells HCl in the yard. Yet it is a safety device: it stops toxic gases escaping during normal operation and during upsets. Designing and running one well comes down to a few questions: what gas, how much, how fast, and is there still enough caustic left to catch it. ► Watch: Industrial Gas Scrubbing (YouTube Short) In this article What a scrubber does Basics Choosing the liquor Basics How long the caustic lasts Working level Sizing for the peak Working level Running it safely Going deeper Questions people ask What a scrubber does Basics A wet scrubber brings the vent gas into close contact with a liquid that absorbs or reacts with the pollutant. Most process scrubbers are packed columns: gas flows up through packing while the liqu

A wet scrubber brings the vent gas into close contact with a liquid that absorbs or reacts with the pollutant. Most process scrubbers are packed columns: gas flows up through packing while the liquor is pumped from a tank, sprayed on top and trickles down. Venturi or jet scrubbers use a high-velocity liquid jet to draw in and scrub the gas, which also helps pull vapours from the process.

SO2 NaOH Forms sulphite, then bisulphite; 1–2 mol NaOH per mol SO2 depending on pH. Cl2 NaOH Forms hypochlorite; 2 mol NaOH per mol Cl2. Keep excess caustic, or chlorine breaks through and the liquor can decompose. NH3, amines Dilute H2SO4 Forms ammonium sulphate. H2S NaOH (or hypochlorite) Forms NaHS/Na2S; never let it meet acid again. For HF, NOx, HCN, SO3, phosgene, mercaptans and the gases a scrubber cannot treat (H2, CO, CO2), see the full gas scrubbing agent table . Never route incompatible v

t: How long the caustic lasts Working level
x: For HCl: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O, so each kg of HCl uses 40/36.5 ≈ 1.1 kg of NaOH. A 2,000 kg charge of 10 % NaOH holds 200 kg of NaOH. If each batch releases 60 kg of HCl, it uses about 66 kg of NaOH. Keeping at least about 2 % free caustic as a reserve for upsets leaves room for only two batches before the liquor must be changed. Try it: change the HCl per batch, liquor quantity and strength, and see how many batches the scrubber can take before the free caustic is too low. Heat matters too. Neutralisation releases about 13.7 kcal per mol, and absorbing gaseous HCl into water releases roughly as much again. A fast release into a small tank

t: Sizing for the peak Working level
x: A scrubber that handles the average flow can fail at the peak: the first minutes of a thionyl chloride distillation, a quench, or a relief event. Size the gas side for the peak rate, check the pressure drop through the packing at that rate, and keep enough liquid flow to wet the packing fully (manufacturers give a minimum wetting rate). Gas that bypasses the liquid goes straight to the stack.

Measure the liquor: pH or conductivity online, and free caustic by titration on a schedule. Change it at a set strength, not when it smells. Interlock the process: no vent-producing step if the scrubber pump is off or the fan has failed. Alarm on low recirculation flow. Prevent suck-back: when a reactor cools or goes under vacuum, scrubber liquor can be drawn back up the vent line into it, with violent results if the reactor holds thionyl chloride or hydride. Use a dip-leg arrangement with enough height, a vacuum breaker or a knock-out pot, and keep the reactor under slight nitrogen pressure. Watch for solids: salts crystallising from strong

Changing the liquor only when the outlet smells. Sizing for average gas flow, not the peak. No interlock between the scrubber pump and gas-producing steps. Combining incompatible vents in one scrubber. Ignoring suck-back when a reactor cools under vacuum.

t: How much NaOH is needed to scrub HCl?
x: About 1.1 kg NaOH per kg HCl, plus a reserve.

t: When should scrubber caustic be changed?
x: At a set minimum free caustic, commonly about 2–3 %, before it is exhausted.

t: What is suck-back in a scrubber?
x: Liquor pulled back into a cooling or evacuated vessel through the vent line.

s: Why exothermic reactions run semi-batch: accumulation, how dosing time and temperature set the MTSR, plant cooling capacity and the interlocks that matter.
x: Semi-Batch Reactions: Dosing Time, Accumulation and MTSR Scale-up · Reaction Safety · October 2026 “Dose the reagent over 4 hours.” Every batch card for an exothermic reaction has a line like this, and on a busy night someone always asks why it can't be 2 hours. The honest answer is not “because the SOP says so”. It is about how much unreacted reagent is sitting in the reactor at any moment, and what that reagent would do if the cooling failed. This article builds that answer from the ground up. In this article Why we dose instead of mixing everything Basics Accumulation: the reagent waiting to react Basics From accumulation to MTSR Working level Can the plant cool it? Working level Why colder is not always safer Going deeper Protecting a dosing step Going deeper Questions people ask Why we dose instead of mixing everything Basics If two reactants that release a lot of heat are mixed all

t: Why we dose instead of mixing everything Basics
s: Semi-Batch Reactions: Dosing Time, Accumulation and MTSR
x: If two reactants that release a lot of heat are mixed all at once (a batch reaction), the whole heat of reaction is available from the first minute. If cooling fails, there is nothing you can do: everything is already in the reactor. In a semi-batch reaction, one reactant is in the reactor and the other is dosed in slowly. Ideally each drop reacts almost as soon as it arrives, so the heat comes out at the rate you dose. That gives you a control handle: if the temperature rises or cooling fails, stop dosing, and the heat release stops too. At least, that is the idea. Whether it is true depends on accumulation.

t: Accumulation: the reagent waiting to react Basics
s: Semi-Batch Reactions: Dosing Time, Accumulation and MTSR
x: Reagent doesn't react instantly. At any moment during dosing, some of what has been added has reacted and some hasn't. The unreacted part is the accumulation . If the reaction is fast compared with the dosing, accumulation stays low and stopping the feed really does stop the heat. If the reaction is slow, reagent piles up, and stopping the feed doesn't help much: the reagent already in the reactor keeps reacting. Think of filling a bucket with a hole in it. The tap is the dosing rate; the hole is the reaction. The water level in the bucket is the accumulation. Open the tap faster, or make the hole smaller (a colder, slower reaction), and the

t: From accumulation to MTSR Working level
s: Semi-Batch Reactions: Dosing Time, Accumulation and MTSR
x: The worst case is a total cooling failure at the moment accumulation is highest. All the unreacted reagent then reacts with no cooling, and the batch heats up by its share of the adiabatic temperature rise: ΔTad = Qreaction / (m × cp) MTSR = Tprocess + Xacc × ΔTad MTSR: maximum temperature of the synthesis reaction. Xacc: accumulation as a fraction (0 to 1). Then compare the MTSR with two temperatures that matter: the MTT , the maximum technical temperature (usually the boiling point of the solvent, in an open or vented system), and TD24 , the temperature at which a decomposition would reach its maximum rate in 24 hours. Those comparisons giv

s: Semi-Batch Reactions: Dosing Time, Accumulation and MTSR
x: A 3,000 kg batch in toluene with cp 0.43 kcal/kg·°C; the full dose releases 62 kcal per kg of batch. ΔTad = 62 / 0.43 ≈ 144 °C. Toluene boils at 111 °C; the decomposition TD24 is 140 °C. The reaction runs at 60 °C. Dosed over 4 hours : peak accumulation about 14 %, MTSR ≈ 60 + 0.14 × 144 ≈ 80 °C. Below boiling: class 1. Dosed over 1 hour : peak accumulation about 46 %, MTSR ≈ 126 °C. Above boiling but below TD24: class 3, relying on the solvent boiling to stop the temperature. Dosed over 30 minutes : MTSR ≈ 155 °C, above TD24: class 4 or 5, a potential runaway into decomposition. Try it: the line is the MTSR at each moment, the temperature th

t: Can the plant cool it? Working level
s: Semi-Batch Reactions: Dosing Time, Accumulation and MTSR
x: Accumulation is about the cooling failure case. There is a second check for normal operation: can the jacket remove the heat as fast as the reaction makes it? Heat release rate ≈ total reaction heat / dosing time Cooling capacity = U × A × (Tbatch - Tjacket) In the example, the total heat is 3,000 × 62 = 1,86,000 kcal. Over 4 hours that is about 46,500 kcal/h; over 1 hour, about 1,86,000 kcal/h. If the jacket can remove about 60,000 kcal/h (U × A of 1,200 kcal/h·°C and 50 °C between batch and cooling water), the 4-hour dosing is controllable and the 1-hour dosing is not: the temperature will rise even with the cooling working perfectly. This

t: Why colder is not always safer Going deeper
s: Semi-Batch Reactions: Dosing Time, Accumulation and MTSR
x: A natural instinct with an exotherm is to run it colder. It feels safer: more margin to the boiling point. But a colder reaction is slower, and a slower reaction accumulates more reagent during dosing. In the example, dosing over 4 hours at 60 °C gives an MTSR of about 80 °C. The same dosing at 40 °C gives about 126 °C, because the reaction rate roughly quarters and reagent piles up. The batch is cooler while it runs, but much more dangerous if cooling fails. Worse, a reaction that is too cold may stall almost completely; if someone then warms it up, everything accumulated reacts at once. That is why many dosing steps have a minimum temperatu

t: Protecting a dosing step Going deeper
s: Semi-Batch Reactions: Dosing Time, Accumulation and MTSR
x: Measure it. Reaction calorimetry (RC1 or similar) gives the heat of reaction, the heat release profile and the accumulation directly. DSC or ARC on the final mixture gives the decomposition onset and TD24. See thermal safety testing . Limit the dosing rate physically: a restriction orifice, a dosing pump that cannot exceed the safe rate, or a dosing vessel that holds only one batch quantity. Interlock the feed: stop dosing on high temperature, low temperature, agitator stopped (rotation, not just motor current) and cooling failure. Never restart blindly after an agitator stop or a long dosing interruption: sample or wait for the accumulated r

s: Semi-Batch Reactions: Dosing Time, Accumulation and MTSR
x: The fraction of dosed reagent that has not reacted yet. MTSR = process temperature + accumulation × ΔTad.

t: Is it safer to run colder?
s: Semi-Batch Reactions: Dosing Time, Accumulation and MTSR
x: Not always. Colder means slower, which means more accumulation. In the example, 40 °C gives a higher MTSR than 60 °C for the same dosing time.

t: How do you choose the dosing time?
s: Semi-Batch Reactions: Dosing Time, Accumulation and MTSR
x: Long enough that the heat release stays within the plant's cooling capacity and that the MTSR stays below the boiling point and TD24, confirmed by reaction calorimetry.

s: Soft sensors for chemical and pharma plants: what they estimate, physics vs data-driven models, drift, GMP use and a free tool to fit one from your data.
x: Soft Sensors in Chemical Plants Digitalization and AI · Plant Engineering · October 2026 AI basics AI plant examples Predictive maintenance Soft sensors Digital twins GenAI for SOPs and deviations Process historian MES and eBMR OEE in batch plants OT cybersecurity Plant KPI dashboard Digital business case Your lab tells you the impurity four hours after the sample was taken. By then the batch has moved on. A soft sensor fills the gap with an estimate every minute, built from measurements you already log. This article explains what soft sensors can estimate, how to build one, how to keep it honest, and includes a free tool to fit and test one on your own data. In this article What a soft sensor is Basics Three ways to build one Basics Build your own (regression tool) Working level Drift and recalibration Working level Soft sensors under GMP Going deeper Mistakes I see most often Questions

t: What a soft sensor is Basics
x: A soft sensor (also called a virtual sensor or inferential) estimates a quantity that is slow, expensive or impossible to measure online, using measurements the plant already logs. The lab may report an impurity every four hours; the soft sensor gives a best estimate every minute from temperatures, pressures, flows and power. What you want to know Fast inputs that often carry the information Reaction conversion or residual starting material Heat released (jacket flow × ΔT), dosing integral, reaction time, temperature profile Distillate or bottoms purity Tray temperatures, reflux ratio, pressure, feed rate Moisture or residual solvent during d

t: Three ways to build one Basics
x: First-principles: a balance equation. U-value from heat duty and log-mean temperature difference is a soft sensor for fouling. Most robust outside past data, needs good instruments. Data-driven: regression or machine learning from past data. Fast to build where the physics is messy; only valid inside the range it was trained on. Hybrid: a physics model with a data-driven correction for what the physics misses. Often the best choice for reactors and dryers.

t: Build your own soft sensor (regression tool) Working level
x: Paste data exported from your historian and lab: one row per lab sample, up to three input columns, and the lab result in the last column, oldest row first. The tool fits a linear model on the first 70% of rows and tests it on the last 30%, the way a soft sensor would be tested on batches it has not seen. Your data stays in your browser.

Columns separated by tabs, commas or spaces. Header row optional. At least 10 rows. Fit model Load made-up example How to read it: a test R² close to the training R² means the model generalises; a much lower test R² means it learned noise or the process changed. The test error (RMSE) should be well inside the specification width before anyone uses the estimate.

t: Keeping it honest: drift and recalibration Working level
x: Keep taking lab samples. They are the reference that tells you when the soft sensor has drifted. Fewer samples, not none. Set a limit in advance for the difference between estimate and lab; when it is crossed, stop using the estimate for decisions and investigate. Watch the inputs. A soft sensor is only valid inside the range of its training data. Flag inputs outside it: new grade, new scale, new raw material supplier. Recalibrate under change control, with the new model tested on data it has not seen. Try the drift demo in AI in the chemical industry .

t: Soft sensors under GMP Going deeper
x: If a soft sensor only helps operators, treat it as an advisory tool with ordinary engineering change control. If its output is used for a GMP decision, such as an end point, an in-process control or release, it becomes part of the control strategy: document the intended use, validate on independent data, freeze the model version and manage changes formally. The EU draft GMP Annex 22 (July 2025) sets out these expectations for AI models in critical GMP use.

Testing on random rows, so samples from the same batch sit in both training and test data and the model looks better than it is. Lab results matched to the wrong time: the sample time, not the time the result was entered. Using inputs that are set points rather than measurements. Stopping lab sampling once the soft sensor “works”.

t: What is a soft sensor in a chemical plant?
x: A model that estimates a slow or expensive measurement, such as an impurity, conversion or moisture, from fast measurements the plant already logs, such as temperatures, pressures, flows and power.

t: How much data do I need to build a soft sensor?
x: Enough lab results, matched to process data at the sample time, to cover the normal operating range: often a few dozen to a few hundred samples. Always test on the most recent data, not on random rows.

t: Can a soft sensor replace lab testing?
x: Not entirely. Lab results remain the reference that shows when the model has drifted. Many plants reduce sampling frequency once the soft sensor is proven, and keep a check sample on a fixed schedule.

x: Solvent Recovery Calculation: From Boiling Point to Batch Time Chemical Engineering · Distillation · Updated October 2026 Almost every batch in a pharma or agrochemical plant ends the same way: the reaction is done, and now the solvent has to come off. How hot will the batch get? How long will it take? Will the condenser keep up, or will solvent end up in the vacuum pump oil? This article answers those questions in order, from the basic idea to the checks that decide whether a recovery runs smoothly on the plant. t: Why we recover under vacuum Basics
s: Solvent Recovery Calculation: From Boiling Point to Batch Time
x: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure reaches the pressure above it. At sea level that is about 1,013 mbar, so toluene boils at 110.6 °C. Lower the pressure in the reactor and the liquid needs less heat to reach that point, so it boils cooler. Cooler boiling helps in three ways. The product is less likely to degrade. Hot water or low-pressure steam is enough to drive the distillation. And the gap between the jacket and the batch is bigger, so heat flows in faster. Heat from the jacket boils the solvent, vapour travels to the condenser, liquid drains to the receiver, and the vacuum pump removes only air and leakage, if the condenser is doing

t: Boiling point at any pressure: the Antoine equation Basics
s: Solvent Recovery Calculation: From Boiling Point to Batch Time
x: The relation between vapour pressure and temperature is curved: each 10 °C of temperature roughly doubles a solvent's vapour pressure near its boiling point. The Antoine equation describes that curve with three constants per solvent: log₁₀(P) = A - B / (T + C) ⇒ Tb = B / (A - log₁₀P) - C P in mmHg and T in °C for the constants used here. Some tables use bar and kelvin, so always check the units of the set you use. For toluene, A = 6.95087, B = 1342.31, C = 219.187. At 100 mmHg (133 mbar): Tb = 1342.31 / (6.95087 - 2.000) - 219.187 ≈ 271.1 - 219.2 ≈ 52 °C A quick sanity check for any Antoine set: put P = 760 mmHg in and you should get the norm

x: The Antoine equation is for one pure liquid. A mixture boils at a temperature between its components, and that temperature rises as the lighter one leaves. x: Solvent Selection and Solvent Swaps Scale-up · Solvents · October 2026 Many API processes use three or four solvents across a sequence of steps, and every change from one to the next costs time, energy and solvent. The swap is often the longest step in the batch and the one that most often leaves too much of the old solvent behind. This article covers how to choose solvents in the first place and how to swap them efficiently. The chemist picks a solvent for the chemistry: solubility, reactivity, selectivity. At scale, more questions matter: Safety: flash point, static (conductivity), peroxide formation (THF, ethers), toxicity, thermal stability with reagents (DMF and DMSO with strong bases and hydrides). Work-up: water miscibility, density difference from water, emulsion tendency. Recovery: boiling point, azeotropes with water and other solvents, ease of drying. Regulatory and environmental: ICH class, emission limits, effluent load. Cost and supply. Published solvent selection guides (for example from the ACS GCI Pharmaceutical Roundtable and CHEM21) rank common

t: Residual solvents and ICH classes Basics
x: ICH Q3C groups solvents by toxicity: Class 1 (avoid: benzene, carbon tetrachloride), Class 2 (limit, with a permitted concentration for each: toluene 890 ppm, methanol 3,000 ppm, DCM 600 ppm, acetonitrile 410 ppm), and Class 3 (low toxicity, generally up to 5,000 ppm: ethanol, acetone, ethyl acetate, IPA). The class of the last solvents used before isolation matters most, because they are the hardest to remove completely.

t: Two ways to swap Working level
x: To change from a low-boiling solvent (say THF) to a higher-boiling one (say toluene): Put-and-take: distil down to the minimum volume, add the new solvent back to the working volume, distil down again, repeat. Simple to run, with several “chases”. Concentrate, then constant volume: distil down to the minimum volume, then keep distilling while feeding new solvent at the same rate as distillate leaves, holding the volume constant. Finally top up to the working volume. Both work because the old solvent is more volatile: the vapour is richer in it than the liquid. With a relative volatility of 3.5, distilling down to half volume and swapping at t

t: Azeotropes and other traps Working level
x: Azeotropes: methanol and toluene, ethanol and toluene, IPA and water all form azeotropes. A swap that crosses one can't reach low residuals by simple distillation; the residual levels off. Check azeotrope data before designing a swap, and sometimes swap through a third solvent. Product stability: concentrating to a low volume at high temperature can degrade the product or crystallise it on the wall. Use vacuum to keep the temperature down. See vacuum systems . Water: water from a work-up often has to come out with the old solvent; toluene's heterogeneous azeotrope with water helps here (azeotropic drying with a Dean-Stark separator). Swapping

t: Doing it in the plant Going deeper
x: Define the end point by analysis (GC of the pot), not by the number of chases. Know the true minimum stirrable volume of the reactor, with the agitator covered and the temperature probe immersed. Watch the top temperature: as the old solvent runs out, it rises toward the new solvent's boiling point at that pressure. Collect the distillate separately for recovery; mixed distillate of two solvents is harder to recover than either alone. See distillation basics . On the plant If the residual old solvent stalls at the same value after each chase, suspect an azeotrope or a dead volume (a condenser leg, a dip pipe, a sample line) that keeps feeding

Fixing the number of chases instead of testing the residual. Ignoring an azeotrope between the two solvents. Not knowing the true minimum stirrable volume. Overheating the product during concentration. Mixing the distillates of different solvents.

t: What is a put-and-take solvent swap?
x: Repeated distilling down and refilling with the new solvent.
Distilling while feeding new solvent at the same rate, keeping the volume constant.

t: Why does a solvent swap sometimes stall?

s: How static builds up in plants: spark energy ½CV² vs MIE, low-conductivity solvents, bonding and earthing, filling and inerting, with the Barton case.
x: Static Electricity and Solvent Fires Process Safety · Ignition Sources · October 2026 Most solvent fires in pharma and fine chemical plants are not caused by a welding torch or a faulty motor. They start with a spark nobody saw: from a drum on a plastic pallet, an operator's body, or a plastic bag of powder tipped into a reactor. This article explains, from the beginning, how static charge builds up, why a spark too small to feel can ignite a solvent, and which simple controls stop it. In this article What static charge is Basics How charge builds up Basics How much energy is in a spark Working level Solvents that hold their charge Working level The controls that work Working level Powder into a solvent reactor Going deeper When earthing was not enough: Barton Solvents Going deeper Questions people ask What static charge is Basics Every material contains equal amounts of positive and neg

Every material contains equal amounts of positive and negative charge, so normally it is neutral. When two different materials touch, a few electrons cross from one to the other. Pull them apart and those electrons don't all go back: one side is left slightly positive, the other slightly negative. That separated charge is static electricity. It happens whenever things rub or separate: a solvent flowing along a pipe wall, powder sliding out of a bag, a person walking across the floor, a belt running over a pulley, nitrogen blowing through a hose. The more contact and the faster the separation, the more charge. A fine filter is one of the stron

Charge being generated is not, by itself, dangerous. It becomes dangerous only if it cannot escape. Think of a bucket under a running tap with a hole in the bottom. The tap is charge generation; the hole is the path to earth. If the hole is big (earthed metal, a conductive liquid), the level never rises. If the hole is tiny (a plastic container, an unbonded drum, toluene), the level rises until it overflows. In electrical terms, the voltage rises until the air breaks down, roughly 3 kV per millimetre, and the stored charge jumps as a spark. We can rarely stop generation in a process plant. The job is to make sure the leak is always bigger tha

t: How much energy is in a spark Working level
x: A charged object behaves like a capacitor. The energy it can release in one spark is: E = ½ C V² C capacitance in farads (a person about 100–300 pF, a 200 L drum about 100–200 pF, a road tanker about 1,000 pF), V voltage in volts. A person in ordinary shoes on a dry floor easily reaches 10 kV. With 200 pF that is ½ × 200×10^-12 × 10,000² = 0.01 J, or 10 mJ. You start to feel a spark at about 1 mJ. Now compare that with the minimum ignition energy (MIE) , the smallest spark that ignites the most easily ignited mixture of the vapour in air: Solvent MIE (mJ) Flash point Holds charge? Methanol 0.14 11 °C No, conductive Toluene 0.24 4 °C Yes, low

t: Solvents that hold their charge Working level
x: A liquid's electrical conductivity decides how fast charge drains from it. The standard IEC TS 60079-32-1 groups liquids into three classes: Low conductivity, below 50 pS/m: toluene, xylene, hexane, heptane, many hydrocarbons. Charge can stay in the liquid for tens of seconds, even inside an earthed metal tank. Medium, 50 to 10,000 pS/m: some esters and ethers. High, above 10,000 pS/m: alcohols, ketones, water. Charge drains in microseconds, but only if the container is earthed. In a plastic can, even methanol charges up. The time charge stays in a liquid is its relaxation time, τ = εε0/κ (permittivity divided by conductivity). For toluene it

Clamp drums, IBCs and tankers before the lid or valve opens, and remove the clamp last. Bond across anything that breaks the metal path: PTFE-gasketed flanges, glass sections, flexible hoses. Test it: a metal-to-metal bond below 10 Ω shows it is real, and below 1 MΩ to earth is enough to drain static. Earth monitoring clamps with a green light, interlocked to the transfer pump, remove the guesswork. Paint, rust and dirt under a clamp can break the path.

t: 2. Fill slowly and from the bottom
x: Splash filling from a top nozzle breaks the liquid into droplets and mist, which generates charge and fills the vapour space with a fine flammable mist. Use a dip pipe to the bottom. For low-conductivity solvents, keep the velocity at 1 m/s or less until the pipe outlet is covered by liquid. Avoid air or water slugs in the line, and give the liquid time to relax after a filter before it reaches the tank.

Most solvent vapours cannot burn below about 10–12 % oxygen, the limiting oxygen concentration (LOC). Inerting with nitrogen to 8 % or less, checked with an analyser, removes one side of the fire triangle. It is the main control where charge cannot be avoided, such as powder charging or low-conductivity solvents. See the nitrogen purging calculator .

ESD (antistatic) footwear only works on a conductive floor, so check both. No mobile phones in solvent areas. Touch an earthed point before opening a manhole. Cotton or FR clothing rather than synthetics; never take off a jacket or wipe with a dry cloth near open solvent. On the plant Managers set the standard here more than any SOP. If a visitor or a senior person walks into the solvent store in leather-soled shoes, talking on a phone, the rule is dead for everyone who saw it.

t: Powder into a solvent reactor Going deeper
x: Tipping powder from a plastic bag through an open manhole into a reactor that already contains solvent is the most common cause of flash fires in API and intermediate plants. Everything lines up at once: a flammable vapour at the manhole, air coming in, powder and bag both charging as the powder slides out, and an operator standing in the vapour. The discharge from a plastic bag or liner is a brush discharge , up to about 4 mJ. That is too weak to ignite most dusts but easily enough for solvent vapour. A non-antistatic FIBC or a plastic-lined chute can give a propagating brush discharge of 1,000 mJ or more, which ignites almost anything. Char

t: When earthing was not enough: Barton Solvents Going deeper
x: On 17 July 2007, a 15,000-gallon tank exploded at the Barton Solvents distribution facility in Valley Center, Kansas, while a tanker unloaded VM&P naphtha, a low-conductivity solvent. The tank was thrown into the air, fire spread through the tank farm and about 6,000 residents were evacuated. The US Chemical Safety Board found four conditions lined up: the naphtha was nonconductive and held its charge; stop–start filling introduced air and turbulence, adding charge; the tank headspace was flammable and not inerted; a loose linkage on the level float, an isolated conductor inside the tank, likely sparked. The bonding and grounding of the trans

“I didn't feel a spark, so there wasn't one.” Assuming a conductive solvent is safe in a plastic container or an unbonded drum. Assuming nitrogen protection without ever measuring the oxygen. Plastic buckets, funnels and scoops kept “just for small additions”. Thinking static is a winter problem: humidity helps surfaces, but does nothing for charge inside a flowing liquid.

t: Can static electricity ignite solvent vapour?
x: Yes. Most solvent vapours ignite at 0.1–1 mJ, while a charged person can release about 10 mJ in one spark.

t: What resistance is acceptable for earthing?
x: Below 1 MΩ to earth is enough to drain static; a metal bond below 10 Ω confirms the connection is real.

t: Why are toluene and hexane worse than methanol?
x: Their very low conductivity keeps charge in the liquid for seconds to minutes, even in an earthed tank. Methanol drains its charge almost instantly if the equipment is earthed.

s: How much heat steam gives in a jacket, why low-pressure steam heats better, steam consumption, and how to size a reactor condenser and vent condenser.
x: Steam Energy and Condenser Selection Plant Engineering · Heat Transfer · October 2026 Two questions come up in almost every new batch process: how much steam will this heating step need, and is the reactor condenser big enough for the distillation? Both come down to the same physics: latent heat, given up by steam when it condenses in the jacket, and taken up again by the solvent vapour that has to condense in the condenser. This article goes through both, with the numbers engineers actually use. In this article What steam gives you Basics Which steam pressure to use Basics Steam consumption for a duty Working level Selecting a reactor condenser Working level Vacuum, vent condensers and non-condensables Going deeper Questions people ask What steam gives you Basics The enthalpy of saturated steam has two parts. Sensible heat (hf) is what it took to heat the water to boiling. Latent heat (

The enthalpy of saturated steam has two parts. Sensible heat (hf) is what it took to heat the water to boiling. Latent heat (hfg) is what it took to boil it. In a jacket or coil, steam condenses and gives up its latent heat; the condensate leaves through the trap still carrying its sensible heat. So the useful heat per kg in ordinary heating is the latent heat, about 500 kcal/kg at typical process pressures. Try it: raise the steam pressure. The total enthalpy hardly changes, but more of it is sensible heat that leaves with the condensate, and the latent heat per kg falls.

t: Which steam pressure to use Basics
x: Higher pressure gives a higher temperature, so a bigger temperature difference and faster heating. But it gives less latent heat per kg, and the hot condensate carries more energy away (recoverable only as flash steam). The rule: use the lowest steam pressure that gives the temperature difference you need . Many plants distribute at 8–10 barg to keep pipe sizes small and reduce to 2–4 barg at the users. Remember the product's wall temperature limit and the glass-lined vessel's thermal shock limits when choosing.

t: Steam consumption for a duty Working level
x: Steam (kg/h) = Q (kcal/h) / hfg (kcal/kg) × (1 + losses) 86,000 kcal/h of heating at 3 barg (hfg ≈ 509 kcal/kg) needs about 169 kg/h of steam, plus 10–15 % for losses from the vessel and lines. To distil 1,850 kg of toluene, about 1,59,000 kcal of latent heat, needs roughly 360 kg of steam with losses. See material and energy balance and the steam and boiler calculators . Wet steam (with water droplets), a failed trap that waterlogs the jacket, or air in the steam all reduce the heat delivered. If a jacket heats slowly, check the trap and the condensate drain before blaming the steam pressure.

t: Selecting a reactor condenser Working level
x: The condenser must remove the latent heat of all the vapour the reactor boils off, at the highest rate the steam can produce it: Duty = vapour rate × [λ + cp (Tcondensing - Tcondensate)] Area = Duty / (U × LMTD) Start from the reboil rate : the jacket heat input at full steam sets the maximum vapour rate. A condenser sized for the “normal” rate will be overloaded the first time someone opens the steam valve fully. Use the latent heat of the solvent at the condensing temperature: methanol (about 263 kcal/kg) needs three times the condenser of toluene (about 87 kcal/kg) for the same mass. Check the approach to the cooling water outlet: with 32/

t: Vacuum, vent condensers and non-condensables Going deeper
x: Under vacuum, the condensing temperature drops with the boiling point, the LMTD to cooling water shrinks and the area needed rises fast. Nitrogen bleed and air leaks add non-condensable gas that collects in the condenser and blankets the tubes, cutting U sharply. Keep a vent condenser on chilled water or brine after the main condenser to catch what the main one misses and to cut solvent loss to the vacuum pump. See vacuum systems . On the plant If the distillation rate stalls while the jacket still has steam, feel the condenser vapour outlet and check the vent. A hot outlet means the condenser is overloaded or blanketed with nitrogen, and the

Counting the total enthalpy of steam instead of the latent heat. Heating with high-pressure steam when low pressure would do. Sizing the condenser for the normal rather than the maximum boil-up. Ignoring non-condensables in vacuum condensers. No vent condenser on low-boiling solvents.

t: How much heat does steam give in a jacket?
x: Its latent heat: about 480–540 kcal/kg depending on pressure.

t: Why use low-pressure steam for heating?
x: More latent heat per kg and less energy lost with the condensate.

t: How do you size a reactor condenser?
x: Duty from the maximum boil-up and latent heat, then area = duty / (U × LMTD) with margin.

The condensed water, called condensate, drains through a steam trap , a small automatic valve that lets water out but holds steam in, and in a good system flows back to the boiler feed tank to be used again. s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: Every loss calculation needs this one number. The fuel part of it comes from an energy balance on the boiler: Heat per kg of steam = hg (at boiler pressure) - hfw (feed water) Fuel per tonne of steam = 1,000 × (hg - hfw) / (η × GCV) Fuel cost per tonne of steam = Fuel per tonne × fuel price hg comes from steam tables (about 664 kcal/kg at 10 barg), hfw ≈ 1 × feed water temperature (kcal/kg), η is the boiler efficiency and GCV the fuel's gross calorific value in kcal/kg.

s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: 10 barg steam, feed water 80 °C: 664 - 80 = 584 kcal/kg Coal at 4,000 kcal/kg, 75 % efficient: fuel = 1,000 × 584 / (0.75 × 4,000) ≈ 195 kg per tonne of steam At ₹8/kg: about ₹1,560 per tonne of steam (fuel only) The same steam from furnace oil at 10,200 kcal/kg, 85 % efficient and ₹55/kg costs about ₹3,700 per tonne. Add power for the FD/ID fans and feed pumps, water treatment, chemicals, ash handling, labour and maintenance, and the full cost is usually 15–30 % higher than the fuel cost alone. Use the full cost when you value savings. Try it: the fuel cost of one tonne of 10 barg steam for different fuels at their typical boiler efficiency.

t: Where the fuel goes Working level
s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: A coal or biomass boiler at 75 % efficiency loses a quarter of the fuel's heat before the steam leaves the boiler house. The usual split: Dry flue gas: the biggest loss. It rises with stack temperature and with excess air. Check O₂ in the flue gas: about 3–4 % on oil and gas, 6–8 % on solid fuel. Moisture: water in the fuel and water formed from hydrogen leave as vapour up the stack. Wet husk or wet coal costs real money. Unburnt carbon in ash: shows up as black ash. Grate speed, air distribution and fuel sizing matter. Radiation and convection: small at full load, larger at low load. Blowdown: hot boiler water drained to control TDS.

s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: Dissolved solids in the feed water stay behind when water boils, so the boiler water gets more concentrated until some of it is drained off. The blowdown needed to hold a TDS limit is: Blowdown (% of steam) = TDSfeed / (TDSboiler, max - TDSfeed) × 100 With 150 ppm feed water and a 3,000 ppm limit, blowdown is about 5.3 % of the steam. For a 5 t/h boiler at 10 barg that is about 263 kg/h of water at 184 °C, carrying (187 - 80) kcal/kg more heat than the feed water, about 28,000 kcal/h or roughly 0.7 % of the fuel. s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: A trap that fails open passes live steam into the condensate line. Napier's formula gives an upper estimate of the steam through an orifice: Steam (kg/h) ≈ 0.412 × d² (mm²) × P (bar abs)

s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: A survey of 200 traps on 7 barg steam finds 15 % (30 traps) blowing through. Taking an equivalent 2 mm hole for each: Per trap: 0.412 × 4 × 8.0 ≈ 13 kg/h 30 traps: ≈ 400 kg/h, about 3,200 tonnes a year over 8,000 hours At ₹2,500 per tonne: up to ₹80 lakh a year The real figure is usually lower, because a failed trap rarely blows the full seat area all the time. Even half of it pays for a trap survey and spares many times over. Test traps with an ultrasonic tester or a surface thermometer, tag the failed ones and recheck after repair.

s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: Condensate leaving a trap at 8 barg is at about 175 °C. In a return line at 0.5 barg water can only exist up to about 111 °C, so the extra heat boils part of it: Flash fraction = (hf,high - hf,low) / hfg,low = (743 - 467) / 2,226 ≈ 12 % That flash steam is ordinary low-pressure steam. If a flash vessel sends it to a low-pressure user such as a tank heater, an air heater or a deaerator, it replaces live steam. If not, it plumes from the feed tank vent, which also means the feed tank cannot be held at a high temperature.

s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: Returned condensate is hot, already treated water. Each kilogram returned saves: the fuel to heat make-up water from ambient to the condensate temperature: m × 4.186 × (Tc - Tmakeup); the treated water itself, and its softener or RO cost; chemicals and blowdown, because condensate has almost no dissolved solids. Returning 3 t/h of condensate at 90 °C instead of 30 °C make-up recovers about 1,80,000 kcal/h, roughly 60 kg/h of coal in a 75 % efficient boiler, plus 72 m³ a day of treated water. t: A steam audit checklist Going deeper
s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: Calculate the cost of steam per tonne and agree it with finance. Measure boiler efficiency monthly (direct method) and trend the evaporation ratio. Check flue gas O₂ and stack temperature every shift. Survey every steam trap at least once a year; keep a trap register. Walk the steam mains for leaks, missing insulation and wet lagging. Measure condensate return as a percentage of steam generated; most plants can reach 60–80 %. Look for vents with a steam plume: feed tank, condensate receivers, flash vessels. Set blowdown from boiler water TDS, not from habit.

s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: Valuing savings at the fuel cost only, which undervalues them; using hfg instead of hg - hfw for the boiler heat duty; measuring boiler efficiency over a short period at changing load; and assuming condensate return is happening because a return pump exists.

t: How do you calculate the cost of steam?
s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: Fuel per tonne = 1,000 × (hg - hfw) / (η × GCV × 4.1868), then multiply by the fuel price. For 10 barg steam from 80 °C feed water, a 75 % efficient boiler on ₹8/kg coal of 4,000 kcal/kg gives about ₹1,560 per tonne for fuel alone.

t: How do you calculate boiler blowdown?
s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: Blowdown (% of steam) = feed TDS / (maximum boiler TDS - feed TDS) × 100. With 150 ppm feed water and a 3,000 ppm limit it is about 5.3 %.

s: Solvent tank filling and breathing losses, conservation vents, nitrogen blanketing, flame arresters, vapour balancing and tank pressure-vacuum protection.
x: Solvent Storage Tanks: Breathing Losses and Vents Process Design · Storage · October 2026 A solvent tank farm loses solvent every day without a single leak. Each time a tanker fills a tank, the gas pushed out of the vent carries vapour with it; each sunny afternoon, the tank warms and breathes out a little more. The amounts look small per event and add up to tonnes a year. This article explains where the losses come from and the equipment that controls them and keeps the tank safe. In this article Why tanks lose solvent Basics Estimating filling losses Working level Conservation vents and arresters Working level Nitrogen blanketing Working level Reducing losses Going deeper Questions people ask Why tanks lose solvent Basics The space above the liquid in a solvent tank is saturated with vapour. Whenever gas leaves the tank, vapour leaves with it: Filling (working) losses: each m³ of liqui

s: Solvent Storage Tanks: Breathing Losses and Vents
x: The space above the liquid in a solvent tank is saturated with vapour. Whenever gas leaves the tank, vapour leaves with it: Filling (working) losses: each m³ of liquid pumped in pushes out about one m³ of saturated headspace gas. Breathing losses: daytime heating expands the headspace and raises the vapour pressure; the tank breathes out. At night it cools and breathes in air, which then saturates again. The amount depends almost entirely on the solvent's vapour pressure at the tank temperature. Acetone, MDC and methanol lose far more than toluene or xylene.

s: Solvent Storage Tanks: Breathing Losses and Vents
x: Solvent in vented gas (kg/m³) = Pvap × M / (R × T) Pvap in Pa from the Antoine equation, M in kg/mol, R = 8.314 J/mol·K, T absolute (°C + 273.15). Toluene at 30 °C has a vapour pressure of about 4.9 kPa, so each m³ of vented gas carries 4,890 × 0.092 / (8.314 × 303) ≈ 0.18 kg. Filling 100 m³ a month loses about 214 kg of toluene a year from filling alone. The same tank of acetone loses several times more. Try it: change the solvent, tank temperature and monthly throughput, and compare venting to air with a vent condenser and vapour balancing. For full estimates including breathing losses, use the US EPA AP-42 Chapter 7 methods, which account

t: Conservation vents and arresters Working level
s: Solvent Storage Tanks: Breathing Losses and Vents
x: A pressure-vacuum conservation vent (breather valve) stays closed over a small pressure range, for example opening at +20 mbar and -5 mbar. Small daily temperature changes are absorbed without venting, which cuts breathing losses. It also protects the tank: storage tanks are very weak, often designed for only tens of millibars, and a blocked vent can collapse a tank under vacuum when it is pumped out or cooled by rain. On flammable solvent tanks, a flame arrester or an end-of-line deflagration arrester stops an external flame entering the tank through the vent. Arresters block with polymer, dust or ice, so they need inspection. A separate eme

s: Solvent Storage Tanks: Breathing Losses and Vents
x: A blanketing regulator admits nitrogen whenever tank pressure falls (during emptying or cooling) and the conservation vent releases gas when it rises. This keeps air out, so the headspace stays below the LOC and cannot burn, and keeps moisture out of hygroscopic solvents. See inerting and LOC . Blanketing does not reduce filling losses: the gas pushed out is now nitrogen saturated with vapour instead of air saturated with vapour. Set the blanketing pressure below the vent's opening pressure, with enough margin that nitrogen isn't vented continuously.

s: Solvent Storage Tanks: Breathing Losses and Vents
x: Vapour balancing: connect the tank vent back to the road tanker during unloading, so the displaced vapour goes into the tanker instead of the air. It is the cheapest large reduction. Vent condenser: cool the vented gas with chilled water or brine to condense most of the solvent. At 5 °C, toluene's vapour pressure falls to about 1.2 kPa, removing roughly three-quarters of the loss. Insulation and white paint reduce the daily temperature swing and breathing loss. Carbon adsorption or a scrubber for toxic solvents where the remaining emission must be very low. On the plant Watch the breather valve during a tanker unloading. A vent that blows con

s: Solvent Storage Tanks: Breathing Losses and Vents
x: Assuming nitrogen blanketing reduces filling losses. Blanketing pressure set above the conservation vent setting. Uninspected flame arresters blocked with polymer or ice. No vacuum protection, risking tank collapse when emptied. Unloading tankers without vapour balancing.

x: Technology Transfer from R&D to Plant Plant Departments · Technology Transfer · October 2026 Technology transfer is where a lab process becomes a plant process. Done well, the first plant batch behaves like the lab. Done badly, the plant spends months rediscovering what R&D already knew. The difference is mostly in the documents and in the conversations around them.
