x: Q5. NAT · 2 marks A loop has ultimate gain Ku = 4 and ultimate period Pu = 10 min. Using Ziegler–Nichols settings for a PI controller, find the controller gain Kc. (round to 2 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 1.8 (accepted range 1.79 to 1.81) Z-N PI: Kc = 0.45 Ku = 1.80 , τI = Pu/1.2 = 8.33 min.

t: An air-to-open control valve, on loss of instrument air, will:
x: Q6. MCQ · 1 mark An air-to-open control valve, on loss of instrument air, will: fail open fail closed stay in its last position open to 50% Show answer and solution Answer: (B) fail closed Air opens it, so with no air the spring closes it: fail closed.

x: Q7. MCQ · 2 marks The closed-loop characteristic equation is s³ + 2s² + 3s + K = 0. The system is stable for: K > 0 0 0 K > 6 Show answer and solution Answer: (C) 0 Routh array: rows (1, 3), (2, K), ((6 - K)/2, 0), (K). Stability needs 6 - K > 0 and K > 0: 0 .

t: In cascade control, the inner (secondary) loop should be:
x: Q8. MCQ · 1 mark In cascade control, the inner (secondary) loop should be: faster than the outer loop slower than the outer loop tuned with integral action only open loop Show answer and solution Answer: (A) faster than the outer loop The secondary loop must be faster than the primary so it can correct disturbances before they reach the primary variable.

t: In ISA 5.1 P&ID symbols, an instrument bubble (circle) with a single solid horizontal line through it means the instrument is:
x: Q9. MCQ · 1 mark In ISA 5.1 P&ID symbols, an instrument bubble (circle) with a single solid horizontal line through it means the instrument is: field mounted in the main control room, accessible to the operator behind the panel, not accessible a software function only Show answer and solution Answer: (B) in the main control room, accessible to the operator A plain circle is field-mounted; a solid line means it is in the main control room or panel, accessible to the operator .

x: Q1. NAT · 2 marks Equipment costing ₹10 lakh has a salvage value of ₹1 lakh after a 9-year life. Using straight-line depreciation, find its book value in ₹ lakh after 4 years. Show answer and solution Answer: 6 (accepted range 5.99 to 6.01) Annual depreciation = (10 - 1)/9 = 1 lakh. Book value after 4 years = 10 - 4 = ₹6 lakh .

x: Q2. NAT · 2 marks A 2000 L reactor costs ₹5 lakh. Using the six-tenths rule, estimate the cost of an 8000 L reactor of the same type, in ₹ lakh. (round to 2 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 11.487 (accepted range 11.4 to 11.6) C2 = C1(V2/V1)^0.6 = 5 × 4^0.6 = ₹11.49 lakh .

t: Equipment cost ₹20 lakh when the cost index was 500. The index is now 650. Estimate its present cost in ₹ lakh.
x: Q3. NAT · 1 mark Equipment cost ₹20 lakh when the cost index was 500. The index is now 650. Estimate its present cost in ₹ lakh. Show answer and solution Answer: 26 (accepted range 25.9 to 26.1) Present cost = 20 × 650/500 = ₹26 lakh .

t: The payback period is the time needed for:
x: Q4. MCQ · 1 mark The payback period is the time needed for: the plant to reach design capacity the loan interest to be paid the cash flow to recover the fixed capital investment equipment to be fully depreciated Show answer and solution Answer: (C) the cash flow to recover the fixed capital investment Payback = fixed capital investment / annual cash flow (profit after tax + depreciation): the time to recover the fixed capital from cash flow.

x: Q5. NAT · 2 marks Find the present worth, in ₹ lakh, of ₹1 lakh to be received 5 years from now at 10% interest compounded annually. (round to 3 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 0.620921 (accepted range 0.619 to 0.622) PW = 1 / 1.1^5 = ₹0.621 lakh .

t: The optimum economic pipe diameter balances:
x: Q6. MCQ · 1 mark The optimum economic pipe diameter balances: pumping cost against the fixed cost of the pipe velocity against density insulation against heat loss only corrosion against erosion Show answer and solution Answer: (A) pumping cost against the fixed cost of the pipe A larger pipe costs more to buy and install but less to pump through: the optimum minimises the sum of pumping and fixed pipe costs .

x: Q6. MCQ · 1 mark Ethylene oxide is made commercially by direct oxidation of ethylene over a catalyst of: silver vanadium nickel platinum Show answer and solution Answer: (A) silver Silver on alumina.

Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Distillation separates the components of a liquid mixture by differences in volatility (boiling point). The mixture is heated so the more volatile component vaporizes preferentially, and that vapor is then condensed back to a liquid richer in that component. It's one of the most common separation and purification techniques in chemical and pharmaceutical processing, used both to purify a product and to recover or remove solvents. t: What is evaporation, and how is it different from distillation?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Evaporation removes a volatile solvent from a solution by vaporizing it, leaving behind a more concentrated solution or, if carried far enough, a solid residue. Unlike distillation, evaporation isn't mainly about collecting the vapor as a purified product; the vapor is often just discarded or recovered as a byproduct. Distillation uses that vapor deliberately to separate two or more components. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Distillation Column Solvent Recovery Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Filtration separates solid particles from a liquid (or gas) by passing the mixture through a porous medium that retains the solids while letting the liquid pass through. In chemical and pharmaceutical processing it's the standard way to isolate a crystallized or precipitated solid product from its mother liquor. Related on PharmaChemE: Filtration Calculator Virtual Plant Tour (3D) ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What is drying, in a process engineering sense?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Drying removes residual liquid (usually solvent or water) from a wet solid, typically by applying heat, reducing pressure, or both, until the material reaches an acceptable residual moisture or solvent specification. It's usually the final step before a solid product is packaged, and it needs to balance thorough solvent removal against avoiding thermal degradation of the product. Related on PharmaChemE: Lesson: Dust & powder hazards Virtual Plant Tour (3D) ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What is absorption, and how is it different from adsorption?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Absorption is when a gas (or sometimes a liquid) is taken up into the bulk volume of a liquid or solid, becoming dissolved or incorporated throughout, like carbon dioxide absorbing into water. Adsorption is when a substance sticks to the surface of a solid (or sometimes liquid) without going into the bulk, like activated carbon adsorbing color bodies from a solution. The difference matters because it changes what controls the rate and capacity: bulk solubility for absorption, surface area for adsorption. Related on PharmaChemE: Virtual Plant Tour (3D) ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What is centrifugation used for in process engineering?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Centrifugation uses rapid rotation to generate centrifugal force that separates components of different density. It's commonly used to separate solids from a liquid (as an alternative or complement to filtration) or to split two immiscible liquid phases faster than gravity settling alone would. In pharmaceutical and fine chemical manufacturing, centrifuges are often used to isolate crystallized solids from their mother liquor. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Centrifuge Centrifuge Cake Weight Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

Fresher Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Size reduction mechanically breaks larger solid particles into smaller ones, using equipment ranging from simple mechanical mills to jet mills that use high-velocity gas to shatter particles through collisions. In pharmaceutical processing, controlling final particle size is often important for how a drug substance dissolves, flows, and is handled during formulation. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Mills Lesson: Dust & powder hazards ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What is agitation/mixing, and why does it matter?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Agitation is the mechanical action of stirring a liquid or slurry, typically with a rotating impeller, to blend materials, suspend solids, disperse gases or a second liquid phase, or improve heat transfer. Many reactions and physical processes (like crystallization or extraction) depend on bringing materials into close contact at the rate the process needs. Poor mixing can become the rate-limiting step even when the underlying chemistry is fast. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Agitators and Impellers Mixing / Scale-up Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What is heat exchange, and what's a heat exchanger?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Heat exchange is the transfer of thermal energy from a hotter fluid to a cooler one without the two fluids mixing, typically across a solid wall (like a metal tube or plate). A heat exchanger is the equipment that does this, from a simple jacketed vessel to dedicated shell-and-tube or plate heat exchangers. Heating, cooling, condensing and evaporating all over a chemical plant depend on it. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Shell and Tube Heat Exchanger Heat Load & Recovery Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What is scrubbing, in the context of chemical plant operations?
x: Fresher Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Scrubbing removes unwanted gases, vapors, or particulates from a gas stream by contacting it with a liquid (or sometimes a solid) that absorbs or reacts with the contaminant, commonly used to treat vent gases before they're released to the atmosphere or to recover a valuable solvent vapor. A scrubber is the equipment that provides this gas-liquid contact, often using packing or trays to maximize contact area. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Absorber / Scrubber Virtual Plant Tour (3D) ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

Fresher Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Decantation separates two immiscible liquids, or a liquid from settled solids, simply by carefully pouring or draining off the upper layer once the mixture has been allowed to settle and separate by gravity. It's one of the simplest separation techniques, often used as a quick first step before a more thorough separation like filtration or centrifugation. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Liquid-Liquid Separator / Decanter Virtual Plant Tour (3D) ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What's the difference between a batch process and a continuous process?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ A batch process takes a fixed quantity of material through a complete sequence of steps before the next batch starts. It's common in pharmaceutical and fine chemical manufacturing, where flexibility, smaller volumes and traceability of each batch matter. A continuous process runs material through the system steadily without starting and stopping, which is typically more efficient at very large scale and consistent product volumes, but less flexible for making different products or smaller quantities. Related on PharmaChemE: Virtual Plant Tour (3D) Game: Plant Operator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise late

t: What is a theoretical plate (or theoretical stage) in distillation?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ A theoretical plate is one full equilibrium contact between vapor and liquid: the ideal case where the vapor and liquid leaving that stage are in perfect equilibrium with each other. Real distillation columns are rated by how many theoretical plates' worth of separation they achieve. It's the standard way to compare and design separation equipment, even though no real tray reaches perfect equilibrium. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Distillation Column Solvent Recovery Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Residence time is how long material actually spends inside a piece of equipment or a process step. For a continuous process it's typically the vessel volume divided by the volumetric flow rate; for a batch process it's simply the duration of that step. Many processes (reactions, drying, heat transfer) need a minimum residence time to reach completion, and too little residence time is a common cause of incomplete processing. Related on PharmaChemE: Virtual Plant Tour (3D) Game: Plant Operator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What's the difference between yield, conversion, and selectivity?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Conversion is the fraction of starting material that has reacted at all; selectivity is the fraction of that converted material that went to the desired product rather than side products; and yield is the overall fraction of theoretical product actually obtained, which combines both conversion and selectivity (yield equals conversion times selectivity, roughly speaking). A reaction can have high conversion but poor yield if selectivity to the desired product is low. Related on PharmaChemE: Virtual Plant Tour (3D) Game: Plant Operator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What is viscosity, in practical terms?
x: Fresher Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Viscosity is a fluid's resistance to flow. A high-viscosity fluid (like honey) flows sluggishly and resists being pumped or stirred, while a low-viscosity fluid (like water) flows easily. It directly affects pump selection, mixing, heat transfer rates and filtration behavior, which is why it's one of the first physical properties checked when handling an unfamiliar material. Related on PharmaChemE: Virtual Plant Tour (3D) ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What is vapor pressure, and why does it matter for process engineering?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Vapor pressure is the pressure exerted by a substance's vapor when it's in equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature, and it increases with temperature. A substance boils when its vapor pressure equals the surrounding pressure. Vapor pressure sets a solvent's volatility, flammability risk and evaporation rate, and how distillation or vacuum operations will behave for that material. Related on PharmaChemE: Solvent Recovery Calculator Article: Solvent recovery explained ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What is boiling point, and how does pressure affect it?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid's vapor pressure equals the surrounding (ambient or system) pressure, causing it to vaporize throughout the bulk liquid rather than just at the surface. Reducing the surrounding pressure (as in vacuum distillation) lowers the boiling point, which is exactly why vacuum is used to distill heat-sensitive materials at a lower, safer temperature. Related on PharmaChemE: Solvent Recovery Calculator Article: Solvent recovery explained ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

Fresher Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ A slurry is solid particles suspended in a liquid, thick but still able to flow, with a significant proportion of undissolved solids. Slurries are common in crystallization (crystals suspended in mother liquor) and when solid raw materials are charged as a pumpable mix rather than a dry powder. Pumps, valves and agitators need to be suited to slurry service, since standard liquid-handling equipment can struggle with abrasive or settling solids. Related on PharmaChemE: Virtual Plant Tour (3D) ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What's the difference between a suspension and an emulsion?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ A suspension is solid particles dispersed in a liquid (like a slurry), while an emulsion is one liquid dispersed as tiny droplets within another liquid it doesn't naturally mix with (like oil droplets dispersed in water). Both are inherently unstable over time and will eventually separate unless stabilized, which is why suspensions and emulsions often need continued agitation or a stabilizing agent to remain uniform. Related on PharmaChemE: Virtual Plant Tour (3D) ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What's the difference between an exothermic and an endothermic reaction?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ An exothermic reaction releases heat as it proceeds (the products have lower energy than the reactants), while an endothermic reaction absorbs heat from its surroundings to proceed (the products have higher energy than the reactants). This difference is central to process safety. An exothermic reaction can self-accelerate and potentially run away if the heat it generates isn't removed fast enough, which is why reaction calorimetry is done before scaling up a new exothermic process. Related on PharmaChemE: Lesson: Thermal testing (DSC, ARC, RC1) Game: Runaway! Stoessel Challenge ✓ I knew this ↻ R

t: What does validation mean in a pharmaceutical manufacturing context?
x: Fresher Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Validation is documented evidence that a process, piece of equipment, or analytical method consistently does what it's intended to do, produced by executing predefined tests or trial runs against predetermined acceptance criteria. It's a core regulatory requirement in pharmaceutical manufacturing. A process isn't considered proven because it worked once; it has to be shown to work reliably and reproducibly under real operating conditions. Related on PharmaChemE: Virtual Plant Tour (3D) ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What's the difference between a raw material, an intermediate, and an API?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ A raw material is a starting substance brought into the process from outside (a reagent, solvent, or starting chemical); an intermediate is a substance produced partway through a multi-step synthesis that isn't the final desired product but is used to make it; and the API (Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient) is the final biologically active substance that goes into a drug product. A single synthesis might pass through several intermediates before reaching the API. Related on PharmaChemE: Virtual Plant Tour (3D) ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What is a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)?
x: Fresher Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ An SOP is a documented, step-by-step set of instructions for carrying out a specific task or process the same way every time, covering everything from equipment setup to the exact sequence of actions and the acceptance criteria for each step. SOPs are central to GMP manufacturing because consistency and reproducibility depend on everyone following the same validated procedure, not on individual judgment each time. Related on PharmaChemE: Virtual Plant Tour (3D) ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What does 'unit operation scale-up' actually mean, in plain terms?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Basic Concepts & Terminology ▸ Scale-up means taking a process that's been developed and proven at small (lab or pilot) scale and getting the same result at a much larger, commercially useful scale. That's harder than it sounds, because many physical effects (mixing time, heat transfer rate, addition time) don't change in proportion to size. Good scale-up work identifies which of these effects actually control the process outcome, then designs the larger equipment and procedure to preserve those conditions. Related on PharmaChemE: Lesson: Scale-up & tech transfer Mixing / Scale-up Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: Why does a reaction that works perfectly in the lab behave differently at pilot scale?
x: 1–3 yrs ★ Top 50 Scale-Up & Process Development ▸ Scale-up changes physical parameters that don't scale linearly with volume: mixing time typically increases, heat transfer surface area per unit volume decreases, and addition/charging times get longer relative to the reaction rate. A reaction that's mixing-limited or heat-transfer-limited at large scale can behave completely differently even though the chemistry itself hasn't changed. Always ask what's actually controlling your reaction rate at lab scale before assuming it will scale directly. Related on PharmaChemE: Lesson: Scale-up & tech transfer Mixing / Scale-up Calculator ✓ I knew this

t: What are the most important factors to check before scaling up a reaction?
x: 1–3 yrs ★ Top 50 Scale-Up & Process Development ▸ Focus on heat transfer capability (can the plant reactor add/remove heat as fast as the reaction needs?), mixing time versus reaction rate, addition/charge time relative to reaction kinetics, and whether the reaction is adiabatic-safe if cooling is lost. Reaction calorimetry data (heat of reaction, adiabatic temperature rise) is usually the single most valuable piece of information before committing a new reaction to a larger vessel. t: Why does mixing take longer at larger scale even with a similarly powerful agitator?
x: 1–3 yrs ★ Top 50 Scale-Up & Process Development ▸ Mixing time generally scales unfavorably with vessel size for a fixed impeller tip speed or fixed power per unit volume. Larger vessels have proportionally longer blend times because the ratio of impeller-swept volume to total volume shrinks. This is one of the most common reasons a reaction that seemed instantaneous on the bench becomes addition-rate or mixing limited in the plant. t: Why is reaction calorimetry important before running a new process?
x: 1–3 yrs ★ Top 50 Scale-Up & Process Development ▸ Calorimetry measures the heat of reaction and the rate at which heat is generated, which tells you whether your reactor's cooling capacity can keep up with the reaction, and what the adiabatic temperature rise would be if cooling were lost. Without this data you don't actually know whether a runaway is possible, so it's the single most important safety screening step before scaling up an exothermic reaction. This explains why calorimetry matters in general. The specific safety screening tests required for a given reaction should be determined by a qualified process safety specialist based on t

t: What should a batch record capture?
x: Fresher Scale-Up & Process Development ▸ A batch record should capture every material charged (with lot numbers and quantities), every process step performed with actual times and observed conditions (temperature, pressure, pH, etc.), in-process sample results, deviations from the procedure, and who performed and verified each step. It needs to be complete enough that someone could reconstruct exactly what happened without being present. t: What's the purpose of a process flow diagram in pilot plant work?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Scale-Up & Process Development ▸ A process flow diagram shows the sequence of unit operations, the equipment involved, and the major streams (raw materials, intermediates, waste) flowing between them. It's the reference document operators and engineers use to understand how the whole process fits together, and it's usually the starting point for a Haz-Op. t: What are common mistakes to avoid when developing a process meant to be scaled up?
x: Experienced Scale-Up & Process Development ▸ Common ones: relying on very fast additions or instantaneous mixing that won't be achievable at scale, using lab techniques that don't translate (like swirling a flask by hand), not characterizing the heat of reaction, assuming filtration or drying rates from a Buchner funnel will hold at plant scale, and not building in enough margin for longer hold times and addition times. Related on PharmaChemE: Lesson: Scale-up & tech transfer Mixing / Scale-up Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: Why do batches typically take longer at pilot or plant scale than at the bench?
x: 1–3 yrs ★ Top 50 Scale-Up & Process Development ▸ Charging, heating, cooling, and phase separations all take proportionally longer as equipment gets larger, because heat transfer area and addition rates don't scale at the same rate as volume. A charge that takes seconds from a pipette can take an hour from a plant-scale addition vessel, and a reaction that seemed to run to completion instantly on the bench may take hours to reach the same conversion once mixing and heat transfer become rate-limiting. Related on PharmaChemE: Lesson: Scale-up & tech transfer Mixing / Scale-up Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What does GMP mean for pilot plant operations?
x: Fresher Scale-Up & Process Development ▸ Good Manufacturing Practice means documented, reproducible procedures, calibrated and qualified equipment, traceability of materials and actions (who did what, when), and a quality system that reviews deviations. Even in early-stage pilot work, building GMP-friendly habits (good batch records, equipment logs, clear procedures) makes the eventual transfer to full GMP manufacturing much smoother. Related on PharmaChemE: Lesson: Scale-up & tech transfer Mixing / Scale-up Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: Why does my reaction seem to be mixing-limited at larger scale?
x: 1–3 yrs Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ If a reaction's rate depends on how quickly two phases or reagents are brought into contact, blend time becomes the limiting factor once the mixing rate falls below the intrinsic reaction rate. Signs of this include yield or selectivity dropping as scale increases even though temperature and stoichiometry are unchanged. The fix is usually to slow the addition rate, improve impeller design, or add the reagent closer to the impeller discharge. t: What causes poor reaction control (temperature excursions) during scale-up?
x: Experienced ★ Top 50 Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ Usually a mismatch between the rate of heat generation (which can scale faster than expected if addition is fast) and the rate of heat removal (which is often limited by jacket area per unit volume, which shrinks as the vessel gets bigger). Slowing the addition rate, using a controlled semi-batch addition, or pre-cooling reagents are the standard fixes. Related on PharmaChemE: Lesson: Thermal testing (DSC, ARC, RC1) Game: Runaway! t: How do I know if a process sample is representative of the whole batch?
x: Experienced ★ Top 50 Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ Sample from a well-mixed zone, ideally while the agitator is running, and avoid sampling right after a charge before it's had time to distribute. For heterogeneous or viscous systems, take samples from more than one location or depth and compare. If results vary noticeably between samples, that's a sign the batch isn't fully mixed yet. t: What makes an extraction efficient or inefficient?
x: 1–3 yrs Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ Extraction efficiency depends on the partition coefficient of the solute between the two phases, the volume ratio of the phases, and the number of extraction stages. A single extraction with a favorable partition coefficient can still leave significant product behind. Several smaller extractions are almost always more efficient than one large one for the same total solvent volume. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Liquid-Liquid Extraction Virtual Plant Tour (3D) ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: Why does batch distillation performance change when I scale it up?
x: Experienced Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ Larger stills often have proportionally less surface area for heat input relative to the batch volume, meaning distillation takes longer. Column efficiency (theoretical plates) can also differ if the plant column's packing or trays aren't equivalent to whatever was used at bench scale, changing the separation you actually achieve for the same reflux ratio. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Distillation Column Lesson: Scale-up & tech transfer ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What causes poor crystal quality: too many fines or hard agglomerates?
x: 1–3 yrs Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ Fines are usually caused by excessive supersaturation (cooling or antisolvent addition too fast, or too much local supersaturation at the addition point), which favors nucleation over growth. Agglomerates often come from poor mixing that lets locally over-concentrated zones stick particles together, or from seeding technique issues. Slower, better-controlled addition rates and adequate seeding usually improve both problems. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Crystallizer Game: Troubleshooter ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What's the difference between cake filtration and depth filtration, and when do I use each?
x: 1–3 yrs ★ Top 50 Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ Cake filtration collects a visible layer of solids on a filter medium and is used when you want to recover a solid product (like isolating a crystallized API). Depth filtration passes liquid through a thick porous medium to capture fine particulates for clarification, typically used for polishing a solution rather than recovering solids. Choosing the wrong one either clogs quickly (using depth media for heavy solids loading) or fails to clarify properly (using cake filtration for trace particulates). t: Why does drying take so much longer at production scale than in a lab oven?
x: 1–3 yrs ★ Top 50 Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ Larger cake beds have longer diffusion paths for moisture or solvent to escape, and heat transfer to the center of a large cake or through a jacketed dryer wall is slower per unit mass than in a thin lab tray. Poor airflow or vacuum distribution across a larger surface area makes it worse. Bed depth and agitation (if using an agitated dryer) are usually the first things to check when drying is slower than expected. These are the usual suspects, but drying behavior is often product-specific, so verify with actual scale-down or pilot trials before settling on a cause. Related on PharmaChem

t: What's the right way to clean a reactor between batches of different products?
x: 1–3 yrs Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ Use a validated cleaning procedure suited to the residue's solubility (solvent rinse, caustic wash, or dedicated cleaning agent), verify cleanliness with a rinse sample or swab test where cross-contamination matters, and pay special attention to dead legs, gaskets, and agitator shafts where residue can hide. For potent or highly reactive residues you need documented cleaning validation, not just a visual check. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Batch Reactor Virtual Plant Tour (3D) ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What causes a rotary (gear or lobe) pump to stop delivering flow?
x: 1–3 yrs Liquid Handling & Fluid Systems ▸ Common causes include excessive clearance from wear letting liquid slip back internally, a relief valve stuck open or set too low, entrained air or vapor in the pumped fluid, or the fluid viscosity being outside the pump's design range. Rotary pumps depend on close internal clearances, so wear is a very common root cause of gradually declining output. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Gear Pump Pump Power Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What's the difference between a diaphragm pump and a peristaltic pump, and when should I use each?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Liquid Handling & Fluid Systems ▸ A diaphragm pump uses a flexing membrane and check valves to move fluid and can handle higher pressures and a wide range of chemical compatibility depending on diaphragm material; a peristaltic pump squeezes fluid through flexible tubing with rollers, keeping the fluid completely isolated from any pump internals, which is ideal for sterile, shear-sensitive, or highly corrosive fluids at lower pressures and flow rates. Choose peristaltic when you need to avoid any fluid contact with pump internals, and diaphragm when you need higher pressure or flow capability. Related on PharmaChemE: How it w

t: Why won't my diaphragm pump prime?
x: 1–3 yrs Liquid Handling & Fluid Systems ▸ Common causes are a worn or torn diaphragm, a stuck or fouled check/ball valve, air trapped on the suction side that the pump can't purge, or a suction lift beyond the pump's dry-priming capability. Diaphragm pumps rely on their check valves sealing properly to build suction, and a valve held open by debris is one of the most common culprits. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Diaphragm Pump Pump Power Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What causes excessive pressure drop in a transfer line?
x: 1–3 yrs ★ Top 50 Liquid Handling & Fluid Systems ▸ Undersized pipe diameter for the flow rate, too many fittings and elbows (each adds equivalent length), a partially closed or fouled valve, or a highly viscous fluid all increase pressure drop. Pressure drop increases roughly with the square of velocity, so a line sized even slightly too small can cause a disproportionate increase in required pump head. Related on PharmaChemE: Pump Power Calculator Article: How to calculate pump power ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: How do I select the right gasket material for a flange?
x: 1–3 yrs Liquid Handling & Fluid Systems ▸ Match the gasket material's chemical compatibility to the process fluid first (this rules out most options quickly), then confirm it can handle the operating temperature and pressure, and consider whether the flange faces are smooth or serrated, which affects which gasket types will seal properly. When in doubt, check a material compatibility chart for the specific chemical against the elastomer or fluoropolymer first, instead of just picking a common general-purpose gasket. This is only a general starting point. Always verify against the gasket manufacturer's chemical compatibility data at your actua

t: How do I pick the right size O-ring to fix a leaking seal?
x: 1–3 yrs Liquid Handling & Fluid Systems ▸ Measure the groove's inner diameter and cross-section width (or measure the failed O-ring itself if it hasn't distorted too much) and match against a standard O-ring size chart (AS568 dash sizes are the common reference). Always confirm the elastomer is chemically compatible with the process fluid, not just that the dimensions match. A correctly sized but incompatible O-ring will still fail. t: How do I estimate how much liquid a storage tank or drum actually holds?
x: 1–3 yrs Liquid Handling & Fluid Systems ▸ For a vertical cylindrical vessel, volume is simply cross-sectional area times liquid height, but always subtract for any dished or sloped bottom, and never plan to fill to 100% of nominal capacity. Leave enough freeboard for thermal expansion and to prevent overflow during filling. For common container sizes, standard drum and tank capacity references (by diameter and standard sizes) are a faster check than calculating from scratch. t: Why does my reactor take longer to heat up or cool down as batch size increases?
x: 1–3 yrs ★ Top 50 Heat Transfer & Utilities ▸ Heat transfer area (jacket surface) scales with the square of a vessel's linear dimension, while volume scales with the cube. So larger vessels have proportionally less jacket area per unit volume, which directly increases heating and cooling times. This is one of the most predictable and unavoidable effects of scale-up, and it's why plant-scale temperature ramps are almost always slower than lab-scale ones. Try the Heat Load & Recovery Calculator → Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Batch Reactor Lesson: Scale-up & tech transfer ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: How do I estimate the heat transfer coefficient of a jacketed reactor?
x: Experienced Heat Transfer & Utilities ▸ The overall coefficient combines the inside film coefficient (driven by agitation and fluid properties), the wall and jacket-side resistances, and any fouling. In practice, it's most reliable to determine it experimentally by measuring the actual heating or cooling rate of a known mass and comparing to the temperature driving force, rather than relying solely on theoretical correlations, since fouling and real agitation conditions vary significantly from vessel to vessel. t: What is LMTD and why does it matter for heat exchanger sizing?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Heat Transfer & Utilities ▸ Log mean temperature difference is the properly-averaged temperature driving force between two fluids exchanging heat when that difference changes along the length of the exchanger (as it does in any real heat exchanger). Using a simple arithmetic average instead of LMTD will give an inaccurate (usually optimistic) estimate of the required heat transfer area, especially when the temperature difference varies a lot between the inlet and outlet ends. t: Why won't my temperature control unit (TCU) reach its setpoint?
x: 1–3 yrs Heat Transfer & Utilities ▸ Check first whether the heat transfer fluid flow rate through the jacket is adequate (a partially closed valve or air-locked line will starve heat transfer), whether the TCU's own heating or cooling capacity is actually sufficient for the vessel size and duty, and whether the fluid has degraded or lost its heat transfer properties over time. An undersized TCU relative to the vessel's heat duty is a very common root cause, especially after moving a process to a larger reactor. Related on PharmaChemE: Heat Load & Recovery Calculator Article: Heat load & recovery time ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: How do I choose the right heat transfer fluid for my application?
x: 1–3 yrs Heat Transfer & Utilities ▸ Match the fluid's useful temperature range to your process's full operating range (including any planned excursions), check viscosity at the coldest temperature you'll see (high viscosity kills circulation and heat transfer), and consider flammability and toxicity if a leak into the process is a credible scenario. Glycols are common for moderate temperature ranges; specialized synthetic heat transfer fluids or silicone oils are used for wider or more extreme ranges. Related on PharmaChemE: Heat Load & Recovery Calculator Article: Heat load & recovery time ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What's the difference between using a glycol solution and using a brine for cooling?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Heat Transfer & Utilities ▸ Glycol/water mixtures are generally less corrosive and easier to handle but have a practical low-temperature limit around -30 to -40°C depending on concentration; brines (like calcium chloride solutions) can reach lower temperatures but are more corrosive to many common materials. Choose based on the coldest temperature you actually need and the material compatibility of your cooling loop. Related on PharmaChemE: Heat Load & Recovery Calculator Article: Heat load & recovery time ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: Why does my process chiller lose cooling capacity in hot weather?
x: 1–3 yrs Heat Transfer & Utilities ▸ Chillers reject heat to ambient air or cooling water, and their capacity drops as the temperature difference between the condenser and ambient shrinks. A chiller rated for a cold winter day can lose a significant fraction of its rated capacity on a hot summer day. Always check a chiller's capacity curve at the worst-case (highest) ambient or cooling water temperature you expect, not just the nominal rating. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Chiller Heat Load & Recovery Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: How does cooling water inlet temperature affect condenser performance?
x: 1–3 yrs Heat Transfer & Utilities ▸ Higher cooling water inlet temperature reduces the temperature driving force across the condenser and directly cuts its heat rejection capacity. This can show up as poor vacuum distillation performance or incomplete condensation on hot summer days even when nothing else in the system has changed. If condenser performance is seasonal, cooling water temperature is usually the first thing to check. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Condenser Heat Load & Recovery Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: How do I estimate the steam pressure needed to reach a given process temperature?
x: 1–3 yrs ★ Top 50 Heat Transfer & Utilities ▸ Saturated steam temperature and pressure are directly linked (steam tables or a pressure-temperature chart give this relationship), so you size steam pressure based on the saturation temperature needed, plus a margin to overcome the added resistance of the heat exchanger or jacket wall. Remember you need the steam temperature to exceed your target process temperature by enough margin to actually drive heat transfer at a reasonable rate. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Steam Trap and Condensate System Heat Load & Recovery Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What's the difference between a single-phase and a three-phase motor?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Electrical & Instrumentation ▸ A single-phase motor runs on standard single-phase power (common in smaller equipment and residential-style circuits) and generally has lower efficiency and higher starting current relative to its size; a three-phase motor uses three alternating currents offset in phase, giving smoother torque, higher efficiency, and easier starting, which is why almost all significant industrial motors (pumps, agitators, compressors) are three-phase. Related on PharmaChemE: Virtual Plant Tour (3D) ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What's an intrinsically safe circuit and when do I need one?
x: 1–3 yrs Electrical & Instrumentation ▸ An intrinsically safe circuit is designed so it can never release enough electrical or thermal energy, even under fault conditions, to ignite a specified flammable atmosphere. You need intrinsically safe instrumentation and wiring in any area classified as hazardous due to flammable vapors, gases, or dusts, such as around solvent transfer points or inside a vessel headspace containing flammable vapor. Hazardous area classification and intrinsic safety requirements are governed by local electrical codes and should always be confirmed by a qualified electrical/process safety engineer for your specific site

t: What does a Class 1, Division 1 rating mean for electrical equipment?
x: 1–3 yrs Electrical & Instrumentation ▸ It designates an area (Class 1) where flammable gases or vapors may be present, and where that flammable atmosphere is expected to exist under normal operating conditions (Division 1, as opposed to Division 2, where it would only be present under abnormal conditions like a leak or spill). Electrical equipment installed in a Division 1 area must be specifically rated for that classification; standard general-purpose equipment is not acceptable. Area classification for a specific plant or process must be formally determined by a qualified engineer following applicable codes (such as NEC or IEC standards).

t: Why is my electric motor drawing more current than its nameplate rating?
x: 1–3 yrs Electrical & Instrumentation ▸ Common causes are the motor being mechanically overloaded (driving a pump or agitator against more resistance than designed for), a bearing or alignment problem creating extra friction, low supply voltage forcing higher current to deliver the same power, or a developing winding fault. Sustained overcurrent will overheat the motor and shorten its life even if it doesn't trip immediately. Related on PharmaChemE: Game: Troubleshooter Game: Plant Operator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What's the difference between a thermocouple and an RTD?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Electrical & Instrumentation ▸ A thermocouple generates a small voltage from the junction of two dissimilar metals and works over a very wide temperature range with a fast response, but is less accurate; an RTD (resistance temperature detector) measures temperature via the predictable change in a metal's electrical resistance and is more accurate and stable but generally has a narrower range and slower response. For precise process control at moderate temperatures, RTDs are usually preferred; thermocouples are chosen for very high temperatures or fast transient measurements. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Thermocouple

t: How does a 4-20 mA transmitter work, and why is it used?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Electrical & Instrumentation ▸ A 4-20 mA transmitter converts a sensor's measurement (temperature, pressure, level, etc.) into a proportional current signal between 4 and 20 milliamps, where 4 mA represents the low end of the measurement range and 20 mA the high end. With a live zero of 4 mA (rather than 0 mA), a broken wire or dead transmitter reads as 0 mA, which is easy to tell apart from a genuine low reading. That's why it's the standard for reliable process instrumentation. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Pressure Transmitter Virtual Plant Tour (3D) ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: Why does my pH probe give inconsistent or drifting readings?
x: 1–3 yrs Electrical & Instrumentation ▸ Common causes include a fouled or coated glass membrane reducing responsiveness, a depleted or contaminated reference electrolyte, temperature effects not being compensated for, or the probe simply being past its calibration interval or end of life. Regular calibration against fresh buffer solutions and periodic cleaning are the standard first troubleshooting steps before assuming a probe needs replacement. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: pH Analyser Game: Troubleshooter ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What causes an electric motor to overheat in continuous duty?
x: 1–3 yrs Electrical & Instrumentation ▸ Insufficient cooling airflow (blocked vents, wrong orientation), running above rated load for the duty cycle, high ambient temperature, or voltage imbalance across phases in a three-phase motor can all cause overheating. Motors have a rated duty cycle and service factor. Running continuously beyond what the nameplate specifies will shorten insulation life even without an obvious immediate fault. Related on PharmaChemE: Heat Load & Recovery Calculator Article: Heat load & recovery time ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: How do I tune a PID controller that's oscillating around setpoint?
x: Experienced Electrical & Instrumentation ▸ Oscillation usually means the proportional gain is too high or the integral time is too short (too aggressive) for the process's actual response speed. Reduce the proportional gain first and observe, then adjust integral time. A systematic tuning method (like Ziegler-Nichols or trial-and-error step response testing) is more reliable than guessing individual parameters in isolation. Treat this as a general troubleshooting starting point, and confirm the tuning approach and safe parameter ranges against your specific control system and process dynamics. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: PID Control

t: How do I size wire gauge correctly for an electrical circuit?
x: Experienced Electrical & Instrumentation ▸ Wire gauge needs to be sized for the expected current draw (including motor starting current, which can be several times the running current) with an adequate safety margin, and also checked against voltage drop over the run length. A wire that's technically rated for the current can still cause unacceptable voltage drop over a long run. Local electrical code tables for ampacity by wire gauge and insulation type are the standard reference, not a rule of thumb. Related on PharmaChemE: Virtual Plant Tour (3D) ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: Is it more efficient to run a distillation at atmospheric pressure or under vacuum?
x: 1–3 yrs ★ Top 50 Solvents & Distillation ▸ Vacuum distillation lowers the boiling point of the material, which is a must for heat-sensitive compounds that would decompose at their atmospheric boiling point, and it can also improve separation for close-boiling or high-boiling mixtures. But vacuum systems add complexity (leak-tightness, vacuum pump capacity) and can reduce relative volatility for some systems. The right choice depends on the specific compound's thermal stability and the separation you're attempting; there's no universal rule. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Distillation Column Solvent Recovery Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ R

t: What happens to azeotrope composition under vacuum?
x: Experienced ★ Top 50 Solvents & Distillation ▸ Azeotrope composition is generally pressure-dependent and often shifts (and can sometimes disappear entirely) as pressure is reduced, because the relative volatilities of the components change differently with temperature. So a mixture that's difficult to separate by simple distillation at atmospheric pressure may separate more easily under vacuum, or the other way round. Check it for the specific system instead of assuming. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Distillation Column Solvent Recovery Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What are good solvents for azeotropic removal of water from a reaction mixture?
x: 1–3 yrs Solvents & Distillation ▸ Solvents that form a low-boiling, water-immiscible (or partially immiscible) azeotrope work best, since the water separates cleanly in a Dean-Stark type trap after condensation. Toluene and other aromatic or moderately non-polar solvents are classic choices for this reason. The solvent also has to be compatible with the reaction chemistry, so the choice always balances azeotropic behavior against chemical compatibility. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Distillation Column Solvent Recovery Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: How do I choose a good solvent for crystallization?
x: 1–3 yrs Solvents & Distillation ▸ Look for a solvent (or solvent pair) where the target compound is quite soluble hot and much less soluble cold, giving a wide usable window for cooling crystallization, while impurities stay in solution throughout. Solubility curves, and sometimes an antisolvent addition strategy, are the standard tools for screening candidate solvents rather than guessing from general polarity rules. Use this as a starting point for screening, not a final answer. Confirm with actual solubility data and small-scale trials for your compound before committing to a solvent at scale. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Crystall

t: What does the NFPA flammability classification tell me about a solvent?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Solvents & Distillation ▸ NFPA flammability ratings (typically 0 to 4) reflect how readily a material will burn based on its flash point and boiling point, with higher numbers meaning a more severe fire hazard. This rating directly drives decisions about storage, electrical area classification, and handling precautions. A solvent with a low flash point needs much stricter controls than one with a high flash point, even if both are technically 'flammable.' Related on PharmaChemE: Solvent Recovery Calculator Article: Solvent recovery explained ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: Why does solvent viscosity matter for distillation efficiency?
x: 1–3 yrs Solvents & Distillation ▸ Higher viscosity reduces mass transfer rates on distillation trays or packing, which can reduce the effective number of theoretical stages achieved and slow down the whole operation. It also affects reboiler and condenser heat transfer coefficients, so a viscous solvent mixture may need a longer distillation time or reduced throughput compared to a low-viscosity system with the same nominal separation. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Distillation Column Solvent Recovery Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What's the difference between a binary and a ternary azeotrope?
x: Experienced Solvents & Distillation ▸ A binary azeotrope involves two components that boil at a constant composition and temperature (neither simple distillation nor further heating changes the vapor composition), while a ternary azeotrope involves three components behaving the same way. Ternary azeotropes are especially relevant when a third component (often water) is present alongside the solvent pair you're trying to separate, and they can make an otherwise straightforward-looking distillation surprisingly difficult. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Distillation Column Solvent Recovery Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: How do I estimate a solvent's boiling point at reduced pressure?
x: 1–3 yrs Solvents & Distillation ▸ The Clausius-Clapeyron relationship (or a nomograph / boiling point vs. pressure chart) lets you estimate how boiling point drops as pressure is reduced, starting from a known boiling point at one pressure. You need this when planning a vacuum distillation of a heat-sensitive compound, to know what vacuum level will actually bring the boiling point below the compound's decomposition temperature. t: Are there solvents that are restricted or discouraged for pharmaceutical use?
x: Fresher Solvents & Distillation ▸ Yes. Regulatory guidance (such as ICH Q3C) classifies residual solvents by toxicity: Class 1 solvents (like benzene) are to be avoided entirely in pharmaceutical manufacturing unless justified, Class 2 solvents are limited to specific concentration thresholds in the final product, and Class 3 solvents are considered lower risk. Solvent selection for any pharmaceutical process needs to check the current regulatory solvent class, not just general chemical suitability. Related on PharmaChemE: Solvent Recovery Calculator Article: Solvent recovery explained ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What causes poor water removal during an azeotropic drying distillation?
x: Experienced Solvents & Distillation ▸ Incomplete phase separation in the Dean-Stark trap (often due to emulsification, especially if surfactant-like impurities are present), insufficient reflux, or simply not running the distillation long enough for equilibrium to be reached are the most common causes. If water removal stalls, check whether the two liquid phases are actually separating cleanly in the trap rather than assuming the chemistry is the problem. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Distillation Column Solvent Recovery Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What special precautions are needed when handling gaseous hydrogen?
x: 1–3 yrs Compressed Gases & Vacuum Systems ▸ Hydrogen has an extremely wide flammability range and very low ignition energy, so leak-tight connections, adequate ventilation, elimination of ignition sources, and hydrogen-specific leak detection are all required. Hydrogen is also lighter than air and can collect at ceiling level, so ventilation and detection have to account for that, unlike heavier gases that pool near the floor. t: How do I estimate how much gas is left in a compressed cylinder?

t: What's the relationship between dew point and relative humidity?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Compressed Gases & Vacuum Systems ▸ Dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated and water begins to condense, while relative humidity is the percentage of saturation at the current temperature. The same absolute moisture content gives a fixed dew point but a relative humidity that changes with temperature. For compressed air systems, dew point (not relative humidity) is the meaningful spec, since it tells you the actual temperature at which condensation will start to form in your lines. t: How do I safely prepare a dilute acid or base solution?

t: What's the difference between pKa and pH?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Chemical Properties & Data ▸ pH describes the actual hydrogen ion concentration of a specific solution at a given moment, while pKa is an intrinsic property of a particular acid or base that describes its inherent strength: specifically, the pH at which that acid is exactly half dissociated. Knowing a compound's pKa tells you how its ionization (and often its solubility and extraction behavior) will change as you adjust the pH of the solution it's dissolved in. t: How does temperature affect the aqueous solubility of a compound?
x: Fresher Chemical Properties & Data ▸ For most solid solutes, solubility in water increases with temperature, though the relationship isn't always linear and some compounds show unusual or even inverse behavior. This temperature dependence is what makes cooling crystallization possible: dissolve the compound hot, then cool to force it back out of solution as crystals. t: What is heat of solution and why does it matter?
x: Fresher Chemical Properties & Data ▸ Heat of solution is the heat absorbed or released when a substance dissolves, and it can be large enough to noticeably heat or cool a solution during dissolution. Some salts dissolve endothermically enough to freeze condensation on the outside of a vessel; others release enough heat to need cooling. Always check heat of solution before dissolving a large quantity of an unfamiliar material, especially at production scale where the total heat effect is large. t: What causes stainless steel to corrode in a process that's supposedly compatible?

Anything that disrupts that layer locally (mechanical damage, chloride pitting, weld heat-affected zones) can cause corrosion even in an otherwise 'compatible' environment. t: Why does borosilicate glass sometimes get attacked by certain chemicals?

t: What is galvanic corrosion and how do I avoid it in mixed-metal systems?
x: Fresher Safety & Materials ▸ Galvanic corrosion happens when two dissimilar metals are in electrical contact in the presence of an electrolyte (like moisture or a conductive process fluid), causing the more active (anodic) metal to corrode faster than it would alone. Avoid it by using compatible metal combinations close together on the galvanic series, or by electrically isolating dissimilar metals (insulating gaskets or fittings) where mixed-metal contact is unavoidable. Kinematic similarity adds the requirement that characteristic velocities scale proportionally, and dynamic similarity further requires that the relevant forces (like inertial versus viscous forces) scale proportionally too. t: What does 'constant power per unit volume' mean as a scale-up criterion, and when should I use it?
x: Experienced Scale-Up & Process Development ▸ It means keeping the energy dissipation rate (power input divided by batch volume, often called epsilon) the same at both scales, which is a common approach for reactions where mass transfer or turbulence intensity controls performance. It's most appropriate for processes like liquid-liquid dispersions or gas-liquid mass transfer where turbulent energy dissipation directly governs how well phases are mixed or dispersed, rather than for reactions primarily controlled by bulk blend time. t: When should I scale up using constant tip speed instead of constant power per volume?
x: Experienced Scale-Up & Process Development ▸ Tip speed (the impeller's tangential velocity at its outer diameter) is the right scale-up parameter when maximum shear rate is the critical factor. For example, a reaction may need high local shear to disperse an added reagent quickly, or a precipitated solid may be shear-sensitive, so excessive tip speed would cause particle attrition or fines. If shear-sensitive solids or shear-driven dispersion are central to your process outcome, tip speed usually matters more than bulk power per volume. t: What is blend time and why does it matter for scale-up?
x: 1–3 yrs Scale-Up & Process Development ▸ Blend time is how long it takes the contents of a vessel to become homogeneous (commonly measured to a target like 95% uniformity). It matters most in semi-batch reactions, where a reagent is added gradually and needs to disperse before it can react locally in an uncontrolled way. Blend time depends strongly on impeller type and vessel geometry. Impellers designed mainly for wall-scraping (like anchors) tend to have much longer blend times than turbine-style impellers built for bulk circulation. t: What's the advantage of an agitated Nutsche filter-dryer over a standard filter?
x: 1–3 yrs Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ An agitated Nutsche filter-dryer combines filtration, washing, and drying in the same vessel, which avoids transferring a wet cake to a separate dryer and reduces product handling, exposure, and potential for cross-contamination. It's especially valuable for potent or air-sensitive compounds where minimizing transfers and open handling steps is a priority, even though cycle times per batch can be longer than using dedicated, separate filtration and drying equipment. t: When would I choose a pressure/vacuum Nutsche filter over an agitated one?
x: 1–3 yrs Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ A non-agitated pressure or vacuum Nutsche filter is a simpler, often lower-cost option when the cake doesn't need in-vessel mixing or discharge assistance. It typically suits free-filtering solids that form a cake easily and don't need agitation to wash or dry well. If the cake tends to crack, channel, or dry unevenly without help, or if in-situ drying is needed, the agitated version becomes the better choice despite the added complexity. t: When should I use a centrifuge instead of a Nutsche filter for isolation?

However, centrifuges can subject crystals to higher mechanical stress (risking attrition or fines) and are less suited to fine, slow-filtering, or fragile particles compared to a gentler Nutsche filtration. x: 1–3 yrs Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ A vacuum tray dryer removes solvent under reduced pressure, which lowers the boiling point of residual solvent and allows drying at lower temperature (important for heat-sensitive or thermally unstable products). An air tray dryer relies on heated air circulation at atmospheric pressure, which is simpler but exposes the product to higher temperature for a given solvent removal rate. Choose vacuum tray drying whenever the product's thermal stability or the solvent's flash point makes atmospheric hot-air drying unsuitable. t: What is a spray dryer used for, and how is it different from other dryer types?

t: How do I decide which size reduction equipment to use?
x: Experienced Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ The target particle size range is the main driver: if you need very fine, narrow particle size distribution (micronization for improved dissolution or bioavailability), a jet mill is usually necessary; if a coarser, more moderate size reduction is sufficient, a multi mill or similar mechanical mill is simpler, cheaper to operate, and easier to clean. Material properties like heat sensitivity, potency (containment needs), and friability also factor into the choice. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Mills Lesson: Dust & powder hazards ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What's the difference between supersaturation and the metastable zone in crystallization?
x: Fresher ★ Top 50 Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ Supersaturation is the condition where a solution holds more dissolved solute than its equilibrium solubility at that temperature; the metastable zone is the range of supersaturation within which spontaneous (uncontrolled) nucleation doesn't occur, so crystal growth can proceed in a controlled way on existing seed crystals. If supersaturation is pushed beyond the metastable zone limit, spontaneous nucleation occurs, typically producing more, smaller crystals and less control over the final particle size and polymorph. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Crystallizer Virtual Plant Tour

t: Why does the metastable zone width often narrow when a crystallization is scaled up?
x: Experienced Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ Larger vessels often have different mixing characteristics and different cooling or addition rates in practice, and a narrower metastable zone at scale means spontaneous nucleation can occur before intentional seeding takes place, leading to poor control over polymorph and particle size. That's why metastable zone width should be measured as a function of agitation, cooling rate, and antisolvent addition rate before finalizing a crystallization's scale-up conditions. This is a common tendency, not a certainty for every system, so always characterize metastable zone width experimentally for yo

t: Why is seeding important for a controlled crystallization, and what problems can occur with seed addition at scale?
x: Experienced Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ Seeding provides existing crystal surface for controlled growth within the metastable zone, avoiding the loss of polymorph and particle size control that comes from spontaneous nucleation. At larger scale, some equipment makes it harder to add a small quantity of dry seed effectively (seeds may need to go in as a slurry instead), and getting the seed charge evenly distributed so it actually reaches and contacts the bulk solution can be harder than at lab scale. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Crystallizer Lesson: Scale-up & tech transfer ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: How does mixing intensity affect crystallization outcomes?
x: Experienced Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ Inadequate mixing can create localized zones of high supersaturation (hot spots) that trigger uncontrolled nucleation even if the bulk solution is within the metastable zone, while excessive agitation can narrow the metastable zone width or cause attrition of crystals already formed. The right mixing intensity balances preventing local supersaturation spikes against avoiding unnecessary mechanical stress on the growing crystals. This is very product- and equipment-specific and needs to be evaluated experimentally. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Crystallizer Mixing / Scale-up Calculator

t: Why do temperature measurements sometimes give misleading readings during a crystallization?
x: 1–3 yrs Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ A thermocouple can get coated with crystals during the batch, which insulates it from the true bulk temperature and gives false readings. This becomes a real process risk if the control system is in batch temperature control mode, since it may then adjust jacket temperature wrongly and push the batch outside its intended operating range. Using jacket temperature control instead of relying only on a batch temperature probe, and watching for coating, help avoid this. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Crystallizer Virtual Plant Tour (3D) ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What causes particle attrition during crystallization, and why does it matter?
x: 1–3 yrs Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ Attrition happens when crystals are broken apart by mechanical stress from agitation, especially when the crystals are inherently fragile or when agitation intensity or duration is more than they can take. Attrition shifts the particle size distribution finer, which can affect downstream filterability, drying behavior, and the final powder's flow and handling. So agitation during crystallization is often a compromise between adequate mixing and minimizing particle damage. Related on PharmaChemE: How it works: Crystallizer Mixing / Scale-up Calculator ✓ I knew this ↻ Revise later

t: What's involved in an energy and mass balance for sizing crystallization equipment?
x: Experienced Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ The energy balance accounts for the sensible heat needed to cool or heat the solution, the heat of crystallization released or absorbed as solid forms, and (for evaporative crystallizers) the latent heat of vaporization of any solvent removed. This sets the utility (cooling or heating) capacity needed. The mass balance uses the solubility difference between the starting and final conditions to calculate the theoretical crystallization yield, which in turn sets the vessel size needed for a target batch quantity. t: Is heat of crystallization usually significant compared to other heat effects in the process?
x: Experienced Reactors, Mixing & Solids Processing ▸ For a cooling crystallization, the heat released by crystallization can be a meaningful fraction of the total heat that needs to be removed, though it's usually smaller than the sensible heat of cooling the bulk solution; for an evaporative crystallization, the heat of crystallization is typically negligible compared to the much larger latent heat needed to vaporize the solvent being removed. Which effect dominates depends on the specific system, so it's worth checking rather than assuming one is always negligible. t: Why plant batches heat and cool slower than the lab
s: Batch heating and cooling time simulator
x: The time scales with m cp/UA. Volume grows with the cube of the vessel size but jacket area only with the square, so a 10 KL reactor has roughly one tenth of the area per kg of a 10 L lab reactor. A step that heats in 20 minutes in the lab can take hours in the plant. Use this tool before tech transfer to set realistic heat-up and cool-down times in the batch record.

t: How do you calculate the heating time of a batch reactor?
s: Batch heating and cooling time simulator
x: With a fixed jacket temperature, t = (m cp / UA) x ln((Tu - T0)/(Tu - Ttarget)). For limited utility flow, glass-lined ΔT limits, agitator heat or losses, step through time numerically as this simulator does.

t: Why is heating slower near the target temperature?
s: Batch heating and cooling time simulator
x: The jacket duty is proportional to the temperature difference between jacket and batch. As the batch approaches the utility temperature the difference shrinks, so the last few degrees take the longest. A free screening tool for engineers and students. Two simple lab observations make the plant prediction far more reliable: the speed at which no solid rests on the base for more than 1 to 2 seconds (enter it as the lab Njs and the tool back-calculates S), and if gas matters, a measured kLa. t: What is the just-suspended speed Njs?
x: The lowest agitator speed at which no particle stays on the vessel base for more than 1 to 2 seconds (Zwietering). Below it, solids settle; well above it, extra power adds little to mass transfer from the particles.

t: How does kLa change on scale-up?
x: At the same P/V and superficial gas velocity, kLa from van't Riet stays about the same. At the same vvm the superficial velocity rises with vessel size, so kLa usually rises if P/V is kept. For headspace hydrogenation without a sparger, kLa usually falls on scale-up. A free screening tool for engineers and students. s: Free reaction kinetics fitting tool: paste conversion vs time at several temperatures, fit rate constant and activation energy, and predict plant batch time.
x: Reaction kinetics fitting Paste HPLC or GC conversion results from lab runs at two or more temperatures. The tool fits the rate constant at each temperature, draws the Arrhenius plot to get the activation energy, and predicts the time to your target conversion at the plant temperature. It is the first step of any process model. How it works First order : X = 1 - e^-kt. Second order, A + B , with M = [B]0/[A]0: ln[(M - X)/(M(1 - X))] = [A]0(M - 1) k t (and X = k[A]0t/(1 + k[A]0t) when M = 1). nth order : (1 - X)^1-n = 1 + (n - 1) k [A]0^n-1 t, with n fitted across all temperatures. For each temperature, k is found by least squares on conversion. With two or more temperatures, a straight line through ln k against 1/T gives the activation energy: ln k = ln A - Ea/(RT) . Getting good data Run at least three temperatures, 10 to 15 °C apart, around the planned plant temperature. Take 6 to 10 s

Run at least three temperatures, 10 to 15 °C apart, around the planned plant temperature. Take 6 to 10 samples per run, more at the start when conversion changes fastest, and quench each sample immediately. Keep the temperature steady. Add the reagent quickly (or all at once) so the start time is clear. Use the same stoichiometry and concentration as the plant process. The sample data loaded in the tool is made up for illustration. Try each rate law and keep the one with the highest R² at every temperature and no pattern in the misfit. A rate that changes about 2× per 10 °C is typical (Ea around 12 to 17 kcal/mol). Use the fitted k and Ea in the semi-batch dosing simulator to check heat release and accumulation at plant scale.

t: How do you find the activation energy from lab data?
x: Fit the rate constant k at each temperature, then plot ln k against 1/T, with T absolute (°C + 273.15). The slope is -Ea/R, so Ea = -slope x 1.987 cal/mol·°C, giving Ea in cal/mol (divide by 1,000 for kcal/mol). You need at least two temperatures; three or more give a check on the fit.

t: How do you predict batch time at a different temperature?
x: Calculate k at the new temperature from the Arrhenius equation, then use the integrated rate law to find the time to the target conversion. Stay within about 15 °C of the lab data to avoid large extrapolation. A free screening tool for engineers and students. Lower the reaction temperature in the tool and watch the accumulation rise. t: What is accumulation in a semi-batch reaction?
x: The dosed reagent that has not yet reacted. If cooling fails, it can still react and release its heat, so the MTSR rises with accumulation. It is highest when the reaction is slow compared with the dosing rate.

t: How do you choose the dosing time?
x: Long enough that the jacket can remove the heat at the peak and the MTSR stays below the MTT and TD24 throughout, with a margin. s: Free solvent swap simulator: compare put-and-take and constant-volume distillation for 86 solvents, with solvent used, distillate, time and residual solvent.
x: Solvent swap simulator Changing from one solvent to another in the reactor is one of the longest steps in many API processes. Choose the two solvents, the pressure and the volumes, and the simulator works out how much new solvent and distillation time each method needs to bring the old solvent below your limit. How it works The batch is treated as a single-stage still (no column). At each step the bubble point is found from Raoult’s law with Antoine vapour pressures, the vapour composition is yA = xA PA^sat/P, and a small amount of vapour is removed. Put-and-take : distil down to the minimum stirrable volume, refill with the new solvent to the maximum volume, repeat until the residual target is met. Constant volume : distil down to a set level, then feed the new solvent at the same rate as the distillate so the level stays constant. Constant volume almost always needs less new solvent be

The batch is treated as a single-stage still (no column). At each step the bubble point is found from Raoult’s law with Antoine vapour pressures, the vapour composition is yA = xA PA^sat/P, and a small amount of vapour is removed. Put-and-take : distil down to the minimum stirrable volume, refill with the new solvent to the maximum volume, repeat until the residual target is met. Constant volume : distil down to a set level, then feed the new solvent at the same rate as the distillate so the level stays constant. Constant volume almost always needs less new solvent because every litre of distillate removes old solvent at its highest concentra

It assumes an ideal mixture. Alcohols or water with hydrocarbons, esters, ketones, ethers or chlorinated solvents often form azeotropes, which make the swap harder than shown. The tool warns you about likely pairs. The dissolved product is ignored. It raises the boiling point a little and may crystallise as the solvent changes, so check solubility at each stage. A real reactor gives some reflux on the walls and vapour line, so the separation is slightly better than a single stage. Confirm the end point by GC. Vapour pressure data is from our solvent data pages . For the background, read solvent selection and solvent swaps .

t: Which is better, put-and-take or constant-volume solvent swap?
x: Constant-volume distillation usually needs much less new solvent and less distillation time, because the new solvent is added continuously while the old one is at its highest concentration. Put-and-take is simpler where there is no metering pump or reliable level control.

t: How much solvent does a solvent swap need?
x: It depends on the relative volatility of the two solvents, the minimum stirrable volume and the residual limit. For a well-separated pair, a constant-volume swap typically needs about 1.5 to 3 times the held volume of new solvent; azeotropes can need far more. A free screening tool for engineers and students. x: Process Safety · Case study Bhopal, 1984: methyl isocyanate release Water entered a storage tank of methyl isocyanate (MIC). The runaway reaction that followed released a toxic cloud over a sleeping city. Date 2–3 Dec 1984 Where Union Carbide India Ltd, Bhopal Material Methyl isocyanate (MIC) Released About 40 tonnes Deaths Thousands: the Madhya Pradesh government confirmed 3,787; other estimates are far higher Exposed Over 500,000 people What happened The plant made the pesticide carbaryl using MIC, a volatile, highly toxic and water-reactive intermediate stored in large underground tanks. Late on 2 December 1984, water got into tank E610. MIC reacts exothermically with water; the temperature and pressure rose, the relief valve lifted, and MIC vapour poured out of the vent stack for about two hours. The cloud drifted over densely populated neighbourhoods next to the plant. The way the w

The plant made the pesticide carbaryl using MIC, a volatile, highly toxic and water-reactive intermediate stored in large underground tanks. Late on 2 December 1984, water got into tank E610. MIC reacts exothermically with water; the temperature and pressure rose, the relief valve lifted, and MIC vapour poured out of the vent stack for about two hours. The cloud drifted over densely populated neighbourhoods next to the plant. The way the water got in has been disputed (a pipe-washing operation without a blind, or deliberate introduction), but the scale of the disaster came from what failed to stop it.

Late evening Water enters MIC tank E610, which holds about 40 t of MIC. Before midnight Workers notice eye irritation; the tank pressure is rising. Around midnight Pressure and temperature climb fast; the relief valve lifts. Next 1–2 hours MIC vapour pours out of the vent stack; the scrubber and flare cannot stop it. By morning The cloud has covered large parts of the city; thousands are dead or dying.

Large inventory of a highly hazardous intermediate : far more MIC was stored than the process needed (an inherent-safety failure). Safeguards out of service : the refrigeration that should have kept MIC near 0 °C had been shut down; the vent gas scrubber was on standby and too small for a runaway; the flare was out of service for maintenance; water sprays could not reach the height of the release. Maintenance and procedures : no slip-blinds when washing lines; alarms and gauges known to be unreliable. Siting and emergency planning : dense housing up to the fence, no community warning or evacuation plan, no information on antidotes or shelteri

Minimise inventories of highly hazardous intermediates: “what you don’t have can’t leak”. A safeguard that is out of service is not a safeguard. Track impairments and stop operation when critical layers are missing. Size scrubbers, flares and relief for the worst credible runaway, not the normal vent load. Plan for the community: land-use planning, sirens, shelter-in-place advice, coordination with local authorities. Water-reactive materials need positive isolation (blinds) during line washing.
