s: Buncefield 2005: how a petrol tank overfilled when its level gauge and high-level switch failed, why the vapour cloud exploded, and lessons for overfill.
x: Process Safety · Case study Buncefield, 2005: filling blind A petrol storage tank overflowed for about 40 minutes because both its level protections had failed. The vapour cloud exploded. Date 11 Dec 2005 Where Buncefield oil depot, Hemel Hempstead, UK Released About 300 t of petrol Deaths None Injuries 43 Fire Burned for about 5 days, 20+ tanks What happened Tank 912 was being filled with unleaded petrol from a pipeline overnight. Its automatic level gauge had been sticking intermittently since a service in August, and on that night it stuck, showing a constant level while the tank kept filling. The independent high-level switch, which should have shut off the flow, was inoperative: a test lever had not been put back in place after testing. Petrol cascaded over the tank roof, broke up into droplets and evaporated, forming a large vapour cloud in still, cold air. At 06:01 it ignited, cau

Tank 912 was being filled with unleaded petrol from a pipeline overnight. Its automatic level gauge had been sticking intermittently since a service in August, and on that night it stuck, showing a constant level while the tank kept filling. The independent high-level switch, which should have shut off the flow, was inoperative: a test lever had not been put back in place after testing. Petrol cascaded over the tank roof, broke up into droplets and evaporated, forming a large vapour cloud in still, cold air. At 06:01 it ignited, causing a vapour cloud explosion far more violent than expected and the largest fire in peacetime Europe.

~19:00 (10 Dec) Tank 912 starts receiving petrol. ~03:00 The level gauge sticks; the reading stays flat. ~05:20 The tank is full; the high-level switch does not trip. Petrol overflows. 06:01 The vapour cloud ignites: explosion, then fire across the site.

Both layers of overfill protection failed : a gauge known to stick, and an independent switch left inoperative after testing. No alarm on “no level change while filling” , and limited control of incoming flow by the site. Containment failed : bund walls and joints leaked and fire-water and fuel escaped, polluting groundwater. Unexpected severity : a vapour cloud in a moderately congested area exploded far more strongly than models of the time predicted.

Overfill protection must be truly independent, tested properly, and returned to service after testing (functional safety, SIL). Treat repeated instrument faults as warnings, not nuisances. Design secondary and tertiary containment (bunds, drainage) to hold fuel and fire-water. Do not assume a vapour cloud will only flash: congestion can make it explode. The plant oxidised cyclohexane in a train of six reactors at about 155 °C and 8.8 bar. In March 1974 a crack was found in reactor 5, so it was removed and a 20-inch bypass pipe was installed between reactors 4 and 6 to keep production going. Because the reactor nozzles were at different heights, the bypass had a “dog-leg” shape and was supported on scaffolding, with bellows at each end. No design calculation was made, no drawing beyond a chalk sketch on the workshop floor, no pressure test of the assembly, and the bellows manufacturer’s guidance was not followed. On 1 June the bypass failed. About 30–40 tonnes of hot cyclohexane flashed into

Mar 1974 Crack found in reactor 5. Decision to bypass it and restart quickly. Days later Bypass designed and built by site staff; no qualified mechanical engineer in post. Apr–May Plant runs with the bypass. 1 Jun, 16:53 Bypass ruptures during a pressure rise. Vapour cloud forms and explodes within about a minute. The control room is destroyed.

No management of change : a major modification treated as a quick repair; no hazard review. No engineering design : forces on the dog-leg and bellows not calculated; no reference to the design code; no pressure test. Missing expertise : the works engineer post was vacant and nobody with the right competence was involved. Production pressure : restarting fast took priority over understanding the original crack. Large inventory under pressure and an occupied control room close to the plant.

Every modification, temporary or permanent, must go through MOC and be designed, built and tested to the same standard as the original plant. When a key post is vacant, decisions that need that expertise must get it elsewhere. Find the cause of a failure (the crack) before restarting. Locate control rooms and occupied buildings away from large flammable inventories, or make them blast-resistant. s: T2 Laboratories, 2007: a runaway nobody expected
x: Hazard not recognised : the owners were chemists and chemical engineers, but did not recognise the runaway potential of the side reaction, nor that scale-up removed the safety margin seen in small batches. Single safeguard : the whole protection was the cooling water. No redundant cooling, no automatic shutdown, no quench. s: T2 Laboratories, 2007: a runaway nobody expected

Educational overview. The principles here are general and simplified, and the figures and rules of thumb are typical values, not limits for your plant. Decisions need process-specific data, the applicable codes and standards, and a qualified assessment. The scenario The question is always the same: the cooling fails at the worst possible moment. What happens? Answering it in a structured way gives you the four temperatures of the Stoessel diagram. 1 The reaction runs at the process temperature Tp . 2 Cooling fails. Dosing stops (it must be interlocked). The unreacted reagent still in the reactor reacts adiabatically and the temperature climbs to the MTSR . 3 If the MTSR is high enough, a decompo

The question is always the same: the cooling fails at the worst possible moment. What happens? Answering it in a structured way gives you the four temperatures of the Stoessel diagram. 1 The reaction runs at the process temperature Tp . 2 Cooling fails. Dosing stops (it must be interlocked). The unreacted reagent still in the reactor reacts adiabatically and the temperature climbs to the MTSR . 3 If the MTSR is high enough, a decomposition or secondary reaction starts. How long that takes is the TMRad at the MTSR. 4 On the way, the batch may reach its boiling point or relief pressure, the MTT , which can act as a barrier (lesson 5).

t: 1 · How much energy? Heat of reaction and ΔTad
x: Q′rx = c · (-ΔHr) / ρ [kcal/kg] (c in mol/m³, -ΔHr in kcal/mol, ρ in kg/m³) ΔTad = Q′rx / c′p [K] c′p,mix = Σ mi·c′p,i / Σ mi From reaction calorimetry: Qrx = ∫ qrx dt (the area under the heat-flow curve). For a roughly constant heat flow during dosing, Qrx ≈ qrx × tdosing.

t: 2 · Can the plant cool it? Cooling capacity
x: qex = U · A · (Tr - Tc) U is the overall heat-transfer coefficient (typically 85–345 kcal/h·m²·°C for jacketed vessels with organic batches), A the wetted jacket area (it grows as you dose), Tc the coolant temperature. Keep the cooling capacity at least 20 % above the maximum heat release rate. In a semi-batch reaction that keeps pace with the dosing, the heat release rate is roughly the total heat divided by the dosing time. That gives the shortest dosing time the cooling can handle : tdosing,min = Qrx,total / (qex / 1.2)

x: From the total reaction heat and the reactor’s cooling capacity. Educational screening tool Results are illustrative and depend on the stated assumptions. They are not a substitute for a qualified process-safety assessment, the applicable design code, vendor data, laboratory testing or engineering review. Reaction heat Q′rx (kcal/kg) Final batch mass (kg) U (kcal/h·m²·°C) Jacket area A (m²) Reaction temperature Tr (°C) Coolant temperature Tc (°C) Safety margin (%)

t: 3 · How hot can it get? Accumulation and MTSR
x: In a batch (all reagents charged, then heated) everything is unreacted at the start: Xacc = 100 %. In a semi-batch the dosed reagent may react instantly or may pile up. The fraction that has been added but not yet reacted is the accumulation . It is measured in the reaction calorimeter by comparing the heat released with the amount dosed. MTSR = Tp + Xacc,max · ΔTad Colder is not automatically safer. Lowering Tp slows the reaction, so more reagent accumulates. Many runaways happened in reactions run “cold for safety”, sometimes with a stopped agitator or a forgotten catalyst, where the reagent sat unreacted and then reacted all at once.

t: 4 · How much time is left? TMRad and TD24
x: For a decomposition with an initial heat release rate q′0 (kcal/h·kg) at temperature T0, the adiabatic time to maximum rate is approximately: TMRad = c′p · R · T0² / (q′0 · Ea) q′(T) = q′0 · exp[ (Ea/R)·(1/T0 - 1/T) ] Zero-order, adiabatic approximation. T is absolute temperature (°C + 273.15) and R = 1.987 × 10⁻³ kcal/mol·°C, so with c′p in kcal/kg·°C, q′0 in kcal/h·kg and Ea in kcal/mol the answer is in hours. TD24 is the temperature at which TMRad = 24 h: below it, a decomposition develops slowly enough to restore control. As a rough rule the heat release rate doubles every 10 °C (van ’t Hoff), so TMRad roughly halves.

Cooling-failure scenario: Tp → MTSR (accumulated reagent reacts) → decomposition after TMRad. ΔTad = Q′ / c′p; MTSR = Tp + Xacc·ΔTad. Cooling capacity qex = UA(Tr - Tc), with a ≥ 20 % margin, sets the shortest dosing time. Lower Tp can mean more accumulation and a higher MTSR. t: Static electricity: the usual ignition source
x: Powders become charged whenever they flow, slide, are pneumatically conveyed or poured from a bag. Insulating plastics (liners, FIBCs, funnels) and isolated metal parts store that charge until it discharges as a spark. A typical spark from a person is 10–30 mJ; many fine organic powders and almost all flammable vapours ignite below that. Hybrid mixtures are the trap. Pouring a powder into a reactor that contains flammable solvent vapour creates a hybrid mixture that ignites far more easily than either alone. Charge solids before the solvent, or through an inerted closed system, never by hand into a hot solvent.

x: A 1 L flask and a 5 m³ reactor run the same chemistry under very different heat-transfer conditions. Volume, and so heat production, grows with the cube of the size; jacket area, and so heat removal, grows only with the square . Lab flask (1 L) Plant reactor (5 m³) Area / volume ~50–100 m²/m³ ~2–4 m²/m³ Heat loss when cooling fails High: the flask cools itself in air Almost none: practically adiabatic Mixing time Seconds Tens of seconds to minutes Time to heat / cool Minutes Hours So a reaction that “just got warm”

t: Things that change reactivity during scale-up
x: Batch vs semi-batch. In an all-in batch there is no control of the rate: all the energy may be released at once. Proving that an addition is dose-controlled (sample just after the end of the addition: little unreacted reagent left) removes most of the risk. Concentration. Reactions in 7–10 volumes of solvent are rarely hazardous; below about 5 volumes, ΔTad rises and more testing is needed. Large excesses of reagent. Often a sign the chemistry is not understood; the excess may cause side reactions or decompositions and needs a planned quench. Longer times at temperature. Distillations, hold times and filtrations are much longer in the plant.

t: Changes that need new safety data
x: If the initial assessment was lean, many changes are fine without re-testing. These are not, and should go back to the process safety lab: Anything that increases heat or gas generation, or their rates: new reagents, molar ratios, higher concentration, faster addition, a significantly different reaction or work-up temperature. Changing a dose-controlled step into an all-in process. A change in the composition of a distillation residue . Charging a reactive reagent as a concentrated solution instead of a solid (compatibility: e.g. NBS in NMP or DMF, nitric acid with organic solvents). Management of change (MOC). Every change to chemistry, equi

Heat production scales with volume, cooling with area: plants are nearly adiabatic. Dose-controlled operation, enough dilution and modest excesses reduce scale-up risk. Changes that raise heat or gas generation, all-in charging, new residues or concentrated reagent solutions need new data and MOC. Consequence analysis follows the material: source term (how much escapes, how fast) → pool and evaporation (for liquids) → dispersion in the wind → effect on people (toxic dose, flash fire, heat radiation, overpressure). Liquid through a hole: Q = Cd · A · √(2·ρ·ΔP) (Cd ≈ 0.61) ΔP = pad / pump pressure + ρ·g·h (liquid head) Gases and liquefied gases (Cl₂, NH₃) escape much faster and partly flash; a 6 mm hole in a chlorine tonner can empty it in well under an hour.

Level Meaning (60-minute exposure) AEGL-1 Notable discomfort, irritation; reversible AEGL-2 Irreversible or serious long-lasting effects, or impaired ability to escape AEGL-3 Life-threatening effects or death Example 60-min values: chlorine 0.5 / 2 / 20 ppm; ammonia 30 / 160 / 1,100 ppm. Chlorine’s are tiny, which is why a small chlorine leak needs a far larger emergency zone than a large solvent leak.

LFL / UFL : a vapour–air mixture burns only between the lower and upper flammable limits (methanol 6–36 %, toluene 1.1–7.1 %). Zones are usually drawn to ½ LFL to allow for pockets of richer mixture. Flash fire : a cloud ignites and burns back to the source. Deadly inside the cloud, little effect outside. Vapour cloud explosion : the same cloud in a congested area (pipe racks, buildings) can accelerate into a damaging blast (Flixborough, Buncefield). Pool fire : harm is by heat radiation: 32,250 kcal/h·m² (37.5 kW/m²) damages equipment and is fatal; 10,750 kcal/h·m² (12.5 kW/m²) ignites wood and is lethal within minutes; 3,440 kcal/h·m² (4 kW

The same leak is far more dangerous on a calm, clear night (Pasquill stability class F, low wind) than on a windy afternoon (class D): the cloud stays concentrated and travels further. Dense gases (chlorine) hug the ground and flow into drains and basements.

Detect fast: gas detectors, CCTV, manual call points, siren. Evacuate crosswind, then upwind , to the assembly point the control room names for the current wind. Head count at the assembly point. Isolate from a safe place: remote shut-off valves, king valves, emergency kits (e.g. chlorine kit B). Water curtains knock down soluble clouds (NH3, HCl, Cl2); foam blankets cut evaporation from solvent pools. Never spray water onto a leaking chlorine container: it forms acid and enlarges the hole. t: The runaway problem in one picture
x: An exothermic reaction stays under control only while heat is removed as fast as it is produced. Heat production rises exponentially with temperature (Arrhenius), while heat removal through the jacket rises only linearly (UA × ΔT). Above a certain temperature, production wins: the batch heats itself, which speeds the reaction, which heats it faster. That positive feedback is a thermal runaway . If the batch reaches a temperature where a decomposition starts, the energy and gas released can be many times larger than the main reaction. t: Terms you will meet in every lesson
x: Term Meaning Exothermic reaction Releases heat: the reaction enthalpy ΔHr is negative. Adiabatic No heat exchange with the surroundings. A large, well-insulated reactor with failed cooling is close to adiabatic, so it is the worst case. Adiabatic temperature rise, ΔTad How much the temperature would rise if all the remaining reaction heat stayed in the mass: ΔTad = Q′ / c′p. Activation energy, Ea Sets how strongly the rate rises with temperature. A higher Ea means a steeper rise once things get hot. Runaway A thermally unstable system in which temperature and rate keep accelerating, possibly to an explosion. Induction time / TMRad The time, u

Some groups of atoms store a lot of energy or release gas when they break down. If one of them is in a starting material, intermediate, product or residue, treat the process as potentially hazardous until thermal testing says otherwise. Process safety is about keeping energy and hazardous material inside the equipment. It is measured differently from personal safety. Runaway = exponential heat production beating linear heat removal. ΔTad, Ea and TMRad describe how big, how steep and how fast a runaway is. Energetic functional groups (azides, nitro, peroxides, diazo, N–O, acetylenes…) mean: test before you scale up. t: What an azeotrope means on the plant
x: An azeotrope is a mixture that boils at constant temperature and gives a vapour of the same composition as the liquid. Simple distillation stops at that composition: you cannot get dry ethanol by distilling 95 % ethanol, however many plates you add. Minimum-boiling azeotropes (most of them) boil below both pure components and come over first. Toluene and water distil together at about 84 °C, which is how toluene is used to dry a batch. Maximum-boiling azeotropes boil above both components and stay behind in the still, as acetone with chloroform and water with formic acid do. Heterogeneous azeotropes condense into two layers. Decant the water

t: How the estimates are made, and how good they are
x: The calculator finds the boiling point of every liquid composition at your pressure, and looks for the point where the vapour has the same composition as the liquid. It uses: Activity coefficients from modified UNIFAC (Dortmund), with the published group parameters. Pairs whose groups have no published interaction parameters are not estimated. Vapour pressure from the Antoine constants on each solvent page. Two liquid layers: when the model predicts that the liquid splits, the azeotrope is found at the three-phase temperature, as a heterogeneous azeotrope. An ideal vapour, which is reasonable from deep vacuum up to a few bar. Check against th

A liquid mixture that boils at constant temperature with a vapour of the same composition as the liquid, so simple distillation cannot separate it beyond that composition. Ethanol and water form one at 78.1 °C and 95.5 % ethanol by weight.

t: Does an azeotrope change with pressure?
x: Yes. Both the boiling temperature and the composition shift with pressure, and some azeotropes disappear under vacuum. Pressure-swing distillation uses this to separate azeotropes such as THF and water.

One in which the condensed liquid separates into two layers, as with toluene and water. Decanting the layers breaks the azeotrope, which is why toluene is used to remove water from a batch by azeotropic distillation.

It runs on electricity. A vapour absorption machine (VAM) uses water as the refrigerant and lithium bromide solution to absorb it. t: Two ways to make chilled water
x: An electric (vapour compression) chiller uses a compressor to push refrigerant from the evaporator, where it boils and takes heat from the chilled water, to the condenser, where it gives that heat to the cooling water. It runs on electricity. A vapour absorption machine (VAM) uses water as the refrigerant and lithium bromide solution to absorb it. Instead of a compressor, heat drives the water back out of the solution: steam, hot water, exhaust gas or a burner. It uses very little electricity, so it makes sense where heat is cheap or free.

Cooling (kcal/h) = flow (m³/h) × ρ × cp × ΔT TR = Cooling (kcal/h) / 3,024 (for water: TR ≈ m³/h × ΔT / 3.024) kW/TR = power input (kW) / TR COP = cooling (kcal/h) / (power input kW × 860) One ton of refrigeration (TR) is 3,024 kcal/h, the heat to melt one short ton of ice in a day. Use a calibrated flow meter or a clamp-on ultrasonic meter and accurate temperature sensors: at a 5 °C difference, a 0.25 °C sensor error is a 5 % error in TR.

120 m³/h of water, 12 °C → 7 °C: cooling = 120 × 1,000 × 1 × 5 = 6,00,000 kcal/h ≈ 198 TR Measured power 140 kW → 140 / 198 ≈ 0.71 kW/TR, COP ≈ 5.0 For glycol or brine, choose the fluid in the calculator: a 30 % glycol has a specific heat of about 0.88 kcal/kg·°C, so the same flow and ΔT carries about 8 % less heat than water.

Heat input (kcal/h) = TR × 3,024 / COP Steam (kg/h) = Heat input / hfg (kcal/kg) at the steam pressure Heat to cooling tower = cooling + heat input = TR × (1 + 1/COP) A 200 TR double-effect machine with COP 1.3 on 8 barg steam needs about 4,65,000 kcal/h of heat, or about 960 kg/h of steam (4.8 kg/h per TR). Its cooling tower must reject about 1.77 times the cooling load, against about 1.2–1.25 times for an electric chiller, so a VAM needs a bigger tower, more condenser water and a bigger condenser water pump.

Compare the yearly power cost of the chiller (TR × kW/TR × hours × ₹/kWh) with the VAM's steam cost plus its pump and fan power. The break-even steam cost tells you how cheap steam must be before the VAM wins. With 0.85 kW/TR including the chiller's share of pumps and fans, power at ₹8/kWh and a VAM using 4.6 kg/h per TR, the break-even is about ₹1,200 per tonne of steam. Steam from a coal or biomass boiler can come close to this; waste heat or back-pressure steam from a turbine easily beats it.

Machine Typical efficiency Notes Water-cooled centrifugal 0.55–0.65 kW/TR Large loads, chilled water 6–7 °C Water-cooled screw 0.65–0.8 kW/TR Common in process plants Air-cooled screw or scroll 1.0–1.3 kW/TR No cooling tower, worse in hot weather Brine chiller, -10 to -20 °C Much higher per TR Compare only with machines at the same temperature VAM single-effect COP 0.65–0.75 Low-pressure steam or 85–95 °C hot water, ≈ 8 kg/h steam per TR VAM double-effect COP 1.2–1.4 8–9 barg steam, ≈ 4.5–5 kg/h steam per TR A VAM makes chilled water down to about 5–7 °C; it cannot make sub-zero brine. For brine duties use a vapour compression chiller.

t: Simple ways to save chiller energy
x: Raise the chilled water supply temperature as far as the process allows: each 1 °C saves roughly 2–3 % of compressor power. Keep the condenser water cold and the tubes clean: each 1 °C lower condenser water also saves about 2–3 %. Run one chiller well loaded rather than two at half load. Fix a low chilled water ΔT: it usually means too much flow or bypassing through three-way valves. Insulate chilled water and brine lines; check for condensation and wet insulation.

t: How do I calculate chiller TR in the field?
x: Measure the chilled water flow and the return and supply temperatures. For water, TR = m³/h × ΔT / 3.024. Divide the measured compressor power by this TR for kW/TR.

t: Why does a VAM need a bigger cooling tower?
x: Its cooling tower removes both the heat taken from the chilled water and the heat put in by the steam. With COP 1.3 that is 1.77 times the cooling load.

t: Can a VAM run on hot water from a process?
x: Yes. Single-effect machines run on hot water at about 85–95 °C, which makes them a good use of waste heat from engines, condensate or process coolers.

s: Free compressed air and nitrogen calculators: leak flow and cost, receiver size, compressor specific power, N2 for pressure, vacuum and sweep purging.
x: Compressed Air & Nitrogen Calculations Compressed air is one of the most expensive utilities per unit of useful energy, and nitrogen is a safety utility. Work out what leaks cost, size a receiver, estimate compressor power and plan nitrogen for purging and blanketing. Full article Air leak cost Receiver size Compressor power N₂ purging N₂ blanketing How it works Why compressed air is expensive Only about 10–15 % of the electricity a compressor draws comes out as useful work at the tool; the rest becomes heat in the compressor. A compressor making 10 m³/min at 7 barg draws about 60–65 kW. Leaks, pressure set higher than needed and air used for cleaning or cooling waste a large share of it. Air leaks Air through a hole (choked flow): m = Cd × A × P0 × √[k / (R T) × (2/(k+1))^(k+1)/(k-1)] Power wasted (kW) = leak (m³/min free air) × specific power (kW per m³/min) Above about 0.9 barg the fl

Only about 10–15 % of the electricity a compressor draws comes out as useful work at the tool; the rest becomes heat in the compressor. A compressor making 10 m³/min at 7 barg draws about 60–65 kW. Leaks, pressure set higher than needed and air used for cleaning or cooling waste a large share of it.

Air through a hole (choked flow): m = Cd × A × P0 × √[k / (R T) × (2/(k+1))^(k+1)/(k-1)] Power wasted (kW) = leak (m³/min free air) × specific power (kW per m³/min) Above about 0.9 barg the flow through a hole is choked, so it rises in step with the absolute pressure. With a discharge coefficient of 0.65, a 3 mm hole at 7 barg leaks about 0.43 m³/min. Ten such leaks waste about 4.3 m³/min, roughly 28 kW, or about ₹18 lakh a year at ₹8/kWh. A simple check: with all users stopped, time how fast the receiver pressure falls, or how long the compressor stays loaded.

V (m³) = Q (m³/min free air) × t (min) × 1.013 / (P1 - P2) To cover a 10 m³/min demand for 1 minute while the pressure falls from 7.5 to 6.5 barg needs about 10 m³ of storage. A receiver near a large intermittent user, such as a filter press, centrifuge or bag filter pulse cleaning, smooths peaks and stops a second compressor starting for a few seconds of demand.

Adiabatic power = n × k/(k-1) × P1 × Q × [(P2/P1)^(k-1)/(n k) - 1] Shaft power = adiabatic power / overall efficiency n is the number of stages and k = 1.4 for air. For 10 m³/min to 7 barg in one stage, the adiabatic power is about 48 kW and the shaft power about 64 kW at 75 % efficiency, about 6.4 kW per m³/min. Every extra 1 bar of discharge pressure costs roughly 6–8 % more power, so set the compressor to the lowest pressure the users need.

Pressure or vacuum purge: O₂ after n cycles = O₂start × (Plow / Phigh)^n (absolute pressures) N₂ per cycle (Nm³) = V × (Phigh - Plow) / 1.013 Sweep purge (well mixed): N₂ (Nm³) = V × ln(O₂start / O₂target) For a 6 m³ reactor headspace purged to 2 barg and vented to atmosphere, each cycle cuts oxygen to about a third: 7.1 % after one cycle and 2.3 % after two. Most solvent vapours cannot burn below about 10 % oxygen (the limiting oxygen concentration), and plants commonly aim for 8 % or less, so one cycle leaves almost no margin. Two cycles use about 24 Nm³. Always confirm with an oxygen analyser; a sweep purge with poor mixing can leave pocke

Item Typical Specific power, screw compressor at 7 barg 5.5–7 kW per m³/min of free air Leaks in a plant without a leak programme 20–30 % of compressor output Pressure drop, compressor to farthest user Under about 0.5 bar Dew point: refrigerated dryer ≈ +3 °C pressure dew point Dew point: desiccant dryer (instrument air) -40 °C pressure dew point Nitrogen purity for inerting (PSA) 95–99.9 %, chosen against the LOC of the solvent

t: How much power does a compressed air leak waste?
x: Multiply the leak flow in m³/min by the compressor's specific power. A single 3 mm leak at 7 barg wastes about 2.8 kW, all day and all night.

t: Can I use compressed air instead of nitrogen to push a solvent?
x: No. Air adds oxygen to a flammable vapour space. Use nitrogen, or a pump, and keep the vessel inerted.

t: Pressure purge or sweep purge: which uses less nitrogen?
x: For a vessel that can take pressure, pressure purging is predictable and easy to check. Vacuum purging uses the least nitrogen. Sweep purging suits vessels that cannot take pressure or vacuum, but needs good mixing and an oxygen check at the vent.

s: Free cooling tower calculators: range, approach, heat rejected in kcal/h and TR, evaporation loss, make-up and blowdown from cycles of concentration.
x: Cooling Tower Calculations Check how well a cooling tower is working, how much water it consumes and what higher cycles of concentration would save, and size the cooling water for a condenser or cooler. Full article Range & approach Make-up & blowdown Water for a heat load How it works How a cooling tower works Hot return water is sprayed over the fill while fans draw air through it. A small part of the water evaporates, and its latent heat cools the rest. That is why a cooling tower can cool water below the dry-bulb air temperature but never below the wet bulb temperature: the wet bulb is the limit set by how much more moisture the air can take. Range, approach and effectiveness Range = Thot in - Tcold out Approach = Tcold out - Twet bulb Effectiveness = Range / (Range + Approach) Heat rejected (kcal/h) = flow (kg/h) × 1 × Range Range is set by the plant's heat load and the water flow.

Hot return water is sprayed over the fill while fans draw air through it. A small part of the water evaporates, and its latent heat cools the rest. That is why a cooling tower can cool water below the dry-bulb air temperature but never below the wet bulb temperature: the wet bulb is the limit set by how much more moisture the air can take.

Range = Thot in - Tcold out Approach = Tcold out - Twet bulb Effectiveness = Range / (Range + Approach) Heat rejected (kcal/h) = flow (kg/h) × 1 × Range Range is set by the plant's heat load and the water flow. Approach shows the tower's condition: a tower that held 4 °C approach when new and now gives 7 °C at the same wet bulb has fouled fill, blocked nozzles or weak fans.

Evaporation E (m³/h) = 0.00085 × 1.8 × Circulation (m³/h) × Range (°C) Cycles of concentration COC = TDS (or conductivity) of circulating water / that of make-up Blowdown B = E / (COC - 1) - Drift Make-up M = E + B + Drift = E × COC / (COC - 1) Evaporation removes pure water and leaves the dissolved salts behind, so the circulating water gets more concentrated. Blowdown bleeds off some of it to keep the salts below the scaling limit. More cycles means less blowdown and less make-up, but only as far as the water chemistry and treatment programme allow.

500 m³/h circulation, hot water 37 °C, cold water 32 °C, wet bulb 28 °C, COC 4, drift 0.02 %: Range = 5 °C, approach = 4 °C, effectiveness = 5 / 9 ≈ 56 % Heat rejected = 500 × 1,000 × 5 = 25,00,000 kcal/h ≈ 827 TR Evaporation = 0.00085 × 1.8 × 500 × 5 ≈ 3.8 m³/h Blowdown = 3.8 / 3 - 0.1 ≈ 1.2 m³/h; make-up ≈ 5.1 m³/h (about 122 m³/day) Raising the cycles from 4 to 5 cuts the make-up to about 4.8 m³/h, roughly 8 m³ a day saved on this one tower.

Item Typical Notes Approach 3–5 °C Under 2.5 °C is expensive to build; over 6 °C points to a problem Range 4–8 °C Set by the heat load and water flow Evaporation ≈ 0.15 % of flow per °C of range About 1 % of flow for a 6–7 °C range Drift loss 0.005–0.02 % (modern eliminators) 0.1–0.2 % on old towers without eliminators Cycles of concentration 3–6 Limited by hardness, silica and chloride in the make-up The heat rejected is shown in kcal/h and in refrigeration tons (1 TR = 3,024 kcal/h). Some cooling tower makers rate towers in “cooling tower tons” of 15,000 BTU/h, which already includes the chiller's compressor heat, so check which ton a datas

t: Simple checks that save energy and water
x: Log hot, cold and wet bulb temperatures every shift and trend the approach. Clean the hot water basin nozzles and replace broken fill and drift eliminators. Control blowdown on conductivity, not on a fixed valve opening. Use fan VFDs or switch fans by cold water temperature in winter. Check the cooling water pump is not throttled against a half-closed valve.

t: Why can't a cooling tower cool below the wet bulb temperature?
x: The cooling comes from evaporation. At the wet bulb temperature the air in contact with the water is saturated and can take no more vapour, so evaporation, and the cooling, stops.

t: How much water does a cooling tower lose?
x: Evaporation is about 0.15 % of the circulation for every degree of range, plus blowdown and a little drift. The calculator above gives the full make-up for your cycles.

t: What happens if cycles of concentration are too high?
x: Scale forms on condenser tubes and heat exchangers, and corrosion and biological growth speed up. The safe maximum depends on the make-up water analysis and the treatment chemicals used.

s: Free MEE steam economy calculator: live steam, kg water per kg steam, per-effect evaporation, condenser load and cost per m³ for a forward-feed evaporator.
x: MEE Steam Economy Calculator Steam economy is the water evaporated per kg of live steam. A multiple-effect evaporator (MEE) reuses the vapour from each effect to boil the next, so the economy rises with the number of effects. For example, a 4-effect MEE taking 10,000 kg/h of 5 % solids effluent to 30 % evaporates 8,333 kg/h. With 3 barg steam and a 55 °C last effect it needs about 3,580 kg/h of steam (economy 2.33) when the feed is at 40 °C, and about 2,620 kg/h (economy 3.18) when the feed is preheated to 90 °C. How it works Worked example Effects vs economy Why economy falls Questions How it works In the first effect, live steam condenses in the calandria and boils the liquor. The vapour from that boiling becomes the heating steam for the second effect, which runs at a lower pressure so its liquor boils at a lower temperature. The chain continues to the last effect, whose vapour goes t

In the first effect, live steam condenses in the calandria and boils the liquor. The vapour from that boiling becomes the heating steam for the second effect, which runs at a lower pressure so its liquor boils at a lower temperature. The chain continues to the last effect, whose vapour goes to a surface condenser under vacuum. Each kg of live steam therefore evaporates water several times over. Water to evaporate: E = F × (1 - xF / xP) Each effect: qin × (1 - loss) = Lin × cp × (ti - tin) + Vi × λi Heat into the next effect: qi+1 = Vi × λi Steam economy = E / S Steam per kg water = S / E F feed (kg/h), xF and xP feed and concentrate solids (%

An ETP MEE takes 10,000 kg/h of effluent at 5 % TDS and concentrates it to 30 % before the ATFD. It has 4 effects in forward feed, 3 barg steam (condenses at 143.7 °C), and a last-effect vapour temperature of 55 °C (about 157 mbar abs). Average BPR is 2 °C per effect, liquor cp 0.95 kcal/kg·°C, heat loss 3 % per effect, feed at 40 °C. E = 10,000 × (1 - 5/30) = 8,333 kg/h; concentrate 1,667 kg/h Driving force per effect = (143.7 - 55 - 4 × 2) / 4 = 20.2 °C Effects boil at 123.5, 101.4, 79.2 and 57.0 °C Evaporation by effect: 1,848 + 2,068 + 2,192 + 2,224 = 8,333 kg/h Live steam S = 3,583 kg/h; economy = 8,333 / 3,583 = 2.33 Condenser load = 2,

t: Number of effects vs steam economy
x: Same feed and conditions as the example, changing only the number of effects and the feed temperature: Effects Driving force per effect, °C Economy, feed at 40 °C Economy, feed at 90 °C Live steam at 90 °C feed, kg/h 1 86.7 0.84 0.93 8,914 2 42.4 1.47 1.77 4,704 3 27.6 1.95 2.51 3,316 4 20.2 2.33 3.18 2,622 5 15.7 2.63 3.78 2,203 6 12.8 2.89 4.34 1,921 Each extra effect saves less steam than the one before, while the temperature difference per effect shrinks. That makes the heating surface, and the capital cost, of each effect larger. The economic number of effects is where the steam saved no longer pays for the extra surface. Feed preheating

Preheat the feed with hot condensate or with vapour from a later effect, so the first effect's steam goes into evaporation. Add an effect where the steam price justifies the extra surface and there is enough temperature difference. Thermal vapour recompression (TVR): a steam jet compresses part of the vapour back to heating pressure. It does the work of roughly one more effect. Mechanical vapour recompression (MVR): a fan or compressor recompresses the vapour, replacing most of the live steam with electricity. Flash the condensate from each effect into the next, and return clean first-effect condensate to the boiler.

t: Why plant steam economy falls below design
x: Cause What you see Check Scaling or fouling (CaSO4, silica, organics) Steam rises over weeks; temperature difference across an effect grows Track ΔT per effect; schedule cleaning by trend Non-condensable gases in steam chests Calandria temperature below saturation for its pressure Vent lines open and sized; compare shell temperature with the steam table Poor last-effect vacuum Last effect boils hot; less driving force for all effects Condenser cooling water temperature and flow; air leaks; vacuum pump Condensate not draining Waterlogged calandria, falling evaporation Traps, condensate pumps, level in condensate pots Cold or variable feed Firs

t: What is steam economy in an MEE?
x: Steam economy is the water evaporated divided by the live steam used, in kg per kg. A single effect gives a little under 1; each extra effect reuses the vapour of the one before, so a 4-effect evaporator with a preheated feed gives about 3.

t: How do you calculate steam consumption of a multiple-effect evaporator?
x: Find the water to evaporate, E = F × (1 - xF/xP). Then balance each effect: the heat from the previous effect's vapour heats or flashes the incoming liquor and evaporates water. Solve for the live steam that gives the total E. Live steam = E / economy.

t: Why is my MEE steam economy lower than design?
x: Usually a cold feed, scaled tubes, non-condensable gases in the steam chests, poor last-effect vacuum, condensate not draining, low or wet steam, or a higher boiling point rise as the liquor concentrates. The table above lists the checks.

Forward feed, equal temperature difference per effect, latent heat of water at each effect (λ ≈ 597.3 - 0.566 T kcal/kg), condensate leaving each calandria at saturation, and a fixed heat loss per effect. Backward and mixed feed, TVR and MVR are not modelled. Live-steam feed preheating is not counted. Use the calculator to compare options and check plant performance; the evaporator supplier's heat and mass balance governs the design.

s: Free steam and boiler calculators: fuel consumption, evaporation ratio, boiler efficiency (direct method), flash steam, condensate savings and leak loss.
x: Steam & Boiler Calculations Work out what your steam costs and where it goes: fuel for a steam load, boiler efficiency from a test, flash steam, the value of returned condensate, and what a leaking trap throws away. Results update as you type. Full article Boiler fuel Boiler efficiency Flash steam Condensate recovery Steam leak loss How it works How a steam system works The boiler burns fuel to turn feed water into steam. Steam travels through the mains to jackets, coils and heat exchangers, where it condenses and gives up its latent heat. The condensate drains through steam traps and, in a good system, returns hot to the boiler feed tank. Every kilogram of steam that leaks, every trap that blows through and every litre of condensate sent to drain has to be made again from cold water with more fuel. Boiler fuel consumption Fuel (kg/h) = S × (hg - hfw) / (η × GCV × 4.1868) Evaporation rat

The boiler burns fuel to turn feed water into steam. Steam travels through the mains to jackets, coils and heat exchangers, where it condenses and gives up its latent heat. The condensate drains through steam traps and, in a good system, returns hot to the boiler feed tank. Every kilogram of steam that leaks, every trap that blows through and every litre of condensate sent to drain has to be made again from cold water with more fuel.

Fuel (kg/h) = S × (hg - hfw) / (η × GCV × 4.1868) Evaporation ratio = S / Fuel S is steam flow (kg/h), hg the enthalpy of saturated steam at the boiler pressure (kcal/kg, from steam tables), hfw ≈ 1 × feed water temperature (kcal/kg), η the boiler efficiency as a fraction and GCV the fuel's gross calorific value in kcal/kg.

5,000 kg/h of steam at 10 barg, feed water at 80 °C, Indian coal at 4,000 kcal/kg, boiler efficiency 75 %: hg at 10 barg (11 bar abs) ≈ 664 kcal/kg; hfw = 1 × 80 = 80 kcal/kg Heat per kg = 664 - 80 = 584 kcal/kg Fuel = 5,000 × 584 / (0.75 × 4,000) ≈ 973 kg/h → about 23 t/day Evaporation ratio = 5,000 / 973 ≈ 5.1

Measure steam (from a flow meter or feed water meter) and fuel (weighed or metered) over the same few hours at steady load, then turn the fuel formula around: η = S × (hg - hfw) / (Fuel × GCV × 4.1868). It is quick, but a 5 % error in the steam meter is a 5 % error in efficiency. The indirect (heat loss) method, which adds up flue gas, moisture, unburnt and radiation losses, tells you why efficiency is low.

Flash fraction = (hf,1 - hf,2) / hfg,2 Condensate leaving a trap is at the saturation temperature of the higher pressure. When it drops to the return line pressure it carries more heat than water can hold there, so part of it boils. From 8 barg to 0.5 barg about 12 % flashes: 2,000 kg/h of condensate gives roughly 250 kg/h of low-pressure steam. Collect it in a flash vessel and use it for a low-pressure heater, or it simply vents from the feed tank.

Returned condensate saves treated water, chemicals and the fuel to heat cold make-up water. A rule of thumb: every 6 °C rise in feed water temperature saves about 1 % of boiler fuel. Returning 3,000 kg/h at 90 °C instead of 30 °C make-up recovers about 1,80,000 kcal/h, worth roughly 60 kg/h of coal.

Napier's formula gives the steam through a sharp hole: m (kg/h) ≈ 0.412 × d² (mm²) × P (bar abs). A 3 mm hole at 7 barg passes about 30 kg/h, around 240 tonnes a year. Treat it as an upper estimate for a trap blowing through; a proper trap survey with ultrasound or temperature tells you which ones.

Fuel GCV (typical) Boiler efficiency Evaporation ratio Indian coal 3,500–4,500 kcal/kg 70–80 % 4–5.5 Biomass briquette 3,500–4,000 kcal/kg 68–75 % 4–5 Rice husk 3,000–3,400 kcal/kg 65–72 % 3.5–4.5 Furnace oil ≈ 10,200 kcal/kg 82–88 % 13–15 Natural gas / PNG ≈ 9,500 kcal/Sm³ 85–90 % ≈ 14 kg/Sm³ Ranges depend on the fuel lot, boiler type and load. Use your own fuel analysis and test data when you have them.

t: Where steam money is usually lost
x: Failed-open steam traps: a survey often finds 10–20 % failed in systems without a programme. Condensate sent to drain instead of back to the feed tank. Flash steam venting from the feed tank or condensate receivers. Bare or wet insulation on mains, valves and flanges. Too much excess air: aim for about 3–4 % O₂ in flue gas on oil or gas, 6–8 % on solid fuel. Continuous blowdown set by habit instead of by the boiler water TDS.

t: How do you calculate boiler fuel consumption?
x: Fuel = steam × (steam enthalpy - feed water enthalpy) / (efficiency × GCV). In the example above, 5,000 kg/h of 10 barg steam needs about 973 kg/h of 4,000 kcal/kg coal at 75 % efficiency.

t: What is a good evaporation ratio?
x: It depends on the fuel: about 4–5.5 for Indian coal, 3.5–4.5 for rice husk, 13–15 for furnace oil. A falling evaporation ratio on the same fuel means falling efficiency.

t: Is flash steam the same as live steam?
x: It is ordinary steam at the lower pressure, with the same latent heat as live steam at that pressure. It is only “free” if there is a low-pressure user that can take it.

x: Water, DG & Power Calculations Check an RO plant from its flows and TDS, find what DG power really costs, size capacitors for power factor, see how loaded a motor is, and estimate what a VFD saves on a pump or fan. Full article RO recovery DG cost per unit Power factor Motor loading VFD savings How it works RO plant: recovery and rejection Recovery (%) = permeate / feed × 100 Salt rejection (%) = (1 - permeate TDS / feed TDS) × 100 Reject TDS = (feed × feed TDS - permeate × permeate TDS) / reject flow A 20 m³/h feed at 900 ppm giving 15 m³/h of 25 ppm permeate runs at 75 % recovery and 97.2 % rejection; the 5 m³/h reject carries about 3,500 ppm. Pushing recovery higher concentrates the reject further and raises the scaling risk, which is why antiscalant dosing and the reject LSI (Langelier saturation index) set the limit. Falling rejection points to membrane damage, leaking O-rings or sc

Recovery (%) = permeate / feed × 100 Salt rejection (%) = (1 - permeate TDS / feed TDS) × 100 Reject TDS = (feed × feed TDS - permeate × permeate TDS) / reject flow A 20 m³/h feed at 900 ppm giving 15 m³/h of 25 ppm permeate runs at 75 % recovery and 97.2 % rejection; the 5 m³/h reject carries about 3,500 ppm. Pushing recovery higher concentrates the reject further and raises the scaling risk, which is why antiscalant dosing and the reject LSI (Langelier saturation index) set the limit. Falling rejection points to membrane damage, leaking O-rings or scaling; rising feed pressure at the same flow points to fouling.

t: DG set: what a unit of DG power costs
x: Cost per kWh = diesel price (₹/litre) / specific energy (kWh per litre) Loading (%) = kW / (kVA rating × 0.8) × 100 Read the specific energy from the DG log: kWh from the energy meter divided by litres from the day tank. A healthy diesel set gives about 3.2–3.8 kWh per litre at 60–80 % load, so at ₹90 per litre DG power costs ₹24–28 per kWh, three times grid power. Below about 40 % load the engine wastes fuel and wet-stacks, so run fewer DG sets at higher load.

kVAR = kW × (tan φ1 - tan φ2), where φ = cos^-1(PF) Raising 800 kW from 0.82 to 0.98 power factor needs about 396 kVAR and cuts the kVA from 976 to 816 and the current by about 16 %. That lowers the kVA demand charge, cable and transformer losses, and frees transformer capacity. Where there are many VFDs, use detuned (reactor-protected) capacitors or an active filter, because harmonics can overload plain capacitors.

Input power (kW) = √3 × V × I × PF / 1,000 Loading (%) = input × efficiency / rated kW A 37 kW motor drawing 52 A at 415 V and 0.85 PF takes about 31.8 kW and is about 80 % loaded. Motors below about 50 % load lose efficiency and power factor; a smaller motor or a VFD may pay.

t: VFD savings on pumps and fans
x: Flow ∝ speed Head ∝ speed² Power ∝ speed³ (no static head) A pump throttled to 70 % flow with a valve still draws most of its full power. Slowing it to 70 % speed with a VFD needs only about 34 % of the power, plus 2–3 % VFD losses. For a 45 kW pump that is about 16 kW instead of about 40 kW. Where most of the head is static (lifting to an overhead tank), the cube law overstates the saving, because the pump still has to lift the water at low speed; enter the static head share in the calculator.

t: Why is DG power so much costlier than grid power?
x: A diesel engine turns only about 35–40 % of the fuel's energy into electricity, and diesel is an expensive fuel. At ₹90 per litre and 3.4 kWh per litre, each unit costs about ₹26.

t: Does improving power factor reduce my kWh bill?
x: It mainly reduces the kVA demand charge, any PF penalty and the losses in your own cables and transformers. The kWh used by the load itself does not change.

t: When does a VFD not save much?
x: When the pump already runs at full flow most of the time, or when most of the head is static lift. The biggest savings are on throttled pumps and fans with mostly friction head.

t: Getting there: three ways to purge Working level
x: Pressure purging Pressurise the vessel with nitrogen, let it mix, vent back to atmosphere, repeat. Each cycle reduces the oxygen by the ratio of the absolute pressures: O2 after n cycles = O2 initial × (Plow / Phigh)^n Purging to 2 barg (3.01 bar abs) and venting to 1.01 bar abs multiplies the oxygen by 0.34 each cycle: 21 → 7.1 → 2.4 %. Two cycles reach a 5 % target. Check the vessel's rating first: a glass-lined reactor or a vessel with a sight glass may not take 2 barg. Try it: change the nitrogen pressure and run the purge. Higher pressure means fewer cycles, but more nitrogen per cycle. Vacuum purging Pull a vacuum, break it with nitroge

t: The controls that work Working level
x: 1. Bond and earth every conductor Clamp drums, IBCs and tankers before the lid or valve opens, and remove the clamp last. Bond across anything that breaks the metal path: PTFE-gasketed flanges, glass sections, flexible hoses. Test it: a metal-to-metal bond below 10 Ω shows it is real, and below 1 MΩ to earth is enough to drain static. Earth monitoring clamps with a green light, interlocked to the transfer pump, remove the guesswork. Paint, rust and dirt under a clamp can break the path. 2.
